News.title: Brits warned ‘do not travel’ as Storm Austen hits with 80mph winds as schools close & 1000s without power in amber zone
News.content:
BLOWN AWAY Brits warned ‘do not travel’ as Storm Austen hits with 80mph winds as schools close & 1000s without power in amber zone







Next

BRITS have been warned to not travel as Storm Austen batters the country with 80mph winds, leaving schools closed and thousands without power.

The Met Office has issued amber and yellow weather warnings, saying gusts could cause power cuts, travel delays, and a danger to life along coastal areas.



The first named storm of the season is sweeping across South West England with gusts expected from 60mph to 80mph, according to the Met Office.

The forecaster has issued an amber warning for wind, covering Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly, that came into effect from 1am and remaining in place until 10am.



The Met Office said Storm Austen is “likely to bring some disruption and possible damaging winds” and warned of disruption on the roads and public transport networks.

Flying debris is “likely”, and the storm will “probably” bring some damage to buildings, such as tiles blown from roofs, it added.

A number of schools across Cornwall have said they will open later today to help children and parents arrive safely.

Many will open after 10am, when the Met Office’s amber warning for wind is due to end.



Others have said they will temporarily shut ahead of the weekend.

The National Grid is now reporting 6,980 homes in Cornwall are without power this morning, mainly in the Penzance and central Cornwall area.

This includes 2,241 vulnerable households.

The Met Office has warned of likely power cuts, building damage and travel chaos, as well as a “danger to life” along the coast due to stray debris and large waves.

Mobile phone coverage and the power supply could also be affected, the Met Office said.



Exeter Airport has announced the flight due to arrive from Jersey just after 11am and another from Edinburgh at 12.50pm have been cancelled.

Departures to those locations also cancelled due to the stormy conditions.

Ferries and trains have also been cancelled in the South West.

The Isles of Scilly Steamship Group says its vessels will not be travelling between Penzance and the islands on Friday and Saturday due to the forecasted conditions.

Along with passenger ferry Scillonian III, the firm says its Menawethan freight service is also cancelled.



It says sea heights of up to 5m (16.5ft) are expected.

Wind gust of 45 to 60mph are forecast more widely across most of England and Wales, where two less severe yellow warnings will be in force throughout Friday.

Chief Met Office forecaster Neil Armstrong said: “This is the first stormy weather in the south of the UK this season and we expect some disruption as it moves through.

“With trees in leaf, it is likely fallen branches and trees could obstruct roads and railways so take extra care on the Friday morning commute.”

Strong winds will be combined with spells of heavy rain today though gusts will gradually ease.



Once the peak of Storm Austen has passed, winds will gradually ease through Friday afternoon, offering a brief respite early on Saturday.

But Storm Boelo is due to bring more rain, wind and low temperatures to the nation when it arrives on Saturday.

Amber and yellow weather warnings for wind and “persistent” rain are covering large swathes of the UK from midnight until 3am on Saturday.

Forecasters said the storm will be invigorated by an active jet stream as it crosses the Atlantic before reaching Northern Ireland and western Scotland on Saturday afternoon.

Heavy rain will move in from the west on Saturday, while wind strengths will build through the evening.



The disruptive weather is expected to last through Sunday, bringing difficult travel conditions and potential building damage.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Brits across the country have been battening down the hatches in preparation for the storm, with the Met Office advising people to protect their property.

It recommends checking for loose items outside homes and securing them, including bins, garden furniture, trampolines, tents, sheds and fences.

News.title: Woman, 19, ‘sexually assaulted at bus stop by stranger’ as man, 49, arrested
News.content:
STREET 'ASSAULT' Woman, 19, ‘sexually assaulted at bus stop by stranger’ as man, 49, arrested







Next

A WOMAN has allegedly been sexually assaulted at a bus stop by a stranger, with cops arresting a 49-year-old man.

The incident was reported on September 29, after the 19-year-old encountered a man she did not know at a stop in Sandown, Hampshire.

The man is said to have repeatedly put his arm around her waist before touching her leg – despite her efforts to move away.

He then got on the Number 8 bus at around 9pm.





Cops are appealing to a woman who was standing slightly downhill from the Beachfield Road stop as part of their enquiry.

She is described as black, wearing white headphones, a hoodie, dark trousers, dark shoes and a backpack.

She also boarded the Number 8 bus.

A 49-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of sexual assault and has been bailed until January 2 as the investigation continues



The force is urging anyone with information to contact police directly or submit information online.

More to follow… For the latest news on this story keep checking back at The Sun Online

News.title: At least 16 dead after 7.0-mag earthquake forces thousands to flee homes in Tibet sparking ‘all-out’ rescue efforts
News.content:
Next

AT LEAST 16 people have been killed by a powerful 7.0-magnitude earthquake that flattened hundreds of buildings in Tibet.

Over 12,400 people have been forced to flee their homes with 65 injured as China’s Xi Jinping calls for “all-out” rescue efforts to find survivors.



Seven aftershocks with magnitudes between 4.3 and 5.2 were felt after the initial major tremor.

Urgent search and rescue efforts have seen over 1,600 people rush to the quake’s epicentre in Tibet’s northern regional city of Nagqu.



At least 339 homes collapsed due to the huge shockwaves.

Recovery teams have been sending supplies including 1,000 easy-build housing units, 3,000 tents and folding beds.

The US Geological Survey said the quake was first registered at 10.33pm local time on Thursday.

Its epicentre sat 119 miles east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, mountainous region of northern Tibet.



The earthquake’s depth was around 11 miles.

The 7.0-mag quake marks the biggest earthquake in the region in the last five years, according to China’s national broadcaster CCTV.

One local Nagqu resident said the tremors were so strong it felt “as if several hundred yaks were running past”.

Another told Tibet Daily she was asleep in her bed when her house started to violently shake and left her legs trembling uncontrollably as she fled her home.

Chinese President Xi ordered a mass rescue operation as he was quoted by state media as saying: “All-out efforts must be made to search for and rescue people trapped by the earthquake.”



“Xi stressed that the affected area is at a high altitude and temperatures are cold.”

China has controlled Tibet since it was annexed in the 1950s.

Xi added that rescuers must do all they can to “minimise casualties”.

It follows a deadly 7.1 magnitude quake that destroyed “many buildings” in the region of Shigatse and wreaked havoc in parts of Nepal and India.

Over 125 people died in the devastating earthquake that ripped through one of Tibet’s holiest cities.

News.title: ‘Precious’ teenager, 17, riding an e-bike died in crash with car as man, 60, arrested for ‘drink-driving’
News.content:
CRASH HEARTBREAK ‘Precious’ teenager, 17, riding an e-bike died in crash with car as man, 60, arrested for ‘drink-driving’







Next

A 17-YEAR-OLD boy riding an e-bike has died after a horror crash with cops arresting a man aged 60 on suspicion of drink driving.

Ishmael Sankoh was riding his bike when the fatal collision happened on Elsinge Road in Enfield, London, just before 11pm on Sunday October 4.



Police said the collision involved a car and an e-bike, with Ishmael tragically pronounced dead at the scene.

His family are now being supported by specialist officers, the force said.



The driver of the car, a 60-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and driving while unfit through drink.

He has since been released on bail pending further enquiries, said the Met Police.

Ishmael’s family said in a heartfelt tribute: “It’s hard to find the words to express the pain of losing you, Ishmael. You were more than a son, a brother, a nephew, a cousin and a friend; you were a precious part of our family, and your presence brought something special into all our lives.

“God called you too soon. You were smart, you were kind, and you made your family so proud in everything you did.

“You loved football, you loved computers, you loved life.

“Although our hearts are broken, we are grateful for the memories, the laughter, the love and the moments we were blessed to share with you. We wish we had more time, more conversations and more laughter.



“Rest peacefully, our beloved Ishmael. You were loved beyond words and will never, ever be forgotten. We will carry your name, your smile and your memory with us always. Until we meet again, may your soul rest in eternal peace.”

Cops urged anyone with information to come forward immediately.

Detective Inspector Simon Ager, from the Met Police, said: “Our thoughts remain with Ishmael’s family and loved ones following his tragic death.

“The loss of someone so young in these circumstances is devastating, and we recognise the profound impact this will have on all those who knew and cared for him.

“Specialist officers continue to support Ishmael’s family, and we ask that their privacy is respected as they come to terms with this heartbreaking loss.



“Our investigation remains ongoing and we are working to establish the full circumstances of the collision. We are particularly keen to hear from anyone who witnessed what happened, or who has dashcam, CCTV or mobile phone footage from the area at around the time of the incident.”

News.title: White Van Man saved from red tape nightmare as govt launches £800m paperwork savings bonanza ahead of budget
News.content:
Next

WHITE Van Man will be saved from a red tape nightmare as part of an £800 million of savings for business.

A mountain of bureaucracy has been staved off for electricians, plumbers and carpenters in a move from government ahead of next week’s Budget.



John Healey has intervened to slash the bureaucracy choking firms as the government accepts a series of recommendations from business leaders.

The changes from the Chancellor will mean paperwork required for Companies House will stay minimal – rather than filling out full profit and loss requirements for April 2028.



Streamlining company reporting will save businesses overall £290 million a year amongst other changes.

Small firms will also be aided by making it easier to bid for public contracts especially in construction.



Chancellor John Healey said: “British firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money when they simply want to get on with running their businesses.

“That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.”

Andy Burnham said: “If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms.

“It’s not right that pointless bureaucracy gets in the way of people working hard to build something that matters to their high street.”



Tina McKenzie, National Chair, Federation of Small Businesses, said it’s “a huge step in the right direction, averting a huge new weight of red tape on the very businesses with the fewest resources to deal with it”.

Rain Newton-Smith, CBI boss, said: “Cutting unnecessary admin can free firms to invest, compete and grow – and business will want to see that ambition translated quickly into meaningful reductions in the burden they face.”

Other measures include streamlining the home-buying and selling process saving £116 million a year and a further £105 million saved for asset managers in reducing duplacative reporting.

The changes are part of government plans to reduce the admin burden on firms by 25 per cent by the end of the Parliament.

Ministers believe this will save firms with employees some 280 million hours per year.

News.title: Getaway driver for gang that killed PC Sharon Beshenivsky jailed for life again after supplying guns to criminals
News.content:
BACK TO JAIL Getaway driver for gang that killed PC Sharon Beshenivsky jailed for life again after supplying guns to criminals







Next

THE getaway driver for the gang that killed PC Sharon Beshenivsky has been jailed for life again.

Faisal Razzaq, 45, was sentenced yesterday for supplying reactivated guns to criminals.



The weapons were converted by far-right extremist Thomas McKenna, 60, who lived on a caravan site in South Ockenden, Essex, and had set himself up as an armourer for the criminal underworld.

In one bugged conversation, Razzaq told an associate, Abdul Rahman Saleh, that if police ever tried to detain him, he should not hesitate to shoot at them in order to escape.



He told Saleh: “Feds try and grab you, just shoot at the car, shoot in the air.

“I don’t care where you shoot but you’ve got to shoot bro.”

An officer from the Met’s specialist crime command said: “This is a shocking thing to hear for someone who had already served a lengthy prison sentence over the fatal shooting of a police officer.”

Mum-of-three Sharon, 38, was shot dead in 2005 when answering a call to a robbery at a travel agency in Bradford.

When the robbers burst from the premises, one of them shot at Shron and her fellow colleague, PC Teresa Milburn, who was hit but survived the attack.

Razzaq, originally from Forest Gate, East London, was convicted of ­manslaughter and was sentenced to life with a minimum of 11 years.



After his release in 2017 he sold guns using the cover of a car hire firm in Bushey, Herts.

At Harrow crown court he was jailed for life with a minimum of eight years after admitting offences including conspiracy to sell firearms.

News.title: Alarming advice to stockpile food, water and cash raises questions about just how resilient Britain really is
News.content:
Next

HOW prepared are you to survive three days without electricity, running water or access to the shops?

That is the rather alarming question the Government wants every British household to ask itself.



Families are being urged to stockpile food, water and emergency supplies in case a national crisis leaves them cut off from essential services.

Ministers say the advice is about preparing for everything from storms to cyber attacks and power blackouts.



And while taking a few simple precautions is sensible, it raises questions about just how resilient Britain really is.

After all, keeping the lights on, the taps running and essential services working is surely one of the most basic responsibilities of government.



Of course, even the best-prepared country cannot prevent every storm, flood or major power cut.

But Britain’s ageing infrastructure is already under pressure, and making it more resilient does require serious investment.

It is undeniably another headache for Andy Burnham, whose Government is already grappling with stretched public finances and competing demands for cash.

Encouraging families to prepare for emergencies is sensible but ministers must make sure Britain is just as ready as the people they are asking to stockpile supplies.

News.title: Russell Brand shouted ‘look what you’ve done to my f*****g sheets’ after alleged rape, court hears
News.content:
Next

Russell Brand shouted “look what you have done to my f*****g sheets” after raping a woman, a court has heard.

The complainant, in her early 20s at the time, claims he attacked her at his home in 2009 after picking her out at one of his comedy gigs.



A former colleague said the woman told her through tears that Brand had anally raped her.

The witness added the woman said the comic scolded her for getting blood on his bed.



The colleague said: “He shouted at her and said, ‘look what you’ve done to my f*****g sheets’.”

The complainant’s mum said she told her that she had screamed in pain during the alleged attack in Hampstead, North London.



The trial previously heard the woman attended one of the comedian’s gigs at the Hammersmith Apollo in West London with a friend in 2009.

Jurors were told the comic picked her and her pal out from a crowd of fans in the foyer and then invited the complainant into his dressing room where she performed oral sex on him.

It is said they swapped phone numbers and met at his house the following week.

The woman claims they started having sex when he removed the condom and anally raped her.



Yesterday a friend of the complainant recalled her describing how Brand went from “charming” to “violent and cold-hearted”.

Brand, 51, denies charges including three counts of rape.

The Southwark Crown Court trial, involving six complainants, continues.

News.title: Detective raped by colleague says Met handling of case 'like being raped again'
News.content:
A Metropolitan Police detective, who was raped by a fellow officer, has told the BBC that Scotland Yard's handling of her case was "like being raped all over again".

Det Con Linda Williams was attacked in 2004 by PC David Carrick - a serial abuser jailed for life in 2023 for sexual offences against her and 11 other women.

Linda has post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) because of the attack and sought damages from the Met for failing to protect her from Carrick. The lengthy civil case left her feeling suicidal, she says.

The "worst thing", she says, was when lawyers acting for the Met commissioner challenged the severity of her PTSD on the basis that she had been raped only once.

The Met has told the BBC it "tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams' welfare and has aimed to deal with her claims as quickly and compassionately as possible".

"We recognise the unique and additional impact on DC Linda Williams, whose exposure to Carrick came as a result of her being a Met officer," the force added. "Her continued commitment to public service, in spite of the trauma she experienced, is commendable."

Linda, who has waived her legal right to anonymity to speak to the BBC, has settled her civil case and the Met has now paid her compensation without acceptance of liability.

In an unprecedented move for a serving officer, she is now calling publicly for Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley to resign. She believes he has failed to change police culture as promised and she still does not trust her own force to handle cases like hers.

When he took on the most important job in UK policing in 2022, Sir Mark pledged to change the Met. At the time, the force was viewed as being in crisis - following Sarah Everard's murder by a serving officer and other scandals including officers sharing photos of murdered sisters Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman.

News.title: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
News.content:
Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.

A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the Â£25,000 prize.

"I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry."

It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994.

Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband?

"I made this album not focusing on commercial [success], not focusing on making things cookie-cutter," said the 28-year-old.

"Some of these songs are seven minutes. They're indulgent. They're maximalist."

Across 17 tracks and 73 minutes, the record tells a cinematic story about a relationship that ends in tears on the rainy streets of Paris, then follows our plucky heroine as she dusts off the debris and emerges stronger and more resilient.

Along the way, it features both of her grandparents, the soul legend Al Green, four separate orchestras and more than 100 musicians.

News.title: Blue Planet III: Moment octopus escapes death after hunt gone wrong
News.content:
Filmmakers have captured an octopus's lucky escape after venturing from her normal underwater habitat.

The sequence is part of the latest Blue Planet series from Sir David Attenborough, who has continued to produce nature documentaries into his 101st year.

In the third instalment, viewers are taken around the world - from icy polar waters to the tropics, and out into the open oceans.

For UK audience, Blue Planet III starts on Sunday 1st November, 8pm, BBC One and iPlayer.

For those outside the UK, Blue Planet III will launch from November into 2027 across the world.

News.title: Chancellor plans to cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to £800m
News.content:
The chancellor has announced plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to Â£800m.

Ministers have said the proposed changes in regulations, announced ahead of John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday, will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses.

The move is part of a broader effort in the Budget to offer households and businesses more support amid rising costs.

In response to the announcement, the Conservatives said Labour had only made problems worse for businesses.

"Labour have finally admitted that endless red tape is hammering businesses and killing jobs across the country," shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said.

Healey acknowledged British firms are "fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork" eating into time and money that would be more valuable invested into their businesses.

He becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to slash red tape, which he said will allow businesses more "breathing space" to invest and create good jobs.

The changes should make compliance guidance easier, and simplify the reporting rules firms have to follow, the Treasury said.

Ministers have claimed this will save almost Â£800m in administrative and tariff costs.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey are expected to meet some business leaders on Friday at No 10 North.

Burnham said that it's unfair "pointless bureaucracy gets in the way" of hard-working people building their businesses.

"If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms," Burnham said.

The government has set itself a target of cutting regulation by 25% by the end of the current Parliament.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) Chief Executive Rain Newton Smith has welcomed the plans, but said the test would be in delivering reform.

Meanwhile, the shadow chancellor argued that the unemployment act had only made "the situation worse and has created a youth jobs emergency".

"John Healey must get a grip in his Budget next week. He must back our Conservative plans to cut welfare and cut taxes so we can get Britain working again," he said.

News.title: Lights will stay on this winter, grid operator says after concerns
News.content:
The body in charge of Britain's electricity network has given assurances that the lights will stay on this winter after concerns were raised by some of its engineers.

The National Energy System Operator (NESO) said the country's electricity system was prepared and "resilient to the challenges it may face" during the colder months.

However, its winter outlook report comes after an independent investigation found engineers had "high levels of stress and concern" about their ability to ensure adequate supply due to differences between renewable and gas-fired power generation.

NESO said supplies were expected to remain secure throughout the winter, though warned there could be "tight days".

It added that such days would result in it deploying notices to power producers that additional electricity generation may be needed. It said such an announcement was not a warning of power cuts and was routine.

"While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain's electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world," said Deborah Petterson, director of whole energy system resilience at NESO.

In a separate report, National Gas, a private company that owns and runs the country's gas network, and is separate from NESO, said it expected to have sufficient supply to meet demand this winter, but forecast gas for power generation to increase at peak demand due to the "intermittent" nature of renewables.

News.title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show
News.content:
The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.

During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.

As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa.

They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".

The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.

William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives Â£1m.

The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.

Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.

The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.

At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".

The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday.

News.title: Give more people weight-loss jabs on the NHS, say MPs
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands more people should be given access to the weight-loss injection Mounjaro on the NHS in England, a cross-party group of MPs says.

The Health Committee said the current plan for 220,000 people to have this jab for free on prescription in 2028 was a "woefully small number" and "unambitious".

This represents only around 6% of eligible people and is a key reason why more than a million have been paying privately for weight-loss injections, including Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The committee says a two-tier system is emerging in which only the wealthy can get good access to the medication that curbs appetite.

News.title: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies, Streeting warns
News.content:
Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.

He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.

Streeting also said that cyber incidents - like the recently discovered critical security flaw in the programming language which powers much of the internet - will happen "more and more".

Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that the UK is facing a greater threat to the country, "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime".

Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford earlier on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.

He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and the flooding that is expected this winter.

Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".

The defence secretary referenced the critical security flaw in the PHP programming language which has left organisations around the world scrambling to update their systems.

In the UK, 32 government services were offline while the potential cyber-security issues were addressed.

"It's not just from foreign states engaged in espionage or sabotage; it's also organised criminals," Streeting told Question Time.

"In this world of AI that we live in... it does also present threats if people are innovating and pushing against conventional [cyber] defences."

News.title: Rapid changes to care market risk to National Care Service, regulator says
News.content:
Private companies buying up care homes for older people in England could undermine the government's plan to create a universal care service, the regulator says.

The Care Quality Commission's annual report, external highlights how a rising share of the care home market is owned by large firms - the five biggest increased their share by 26% in the last two years, driven by interest from US property investors, and now own one in seven homes.

While there can be benefits, there are concerns the trend can lead to higher prices and a reduction in quality.

The regulator said rapid changes to the market, including the fragmentation of home help into more smaller services, needed monitoring and clearer planning.

The CQC said the changes to at-home care, which covers support to help people wash and dress, could create inefficiencies - nearly a third of these services are providing care to four or fewer people.

In contrast, there are few smaller care homes judged important for providing specialist and personalised care.

Small care homes have always represented a tiny proportion of the care home market, but over the last 14 years the numbers have fallen significantly, particularly those that combine care with nursing support, which are down by a quarter.

News.title: Monk on Caldey Island gave naked photos of himself to visitors

She said she was stunned but did not say anything to Keet because she thought he would deny it and she might be asked to leave the island.

Natalie said: "I think the worst thing it did, if I'm completely honest, it took away my whole spiritual belief in Catholicism."

But Keet claimed she turned "wickedly against him" after he rejected her attempts to seduce him.

It is also claimed Keet made several unwelcome sexual advances towards an employee of the abbey.

"If it was not so sad, it would be laughable, how she could make up so many allegations spread out over three years, in which we had co-operated so pleasantly together. Very sad," he added.

News.title: Items recovered in search for missing fishing boat and crew
News.content:
Items belonging to a fishing boat that vanished off the north coast of the Isle of Lewis last week have been recovered as the search for the vessel and two missing crew members continues.

Norman "Tam" Murray, 40 and Murdo Morrison, 23, were on board the Kilda when it disappeared on 13 October.

The body of crewmate Douglas Craigie, 49, was recovered from the sea in the early hours of the following morning by rescuers.

On Thursday, police confirmed that items belonging to the vessel had been recovered from what was described as "an area of interest" off the coast near Port of Ness.

The search was carried out by Police Scotland's marine and dive unit and partners.

A Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) exclusion zone has been in place for divers and vessels in an area between the Butt of Lewis and Port of Ness, but this will be lifted from 23:59 on Thursday.

Insp Neil Taylor, local area inspector for the Western Isles, said the search was a "complex operation" and asked for officers to be given "time and space" to carry out inquiries.

He said: "Efforts are continuing to work with partners and we are doing everything we can to get answers.

"While the Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) exclusion zone will be lifted tonight, we would urge people not to put themselves at any risk.

"Please do not attempt to carry out searches in areas which put you at risk of harm."

A GoFundMe for the families affected by the event has raised more than Â£148,000, against a target of Â£110,000.

News.title: Russell Brand accuser said alleged rape 'really hurt', court hears
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

The friend of a woman claiming to have been raped by Russell Brand told a jury the complainant had told her after the alleged attack that it had "really, really hurt".

The witness who spoke via video link at his trial said she had attended the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London with the alleged victim in 2009, where they had been invited to the defendant's dressing room after his comedy show.

Statements from the woman's parents were also heard in court, saying their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, and that she had been "very worried about HIV".

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations span a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009 and involve six female complainants.

The witness said the woman had told her she had visited Brand's house in London soon after meeting at the theatre, and that he then sent a car to collect the woman, which took her to his place in Hampstead.

She said when they spoke about it "quite soon after", she said she "was just crying - really upset".

The witness said Brand had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually.

"He was quite aggressive," she said her friend had told her.

"He forcibly put it in my bum and "it really really hurt".

The witness says she remembers specifically asking the complainant if she had said no to Brand when the alleged attack started.

News.title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
News.content:
Barclays is cutting around 5,000 staff as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.

The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce.

The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.

Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.

Although not all of the cuts are due to AI, their scale will prompt further concern over the impact of the new technology.

Company spending on AI is increasing along with claims new tools can replace some of the basic tasks currently done by staff such as administrative and programming work.

HSBC, Standard Chartered and Danske Bank have also flagged AI-related job cuts this year.

"It is a hot button topic," said AJ Bell investment analyst, Russ Mould.

However, banks had not yet made big moves towards the widespread introduction of AI and they would be considering the implications for security and customer service before implementing AI technology to make financial savings, he said.

"Any company at any time needs to keep on top of its cost base," he said.

"It will be intriguing to see what other banks say in their results in the coming weeks.

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union that represents banking sector workers said the company was "using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce".

"Employers should be focussed on upgrading employees' skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach," she said.

Barclays is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.

AJ Bell's Russ Mould said despite "reaching for the AI lever" Barclays had failed to match expectations with its financial results.

Barclays also revealed it made Â£2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.

Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business.

"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future.

"We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake.

"Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."

Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers.

Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".

"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.

Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further Â£1.1bn of savings in 2027.

News.title: Tommy Robinson hired detectives to find journalists, court told
News.content:
Political activist Tommy Robinson has told a court he hired private detectives to track down and photograph two reporters to "put pressure" on them.

The 43-year-old from Bedfordshire, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, told Southwark Crown Court he was "shocked and scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".

He has denied two charges of harassment causing fear of violence to reporters Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber after the 2024 Southport attacks.

Robinson is accused of writing posts on X, sending direct messages and making phone calls that made the two journalists fear the risk of vigilante attacks.

He denied wanting to expose the journalists to threats of violence, and said he felt his actions were "totally reasonable... under the circumstances".

News.title: Lockerbie bombing accused loses bid to have case thrown out
News.content:
She referred to a longstanding American legal doctrine, which stipulates that a court's right to hold a trial is not impaired if the suspect has been the subject of a forceful abduction.

"This rule rests on the principle that due process of law is satisfied when one present in court is convicted of a crime after a fair trial and in accordance with constitutional procedural safeguards," said the judge.

"Put differently, there's nothing in the Constitution that requires a court to permit a guilty person rightfully convicted to escape justice because he was brought to trial against his will."

In her ruling, the judge said there were two exceptions to that doctrine.

One would apply if Marimi had been brought before the court through the US government's "deliberate, unnecessary and unreasonable invasion" of his constitutional rights.

For that exception to be triggered, the challenged conduct had to be carried out by, or at the direction of, US officials.

The judge said Marimi's allegations "at best suggest that US government officials exerted pressure on Libyan officials to facilitate a rendition, not that US government officials directed or controlled the challenged conduct."

The second exception to the doctrine would apply if the US government had violated an extradition agreement which was the only way a suspect could be transferred between the two countries.

The judge said the US government had invoked two conventions to secure Marimi's appearance in a US court.

Thousands are without power in Cornwall as Storm Austen batters the UK, with National Grid reporting that over 6,000 households have no electricity.

Drivers and passengers are being warned that falling trees could pose deadly risks and disrupt their journeys as two storms are set to sweep across the UK, bringing winds of up to 80mph and heavy rain.

Exeter Airport has cancelled flights and there are a number of traffic delays near Redruth and Truro, with a number of trees reported to have fallen.

The Met Office says there may be flooding, and has issued weather warnings for very strong northwesterly winds, with widespread gusts of 60-70mph in the southwest and some of up to 80mph around exposed headlands.

Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season, is expected to affect southwest England on Friday (23 October), with an amber warning for wind issued in Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly from 1am.

Over the weekend, Storm Boelo will hit Northern Ireland, Scotland and parts of northern England with what the Met Office described as “impactful winds”.

There will be “widespread gusts” of 55-65mph widely, with these reaching up to 70-80mph in more exposed coastal locations, the Met Office added.

Storm Boelo is a separate low pressure system to Storm Austen, which is due to clear into the North Sea by Friday morning.

News.title: Where is Celebrity Traitors filmed and can you stay in the castle?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Things are heating up inThe Traitors' second celebrity season. With just 12 names left in the castle after a tense episode last night, fans might be wondering where the breakfast banquets, muddy missions and turret executions actually take place.

We’ve rounded up everything you need to know about the Scottish castle hosting celebrity royalty on this series of The Traitors.



Where is The Traitors filmed?

Ardross Castle is used in both the UK version of the show and the US adaptation hosted by Scottish actor Alan Cumming.

The 19th-century castle, complete with more than 100 acres of parkland, sits on the banks of the River Alness, just north of Inverness in the Scottish Highlands.

Ardross Castle estate was purchased by the 1st Duke of Sutherland in the late 1700s, where he built a hunting lodge.

The castle as we recognise it now began to take shape once the estate was sold to Sir Alexander Matheson, an MP and opium trader, in 1845 for £90,000.

Aiming to attract tenants to agricultural tenancies, he began developing the land and enlisted the architect Alexander Ross to design the castle building in the Gothic Scottish Baronial style.

Ross added around 30 rooms to the original mansion for £7,000, along with the lawns, pond and fountain.

Ardross Castle passed between owners in the 19th and 20th centuries, and was broken up and sold in 1937. It was purchased by the current owners, the McTaggart family, in 1983, when they began renovating the property, and added new trees.

Generally, the day’s missions take place on site, while the discussions, action and banishments are filmed among the castle’s lavish interiors.

Can you stay at The Traitors castle?

Unfortunately for budding Faithfuls, the rooms of Ardross Castle are not available for individual stays.

While the action on The Traitors takes place overnight at the castle, stars of the show actually tuck into the Courtyard by Marriott hotel near Inverness’s airport during filming.

The Ardross stronghold is used as a wedding and conference venue for corporate and private events when it is not the set of bewilderment and backstabbing. The Times reports that prices to hire the castle for a wedding for up to 130 people over two nights begin at £45,000.

News.title: US to tighten travel rules with new Ebola declaration for arriving passengers
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The US government is set to tighten measures aimed at preventing entry by people exposed to Ebola.

The change will require US-bound air travellers to attest they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the prior 21 days, according to a memo on Thursday.

The US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention in May adopted rules barring ‌airline passengers who have been in the DRC, the centre of the 2026 outbreak, in the prior three weeks.

The restrictions were extended to US citizens in July.

The new CDC order takes effect on November 3 and requires all US-bound airline passengers to file digital or paper attestations.

A worker wearing personal protective equipment (PPE) disinfects a desk at the Kitatumba Ebola treatment centre ( Reuters )

Airlines for America, which represents United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Delta Air Lines, did not immediately comment.

The CDC is holding briefing calls with major US and foreign airlines on Friday to detail how carriers should comply with the new requirements.

Earlier this year, as part of the Ebola measures, the CDC barred any foreign nationals from the US if they have been in Uganda or South Sudan in the prior three weeks.

The Bundibugyo strain of the virus spread undetected for months before ​the outbreak was declared in May. It kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine.

So far, the outbreak is confirmed to have killed about 4,700 people in Africa, according to the Africa CDC.

To date, no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the United States, the CDC said.

News.title: Barcelona v Real Madrid tension is building and El Clasico can light a furious fuse
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

One regular day of LaLiga, that’s all they are asking for. It did not require fluent Spanish to understand the gravity of Real Madrid’s ‘Comunicado Oficial’ last Friday afternoon. A press release containing mention of Javier Tebas, the LaLiga president, alongside Joseph Goebbels and the “ministro de Propaganda del régimen nazi” signalled a drastic escalation in their long-running dispute with the Spanish league and that tensions with rivals Barcelona had reached a peak ahead of this weekend’s Clasico at Camp Nou.

In the statement, Real Madrid demanded Tebas to resign after he compared the club’s criticism of referees through their in-house TV channel to “propaganda techniques” used by the Nazis during the second world war. The 15-time Champions League winners called the language used by Tebas “deeply offensive” and “morally repugnant”. Tebas, in turn, issued his second lengthy social media post of the day in which he largely doubled down in accusing Real Madrid of “intimidation” and seeking to “destroy” the Spanish league.

Barcelona, unsurprisingly, also had their say as club president Joan Laporta criticised Real Madrid for “constantly attacking” LaLiga. Laporta also praised Tebas for being a “counter’ to Madrid’s accusations, which will have done little to dampen the fire building at the Bernabeu. The Madrid supporters had their say during last weekend’s home win over Sevilla, unveiling a banner that played on a LaLiga marketing slogan with the message: “It’s not football, it’s Tebas and Negreira”.

Once again, the Negreira case is likely to feature prominently as Barcelona host Real Madrid in El Clasico this weekend. Real Madrid have demanded a “full clarification” as to why payments of €7.3m (£6.5m) from Barcelona to Jose Maria Enriquez Negreira, the former vice-president of the Spanish football federation’s technical committee of referees, were made between 2001 and 2018. Earlier this month Real Madrid sent Uefa a “50,000-page” dossier of documents which they say relate to the “integrity of the competition and confidence in the refereeing system”.

Barcelona and Negreira deny wrongdoing and were cleared by Uefa investigators in 2023. Laporta said the payments related to consultancy work and providing reports on referees – but Real Madrid president Florentino Perez ramped up the pressure in May by accusing Barcelona of “stealing” seven league titles from his club. Relations between the historic rivals are usually fraught but they took a further turn when Barcelona finally withdrew from the European Super League in February, leaving Real Madrid as the only founding member of the project to remain on board.

It’s an interesting time, then, for the first Clasico of the season to roll around, particularly when Camp Nou will also welcome the return of one of its fiercest opponents: Jose Mourinho.

Prepare for ‘war’?

It’s been 15 years since Barcelona and Real Madrid’s modern rivalry arguably reached its peak: when El Clasico offered the contrast of Pep Guardiola and Jose Mourinho and their clash of styles, the two best managers in the world on the touchline as much of a draw than the best players in the world on the pitch in Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo. Mourinho would prepare his players for “war”, a tactic that will not be forgotten at Camp Nou and could be deployed again now as Real Madrid attempted to halt a Barcelona side who have scored 50 goals in their first 12 matches of the season. Hansi Flick’s team won their first 11 in a row, until Tuesday’s Champions League defeat at Paris Saint-Germain, and lead Real Madrid by six points in LaLiga. Mourinho can’t afford another defeat now.

open image in gallery Real Madrid and Barcelona’s clashes in the 2010/11 season saw the drama of the Clasico reach a peak ( Getty )

open image in gallery Mourinho will take charge of his first Clasico as Real Madrid boss since leaving the club in 2013 ( Reuters )

It did not take Mourinho long on his return to Spain, however, to play into the narrative that Real Madrid have been up against something bigger than just Barcelona. Having suffered their first defeat of the season at Real Betis, Mourinho arrived at his press conference following the heated 2-1 derby defeat at Atletico Madrid holding printouts of the “two clear red cards” Diego Simeone’s team should have received in the first half. Given the attention Mourinho looked to draw towards the two incidents – a studs-up challenge from Cristian Romero on Jude Bellingham’s knee and Lee Kang-in catching Federico Valverde on his ankle – any late challenges in the Clasico which Real Madrid feel are dealt with too leniently or too strongly could be the match that sparks the dynamite.

In between the controversy, it’s easy to forget what the selling point of El Clasico really should be about: the stars. The Premier League may be the most dominant domestic competition in the world but it does not have a fixture that comes close to matching the individual talent on display when Kylian Mbappe faces Lamine Yamal and the midfield battle is decided by either Bellingham or Rodri. The prospect of Yamal enjoying a potential crowning moment at Camp Nou, a night before the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London and in front of a Real Madrid side who were left seething by Vinicius Jr missing out on the award two years ago, adds another delicious storyline into the mix. But the sharp edge to world football’s biggest club fixture is back as well.

News.title: UK retail sales drop after warm weather hits winter clothing demand
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

UK retail sales volumes declined last month as warmer weather dragged on demand for autumn and winter clothing, according to official figures.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said retail sales volumes fell by 0.4% in September, compared with the previous month.

It was a steeper drop than expected, with economists having predicted a decline of 0.1% for the month.

It followed a 0.7% increase in August and a 0.4% fall in July.

These were both revised upwards in the latest figures, improving from a 0.5% estimated rise for August and a predicted 0.5% decline in July.

The ONS added that the volume of products bought from retailers was up 0.7% for the third quarter of 2026, compared with the previous three-month period.

ONS senior statistician Hannah Finselbach said: “Retail sales grew in the latest quarter with growth led by motor fuel which, despite recent price increases at the pump, have now returned to monthly sales levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East.

“Food and drink sales also contributed to growth in the quarter, partly helped by the warm weather and the World Cup, although they fell back slightly in September.”

News.title: How F1 champion-elect Kimi Antonelli has vindicated Toto Wolff’s bravest Mercedes move
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

In the weeks preceding the 2024 Formula 1 season, following the sensational news of Lewis Hamilton’s dramatic ditching of Mercedes for the allure and pageantry of Ferrari, the next quandary was obvious. How would Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff go about replacing the six-time champion who spearheaded the greatest driver-team relationship in the history of the sport?

Typically in the modern-day F1 ecosystem, the omnipresent Netflix boom mic was best placed.

“Have you talked to Toto yet?” Lewis Hamilton asked Carlos Sainz, the man he was replacing at the Scuderia and therefore unattached for 2025, as aired on Season 7 of Drive to Survive. “I haven’t talked to Toto yet…” Sainz replied. “Which makes me feel like if he really had an interest, he would have already called me.”

open image in gallery Carlos Sainz speaks to Lewis Hamilton in a conversation picked up by Netflix in Drive to Survive ( David Davies/PA Wire )

There would be no call. At least not one indicating a straight-driver swap would be forthcoming. In those first few months, Wolff kept his cards close to his chest. Sainz, Lando Norris, Fernando Alonso and Alex Albon were among the obligatory names linked. He flirted with Red bull’s Max Verstappen and made no secret of that lust. Yet the Austrian always had the sense of a man steering away from the staples on the grid; a left-field wildcard pick was incoming.

Wolff would later say: “I made up my mind five minutes after Lewis Hamilton told me that he’s going to Ferrari. Obviously we were discussing other options and looking at the Max idea – we didn’t discount it completely with looking at what happened at Red Bull.

“But instinctively that is the line-up that I always wanted, bearing in mind the fast-tracking that we did with Kimi and everything related there too, but that was immediately what I wanted to do.”

Kimi Antonelli was just 17, fighting for podiums in Formula Two, when he found out that Wolff had plumped for the Italian teenager to replace one of the sport’s greatest-ever drivers. He was just 18 when he smashed into the wall at Parabolica in Monza – a chastening first weekend outing in an F1 car. And he was just 19 when he won his first race, in China in March; a Sunday which would set the tone for the year ahead.

Now, having just turned 20 in August, the curly-haired, happy-go-lucky Antonelli is on the cusp of his first world championship. It is a near-formality that he will become the youngest-ever champion in the history of the sport, an accolade currently held by Sebastian Vettel, who was 23 in 2010.

The boy from Bologna, ironically just 30 miles east of Ferrari’s HQ in Maranello, has a 102-point lead heading into this weekend’s United States Grand Prix in Austin. If he wins the race and second-placed George Russell finishes ninth or lower and third-placed Lewis Hamilton comes home fifth or lower, he will be crowned champion with five rounds remaining.

It has been an astonishing turnaround.

open image in gallery Kimi Antonelli can become F1's youngest-ever world champion this weekend in Austin ( AP )

A year ago, Antonelli was a rookie lacking in confidence after a damaging European summer season which included four retirements in six races. A first-lap crash in Austria into Max Verstappen – with the Dutchman unusually unflustered afterwards – and qualifying 18th at Spa were particular nadirs. Wolff stood by his protege, acknowledging his inexperience and rawness.

There would be less room for sympathy this year, however, particularly early on as Mercedes fulfilled their tags as pre-season favourites. Much like Norris up against Oscar Piastri last year, Russell was declared the heavy favourite with the bookies. Russell won the season-opener in Australia, with Antonelli spinning into the wall in practice. One race in, another inaugural British champion looked extremely likely.

After that, Antonelli won five consecutive races. In total, he has finished higher than Russell in 12 out of 17 grands prix. He even pipped his teammate at Monza, having started at the back of the field, in an iconic home race which will live long in the memory. On the whole, his driving has been exemplary, barely putting a foot wrong in qualifying and in his racecraft. A modicum of calm professionalism, mixed in with a charisma it is near-impossible not to like.

open image in gallery Antonelli took Hamilton's seat at Mercedes ( Getty )

In the aforementioned Netflix episode, Sainz later asks Hamilton: “Do you think they [Mercedes] are declining?” The Briton considers the query and shakes his head: “No, I don’t think so.”

He was right. Not only has Wolff been fully justified in his selection of Antonelli but, conversely, Hamilton’s choice to join Ferrari has proved to be the wrong one (in contrast to 2012, when he joined Mercedes from McLaren). Ferrari, of course, could prove to be the pacesetters next year. The Circuit of the Americas this weekend could go some way in telling us where Mercedes are, with an upgraded car and one eye already on 2027. Red Bull are also on a hot streak, with Max Verstappen winning the last two races in Malaysia and Singapore.

But Austin is all about Antonelli, who, round by round, has vindicated Wolff’s courageous driver pick two years ago. For the Austrian, under pressure himself after Mercedes’ struggles in the ground-effect era, a far simpler choice would have been Sainz, Norris or Alonso. Someone tried-and-tested. Someone consistently able to record podiums. Someone... safe.

Yet sometimes, to unearth a champion, you need to take a gamble. And Wolff’s has paid off big time.

News.title: This personal finance app will encourage users to invest – and you might have already downloaded it
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Personal finance app Plum has received the go-ahead from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) to encourage those with significant cash savings to consider investing some instead.

As part of the government’s wider initiative to get British people back in the investing habit, one of the key changes announced was to try to fill the gap between free, general guidance around personal finances, and the paid professional advice which has long been out of reach for many.

Targeted support is intended to play a key role here, identifying groups of customers of banks or other financial services companies who have similar traits and who have the potential to put some of their money to work in investments.

It is estimated that over seven million adults across the UK have more than £10,000 in cash savings – and now Plum will join the cohort of firms who could get in touch with some customers over utilising some of that money elsewhere.

Plum’s addition to the list is notable, as it’s used by over 2 million people as an all-round personal finance app – for roundups, automations and challenges alongside the usual savings and pension options – rather than the often more formal-feeling banks, insurance firms and asset managers who are already approved to offer targeted support.

A year ago in announcing the plans, Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive of the FCA, said it would be a “game-changing” scheme which would let “millions of people get extra help to make better financial decisions”.

Over longer periods of time, investing can provide significantly better returns than cash savings alone can manage, though the added risk involved means there can be ups and downs along the way.

That uncertainty seems to have put off a generation of Britons from actively investing, but from next April at least £8,000 of each person’s £20,000 annual ISA allowance will be reserved for stocks and shares products, rather than cash ISAs only – another part of the government’s attempt to get more people investing.

Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

Invest at least £100 in Stocks or ETFs of your choice. Get fractional shares worth £50! Terms and conditions apply. Go to website 

In practice, approval will allow Plum and other firms to offer ready-made savings or investment suggestions to groups of consumers who share characteristics, rather than specific individual recommendations or suggesting exactly which investments to make.

The fintech firm will be among the first to offer an AI-led targeted support system, The Independent understands, allowing for automatic and proactive contact with customers who might otherwise leave larger amounts of money sitting in cash.

Customers with big cash piles could be asked if they want to invest some ( Getty Images )

At present, The Independent understands that up to 15 firms have been approved by the FCA to provide targeted support, with 11 of those having publicly announced their involvement: Barclays, Aviva, Forester Life, Legal & General, Quilter Invest, Monzo, Bank of Scotland, Lloyds Bank, Vanguard Asset Management, Royal London Mutual Society and Zopa Bank. The Independent is aware of several more businesses who remain with open applications to also offer the service.

Will Bryant, director of wealth strategy at Plum, said: “It’s currently estimated by the FCA that 23 million consumers are underserved by the advice market. With cost-of-living challenges continuing to squeeze people’s pockets as energy prices rise, consumers need this type of support now more than ever.

“Targeted Support can help make sure people are making their money work harder for them and making strides towards actively building their wealth over the long term through investing - not just saving money and budgeting.

“Now Plum has been approved to offer Targeted Support, our customers will be able to access more helpful, ready-made suggestions to put them in a better position, helping them on their wealth-building journey.”

Victor Trokoudes, CEO and founder of Plum, added: “From day one, Plum has existed to democratise finance. Now, with targeted support approval, we’re going to further help the 91 per cent of people in the UK who don’t access personalised financial advice through the latest AI technology.

“Now we can deliver proactive support that helps customers make smarter financial decisions and find ways to make their money work harder over time.”

Plum is also expected to offer more personalised investment advice options to customers in future.

News.title: Europe’s record-breaking summer heat estimated to have killed 50,000 people
News.content:
More than 50,000 people are estimated to have died across Europe as a result of this summer’s record-breaking heatwaves, according to research.

In the UK alone, researchers estimate there were 4,354 excess deaths this summer.

The number of excess deaths across Europe is double the number recorded in 2025 and it is also far higher than the previous record of 29,000 deaths. This was recorded in 2022 when the continent also endured exceptionally high temperatures, with the mercury hitting 40 degrees celsius for the first time in the UK.

According to the Met Office the UK saw its hottest ever summer this year with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days where the temperature was above 30 degrees celsius. Mainland Europe experienced its third hottest summer, with temperatures particularly high in the south and west.

Researchers from Imperial College, London and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) looked at 854 urban areas in 30 countries across Europe. Using temperature records and modelling based on the relationship between heat and mortality they estimated the number of heat-related deaths that occurred between June and August.

They said findings from previous years’ excess heat mortality modelling matched official figures released later by national health authorities.

Because the study only looked at urban areas – making up 40 per cent of the population of the countries studied – researchers believe the number of deaths is likely to be an underestimate.

According to the study, published in Nature Health, southern and western Europe were hardest hit. Italy experienced the highest number of excess deaths (13,303), followed by France (7,268), Spain (6,824), Germany (6,340) then the UK.

There were an estimated 22,000 deaths among those aged 85 and over but researchers pointed out that an estimated 6,000 people under the age of 65 are also likely to have died as a result of the heat.

Around a third of the deaths took place in late June, when average temperatures across Europe were more than 5°C above what would be expected during this time of year. Researchers say in early summer people were less likely to have acclimatised to the sweltering weather. This period was marked by both extremely high humidity and unusually high night-time temperatures, making it difficult for people to cool down.

Researchers also estimated that more than two thirds of the total excess deaths were attributable to climate change. Across the continent as a whole Europe was an average 2.9°C higher than would have been expected. However, in some places temperatures were as much as 12°C higher.

Dr Clair Barnes, extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College, said extreme heat was having a severe impact on public health.

“It is yet another reminder both of the imperative of rolling out targeted interventions to protect those who are most vulnerable to this increasingly extreme heat, and of the growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming.”

Dr Pierre Masselot, assistant professor of statistics and epidemiology at LSHTM and one of the study’s authors, said “climate change is everybody’s problem”.

“It is not just hot regions that are suffering any more with some parts of Western and Northern Europe experiencing extreme heat and historically high health burden. And the whole population is affected, as shown by the significant death toll among younger age groups.

“It is becoming increasingly clear our cities are poorly adapted to rising heat, and it is critical we improve our efforts towards adaptation. This means cooling the cities through more green spaces and less pollution, and providing health care for affected populations.”

News.title: Bournemouth thrash Milan to seal greatest win in club’s history
News.content:
Milan could not even point to being down to 10 men for the last hour as mitigation; long before, Bournemouth had treated the Rossoneri with contempt. When Ruben Amorim’s side trudged off, soaked and silenced, they had not mustered a single shot on target.

Few nights have better encapsulated the Premier League’s power. Bournemouth have never finished higher than last season’s sixth in the top flight of English football; AC Milan have won seven European Cups. But the Premier League’s financial clout is such that, each season, the bottom club earns more than the champions of Serie A.

The Premier League’s shared riches, allied to years of astute recruitment and management, have underpinned the Bournemouth’s ascent. Even Andoni Iraola’s departure has not stalled the progress at the Vitality Stadium; Marco Rose has relished the new European adventure.

Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz had already been toppled in Bournemouth’s first two European games. Now, Bournemouth have won their first three matches in Europe. Despite middling Premier League form, Rose’s ambitions will extend far beyond securing a berth in the knockout stages of the Europa League. On this evidence, Bournemouth are legitimate contenders to win the competition, and earn a berth in next season’s Champions League.

“It’s a special night for the club,” Ryan Christie, Bournemouth captain, said. “It’s mega – in terms of the story of the club, it’s ridiculous.”

News.title: Harry Brook hits historic double century – but England still lose to Sri Lanka
News.content:
Good morning and welcome to the fourth match of the autumn tri-series in Pakistan. After two wins for the hosts, the two touring sides face each other for the first time in Rawalpindi, the last match here before the circus leaves for Lahore. England and Sri Lanka played each other only last month in this format, England winning at Chester-le-Street and the Oval by a distance, those victories sandwiching a narrow defeat at Headingley where, if you remember, Harry Brook’s side were cruising until Jos Buttler ripped his left hamstring. He did eventually come back out to bat on one leg as his rattled team-mates flapped and fell to Asitha Fernando, Dilshan Madushanka and Eshan Malinga.

On Tuesday against Pakistan, England again were flying with both ball and bat but they let the middle-order rebuild, losing control of the rate. Their two most experienced white-ball bowlers, Adil Rashid, who looked rusty after breaking his hand in August, and Sam Curran, who missed the end of August and all of September following groin surgery, went for 6.87 and eight runs an over respectively. Then, after a promising opening partnership, Ben Duckett top-edged a pull, Tom Banton flicked straight to midwicket and Will Jacks later fell in identical fashion when well-set to marshal the chase. Arafat Minhas ended up with six for 40, bowling Harry Brook with a beauty, and there will be more trial by spin today.

Although there was some talk of England failing in end-of-days Bazball fashion, it most reminded me of the teething troubles of Eoin Morgan’s side in 2015 and 2016 when they were experimenting with players, viz this Rose Bowl collapse. We have to acknowledge that Joe Root, the best player of spin, was undone by one that kept low from Naseem Shah and both Brook and Jordan Cox lost their wickets to very good deliveries from Arafat, a bowler, on a feast day. Dunith Welllalage will return to try to replicate his line of attack today but he is a bowler that England know well. He has had his days against them but they have also given him some tap in the past.

News.title: Health authorities race to investigate first human death linked to Shamonda virus
News.content:
A French man has become the first person to contract Shamonda virus, a disease previously only found in animals and spread through midges.

The patient, who had a weakened immune system, has since died, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).

Shamonda virus was first identified in Nigeria in the 1960s and has this year been detected in farm animals all across Europe.

It was confirmed to have spread to the British Isles in September, after being found in a cattle herd on the island of Jersey. There have also been cases in Ireland.

The French patient, who was immunocompromised, died earlier this month while infected with the virus, but it is unclear if the infection contributed to his death, the ECDC said in a statement.

Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing.

Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director of the World Health Organization (WHO) said in a statement on X that he was “in contact with French authorities, who are collecting information to better understand the source of infection.”

He added the patient was “immunocompromised, which made them more vulnerable to infection and severe disease.”

There was “no health risk to the general public identified at this time”, the French health and agriculture ministries said in a joint statement.

Dr Ben Brennan, Group Leader and Senior Lecturer, MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research, University of Glasgow, said: “This is an important scientific finding, as it is the first reported human infection with Shamonda virus [..] at present, there is no evidence that Shamonda virus causes widespread human disease, although further investigation is needed to understand its ability to infect people.”

In animals, Shamonda virus attacks the central nervous system and can lead to severe inflammation and haemorrhage. It can also lead to miscarriages.

Affected horses have been reported to exhibit seizures, lethargy, fever, muscle twitching, and difficulty walking.

Authorities are also still trying to ascertain whether the man himself was infected by a biting midge – the route of transmission between animals – or if he could have been infected by close contact with livestock.

It is thought he was infected in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating in midges and animals earlier in the year.

“Despite decades of circulation of the Shamonda virus in Africa and Asia, no human cases had been documented until now. This is therefore an exceptional case occurring in a severely immunocompromised patient,” French health authorities said in a statement.

The UK Plant and Health Agency said some of the neurological signs of the disease in horses resemble West Nile fever, human cases of which reached a record high on mainland Europe this year.
