Ghana News.title: University of Ghana orders students with CGPA below 1.00 to withdraw
Ghana News.content:
UG

The University of Ghana (UG) has directed undergraduate students who obtained a Cumulative Grade Point Average (CGPA) below 1.00 at the end of the 2025/2026 academic year to withdraw from their programmes.

In a notice posted on Facebook on Thursday, October 22, the university’s Academic Affairs Directorate said the directive was in accordance with Section 9.26 of the University Regulations for Junior Members (2017), which sets out the requirements for academic progression.

Under the regulation, students must attain a minimum CGPA of 1.00 and meet the academic requirements of their respective schools or departments to qualify for progression to the next level.

The Directorate explained that the university’s regulations do not provide for academic probation. Students whose CGPAs remain below 1.00 after all grades for their registered courses have been released are therefore required to withdraw.

Affected students have been advised to check their academic standing on the university’s Management Information System (MIS) Web and submit their withdrawal requests through the Student and Staff Portal (STS).

“Affected students are to check their CGPAs on the MIS Web, log in to the STS Portal (sts.ug.edu.gh/services) with their Student ID and PIN and select ‘Withdrawal Request’ to initiate the process,” the statement said.

The Directorate noted, however, that for some programmes, the relevant school or department would initiate the withdrawal process on behalf of affected students.

Students who require clarification about their academic standing or the withdrawal procedure have been advised to contact their respective College Academic Offices.

The university added that its Careers and Counselling Directorate would remain available to offer support and guidance to students affected by the directive.

Ghana News.title: NDC bans tally voting for eight positions in constituency elections
Ghana News.content:
The National Democratic Congress (NDC) has banned tally voting for eight positions in its constituency-level elections scheduled for Saturday, October 24, and directed delegates to present valid identification before casting their ballots.

The party’s General Secretary, Fifi Fiavi Kwetey, announced the guidelines at a press briefing on Thursday, October 22, stressing that all aspirants, delegates and election officials must adhere strictly to the prescribed procedures.

Under the guidelines, delegates will be required to present a valid voter ID card, Ghana Card or the party’s plastic membership identification card for verification before voting.

Mr Kwetey said election officials must apply the identification requirements consistently, warning that no delegate should be allowed to bypass the verification process or receive preferential treatment.

The party has also directed that ballots for the women’s and youth conferences be kept securely and counted only after voting in the main constituency executive elections has ended.

The guidelines further prohibit tally voting for eight positions, with each delegate permitted to cast only one vote for each of the affected positions.

Mr Kwetey warned that the rules were binding on all participants and cautioned aspirants and delegates against practices that could undermine the credibility of the elections.

“We expect all participants to comply fully with them. Ignorance of the rules will not justify attempts to circumvent them, and no aspirants or delegates should seek an advantage through practices that compromise the fairness of the process,” he said.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Grenade exercise sparked deadly fire at Canada military base, army says
World.content:
High winds propelled the blaze across the army base in Wainwright, killing four soldiers and injuring dozens more.

Share Grenade exercise sparked deadly fire at Canada military base, army says on social media

A fire that killed four soldiers at a western Canadian military base was sparked by an exercise using live grenades, a military official said.

The deadly fire broke out on a grenade launcher range during military exercises on Saturday, with high winds propelling it across the base, Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan, commander of the Canadian Forces Military Police Group, told reporters on Thursday.

“A subsequent change in wind direction and velocity significantly increased the fire’s intensity,” she added, with the flames spreading to a training area at the Wainwright military base in Alberta.

Due to the blaze being in the “permanent danger area” of the range, firefighters were unable to directly combat it, Hanrahan added.

The fire spread on Saturday afternoon during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

The military base lies in the prairies, a landscape of wide, open grasslands, rolling plains and scattered groves of trees.

About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practised attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.

Four soldiers died and 39 were injured, with 27 requiring hospitalisation. The incident was one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military.

The soldiers and reserve members were participating in exercises ahead of a planned deployment to Latvia, where Canadian forces have their largest international military operation.



The Wainwright base is one of the largest bases operated by the Canadian Armed Forces. It regularly hosts training exercises involving military personnel from NATO countries.

During the final months of World War II and for several months in 1946, the base was used as an internment centre for German prisoners of war.

World.title: Keeping Madhubala alive: The fight for Karachi’s captive elephants
World.content:
Karachi’s last two African elephants remain in captivity. Their sisters are already dead. Will they survive?

At Karachi Zoo, Jude Allen sang, You Are My Sunshine, to an elephant he could not save.

Noor Jehan, the 17-year-old African elephant, was suffering. Allen recalls massaging her legs, nursing her bedsores and spending her final days beside her.

She died on April 22, 2023, surrounded by a few activists. Allen, 45, had held various corporate jobs while volunteering as an animal caregiver since an early age.

But Noor Jehan changed something in him, he said. “The day this wild African elephant rested her painful forehead on mine, and I hugged her for the first time – it all made sense,” he tells Al Jazeera.

“I quit my job without a plan B.”

Now three years later, Allen has turned the grief of Noor Jehan’s loss into care for one of her sisters, Madhubala, who also faces major health challenges. He is part of a growing campaign of Pakistani and international activists and doctors trying to save Madhubala, a victim, her carers say, not just of medical conditions, but also of a system that is simply unable to give animals in captivity the attention and facilities they need.

The elephant sisters

In 2009, four elephant calves captured in Tanzania were brought to Pakistan, allegedly through an animal trader.

Two of them, Noor Jehan and Madhubala, were kept at the Karachi Zoo, while their sisters Sonia and Malika were taken to Safari Park, a larger facility also in Pakistan’s largest city that has both a zoo and other viewing spaces for visitors to watch animals up close.



Then, in 2020, Pakistan was gripped by the story of Kaavan, an Asian elephant that had spent 35 years in the capital city of Islamabad, eight of them alone after his companion Saheli died. Four Paws, an international animal welfare organisation, helped move Kaavan to an animal sanctuary in Cambodia, where he now lives with other elephants.

That episode also shone a light on the Karachi sisters. At the time, Allen was helping a friend with another animal shelter, and came to know Four Paws was in town. He reached out to them, and they led him to Noor Jehan and Madhubala.

By 2021, Noor Jehan’s tusk was infected. She suffered from malnutrition and stress, too.

Allen and the other activists couldn’t save Noor Jehan, but the campaign had turned into a wider cry, demanding care and justice for captive animals in the urban jungle of Karachi, the coastal home to 20 million people.

One animal in particular became the focus of attention.

Named after an iconic Indian film actress from the mid-20th century, Madhubala was now the only African elephant at the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation-run zoo. She was alone, banging her head against the gate of her enclosure, Allen recalls. “She didn’t have a friend.”

Allen says she needed company – she wanted a friend.

Tragic reunion, and a slow recovery

Allen, along with Four Paws, helped prepare her for a move to Safari Park, so she could join her sister elephants, Sonia and Malika.

Four Paws assessed the elephants and found that they needed better diets, enrichment and medical treatment. The organisation recommended reuniting them.

The reunion came in November 2024. Four Paws documented the meeting between the siblings at Safari Park. Sonia approached Madhubala first. Malika followed. The three touched one another with their trunks and drank together.

But days later, on December 8, Sonia died, aged about 19, after collapsing in her enclosure. The park’s director initially described an apparent heart failure. Subsequent findings, reported by Four Paws, identified a severe bacterial infection associated with an advanced abscess on her foot.

Amir Khalil, a Four Paws wildlife vet involved in the elephants’ care, told The Associated Press at the time that “such infections don’t spread in one day”. Four Paws linked her death to prolonged unsuitable living conditions and malnutrition.

Meanwhile, Madhubala and Malika were both diagnosed with tuberculosis, although recent examinations reported by her veterinarian have indicated that Madhubala is no longer testing positive.



Now Madhubala, 22, is recovering after losing more than 200kg (440 pounds) and becoming too weak to get up safely after lying down.

Khalil, who has also rescued wild animals from multiple conflict zones, is one of the carers who has taken charge of Madhubala’s recovery. He told Al Jazeera that Madhubala had recovered 85 percent of her ability to walk, and was a good patient: “She really wants to follow the standard operation procedure and to adhere to the programme that I put in,” he says. That includes a “water massage for the leg with high-pressure water”.

He says the required medication needs to be administered properly, and treating all the wounds – and they were getting better when he left Pakistan a few days ago.

For Allen, the work began with Noor Jehan.

While she was unwell, he says he visited the zoo daily, checking that the elephants received their food on time and in the right quantities. During Noor Jehan’s final 10 days, he was a near-permanent presence there, assisting the medical team however he could.

Her death became the beginning of the “I Am Noor Jehan” movement, which Allen leads for animals in captivity. The Pakistan Animal Welfare Society (PAWS), with I Am Noor Jehan, held a memorial for Noor Jehan with artists, filmmakers, and other animal activists.

Then came Madhubala. Preparing her to enter a transport crate required patience. Allen describes an elephant who could be aggressive and difficult to approach. Four Paws specialists helped him understand her needs.

But delays to the relocation disrupted the training, he says. Madhubala became frustrated and bored. Allen tried football.

He entered her enclosure, an approach he acknowledges Four Paws did not endorse. The caretakers warned him too: Madhubala wasn’t in a playful mood.

But within 20 minutes, he says, Madhubala wanted the ball.

She picked it up with her trunk and hid it between her legs. Then she began teasing her caretakers who were trying to retrieve it, offering the ball before concealing it again.

The sessions helped him build a relationship with her, he says. Madhubala began responding eagerly to training again.

“Earning her trust was the most significant accomplishment.”

That trust is especially important to Allen because he believes that Noor Jehan, and then Sonia, could have been saved.

When Sonia was unwell, Allen says he had raised concerns with local authorities about her weight loss and a swelling beneath her body. He says those warnings were not adequately acted upon.

“I felt I betrayed Sonia.”

‘What was meant to be a sanctuary became a zoo’

The deaths of two of the four African elephants in Karachi raise questions about the resources, expertise and accountability behind keeping wild animals in public institutions, experts say.



Karachi Municipal Corporation has not procured any animals in the last 20 years, and the elephants were brought in long before his time, Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab said, speaking to Al Jazeera.

“I’ve always said that animal welfare should be paramount. Anyone who wants to come join hands, to look after the animal, we would be ready and willing to work with them,” he said.

He argued that his team at KMC had done whatever it could to look after Madhubala with Khalil and other doctors.

“Madhubala was being treated, and the good thing is, now, Dr Khalil is also saying things are moving in the right direction and we’ve got a third-party perspective endorsing whatever was being done,” Wahab said.

But Allen says Safari Park, where Madhubala was moved after Noor Jehan’s death, has been a disappointment. Allen says he helped develop Madhubala’s new enclosure there, working on landscaping and the procedures that caregivers needed to use to help her.

Moving her was supposed to change the conditions of her life. But at Safari Park, he says, people come right up to the elephants, feed them, and treat the facility like a zoo.

“What was meant to be a sanctuary became a zoo,” he says.

Javed Maher, the top wildlife official in the government of Sindh, the province containing Karachi, says elephants and wildlife need to be in their own habitat, and people caring for them need to have knowledge of animals.

Currently, the Safari Park enclosure for elephants is about 14 hectares, roughly 35 acres, according to Four Paws.

Mahar says he offered hundreds of acres in the rural country for these elephants so they can live freely.

“Karachi Zoo, along with the majority of the zoos of the country, is not capable,” he says.

But the elephants have remained at Safari Park.

The above photo needs a credit -TSL

Former Islamabad High Court Chief Justice Athar Minallah, in a landmark 2020 judgement, declared that animals had rights. It was that ruling that enabled the transfer of Kaavan to Cambodia, and two Himalayan bears to a sanctuary in Jordan. The zoo in Islamabad was closed, and all 878 animals kept there were released or relocated.

“That judgement remains the law, as no appeal was filed against it,” says Minallah speaking to Al Jazeera.

“Under this jurisprudence, Madhubala has the right to live in an environment where her social, behavioural, and psychological needs can be met,” he says.

To be sure, the challenges that officials like those at KMC and elsewhere face are also real.

Pakistan already faces profound human hardship. A United Nations account published in March says more than 60 percent of people in the country cannot afford a healthy diet.

Acquiring animals that require specialist care creates obligations lasting decades. Once confined, they depend on people for every meal, for movement, companionship and treatment.

But that, say analysts, is even more reason to “stop keeping them in our custody”, says Allen.

He last saw Madhubala on October 8, when he was assisting the Four Paws team. When there are lots of people, he says, she gets distracted easily.

But she can also get jealous for Allen’s attention. “She will literally throw rocks if she can at anyone talking to me,” he smiled.

World.title: Israel arrests 36 Palestinians in the West Bank, attacks on farmers ramp up
World.content:
Israeli pogroms on Palestinian farmers and their lands during the olive harvest season intensify.

Share Israel arrests 36 Palestinians in the West Bank, attacks on farmers ramp up on social media

Israeli forces have arrested 36 Palestinians during raids across the occupied West Bank, as attacks on Palestinian farmers and their lands during the olive harvest season ramp up.

In Jenin governorate, Israeli forces raided towns and villages on Thursday, arresting 10 Palestinians, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing data from the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.

Israeli forces also raided the town of Tuqu in the Hebron governorate on Thursday and arrested former prisoner Shorok al-Badan, along with five others from other parts of Hebron, according to Wafa.

The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said on Thursday that Israeli forces arrested 14 people in Khirbet Jawaya village of Masafer Yatta in Hebron, while Wafa reported that three other Palestinians were arrested across the Hebron governorate, citing a security source.

In Nablus and Jerusalem, three more Palestinians were arrested during Israeli raids in the village of Burin, the town of Awarta, and the Qalandiya refugee camp.

Attack pattern

The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said it documented 17 pogroms by Israeli forces and settlers on Thursday against Palestinian farmers and their land during the olive harvest.

The incidents were recorded across occupied West Bank governorates, including Hebron, Qalqilya, Nablus, Ramallah and el-Bireh, Jenin and Salfit.

According to the Commission, the attacks included assaults on farmers, preventing them from reaching their land, theft of crops and agricultural equipment, damage and burning of olive trees, as well as arrests, threats at gunpoint and live fire.



The Commission says the pattern represents an escalation in attacks targeting the olive harvest and undermines Palestinians’ ability to access and cultivate their land and maintain their livelihoods.

Israeli attacks on Palestinian farmers garnered international attention and condemnation. US Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was briefly detained on Wednesday by the Israeli military with a warning while volunteering to help Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the occupied West Bank.

World.title: US tech stocks tumble as investors fret over AI spending
World.content:
Tech-heavy Nasdaq falls 2.6 percent as debate rages over whether AI is a bubble.

Share US tech stocks tumble as investors fret over AI spending on social media

US tech stocks have dropped sharply amid market jitters over the sustainability of companies’ enormous capital investments in AI.

The Nasdaq Composite, which is dominated by tech firms linked to the AI boom, fell 2.6 percent on Thursday, its steepest fall since the index tumbled 4.2 percent on June 5.

The broader S&P 500 slid 1.21 percent, the benchmark’s biggest drop since a 1.52 percent decline on July 29.

Apart from Apple, each of the “Magnificent 7”, which make up more than one-third of the overall market, saw substantial losses.

Meta dropped nearly 7 percent after it raised its projected capital spending for this year to $135bn to $145bn in its latest earnings report, even as the Facebook parent company’s net profit fell short of expectations.

Amazon fell 4.6 percent, while Nvidia dropped 4.4 percent.

Tesla and Alphabet both fell 3.1 percent, while Microsoft declined 2.2 percent.

Apple rose 1.2 percent.

The sell-off extended to other major tech players, including Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, both of which fell about 8 percent, and Broadcom, which slid 4.3 percent.

After the losses, the Nasdaq is about 5.8 percent off its all-time high, reached on October 6.

Rising oil prices since February, due to the fallout of the US-Israel war on Iran, added to the downbeat mood.

Brent crude futures rose 4 percent on Thursday and continued to climb on Friday morning, taking the international benchmark above $114.20 a barrel, its highest since May.

Stocks slip in Asian trading

Major stock markets in Asia opened lower on Friday, following the losses on Wall Street.



Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 fell more than 2 percent in morning trading before recovering some ground, while South Korea’s KOSPI dropped as much as 3.5 percent.

The Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong fell about 0.5 percent.

Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners in San Francisco, said the swings in the market appeared to be driven more by sentiment than underlying fundamentals.

“In short, nothing has changed. Investors have just decided to be afraid this week. Everyone I speak to points to a different cause for the downfall … It’s just a giant wall of worry,” Goldberg told Al Jazeera.

“There are legitimate concerns about the AI trade, but this level of shift in the markets is driven much more by investor sentiment than any tangible reason.”

US tech companies’ huge investments in AI have stoked intense debate about whether a market bubble is forming similar to the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.

While some Wall Street analysts view current levels of investment in datacentres and graphics processing units as unsustainable, others argue that AI will revolutionise society to a degree that justifies the eye-watering sums involved.

Global AI investment is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

World.title: Venezuelans demand elections in first national protest in nearly two years
World.content:
No date has been set to decide on a successor for Nicolas Maduro after the former president was captured by US forces.

Share Venezuelans demand elections in first national protest in nearly two years on social media

Thousands of Venezuelans have taken to the streets in several cities to demand free elections and other political changes, in the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years.

US President Donald Trump and acting President Delcy Rodriguez have said there would be elections, but no date has been set for a vote to decide on a successor for Nicolas Maduro, after the former Venezuelan president was captured by US forces in a military raid in January.

Opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado, who has been outside the country for nearly a year after living in hiding following a contested 2024 election, has said elections must take place by July 2027.

Her Vente Venezuela movement organised the protest, which took place in the capital Caracas and other cities, including Valencia, Maracay, San Cristobal and Maracaibo.

“Seeing this makes me happy because I know change is possible,” said 18-year-old cosmetology student Leosmary Hernandez, as she gathered with hundreds of others in northern Maracay. “I’ve been through so many hardships, so many problems because of the dollar, and difficulties studying. I have high hopes for my country and for our next leader and president, Maria Corina.”

“I went out to protest before, when things were much tougher, and I’m even less afraid today because I want my voice to be heard,” she added.

Since January 3, the country has been led by interim President Delcy Rodriguez of the long-governing United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV).



PSUV leaders have been accused of carrying out human rights abuses against political dissidents, including arbitrary arrest, imprisonment and torture.

After the United States launched a military operation to abduct and jail former President Nicolas Maduro, the PSUV remained in power with the support of the White House.

US President Trump has backed Rodriguez’s leadership, despite her having been Maduro’s vice president.

His administration has maintained an active role in Venezuela, exerting control over its oil resources and pressuring the Rodriguez government for reforms.

Minimal security presence

Venezuela’s socialist movement, in power since 1999 under late President Hugo Chavez and then Maduro, has in the past deployed security forces against protesters, but government forces had minimal presence at protest sites on Thursday, and in many smaller cities demonstrators dispersed before dark.

The ruling Socialist Party called for its supporters to march from Caracas’ Plaza Venezuela, the same place the opposition planned to gather two hours later, to a location near the presidential palace to commemorate Breast Cancer Awareness Month.

Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, known for his close ties to the security services, was pictured on state television attending the march, while the opposition supporters moved their protest to a nearby location.

US-backed talks continue

Talks between a faction of the opposition and the interim government, aimed at remaking the top court and the electoral council ahead of eventual elections, held their latest session this month, but changes could take significant time.

The negotiations, backed by the US, do not include Machado’s political movement, though she has said she will not stand in the way of their progress.

Machado’s proxy Edmundo Gonzalez Urrutia claims to have won the 2024 election according to vote tallies by the opposition. But the government, which never released full counts, backed Maduro, as did the country’s legal and electoral institutions.

Machado has for years sought US support, aligning with hawks in the Trump team who argued that Maduro, through alleged links to drug gangs, represented a direct threat to US national security. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are facing drug and torture charges in the US. They have pleaded not guilty.

World.title: Indian developer turns ‘Cockroach’ protests into video game
World.content:
NewsFeed Indian developer turns ‘Cockroach’ protests into video game

A 27-year-old Indian developer has created a satirical video game inspired by the Cockroach Party-led protests over alleged electoral list irregularities. Players can take on the role of protesters facing baton charges, tear gas, water cannons and police attempts to stop them.

World.title: Trump backs Ramaswamy ad featuring rival Amy Acton’s estranged mother
World.content:
Trump advises the Republican gubernatorial candidate to keep running the controversial .

US President Donald Trump has backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy amid controversy over an attack  by the Ohio gubernatorial candidate against his Democratic rival.

Trump said in a social media post on Thursday that Ramaswamy should keep running the  that features Democratic candidate Amy Acton’s estranged mother.

In the , Donna Arthur, Acton’s mother, disputes her daughter’s account of a childhood involving homelessness and ⁠⁠sexual abuse by her stepfather, urging Ohioans not to vote for her.

Acton says she has not seen her mother since 1978. Acton’s brother has supported her account of being sexually abused by her stepfather when she was a child. The stepfather, who died in 2004, was charged with rape.

“Anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in office,” Trump said.

The US president also attacked Republican Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, who advised Ramaswamy to take down the , labelling him “disloyal” to the Republican party.

‘It’s wrong’

At a gathering with reporters at the Ohio Statehouse, DeWine recalled the painful experiences of rape victims he dealt with as a county prosecutor and state attorney general.

“It’s wrong to run this ad,” he said. “And, even at this late time – my wife, Fran, saw the  just run this morning on TV – I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down.”

Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, called the  ⁠⁠a “desperate, disgusting attack”, while Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock called Ramaswamy’s decision to promote it “both despicable and entirely predictable”.



Vice President JD Vance, campaigning on Wednesday with Ramaswamy ⁠⁠and US Senator Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican, had brushed aside ⁠⁠the blowback.

Vance, a former senator from Ohio, expressed disgust with Republicans “whining” about the  as low and in poor taste.

Ramaswamy’s campaign said it was spending $4m to promote the .

Opinion polls suggest Acton is narrowly leading Ramaswamy in a tight race to replace the term-limited DeWine.

World.title: Ilhan Omar plans to move out of her Washington DC home after federal raid
World.content:
Last week, US federal agents raided Omar’s home as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud.

Share Ilhan Omar plans to move out of her Washington DC home after federal raid on social media

US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her home in Washington, DC, citing safety concerns following a recent raid of the property by US federal agents.

In an interview with MS NOW on Wednesday, Omar spoke for the first time about the raid, noting that the incident has made her feel unsafe there.

Last week, officers searched Omar’s home with what a Justice Department spokesperson described as a “judicially authorised search warrant”, adding that the raid was part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation”.

According to NBC News, which cited one person familiar with the matter, potential future charges against Omar may include conspiracy and making false statements in her immigration paperwork. Omar denies wrongdoing and accuses the administration of political intimidation.

Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalised US citizen, said she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong”.

The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of US President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies.

Earlier this week, Trump called the congresswoman “sick” and “dishonest” and slammed her birthplace as a “real s—house”.

For years, Omar, who is Muslim, has been the target of right-wing conspiracy theories about her immigration status, including allegations that she had married her brother.

The Minnesota congresswoman has repeatedly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies”.

Five-hour search

In the interview with MS NOW, Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for re-election in a deep blue district in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat.



Omar recalled waking up at about 6am to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.

Omar came with her family to the US at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a US citizen five years later, in 2000.

“It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I’m sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seems like a leap,” she said in the interview.

The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.

Omar said the agents were “intrusive but polite”, logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.

World.title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
World.content:
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.

UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.

The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.

The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.

Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.

Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.

The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.

"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.

"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."

The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.

Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.

In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.

But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.

UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.

The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.

World.title: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
World.content:
The electricity supply has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, though by Friday morning there were reports of power restored in some areas.

Local media said more than 12,400 people have been relocated after the earthquake.

Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.

The US Geological Survey (USGS) has recorded seven tremors close to the epicentre, all of which are located in the mountainous region. The largest tremor was recorded at 5.2 magnitude at a depth of 10km.

Shallow earthquakes and tremors closer to the Earth's surface are more damaging than deep quakes.

Several survivors of the earthquake have told local media about their harrowing escape from the tremor.

Speaking to Tibet Daily, Nagqu resident Yixi Cuomu said she was asleep in her bed when her house started shaking violently. Realising it was an earthquake, she headed outside barefoot, "her legs trembling uncontrollably" as she descended the staircase in her home.

Another eyewitness said the shaking was so violent "that in that moment I felt as if several hundred yaks were running past us".

Residents chose to spend the night outdoors in subzero temperatures, seeking shelter in tents or their cars, as they feared aftershocks could trap them in their homes, according to the news outlet.

Chinese state media reported on Friday morning that more than 400 aftershocks have been registered since the quake occurred.

China's Premier Li Qiang has called for "urgent efforts" to organise rescue operations and medical treatment for the injured, and relocate and resettle affected residents appropriately, according to state media.

Li noted that the earthquake-hit area is at a high altitude around 4,800 metres and prone to aftershocks.

The Ministry of Emergency Management has dispatched a working group to the affected area to guide rescue and disaster relief operations.

Separately, the Chinese government announced it was allocating 50 million yuan (Â£5.6m, $7.5m) for disaster relief efforts in Tibet.

World.title: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network
World.content:
Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US President Donald Trump has said, after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces.

Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.

Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russian targets in Ukraine and protect itself from attacks.

Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but said: "Bottom line, he put it back."

The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access.

The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise.

Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.

World.title: L'Oreal says weight loss drugs are impacting beauty and skincare sales
World.content:
Beauty giant L'Oreal says the rise of weight loss drugs has affected beauty and skincare sales, as it designs products to specifically target some side-effects of rapid weight loss.

The company's head Nicolas Hieronimus said the beauty market was proving resilient in a challenging global context and that the use of GLP-1s was "a very important phenomenon for us".

He told an investor call that the rise in their use was "having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular".

L'Oreal, which owns other popular brands including Maybelline and La Roche-Posay, announced on Thursday that sales in the three months to September rose by 7.7%, above analyst expectations.

The use of GLP-1s has boomed in popularity in recent years, after drugs developed to treat diabetes such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were found to also lead to significant weight loss because they supress the appetite.

While it is not caused by GLP-1 drugs directly, rapid weight loss can, for some people, come with a side-effect of loose skin - including around the face.

Hieronimus said L'Oreal's brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's have products "that have been designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 and its side-effects on skin sagging" and other effects related to rapid weight loss.

L'Oreal has also moved further into the clinical aesthetic space, increasing its stake in dermatology firm Galderma to 20% last December.

Both companies have been testing products on GLP-1 users worried about loose skin in separate clinical trials, according to Reuters.

Galderma owns popular aesthetic products including Sculptra, an injectable aimed at stimulating collagen production, and Restylane, which is an injectable dermal filler.

Last year the aesthetic firm released a report into the rise of GLP-1 use and related concerns about changes in facial appearance.

Its own survey of weight loss medication users found the vast majority had noticed changes to their facial appearance after using those drugs.

World.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit
World.content:
A US judge has ordered Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump cancelled a previous deposition - an interview under oath - on 16 October, citing "matters of national importance".

But a lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia that day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions.

Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is in the phase known as "discovery", in which the two sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence.

Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, told a court in Miami on Thursday that with two months left in the discovery period, Trump had still not completed a deposition.

US Magistrate Judge EnjoliquÃ© Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December or face sanctions - the most extreme of which could be the dismissal of the lawsuit - unless the discovery period is extended.

In US law, a deposition is an out-of-court statement made under oath in response to questions, which is recorded for use in later proceedings. Depositions carry legal weight - they are recorded verbatim by a court reporter and the transcripts can later be used as evidence in trials.

They typically take place in a lawyer's office without a judge physically present.

In defamation cases, lawyers for both sides are normally present for depositions.

Last week, lawyers asked that Lett compel Trump to face deposition after the last scheduled meeting did not take place.

On that day, Trump attended a midterms campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia and a fundraiser at his Mar-a-Lago property in Florida.

In a separate filing on Wednesday, Trump's lawyers said that the president could appear for the interview between 11 and 22 January next year and claimed the BBC was "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action".

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised for the error and said that the broadcast gave "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

In July, Trump's lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally claimed - or on the BBC's website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.

Trump ultimately agreed to drop the lawsuit against BBC Studios, the broadcaster's commercial arm, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".

World.title: Nigeria and Kenya Ebola patients may have crossed paths at Uganda airport, officials say
World.content:
The Kenyan man had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He later died, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death in the current outbreak.

Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact.

"One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.

Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source.

The WHO said it was too early to determine where the Nigerian woman became infected.

"The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official.

He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital.

Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help investigators understand whether the infection is related to other cases.

"The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria.

Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business, where the current Ebola outbreak began.

However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country.

Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there.

Meanwhile, Africa CDC said Nigeria had identified additional people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially reported.

"Most of those contacts, they are from the healthcare workers in different facilities where this case has been receiving treatment. We have also some few family members," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.

He said Nigerian authorities were working to identify and quarantine those considered at high risk, but declined to give an updated figure before the government released its findings.

"The position of the country [is] to bring those high-risk contact and put them on quarantine," he added.

Dr Ursu said the woman was receiving a high standard of clinical care and that her condition was stable.

In Kenya, the first group of people quarantined after possible exposure to Ebola will begin returning home on Sunday after completing 21 days of monitoring without developing symptoms.

Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission.

"We are not out of the woods," he warned, urging the public to remain vigilant but not panic.

He said the remaining eight patients remained in isolation and were responding well to treatment.

The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between the DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands of people cross daily for trade, work and family visits.

Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points.

The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers.

Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu.

The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before they develop symptoms.

Health authorities say tracing contacts quickly, isolating suspected cases and providing early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.

World.title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
World.content:
"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."

As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhaustedâ¦ there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."

By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.

Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.

Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.

The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet.

World.title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
World.content:
Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.

Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.

Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.

There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.

Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.

"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.

She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".

The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.

A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".

"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.

Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".

"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.

But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.

He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.

World.title: BOI supports 1.68m jobs as lending rises 26% to ₦644.9 billion
World.content:
The Bank of Industry (BOI) said it disbursed N644.9 billion to 12,501 businesses in 2025, a 26 per cent increase from N510.9 billion in 2024.

The intervention supported 1.68 million jobs under its 2025–2027 strategy to drive industrial development in Nigeria.

BOI’s Managing Director and CEO, Olasupo Olusi, disclosed this on Thursday at a meeting in Lagos.

Mr Olusi explained that after he assumed office, the bank embarked on a three-year strategy to spearhead Nigeria’s sustainable and inclusive industrial development from 2025 to 2027.

The BOI boss explained that the bank aimed to achieve its ambition through tailored offerings to underserved and high-impact business segments.

“Our 2X ambition meant to double our loan book, disbursements and impact instruments along these areas within three years,” Mr Olusi said.

The bank’s strategy includes six thematic areas to be pursued over the three years. The first theme includes MSME finance, with a commitment to allocate 35 per cent of the bank’s funding to MSMEs.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The bank also aims to focus on infrastructure by dedicating a quarter of all its credit to financing infrastructure, power, transport and logistics to lower the cost of doing business.

It also aims to support underserved and youth-owned businesses. BOI said it would direct at least 15 per cent of its financing to women-owned businesses while targeting 20 per cent of its SME disbursements to youth-owned or youth-run businesses.

BOI also finances clean energy, climate-resilient businesses and the circular economy, with 10 per cent of its portfolio disbursements dedicated to the sector.

Moreover, to take advantage of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, BOI also dedicated 15 per cent of its disbursements to the digital economy sector.

“We are delivering the strategy in three phases. 2025 was our foundation year, when we put in place the governance, frameworks, products and digital tools the strategy needs. 2026 is the year of execution at scale, and 2027 is the year we consolidate our results and meet our targets,” Mr Olusi said.

Strategy’s midpoint

The lender said its strategy was working, as it was set to consolidate its targets by 2027.

In 2025, BOI said it disbursed N644.9 billion, the highest amount the bank has ever disbursed, a 26 per cent increase on the N510.9 billion disbursed in 2024.

The lender said the financing reached 12,501 businesses and created or supported 1.68 million jobs.

BOI said it disbursed N120.9 billion to women-owned businesses alone, while MSMEs received 41 per cent of its 2025 funding, above its 35 per cent target.

Also, women-owned and youth-owned businesses received 20 per cent each, against the bank’s minimum targets of 15 per cent and 20 per cent, respectively.

In infrastructure, the bank said it deployed over N108 billion, including financing 100 mini-grids to power businesses and households, as well as broadband internet connectivity for over 700 communities.

“We also achieved our disbursement targets for climate and digital financing. For 2026, we are set to exceed our 2025 impact,” Mr Olusi said at the meeting with business editors.

To deliver its strategy and ensure inclusion across the Nigerian economy, the bank said it would prioritise five grouped sectors to achieve its targets.

The prioritised sectors include agro-manufacturing, other manufacturing, infrastructure, extractive industries and services.

Capital for Nigeria’s industrial needs

To provide the long-term capital Nigeria’s industries need to finance operations, BOI said it secured more than €2.2 billion and ₦250 billion in new funding for Nigerian industry over three years.

“Investors have placed this money with us because they trust our governance, our pipeline and our results,” Mr Olusi said.

The funding transactions include a €1.879 billion syndicated facility in 2024, named Syndicated Loan Deal of the Year; €210 million from international development partners in 2025; and a N250 billion development bond in 2026, which was oversubscribed.

The funding also includes €85 million from the European Investment Bank for agriculture in 2026 and €50 million for healthcare manufacturing in 2026.

The BOI boss added that the federal government had also entrusted the bank with its N200 billion intervention, comprising a N50 billion Presidential Conditional Grant Scheme, a N75 billion MSME Intervention Fund and a N75 billion Manufacturing Sector Fund.

“We have delivered more than 95 per cent of it, reaching 957,400 grant beneficiaries, 9,000 MSMEs and 104 large manufacturers. Our reach extends well beyond the cities.

“Through our RAPID programme, we disbursed N6.5 billion to 880 rural enterprises across all 36 states and the FCT, supporting more than 8,000 jobs.

“We financed 100 mini-grids that connected 11,777 households and businesses to electricity, many of them for the first time. We also disbursed about N213 billion to agro-allied businesses and linked 47,508 smallholder farmers to processors,” Mr Olusi explained.

BOI said it was working with the Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment on the National Industrial Finance Compact to bring more long-term capital into industry.

It said it would deploy its new European Investment Bank facilities into agriculture and local healthcare manufacturing so that Nigeria could produce more of the food and medicines it consumes.

It also promised to grow its ICT and digital economy portfolio using the iDICE programme.

World.title: Media Trust Group launches converged digital newsroom
World.content:
Media Trust Group, publisher of Daily Trust, has launched a converged digital newsroom that integrates its newspaper, television, radio and online operations to improve collaboration, speed up news delivery and expand its reach across platforms.

The newsroom, unveiled in Abuja on Thursday, brings together the editorial operations of Daily Trust, Weekend Trust, Aminiya, Teen Trust, Trust TV, Trust Radio and Digital Trust under a unified system supported by artificial intelligence (AI) tools and real-time audience analytics.

Group Editorial Director Ibrahim Shehu said the initiative would allow journalists and editors across the organisation to work together from the reporting stage, rather than operate as separate teams for different platforms.

“This newsroom is one newsroom, many platforms,” he said at the launch.

Mr Shehu said the system would enable reporters to file stories from the field or from home, allowing newspaper editors, television producers, radio presenters and digital journalists to access the material simultaneously and prepare it for their respective audiences.

He said a single investigation could be developed into a newspaper report, a television documentary, a radio discussion, a podcast or a digital explainer, depending on how audiences prefer to consume the story.

“Not the same content repeated everywhere, but the same truth told in the form each audience prefers,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to him, the newsroom’s AI-enabled content management system would improve coordination, support fact-checking and help editors monitor audience behaviour, including what people read, watch and listen to and where they access the content.

Mr Shehu said the technology would support journalists rather than replace them, adding that editorial judgement and responsibility for verification would remain with reporters and editors.

The system is also expected to strengthen collaboration between the organisation’s English- and Hausa-language teams, enabling them to develop stories together and make credible reporting accessible to audiences in both languages.

Media Trust chairman recalls company’s early struggles

The Chairman of Media Trust Group’s Board of Directors, Kabiru Yusuf, recalled the company’s beginnings in Kaduna in 1998, when it was established. He said the company now has about 30 shareholders.

Mr Yusuf said the organisation faced significant difficulties in its early years, including operating with a small workforce. He noted that the first edition of its newspaper was produced before the company had recruited enough staff to handle all its editorial work.

Reflecting on the organisation’s development, he said Media Trust had been misunderstood over the years and recalled the challenges of building a newspaper business during military rule.

He said the company has been wrongly linked in the past to two former military leaders, Muhammadu Buhari (1983 to 1985) and Ibrahim Babangida (1985-1993). He said the link to Mr Buhari was because some of the founders of Daily Trust worked in their personal capacity as media consultants to the former head of state, while the link to Mr Babangida was because the former military ruler’s printing press in Kaduna had a commercial deal with Daily Trust to help print its papers.

Mr Yusuf also spoke about press freedom and the responsibility of journalists to report the truth, including when doing so could affect influential people or personal relationships.

He warned against allowing relationships with powerful individuals to interfere with journalism, stressing the need for fairness in reporting.

“Fairness demands we should listen,” he said.

Media Trust targets audience growth, commercial sustainability

Group Chief Executive Officer Ahmed Shekarau said the converged newsroom was a strategic investment aimed at making the organisation more responsive to changing audience habits and technological developments.

“The future of the media lies in our ability to understand and serve our audiences better,” he said.

READ ALSO: CJID awards local media sustainability grants to seven Nigerian newsrooms

Mr Shekarau said integrating the group’s platforms would improve access to its journalism and enable the organisation to respond more effectively to audience needs.

He added that the investment would create opportunities to deepen relationships with audiences and provide greater value to commercial partners through coordinated campaigns across print, broadcast and digital platforms.

The group said audience data would help editors understand how people engage with their content and use those insights to improve coverage, without allowing audience metrics to dictate editorial decisions.

The initiative forms part of Media Trust Group’s strategy to build a digitally driven media organisation as news consumption increasingly shifts towards online and mobile platforms.

World.title: CJID launches Living Archives Initiative to preserve Africa’s media history
World.content:
