A Vanguard market survey carried out at Mile 12 International Market, one of the biggest foodstuff markets in Lagos, on some food items between August, September and October reflects price swings in items such as tomatoes, fresh onions, fresh pepper, beans, yam, plantain and sweet potatoes, while the prices of rice, horse mackerel (Titus), palm oil and guinea corn remained the same.

In August, a big basket of tomatoes sold for between N65,000 and N80,000 and later settled at N60,000 at the end of September, but has since risen to N70,000 in October.

In the same period, a big sack of fresh onions sold for N130,000 in August, rising to N150,000 at the beginning of September and later to N250,000 at the end of the same month. Currently, a sack of fresh onions sells for N350,000 at Mile 12 International Market, one of the biggest foodstuff markets in Lagos.

Meanwhile, a small bag of fresh pepper, which sold for N40,000 in August, dropped to N25,000 in September and is currently sold for N12,000. Also, a tuber of yam dropped to N4,000 in September from N7,000 recorded in August. The price drop was a result of the new yam harvest witnessed during the period. Prices of beans fluctuated between N6,000 and N7,000 in the same period.

Farmers’ groups react

Deputy National President of the All Farmers Association of Nigeria (AFAN), Mr. Daniel Okafor, blamed the high cost of fuel and poor roads, which he said had increased transportation and logistics expenses.

Speaking with Vanguard AgroBiz, Okafor, who is also the National President of the Potato Farmers Association of Nigeria (POFAN), also blamed insecurity in some farming communities, which he said affects cultivation and disrupts the movement of produce from farms to markets.

Okafor called for better rural roads, improved security, irrigation, timely farm inputs and training, saying agricultural support must be delivered in line with the farming calendar.

On her part, the Acting National President of the Smallscale Women Farmers Organisation in Nigeria (SWOFON), Mrs. Florence Ojo, said farm inputs were often inadequate or distributed too late to meet farmers’ needs.

Ojo said inputs intended for farmers should be distributed early enough for the relevant planting season and should reach genuine smallholder farmers, particularly those in rural communities.

According to her, the government must work with farmers’ organisations to identify genuine smallholders and monitor distribution intended to improve production.

She also called for more accessible extension services, better storage facilities and rural roads, as well as measures to reduce insecurity and post-harvest losses.

Why onion prices are high — NOPPMAN

The National President of the National Onion Producers, Processors and Marketers Association of Nigeria (NOPPMAN), Aliyu Maitassamu Isah, blamed the 2024 poor-quality seed crisis, fire incidents in many warehouses and heavy post-harvest losses as major factors contributing to the rise in onion prices.

He noted that onion prices rose from N25,000 and N30,000 per 120kg bag in March and April, respectively, to about N300,000 due to the crisis in the sector.

Explaining the crisis, Isah said a seed introduced into Nigeria from Algeria during the 2024–2025 growing season was unsuitable for the country’s farming system.

He noted that NOPPMAN had reported the problem to the government and sought intervention to cushion the losses, which were estimated at nearly N100 billion.

According to the account, the sector received a grant of about N2 billion from the Nigerian Agricultural Development Fund, an amount described as inadequate compared with the reported losses.

According to him, the current scarcity could have been avoided or reduced if the government had responded promptly to the seed crisis that disrupted production during that period.

He said the problem was compounded by inadequate storage facilities and fires that destroyed onions kept in local storage centres, leaving less produce available to meet demand.

Isah, explained that the price increase was not necessarily because Nigeria had failed to produce enough onions, but because a significant proportion of the harvest was lost before the next season.

“It’s not that we did not produce enough for the country, but we lost more than 51% from the month of April to October,” he said.

Isah said swift government intervention was necessary when a crisis affected an agricultural subsector, warning that failure to address such problems could lead to further damage.

He said the Minister of Agriculture had held discussions with the Bank of Agriculture and the Nigerian Agricultural Development Fund on support for the onion subsector, particularly seed supply and other farm inputs.

Maitassamu said onion supplies from Sokoto were expected around November and December, followed by Aliero in Kebbi State from late December to January while the main harvest season is expected around March and April next year.

He expressed optimism that the incoming harvest would help bring prices down, while stressing the need for timely intervention and better storage to prevent a recurrence of the crisis.

For the tomato sector, the current price surge is due to seasonal transition and low production.

The National Secretary of the National Tomato Growers, Processors and Marketers Association of Nigeria (NATPAN), Sani Danladi Yadakwari, said farmers were almost out of the wet-season harvest, while dry-season cultivation had just commenced.

However, he said many farmers had cut down on production this year after suffering huge losses last year when prices failed to appreciate.

He said: “We are almost out of the wet-season harvest period and the dry season has just started. Farmers are doing land preparation and putting seeds now. Hopefully, around the end of December, January, new harvest will start coming out. That is why the price is going up.

“Even from our end, the price has changed. That is why you see even onion price, pepper, almost everything. People are afraid because last year the produce price did not appreciate all through the year. Some people lost as much as 100 per cent of their investment. That is why some people are backing out to reserve what they have, otherwise they will invest all and lose all,” he said.

He said the price of tomatoes at the farm gate had changed, with a crate now selling for N16,000 to N17,000, depending on freshness, compared with N20,000 last week.

Yadakwari, who has in the past attributed the high cost of tomatoes partly to the lack of industry off-takers, said: “There are still no new off-takers. The only thing is production is down. Farmers did not produce up to how they used to produce because of last year’s experience of poor market price,” he added.

Emir warns

The Emir of Kano, Muhammadu Sanusi II, also warned that government responses to rising food prices must not undermine local production.

Speaking recently at an event in Lagos, he recalled that opening the market to rice imports from countries including Thailand and India had brought prices down but hurt domestic rice mills and left some investors in the agricultural value chain with bad debts.

He said that although imports could lower prices in the short term, they could undermine local mills, investors and domestic production if policy failed to protect productive capacity.

Nigeria, he said, could not continue relying on food imports from countries such as Thailand, India and China instead of strengthening its own production.

Traders blame high transportation costs, others

Traders in various areas in Lagos attributed the rising prices of food items to higher transportation expenses, spoilage and supply constraints, which they said were putting pressure on their businesses.

Founder of Food Drum and foodstuff seller, Caroline Ani, who buys from the North to sell in Lagos, said the foodstuff business was a good business, but the high cost of moving the goods within Lagos greatly affected the prices at which they were eventually sold.

She said: “Foodstuff business is quite lucrative, but doing it in a place like Lagos is crazy. I experienced a very bitter side of business during my first order. I got the foodstuff cheaper, but by the time it got to Lagos, the transportation from Oyinbo to Lagos Island was the exact fee I paid from Kaduna to Lagos.”

Adeola Adeoye, a tomato seller, faulted inadequate storage systems in Nigeria, which she said caused most of the tomatoes to spoil while in transit.

She said: “Tomatoes are more expensive because our suppliers sell them to us at higher prices, and transportation costs have also increased because of fuel prices. Some tomatoes get spoiled before we sell them, so we lose money. We cannot sell at last year’s prices because we also need to make a profit.”

An onion seller, Shukurat Eniola, said higher supply costs and limited availability had also affected the trade, leaving consumers to adjust the quantities they could afford.

She said: “When we go to buy onions from our suppliers, we spend more money than we did last year. Fuel prices have also increased, affecting transportation. Sometimes, onions are not available in large quantities, and customers who used to buy a bag now buy smaller quantities because of the high price.”

A trader dealing in melon seeds and African wild mango seeds (ogbono) said the cost of labour, processing and transportation also contributed to the prices of the commodities.

The trader said: “When our suppliers increase their prices, we have no choice but to increase ours. The money someone used to buy a reasonable quantity last year cannot buy the same quantity now.”

Consumers bear the cost

For consumers, however, the rising prices mean spending more on food while getting less in return.

Amina Bunu complained to our reporter at Ijeh Market, located in Ikoyi, that the N5,000 she spent on onions could not provide enough for two pots of food, describing the prices as the highest she had experienced.

She said that after buying the onions, her employer complained repeatedly that the quantity was too small for the amount spent.

According to her, she had to explain that food prices had risen so much that N5,000 could no longer buy the quantity people were accustomed to.

Bunu added that tomatoes were also expensive, making it increasingly difficult to buy the quantities needed for household cooking.

Another consumer, Nelson Oche, said the cost of food had made it difficult for him to stock up his home, even with N50,000.

Oche, a bachelor who lives with his younger brother, said that in the past, N50,000 would have enabled him to buy food items to stock the house. However, he said the same amount could no longer cover even two days’ worth of meals.

He showed Vanguard the bag of food items he had purchased for more than N50,000, including tomatoes, onions, melon seeds, pepper and other ingredients.

Stakeholders call for investment in solar-powered storage systems, others to address challenges

For agribusiness stakeholders, there was a need to increase investment in cold storage, aggregation centres and logistics infrastructure to reduce post-harvest losses and limit sharp seasonal increases in food prices.

They said Nigeria needed a coordinated cold chain that could preserve perishable produce after harvest and move it to markets when needed, rather than allowing large quantities of food to be lost while consumers faced high prices.

Speaking at a recent event in Lagos, the Managing Director of Mystrose Agro Commodities Limited and Novachill, Mr. Babatunde Niran-Aluko, said Nigeria faced a major gap in long-term storage for perishable produce.

According to him, this opportunity should attract private investment.

He added that cold-chain logistics were equally important because produce could still be lost after leaving an aggregation centre.

Founder of Century 21 Foundation, Princess Kemdi Chika-Okafor, advocated decentralised cold-storage facilities located near aggregation centres and markets, rather than concentrating investment in large warehouses.

She said solar-powered storage hubs could allow farmers and traders to pay for the space they used, making the facilities more accessible to small-scale operators.

She added that partnerships with non-governmental organisations and public institutions could help private operators access cheaper financing and keep services affordable.

Other stakeholders said costs beyond the farm gate were also contributing to high food prices.

Founder and Chief Executive Officer of City Distro, Olamide Olabisi, said multiple levies imposed during the transportation of goods increased distribution costs, ultimately affecting prices paid by consumers.

Olabisi said moving commodities from the North to the South in trucks meant having to settle touts in each local government area before the goods finally reached Lagos State.

He called for better enforcement of a uniform levy system to reduce the burden on traders and distributors. Olabisi also identified farmer-herder clashes and inadequate irrigation as challenges affecting production.

Vanguard News

World.title: Petrol Supply Crashes 23% as Imports Drop 30%, Local Receipts Fall 21%
World.content:
• Dangote refinery hits 106% production capacity in September

•Nigeria supplies 80.4% of feedstock intake by local facilities

• Indigenous refiners get 618,000 bpd oil, down 9%

•Diesel supply slumps to lowest level in 13 months

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja





Nigeria’s daily petrol supply fell 23 per cent in September despite the Dangote Petroleum Refinery operating above its installed capacity, as declining domestic deliveries and imports coincided with higher petrol prices, which exceeded N1,400 per litre in some cities.

The September 2026 factsheet of the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) released yesterday showed that total petrol receipts dropped from 50.5 million litres per day in August to 38.7 million litres, although consumption rose 7 per cent to 44.4 million litres daily.

Besides, local petrol receipts declined 21 per cent, from 35.9 million litres to 28.5 million litres per day, while imports fell 30 per cent, from 14.6 million litres to 10.2 million litres.

The figures mean that the Nigerian market received 11.8 million fewer litres of petrol daily in September than in August. The decline occurred despite a 13 per cent increase in petrol production at the Dangote refinery, which raised its average daily output from 41.94 million litres in August to 47.22 million litres in September.

The refinery’s average capacity utilisation also rose from 105.21 per cent to 105.98 per cent, above its installed capacity of 650,000 barrels per day. Yet, the volume of petrol it supplied to the domestic market fell by about a fifth, while exports increased.

According to the document, Dangote supplied an average of 28.5 million litres of petrol daily to the domestic market in September, compared with 10.2 million litres from imports. Its recorded domestic deliveries were therefore almost 2.8 times the volume of imported petrol.

Also, in August, domestic deliveries from the refinery stood at 35.87 million litres per day, against imports of 14.6 million litres. Although local refining remained the dominant source, its share of total petrol receipts rose from 71 per cent in August to about 74 per cent in September because imports declined more sharply.

The refinery exported 15.47 million litres of petrol daily in September, up 59 per cent from 9.73 million litres in August. It also added 3.25 million litres per day to its petrol stocks, closing the month with 366.2 million litres, compared with 360.4 million litres at the end of August.

The figures showed that higher production did not translate into increased domestic deliveries. While output increased, local supplies fell as exports rose and stocks accumulated.

The fall in market receipts came amid high fuel retail prices. The NMDPRA’s indicative petrol price stood at N1,371.01 per litre in Lagos, N1,420.01 in Abuja, N1,447.75 in Kano and N1,464.75 in Maiduguri. The highest actual price recorded in the surveyed centres was N1,445 per litre in Abuja, while the lowest was N1,293.75 in Lagos.

Beyond finished products, the report showed that domestic refineries received an average of 618,000 barrels of crude oil daily in September, down 9 per cent from 681,000 barrels per day in August.

Nevertheless, Dangote processed an estimated 689,000 barrels daily, about 71,000 barrels above the volume received during the month. The regulator explained that the refinery made up the difference by drawing on its crude inventory. Its reported utilisation above 100 per cent therefore did not mean it received more crude in September.

Similarly, the authority’s nine-month data showed that local refineries received 156.51 million barrels of crude between January and September. Of this, 125.85 million barrels were sourced domestically and 30.66 million barrels imported, meaning Nigerian crude accounted for 80.4 per cent of the total intake, while imported crude represented 19.6 per cent.

The supply squeeze was more pronounced in the diesel market, where daily receipts fell 40 per cent, from 14.5 million litres in August to 8.7 million litres in September, the lowest level in the 13 months covered by the regulator’s data.

According to the factsheet, domestic diesel receipts dropped 39 per cent, from 13.2 million litres to 8.1 million litres daily, while imports fell 54 per cent, from 1.3 million litres to 600,000 litres, although consumption edged up from 14.3 million litres to 14.5 million litres per day.

Dangote’s diesel production, however, increased 35 per cent to 24.32 million litres per day. Domestic deliveries fell from 12.37 million litres in August to 8.14 million litres in September, while exports rose 82 per cent, from 8.75 million litres to 15.91 million litres daily. The refinery ended September with 232.5 million litres of diesel in stock, against 137.2 million litres a month earlier.

The NMDPRA report showed that among modular refineries, Walter Smith operated at 62.25 per cent capacity utilisation, Edo at 104.24 per cent, Aradel at 31.90 per cent and OPAC at 18.43 per cent, while Duport was shut down. Their combined diesel supply was 620,000 litres per day, equivalent to 4.3 per cent of national consumption.

Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) commonly known as cooking gas, recorded a more favourable trend. Daily receipts rose 9 per cent to 4.7 kilotonnes in September, with domestic supply increasing 50 per cent to 4.5 kilotonnes and imports falling 85 per cent to 0.2 kilotonnes.

In the same vein, domestic sources accounted for about 96 per cent of receipts, although consumption rose 8 per cent to 5.2 kilotonnes daily.

In the gas sector, total average daily supply, including volumes supplied to Nigeria LNG Limited, declined 2.2 per cent to 4.822 billion cubic feet in September. Domestic gas supply fell 6.7 per cent to 2.066 billion cubic feet daily, while supply to NLNG rose 1.5 per cent to 2.756 bcf.

World.title: Oil Firms Decry Long Tender Cycles Delaying Upstream Projects Despite Tinubu’s Directives
World.content:
• PETAN flags double-digit bank rates, 90-day payment delays stifling capacity

Peter Uzoho





Indigenous oil and gas service companies have raised alarm over long tender approval cycles and delayed payments by upstream producers, a situation that negates President Bola Tinubu’s Presidential Directives on Local Content introduced in March 2024.

Service providers under the aegis of Petroleum Technology Association of Nigeria (PETAN) also complained that high bank interest rates was hurting them, warning that the bottlenecks are stifling local capacity and slowing Nigeria’s upstream growth.

They raised the concerns in Lagos at the Nigerian Association of Petroleum Explorationists, (NAPE) Pre-Conference Workshop themed “Navigating Nigeria’s Upstream Future: Exploration and Development Approaches vs. Energy Security Demand.”

Publicity Secretary of PETAN, Dr Joan Faluyi, who spoke on execution capacity of her members, said the blames that Nigerian service providers lack capacity ignore the financial and procurement realities they face.

Faluyi said the biggest problem was cycle time, with tender approval, award and mobilisation taking years to materialise, distorting pricing and execution.

Curiously, the 2024 presidential directive is meant to accelerate oil and gas contract timelines, fast–track tendering process and approvals, incentivize investments in the sector and increase Nigeria’s crude oil production, bringing to question the implementation of the policy by the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB).

Faluyi flagged procurement issues, long lead times, budget constraints and hostile financing environment where local banks lend at double-digit rates even for one year on a five-year project, while producers demand delivery at thin margins.

She cited instances where a tender quoted four years ago becomes unexecutable due to foreign exchange shifts, price changes and geopolitical events, including situations where global shocks alter costs before mobilisation.

“Our banks’ interest rates is double digit. You have a project that is five years, and they’re willing to finance one year. And these producers want you to deliver whatever service at a very small margin,” Faluyi said.

“Some of them even specify your margin and say, you have to make nine percent. Someone that is producing or delivering a rig, it takes him so long to get that rig into the country? His bank is already counting. Then it takes him to mobilise, the bank is counting. Then it now takes him another 90 days in which these producers are saying they’re going to pay you whatever money they’re owing. At the end of the day, where is the profit?”

She said the squeeze leaves service firms without ability to deliver, yet they are labelled as lacking capacity.

She called for faster bid processing and alignment of finance and timing, noting that the same companies secure jobs outside Africa with short cycles and produce immediately.

She said all members of the association share the same complaint that finance and timing must be aligned for effective production.

NCDMB did not respond to the claims as its General Manager, Corporate Communications, Dr Obinna Ezeobi promised to get back to THISDAY but never did as of the time of filing this report.

However, in his contribution to the discourse, Chairman of Energia Limited, Mr George Osahon, said the oil industry cannot work without service providers who hold the technology, recalling that Shell’s operating model discourages operators from owning rigs to avoid conflict of interest and inefficiency.

Osahon said operators also face pressure to ensure contractors have capability and wherewithal to avoid debt and production losses, citing cases where a 25 to 30-day well takes 60 days, compared to the past when ExxonMobil drilled development wells in 10 days.

He attributed part of the drop in performance to declining competencies across the industry, loss of training grounds like Shell’s Intership Training Programme (SITP) that previously built industry-wide skills, and dwindling industry-wide capacity building efforts.

He also admitted that service providers bear the brunt of industry downturns, as when crude crashed to $10 per barrel, operators under financial pressure delayed payments due to non-performing loans, not out of wickedness, but due to the rollercoaster nature of the business.

He noted the situation is now improving with rig count doubling in the last two years.

On regulation, Osahon said regulators cannot monitor enough, contrasting Nigeria’s war room with Saudi Aramco’s real-time drilling control rooms where drill bits are steered remotely, saying Nigeria still has gaps to close.

Delivering the keynote on behalf of Managing Director of Renaissance Africa Energy Company Limited, Tony Attah, Vice President Exploration, Dr Johnbosco Uche, said energy security is not defined by resources underground but by value created above ground.

He said Nigeria must sustain a continuous cycle of discovery, development and production, stressing that exploration is an act of belief in the future that replenishes reserves, while development and production solve today’s needs.

According to him, Renaissance now views itself as an energy security company, with philosophy to safely receive, stabilize and grow assets, leveraging Infrastructure-Led Exploration and Near-Field Exploration to reduce time from prospect to production.

“Pace matters. A resource that arrives too late cannot solve today’s energy challenge,” Uche said, adding that gas remains Nigeria’s most powerful tool for industrialisation and transformation, while people and innovation, not just technology, will determine success”, Uche said. .

World.title: $242m Petroleum Dispute: Court Grants UBA Interim Order Against Vitol, Four Shipping Firms
World.content:
Wale Igbintade





The Lagos State High Court has granted interim preservative orders of Mareva injunction in favour of United Bank for Africa (UBA) Plc against Vitol SA, a Switzerland-based energy trading company, and four other shipping companies over a petroleum products diversion dispute involving $242 million.

UBA alleged that Vitol wrongfully released cargoes of petroleum products consigned to the bank’s order under the relevant bills of lading.

Addressing the court, Bode Olanipekun, SAN, lead counsel to UBA, urged the judge to grant the interim preservative orders against Vitol and the other shipping companies.

In her ruling, Justice K. A. Jose granted three prayers in UBA’s application, including requests to restrain the dissipation of assets and dealings in funds up to the disputed amount by Vitol SA.

“Prayers 1-3 are granted as prayed against the second respondent only,” the judge ruled.

The application was brought pursuant to Order 43, Rule 1 of the High Court of Lagos State (Civil Procedure) Rules 2019 and Lagos State High Court Practice Direction No. 2 of 2019.

In the substantive proceedings, UBA intends to contend that Vitol SA and the owners of the vessels are liable for alleged conversion, misrepresentation, and negligence arising from the non-delivery of the petroleum products.

The bank also cited 34 financial institutions and public agencies, including commercial banks, merchant banks, microfinance banks, Nigerian Ports Authority, and Nigeria Customs Service, in connection with the application.

In an affidavit supporting the application, UBA’s Group Head of Recoveries and Remedial Management, Anthony Chilaka, stated that the bank had issued a letter of credit in favour of Vitol SA to facilitate a petroleum products transaction.

According to the affidavit, the cargo was transported to Nigeria, where the masters of the vessels issued several bills of lading.

UBA further alleged that Vitol subsequently endorsed the bills of lading in favour of the bank and handed over the original copies to it.

The bank maintained that the endorsement entitled it to take possession of the cargo upon completion of the voyage.

However, Chilaka stated that UBA had not received the gasoil, despite the completion of the voyage.

“The applicant has not been given possession of the gasoil despite completion of the voyage,” the affidavit stated.

UBA alleged that the cargo was, instead, diverted for the benefit of another party, arguing that the failure to deliver the petroleum products amount to conversion and negligence.

The bank further contended that the respondents had obligations arising from the transaction and the endorsement of the shipping documents, but failed to fulfil them.

It alleged that cargoes associated with the transactions were diverted to other parties after the completion of their voyages rather than being delivered to UBA.

World.title: BOI Targets N1.35trn Loan Disbursement in 2027, Eyes 10-year Long Term Financing for Manufacturers, MSMEs
World.content:
• Attained N645bn disbursement in 2025, funded 25% of manufacturing GDP, 6.5% agriculture lending

Dike Onwuamaeze





Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Bank of Industry (BOI), Dr. Olasupo Olusi, has announced that the bank is targeting an annual loan disbursement of N1.35 trillion to manufacturers and operators in the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in 2027.

Olusi also said the bank was exploring various sources of capital that would enable it to grant real long-term loans of about 10-year tenure to manufacturers and other businesses. He stated these yesterday during the “MD/CEO BOI Meeting with Media Partners.”

He said the bank disbursed N645 billion in 2025, which was the highest disbursement it had ever achieved.

He also elaborated on BOI’s 2025-2027 corporate strategy that was being executed in three phases.

Olusi said 2025 was “our foundation year, where we put in place the governance, the frameworks, the products and digital tools, while 2026 was the year of execution and scale, and 2027 will be the year we consolidate our results and meet our targets.

He said the bank was currently at the mid-point of the strategy implementation, adding that the results so far tell that the strategy is working.

He said BOI accounted for 6.5 per cent agricultural loans and 25 per cent of the manufacturing GDP.

Olusi stated, “The results so far tell us that the strategy is working. In 2025, we disbursed N645 billion, which is the highest ever disbursement by the bank. This represents a 26 per cent increase on N510 billion we disbursed in 2024.

“And our financing has reached 12,500 more businesses and helped to create or support 1.6 million jobs.

“We disbursed over N120 billion to women-owned businesses, which again shows how much we are committed to delivering on our strategy to enhance opportunities for gender.

“We are also on track across our thematic areas. MSMEs received over 41 per cent of our 2025 funding, even against our 35 per cent target. “Youths and women received 20 per cent each against our 15 per cent and 10 per cent minimum commitment, respectively.

Olusi explained, “In infrastructure, we recorded N108 billion funding, including 100 mini-grids to power businesses and households, as well as broadband internet connectivity to over 700 communities.

“We also achieved our disbursement targets for climate and social financing.”

He stated that the bank embarked on a number of landmark capital raising activities that enabled it to deliver its disbursement targets.

The capital raising activities included a landmark deal of nearly €2 billion (Euros), raised from three international banks, and in 2026, BOI was able to get five commitments from the African Export and Import Bank for a €75 million facility to support the Pharmaceutical Value Chain (PIVAC) in Nigeria.

He stated, “Together, we have done more than €2.2 billion and N274 billion in new funding for Nigerian industries.

“Investors have placed their money with us because they trust our governance, our pipeline, our impact and our financial results.

“We are already advancing new capital raising engagements with quite a number of international partners, including the likes of the African Development Bank, the Agence Française de Dévelopment and also pursuing further fundraising opportunities that are available within our domestic capital markets.

“We have also expanded our financing toolkits with a non-interest banking products, which will enable us to promote financial inclusion and widen the range of financing structures available for eligible businesses who have interests in non-interest banking.”

The CEO recounted that in the course of the last couple of years, the bank had managed the federal government’s N200 billion grants and loans intervention programme to the enterprise sector.

He said the N75 billion MSME intervention funds and N75 billion manufacturing sector funds that were disbursed by BOI had delivered results.

Olusi said, “We delivered more than 85 per cent of all these funds, reaching 957,400 grant beneficiaries, 9,000 MSMEs, and 104 large manufacturers across the country.

“Through our Rural Area Program Investment for Development (RAPID) program, we have disbursed over N6.5 billion to nearly 1,000 rural enterprises across all 36 states and FCT of the country, supporting more than 8,000 jobs.

“We have financed more than 100 mini-grids that have connected 11,000 households and businesses to electricity, many of them for the first time.”

According to him, BOI’s strategy is dedicated to raising long term capital at a scale that would match Nigeria’s unending industrialisation needs, widening its reach to underserved segments of the economy, particularly MSMEs, women, young people, and rural enterprises.

He said BOI’s target was to ensure that 35 per cent of its loans went to MSMEs, while lending to infrastructure and women-owned businesses accounted for 30 per cent and 15 per cent, respectively, of the bank’s loan book.

He added that the bank would allocate 10 per cent and 15 per cent of its credit to digital and climate enterprises, respectively, while youth-owned enterprises will command 20 per cent of credits to MSMEs.

Olusi stated, “Infrastructure remains a big pain on our economic development, so we have dedicated a large chunk of our finance, around 35 per cent for all of our large credits to finance infrastructure.

“Women owned businesses are one of the most underserved in Nigeria. So, we have decided that we will direct at least 15 per cent of our financing to them under our strategy.

“We have targeted 20 per cent of our MSMEs disbursement to youth owned businesses.”

He said, “We are providing about 10 per cent of our entire portfolio to climate and sustainability. We want to finance clean energy, climate resilience investments, and of course the circular economy.

“On the digital front, we are very committed also to financing technology-led businesses and digitisation of Nigerian enterprises by committing 15 per cent of our disbursement to the sector.”

World.title: Tinubu’s Reforms Addressing Fiscal Stability, Structural Weaknesses, Says Idris
World.content:
Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, has said President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms are aimed at addressing longstanding structural weaknesses in the economy, restoring fiscal stability, and creating a foundation for sustainable economic growth. Idris stated this in Abuja when National Convener of Women of Influence for Tinubu 2027, Hauwa Farouk Ibrahim, led a delegation of the organisation on a courtesy visit to Ministry of Information and National Orientation.

The minister described the removal of fuel subsidy and the unification of the foreign exchange rate as critical policy decisions intended to stabilise the economy, improve public finances, and reposition the country for long-term development.

He said the reforms were necessary to address persistent economic challenges and strengthen the capacity of the federal government, states, and local governments to finance infrastructure, essential services, and other development priorities.

He explained that the measures had increased the resources available to the three tiers of government, creating opportunities for greater investment in projects and programmes that directly affect the lives of Nigerians.

Idris acknowledged that the reforms had required difficult adjustments, but maintained their long-term objectives were to strengthen the country’s economic foundations and improve prospects for future generations.

He stated, “It is very, very easy and convenient to forget where we are coming from. These were difficult decisions, but they were taken in the interest of our country and the prosperity of future generations.”

The minister urged members of Women of Influence for Tinubu 2027 to intensify public enlightenment at the grassroots, particularly by explaining the rationale behind the administration’s policies, the economic circumstances that necessitated them, and the opportunities they were intended to create.

He stressed that effective public engagement was essential to improving citizens’ understanding of government policies and fostering constructive dialogue around the country’s economic reform programme.

Idris added, “We want you to, please, influence other Nigerians so that they can understand the policies of this administration and support government as it continues its drive towards repositioning our country.”

He reaffirmed the ministry’s commitment to sustained public enlightenment and engagement with organisations working to improve citizens’ understanding of government programmes and policies.

Idris also welcomed the organisation’s interest in collaborating with the ministry, accepted its request to serve as patron, and pledged to designate a focal person to facilitate continued engagement.

Earlier, Ibrahim said the organisation was established to harness the influence and mobilisation capacity of Nigerian women to promote national development and build grassroots support for President Tinubu’s administration.

She disclosed that the group had commenced activities in Kano State and was expanding its reach through digital platforms and community-based initiatives aimed at engaging women and other citizens across the country.

Ibrahim expressed the organisation’s readiness to work with the ministry in strengthening public enlightenment and engagement on government policies and programmes.

World.title: Nigeria’s $337bn Climate Plan Faces Funding Test as FG Inaugurates Steering Committee
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja





Nigeria’s ambition of cutting emissions by 32 per cent by 2035 and achieving net-zero emissions by 2060 will require an estimated $337 billion over the next decade, putting pressure on the federal government to mobilise investment and translate climate commitments into measurable results.

To address the challenge, the government on Thursday inaugurated an inter-ministerial steering committee to coordinate the implementation of the country’s Nationally Determined Contribution 3.0 (NDC 3.0), Net-Zero Investment Plan, and Long-Term Low-Emissions Development Strategy.

Director-General of National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Mrs. Tenioye Majekodunmi, said the financing requirement for 2026 to 2035 comprised approximately $195 billion for emissions mitigation and $141.5 billion for adaptation.

Majekodunmi said the investments could create jobs and strengthen economic resilience, particularly in energy, agriculture, infrastructure, and other key sectors.

She said the immediate priority was to develop credible investment pipelines, deploy public and concessional finance strategically, attract domestic and international private capital, and establish the policy certainty required to encourage investors.

She explained that the steering committee would provide high-level coordination, integrate climate priorities into national planning and budgeting, and resolve implementation bottlenecks that individual ministries could not address independently.

According to her, the committee’s effectiveness should be measured by the barriers it removes, the investments it unlocks, and the results it delivers, rather than the number of meetings it holds.

The committee is expected to bring together relevant ministries and institutions responsible for finance, energy, agriculture, transportation, industry, and other sectors critical to achieving Nigeria’s climate objectives.

NCCC will provide technical secretariat support, including coordination, analysis, implementation tracking and engagement with development partners.

In a keynote address, Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Senator George Akume, said climate commitments must translate into measurable benefits for Nigerians, urging ministries, departments and agencies to integrate climate considerations into their policies, budgets, and investment decisions.

Akume, who was represented by Professor Babatunde Bernard, a Nigerian scientist, environmental scholar, and Technical Adviser to the SGF, said the country must move beyond policy announcements to tangible results.

“We must, therefore, judge success by implementation, not announcements; by measurable outcomes, not intentions; and by the benefits delivered to our citizens, not documents produced,” he said.

The SGF said climate change could no longer be treated as the exclusive responsibility of the environmental sector because of its implications for food security, infrastructure, public health, water resources, coastal communities, and livelihoods.

He urged state governments and the Federal Capital Territory Administration to incorporate climate priorities into agriculture, transportation, urban development, waste management, infrastructure and community resilience.

He added that Nigeria’s transition to a low-emissions economy must reflect its development needs, including expanding access to affordable and reliable energy, creating jobs, strengthening industrial capacity, and protecting vulnerable communities.

Meanwhile, United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) identified inadequate project preparation as a major obstacle to attracting private investment into Nigeria’s climate initiatives.

UNDP Resident Representative in Nigeria, Ms. Elsie Attafuah, said many potentially viable private-sector projects remained unfunded because they lacked adequate feasibility studies, credible business models, clear delivery arrangements, or appropriate financing instruments.

Attafuah said projects needed to meet those requirements to attract investors, particularly where they offered substantial public benefits but could not generate sufficient commercial returns on their own.

She stated that reliable clean energy could help businesses improve production, while climate-smart agriculture could protect farmers’ incomes, strengthen food security and improve resilience to extreme weather.

She also emphasised the need for transparent carbon-market systems, credible emissions measurement and reporting, and a reliable national carbon registry to strengthen accountability and investor confidence.

Support for developing the registry was cited as part of efforts to track climate-related transactions and verify results.

The UNDP representative stressed that climate projects must respond to local needs and involve the communities affected by them.

Women, young people, farmers, and other affected groups, she said, should participate from the outset, particularly where changes in technology, land use, or employment could affect livelihoods and access to economic opportunities.

State governments were also identified as essential to implementation because decisions on land, infrastructure and public services directly influence climate resilience.

The NCCC’s engagement with states is intended to connect their development priorities with technical assistance and practical investment programmes.

Nigeria’s NDC 3.0 outlines mitigation measures across energy, industry, agriculture, forestry and land use, waste and other sectors.

Its adaptation priorities include food systems, water, health, coastal and urban areas, and disaster-risk management.

The federal government has also launched the Net-Zero Investment Plan and the Long-Term Low-Emissions Development Strategy to align immediate climate commitments with the country’s long-term economic transformation.

The launch comes weeks before the global climate community gathers in Antalya, Türkiye, for COP31, offering Nigeria an opportunity to pursue partnerships around its national priorities.

The immediate test, however, will be whether the new committee can translate the country’s climate targets into costed programmes, develop investment-ready projects, and secure the resources needed to implement them.

Ultimately, the success of NDC 3.0 will depend on whether climate action reduces emissions while improving energy access, protecting livelihoods, creating jobs, and strengthening resilience across the country.

World.title: Oyetola Inaugurates NIMBEX Committee, Eyes Maritime Investment Boom
World.content:
Kasim Sumaina in Abuja





Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, on Wednesday inaugurated a committee to organise the Nigeria Marine and Blue Economy Expo (NIMBEX), in a strategic move to position Nigeria as a leading destination for maritime investment, innovation, and trade in Africa.

The expo is expected to bring together policymakers, international investors, industry leaders, and technology innovators to support the federal government’s efforts to unlock the vast economic potential of Nigeria’s marine and blue economy.

Oyetola said the initiative would provide a platform to translate the country’s maritime advantages into tangible investment opportunities, economic growth, and job creation.

He stated that Nigeria’s marine and blue economy held enormous potential to drive economic diversification, attract investment, and create sustainable employment. NIMBEX, according to him, will provide a strategic platform to bring together the capital, expertise, and partnerships needed to unlock these opportunities.

Oyetola, who was represented at the inauguration by Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy, Mrs Fatima Mahmood, said the expo would help bridge the gap between Nigeria’s vast maritime resources and the investments required to harness them for national development.

The minister, in a statement issued by his Special Adviser, Bolaji Akinola, said, “With an 853-kilometre coastline, more than 10,000 kilometres of navigable inland waterways spanning 28 states, and a substantial domestic market, Nigeria possesses significant assets to strengthen its position in regional and international maritime trade.”

The NIMBEX Organising Committee is chaired by Mr. Husseini Shettima, Director of Marine Conservation, Innovation and Technology at the Federal Ministry of Marine and Blue Economy.

Hajia Kalthum Ibrahim, Director of Planning, Research and Statistics in the ministry, and Professor Busayo Fakinlede, Senior Special Assistant to President Bola Tinubu on Marine and Blue Economy, will serve as co-chairpersons.

The minister’s Special Adviser, Dr. Bolaji Akinola, will serve as a member of the committee and Chief Operating Officer of the expo.

Other members include representatives of the ministry’s technical departments and key agencies and institutions across the maritime sector, including Nigerian Ports Authority, Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency, Nigerian Ports Economic Regulatory Agency, National Inland Waterways Authority, and Council for the Regulation of Freight Forwarding in Nigeria.

Equally represented are Maritime Academy of Nigeria, Oron; Nigerian Institute for Oceanography and Marine Research; Federal College of Fisheries and Marine Technology; National Institute for Freshwater Fisheries Research, New Bussa; and Federal College of Freshwater Fisheries Technology in New Bussa and Baga.

The committee also includes representatives of coastal states, terminal operators, shipowners, freight forwarders, barge operators, and other stakeholders in the maritime industry.

The multi-agency composition is intended to promote coordinated planning and execution while connecting investors with credible, policy-backed opportunities across the sector.

NIMBEX will focus on key areas, such as deep-sea mining, port development, shipping development, inland waterway development, logistics, offshore energy, maritime finance, fisheries, marine biotechnology, maritime security, and environmental sustainability.

The expo will also showcase emerging opportunities in marine renewable energy, green shipbuilding, artificial intelligence-driven logistics, subsea robotics, and coastal tourism.

Beyond showcasing investment prospects, NIMBEX aims to foster collaboration among government, industry, financial institutions, and technology stakeholders while promoting sustainable approaches to harnessing Nigeria’s marine resources.

World.title: Tinubu: We’ll Use Nigeria’s Gas Resources to Create Jobs and Boost Export Earnings
World.content:
• As local firm builds compressor stations to unlock Escravos-Lagos pipeline’s 2.3bn cubic feet daily gas capacity

Deji Elumoye in Abuja





President Bola Ahmed Tinubu on Thursday reaffirmed his determination to unlock Nigeria’s gas resources to power industries, improve electricity supply, create jobs and boost export earnings.

He said this amid indigenous engineering firm, Lee Engineering’s achievement of building two compressor stations to enable the Escravos–Lagos Pipeline System to operate at its full capacity of 2.3 billion standard cubic feet of gas per day.

The President spoke while receiving the Founder and Chairman of Lee Engineering Group, Chief Dr Leemon Ikpea, at the State House, Abuja.

Tinubu reaffirmed his administration’s Nigeria First policy and urged international oil companies operating in the country to give competent Nigerian engineering and manufacturing firms greater opportunities to participate in major energy projects.

Lee Engineering is handling the Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) of two midline compressor stations in Edo State. Although the pipeline’s designed capacity was increased from 1.1 billion to 2.3 billion standard cubic feet of gas per day under the ELPS II expansion, the compressor stations are needed to raise operating pressure and enable the pipeline to deliver at its full capacity.

The project is expected to strengthen gas transportation to power plants and industries along that corridor, support increased gas supplies to neighbouring West African countries through the West African Gas Pipeline, and create opportunities for additional export revenue.

The President, who said Nigeria First must translate into more contracts for capable Nigerian firms, greater use of locally manufactured equipment and more skilled jobs for Nigerians, encouraged international oil companies to build stronger partnerships with indigenous engineering companies that have demonstrated the capacity to deliver complex projects.

He also pointed to his administration’s 2024 executive orders and presidential directives on local content compliance, contracting costs, and approval timelines as measures to attract investment, cut delays, and expand opportunities for Nigerian businesses.

Earlier, Ikpea commended the President’s Nigeria First policy and disclosed that Lee Engineering’s fabrication yard in Warri, Delta State, is manufacturing some components for the compressor stations and houses some of the most advanced fabrication equipment in the industry.

According to him, Nigerian companies have invested heavily in modern equipment, technology and skilled personnel and can now undertake complex EPC projects previously handled by foreign contractors, keeping more jobs, expertise and economic value within Nigeria.

World.title: New rules for motorists travelling between South Africa and Zimbabwe
World.content:
Motorists travelling between South Africa and Zimbabwe with foreign-registered vehicles face tighter checks after the Zimbabwe Revenue Authority (ZIMRA) strengthened controls on Temporary Import Permits (TIPs).

In Public Notice Number 60 of 2026, issued on Wednesday, 21 October, ZIMRA said the measures followed the abuse of the facility, which allows qualifying visitors to bring foreign-registered vehicles into Zimbabwe temporarily without paying the full import duty.

The measures are being implemented under the Customs and Excise Act (Chapter 23:02) and the Customs and Excise (General) Regulations, 2001.



Who qualifies for a temporary import permit?

ZIMRA said TIPs may be issued to bona fide visitors who ordinarily reside outside Zimbabwe and enter the country temporarily for tourism, business, study, employment, sporting activities or other lawful purposes.

Zimbabweans living abroad may qualify, provided they meet the relevant requirements.

Applicants must produce a valid passport and the original vehicle registration book.

Anyone driving a vehicle that is not registered in their name must provide a letter of authority or an affidavit.

Zimbabwean residents abroad must also present a work, employment, study or residence permit.

Non-owner-driven vehicles face extra checks

Under the enhanced measures, ZIMRA may subject certain applications to additional verification, particularly where the vehicle is being driven by someone other than its registered owner.



The move comes as the authority seeks to address the abuse of temporary import arrangements.

Motorists should ensure that their documentation is in order before travelling and should not assume that an affidavit or permission letter will automatically result in a permit being issued.

How long can motorists keep their vehicles in Zimbabwe?

ZIMRA said TIPs will ordinarily be issued for no more than 30 days.

Requests for longer stays will be considered individually, but the total period cannot exceed three months.

Applications for extensions must be submitted before the existing permit expires and supported by valid reasons and relevant documentation.

Permit holders must keep their vehicles under their control and cannot dispose of them in Zimbabwe without ZIMRA’s approval.

Vehicles must also be re-exported before the permit expires unless an extension has been granted. Permit holders should not leave Zimbabwe without their vehicles unless prior arrangements have been made with the nearest ZIMRA office.

What are the Vehicle charges at Beitbridge?

ZIMRA lists carbon tax of US$10 (about R165) and third-party insurance of US$30 (about R495) among the applicable charges.

Travellers using Beitbridge Border Post must also pay a US$9 bridge toll fee (about R149) and a US$28 Zimborders fee (about R462).

This brings the listed charges to US$77 (about R1,271), excluding any other applicable costs.

Motorists seeking clarification can contact ZIMRA through BeitbridgePrivateImports@zimra.co.zw or visit the nearest ZIMRA office.

World.title: Water warning to residents living in and around Mpumalanga
World.content:
The Department of Water and Sanitation has urged communities in Mpumalanga to use water sparingly as dam levels across the province continue to decline. Image: Wikimedia Commons

The Department of Water and Sanitation has urged communities in Mpumalanga to use water sparingly as dam levels across the province continue to decline.

According to the department’s latest weekly state of reservoirs report, the provincial average dam level decreased from 98.7% to 98.3%, with all but three dams recording declines over the past week.

Conservation efforts

The three dams that recorded no change are located in the Lowveld region of the Ehlanzeni District. These include Longmere, which is at 101.6%, Klipkopjes at 100.4%, and Primkop at 101.7%.



The department has called for strengthened water conservation efforts and to prevent water wastage amid declining dam levels and concerns about the potential impact of a Super El Niño weather phenomenon.

The Limpopo-Olifants Water Management Area (WMA) declined from 99.8% to 99.1%, while the Inkomati-Usuthu WMA decreased from 97.8% to 97.5%.

At district level, Ehlanzeni’s average dam levels dropped from 99.9% to 99.6%, Gert Sibande from 97.5% to 97.2%, and Nkangala from 99.6% to 99.0%.



Decreases

“The listed dams that recorded declines in water levels include Kwena Dam from 99.8% to 99.2%, Witklip Dam from 100.4% to 100.3%, Da Gama Dam from 99.8% to 99.3%, Driekoppies Dam from 100.4% to 100.2%, Inyaka Dam from 100.1% to 99.7%, Blyderivierpoort Dam from 100.2% to 100.1%, Buffelskloof Dam from 100.3% to 100.2%, and Ohrigstad Dam from 88.6% to 87.5%,” the department said.

All listed dams in Gert Sibande also recorded decreases. Grootdraai Dam declined from 100.6% to 100.4%, Nooitgedacht Dam from 99.2% to 98.6%, Vygeboom Dam from 100.4% to 100.3%, and Jericho Dam from 91.7% to 90.5%.

Westoe Dam dropped from 52.5% to 51.9%, Morgenstond Dam from 100.3% to 99.9%, and Heyshope Dam from 100.4% to 100.3%.



The report also indicated a decline in dam levels across the Nkangala District, with all listed dams recording decreases.

Witbank Dam declined from 99.2% to 98.4%, Middelburg Dam from 94.6% to 94.2%, Loskop Dam from 100.2% to 99.5%, and Rhenosterkop/Mkhombo Dam from 100.0% to 99.5%.

Use water wisely

The department urged water users to use water wisely and prevent wastage by fixing leaking taps and pipes. Communities are also encouraged to report leaks in bulk water pipelines and incidents of infrastructure vandalism to the relevant institutions and authorities.



The department reiterated that South Africa is a water-scarce country, requiring responsible and efficient water use by households, businesses and other water users.

“Every drop counts as water has no substitute,” the department said.

World.title: Orlando Pirates latest news: Ncikazi, Sebelebele, Dlamini, R100 million
World.content:
Orlando Pirates will be eyeing a spot in the CAF Champions League group stages when they host African Stars at the Orlando Amstel Arena on Friday evening.

The Buccaneers won the first leg 1-0 away from home and just need to avoid defeat to reach the group stages for the fourth time in the last two decades.

Pirates last won the competition in 1995 and will look to go all the way to earn their second title and claim the R100 million prize money.



Ahead of the CAF clash with African Warriors, Abdeslam Ouaddou could give Kabelo Dlamini a rare appearance. The 30-year-old has hardly played under the Moroccan coach.

Kamogelo Sebelebele, who suffered an injury against Mamelodi Sundowns earlier this year, might miss the match. He is training with the team but Ouaddou might not want to risk him ahead of the Soweto Derby.

Orlando Pirates lose coach

On Thursday, Pirates announced that head coach Mandla Ncikazi will be leaving the club.

The move follows discussions with management this morning in which Ncikazi expressed his wish to pursue the opportunity to lead a team again.

Ncikazi departs with 9 trophies earned as part of the Orlando Pirates technical team, where he served predominantly as assistant coach, including a brief spell as co-coach in 2025.

Following his departure, he was announced as the new head coach of Golden Arrows.



The Buccaneers won a treble last season, but their main goal this campaign is to win the CAF Champions League.

Will Pirates win the Champions League?

World.title: Relebohile Mofokeng produces an 8 out of 10 Europa League performance
World.content:
The 21-year-old Mofokeng earned an impressive 8.0/10 match rating against Hapoel Be’er Sheva.

Mofokeng was the fourth-highest ranked performer on the pitch before his 79th minute substitution. Using his technical quality, intelligence and vision, Mofokeng created numerous opportunities for his teammates.

RELEBOHILE MOFOKENG SHINES IN THE EUROPA LEAGUE

The former School of Excellence star enjoyed 53 touches and provided an assist in the 4-0 win.



He completed 34 of his 40 passes, achieving an 85% passing accuracy. His accuracy in the final third stood at 86%, while he completed all his attempted long passes.

Mofokeng laid five key passes, three accurate passes into the penalty area and two progressive passes. He managed six touches inside the opposition penalty area.

Union have now made a firm statement of intent in the UEFA Europa League after an impressive start to the league phase. The Belgian champions are placed in sixth position. They lead the likes of Juventus and AC Milan.



The 4-0 victory over Hapoel Be’er Sheva has boosted the push for automatic qualification to the last 16.

Union SG had also shown their resilience by holding Real Sociedad to a 1-1 draw. Those results have given the Brussels-based club a strong platform to challenge for a place among the top eight and avoid the knockout play-off round.

With their next Europa League fixture against Spanish side RC Celta de Vigo scheduled for 5 November, Union SG will look to maintain their momentum and strengthen their position in the standings.



BRIGHT START IN BELGIUM

Since joining from Orlando Pirates in August, Mofokeng has four goals and three assists in 13 games.

Coming up next is a meet up with Cercle Brugge in the Belgian Pro League. Mofokeng will be facing his compatriot Luke Le Roux in Cercle’s midfield.

The game is set for Sunday 25 October at 20:00 at the Stade Joseph Marien.

World.title: Australia face selection headaches after ‘shambolic’ Proteas loss
World.content:
Australia captain Pat Cummins admits it is hard to "paper over the cracks" after a thumping second Test defeat to South Africa. Image: MARCO LONGARI / AFP

Australia captain Pat Cummins admits it is hard to “paper over the cracks” after a thumping second Test defeat to South Africa, with the fate of at least three players hanging in the balance.

The visitors crashed by an innings and 31 runs at St George’s Park in Gqeberha on Thursday to leave the three-Test series finely poised at 1-1 heading into the decider at Cape Town next week.

few highlights

Australia collapsed to 99 all out in their first innings and were then dismissed for 295, with a superb 121 from Travis Head and defiant 40 off 166 balls by nightwatchman Scott Boland the only highlights.



The manner of the heavy loss did not go down well in Australia, with headlines ranging from “horror show” to “shambolic Aussies” and “brutal failures laid bare”.

“Clearly need to be a lot better than that if we want to compete,” Cummins said.

“I think a loss can sometimes kick you into gear. You can maybe paper over the cracks sometimes in a win. Whereas I think in a loss, it makes you ask questions as a player of yourself.”



Question marks

Heading into the third Test, there are question marks around at least three Australia players, not least the underperforming Marnus Labuschagne who has gone three years without a Test century.

“He’s actually doing the hard bit, he’s getting to 30,” Cummins said of number three Labuschagne.

“I think he’s got to find a way to turn those into bigger scores – 30s aren’t going to win you many matches.



“So, again, we’ll work on that in the next couple of days. It’s one Test match left in the series, we’ve got to win this.”

Recently-recalled opener Nic Maddinson is also on shaky ground after scores of 0, 48, 0 and 8 across the first two Tests, while all-rounder Beau Webster appears vulnerable.

Cameron Green is expected to be available for Cape Town after injury sidelined him from the first two Tests while Josh Inglis is also fit. Cooper Connolly is another option.



Hard to drop

Paceman Boland, who came into the side at Gqeberha at the expense of spinner Nathan Lyon, will be hard to drop given his batting exploits and a five-wicket haul in the first innings.

Much will depend on the nature of the Cape Town pitch on whether Australia again opt for four seamers or Lyon is brought back.

Cummins admitted some hard decisions would have to be made.



“That’s the challenge. Do you give someone one more game, or do you feel like now is the right time to make a move?” he said.

“Does it feel like someone’s just about to turn the corner, and they’re going to be away, or does it now feel like the right time for a change-up?”

By Garrin Lambley © Agence France-Presse

World.title: Donald Trump lashes out at LeBron James over national anthem actions
World.content:
Donald Trump lashed out at NBA superstar LeBron James for what he called disrespectful behaviour during the playing of the national anthem. Image: Wikimedia Commons

US President Donald Trump lashed out at NBA superstar LeBron James on Thursday for what he called disrespectful behaviour during the playing of the national anthem.

Trump posted a video of the basketball legend doing apparent warm-up movements while lined up with his Philadelphia 76ers team-mates before their season opener against the New York Knicks on Tuesday.

‘Total disgrace’

“While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country! I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE,” Donald Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.



“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!” he wrote.

The video used by Trump had an internal caption that read: “LeBron working on his golf swing pregame.” It showed him doing lateral swing motions and basketball shooting movements.

Donald Trump, speaking at a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday night, renewed the attack, calling James’s actions “a big scandal kind of a story.”



Trump and James have traded barbs before, and the NBA’s all-time leading scorer shrugged off the president’s latest criticism.

‘Slow news day’

“It must be a slow news day at the office,” he said after the Sixers completed an epic comeback to beat the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106 in Philadelphia.

“Slow news day at the office.”

James, 41, is entering a record-extending 24th NBA season with his fourth team.



Sixers coach Nick Nurse said Trump’s comments were the kind of distractions he was schooling his team to tune out.

“I think that goes right in with other outside noise we’ve already had,” Nurse said.

“I keep saying the same thing. All I really care about is getting to the practice floor, getting them in the film room, getting them to the game floor.



“The focus that they’ve had and the intent and all the stuff like that has been outstanding.”

Donald Trump has been critical of athletes before – particularly Black athletes – for their behaviour during the playing of the Star Spangled Banner before games.

During his first term, Trump singled out NFL star Colin Kaepernick for his decision to kneel during the “Star-Spangled Banner” to protest at racial injustice and police brutality.



By Garrin Lambley © Agence France-Presse

World.title: South African author defends use of AI: 370 books in 20 months
World.content:
South African writer Coral Hart has published more than 370 books since February 2025 using artificial intelligence. Image: GIANLUIGI GUERCIA / AFP

South African writer Coral Hart has published more than 370 books since February 2025 using artificial intelligence, a process she passionately defends despite criticism and threats.

“Grifter”, “villain” – insults abound on social media to describe the author who, in her forties, has become the symbol of AI’s arrival in publishing.

Pseudonym

Coral Hart – a pseudonym she uses to protect her real name – told AFP in an interview she had received “tens of thousands” of hate messages and several death threats.



In this hostile environment, few authors using AI agree to speak publicly and show their faces.

“I chose to be the one to step up and say, these are conversations we need to start having,” Hart said.

“This is here… They’re not going to switch it off or unplug it because a bunch of authors said so.”



Before she started writing with AI around 20 months ago, Hart had been working in publishing for 14 years and written several dozen works without the technology.

It took her three months to familiarise herself with the various AI models and build a framework capable of producing a book.

Juggles between ChatGPT, Claude and Grok

Now she juggles between ChatGPT, which is “really good at dialogue, terrible at prose”; Claude, “really good story structure, terrible at sex drives”; and others like Grok, “completely unhinged” but good on “spicy scenes”.



“If you say, ChatGPT, write me a book, or, Claude, write me a book, you’re going to get a flaming dumpster fire of trash back because it doesn’t have anything (to work with),” Hart said.

The author defines the story concept, a style, details of the characters, and chapter outlines. And only then will her system generate the books.

Hart said when she started, “we could write one paragraph at a time. I usually took two or three prompts to do that.”



“I can now draft the whole book in one sequence.”

Since last year, AI models have “improved vastly”, Hart said. “The prose has improved. The syntax has improved. The sentence structure has improved.”

‘Books are selling’

The first draft of a book is generally not good, the writer said.



It is run through AI for “developmental edits” and then again “to fix any continuity issues, story issues, flat middles, character arcs that are incomplete, plot threads that have been dropped, people whose eye colour has changed.”

At the end of this process, a human proofreader reads through the text to fix any “AI tells that have slipped through” and do some rewriting. “And it’s usually ready to go.”

Although one of her novels made it into Amazon’s top 100 bestsellers, the vast majority of her 371 titles – many of them romance – are tailored to certain readers based on rigorous market research.



She has sold more than one million books, by her own estimate, in digital, print and audio formats, earning more than $1 million (R16.5 million) so far this year.

Ready to make it public

The South African now heads an operation that has trained several hundred people in her method and is preparing to launch software for AI authors called Authorythm.

As for her own production, she mentions her use of AI only when required by a sales platform.



“For the last 16 years, nobody’s asked me what my creative process was,” said Hart, who publishes under more than 10 other pen names.

Now, she was ready to make it public “for the right reasons”.

Regularly accused of contributing to “AI slop” – low‑quality AI-generated content in text, video, music, or images – Hart points to the ultimate yardstick: “Books are selling.”



“Readers don’t read rubbish books; they return them,” she said.

The writer has followed the debate around a novel by Haitian-Canadian Thelyson Orelien that was withdrawn from the shortlist for France’s Goncourt prize after accusations that he used AI, which his publisher confirmed on Wednesday.

Critics had praised the book and sales were strong before the controversy, she said, asking: “If you need an AI label to hate something, do you hate it, or do you hate AI?”



Would you buy and read a book knowing it was written using AI?

Let us know by clicking on the comment banner below …

By Garrin Lambley © Agence France-Presse

World.title: Godongwana kicks Basic Income Support down the road … Again
World.content:
Despite saying he would, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana did nothing to address Basic Income Support in his MTBPS this week. Image: File

The future of South Africa’s long-anticipate Basic Income Support grant was left unresolved this week. This is despite previous indication that the finer details would be addressed in the next ‘mini-budget.’ Instead, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana’s Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement (MTBPS) simply extended ‘temporary’ R370 SRD for another year.

However, is the minster kicking the Basic Income Support can down the road yet again only intensifying South Africa’s youth unemployment crisis? Latest Quarterly Labour Force figures (Q2 2026) show unemployment among young South Africans (15 to 34) rose to 47.4%, up 1.5 percentage points from the previous quarter. The number of unemployed young people increased by 264 000 to five million.

SILENCE ON BASIC INCOME SUPPORT

Against this backdrop, the future of the ‘temporary’ R370 SASSA SRD grant remains a critical question for millions of destitute South Africans. In his 2026 MTBPS address, Godongwana announced SRD’s extension for another year, to March 2028. The extension provides temporary continuity, but it does not resolve the policy uncertainty surrounding long-term income support.



Instead, Treasury emphasised linking SRD beneficiaries to employment, training and business opportunities. This is meant to take place through something called the MzansiXchange data platform. As well as alongside stronger beneficiary verification and review processes highlighted by the minister. But nothing else was shared on the aforementioned …

NATIONAL TREASURY STALLING

Will Basic Income Support even turn the tide on the youth unemployment crisis in South Africa? Image: File

However, the National Treasury’s reluctance to commit to permanent Basic Income Support is not new. Back in February, it insisted that the proposed policy needed to be properly costed before it could offer support. Moreover, the minister warned that a broader scheme could cost hundreds of billions, placing pressure on an already constrained fiscus.

Furthermore, other fiscal and legal challenges have become more immediate. Treasury awaits news on government’s appeal against a High Court ruling on SRD regulations. If the ruling is upheld, preliminary estimates suggest the annual cost could rise from about R36 billion to R74 billion. Specifically because it will bring millions more people into the system.



FUTURE OF BASIC INCOME SUPPORT LESS CLEAR

Whichever side of the fence you sit, it’s clear is that the Basic Income Support policy process has been extraordinarily slow. A revised costing was expected to go to Cabinet in March 2027, subject to Treasury support. However, the latest extension almost certainly buys government more time, with no firm transition timetable announced …

But what do you think? Should South Africa persist with Basic Income Support, even when it’s clear we cannot afford it? Please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: Police seek another suspect in alleged staged kidnapping case
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Police are pursuing another suspect in the case of 37-year-old Ntombifuthi Rumo, who is accused of staging her own kidnapping to extort money from her cousin.

Rumo and an alleged accomplice have appeared in court, facing charges of fraud, defeating the ends of justice and staging a crime scene.

“A lot of resources were put into investigating the kidnapping of the accused persons, and for us now to discover and alert that this kidnapping was staged it is really concerning," said NPA spokesperson Lumka Mahanjana.

Rumo was reported missing on 7 October. A man later allegedly used her cellphone to demand R40,000 for her release.

Threatening messages followed, along with a video showing Rumo naked, injured and pleading with her mother for help.

During the search, community member Thomas Sibeko was arrested in connection with the alleged kidnapping. He maintains that the incident damaged his reputation and affected his family.

“This thing has dented my name because I see that these people were trying to take my name into the mud," Sibeko said.

Rumo was found near KwaThema cemetery on 20 October, a day before a community prayer service planned for her safe return.

Community leaders say the case has caused distress, particularly amid ongoing concerns about the kidnapping and killing of women.

The matter returns to court on 28 October, when the second accused is expected to appear in person.

World.title: Another secretary general out as MK Party sacks Sibonelo Nomvalo
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has announced the removal of Sibonelo Nomvalo as its secretary-general, marking another change in the party’s top leadership.

In a statement on Thursday, the party confirmed Nomvalo’s removal following a series of complaints from members.

The concerns reportedly include dissatisfaction with the selection of councillors, factionalism within the party and issues relating to parliamentary administration.

Lindiwe Mtshali has been appointed as acting secretary-general following Nomvalo’s departure from the position.

Despite his removal from the party’s leadership structure, the party said Nomvalo remains an MK Party Member of Parliament in the National Assembly.

World.title: Pirates on brink of CAF Champions' League group stage
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Orlando Pirates are just 90 minutes away from securing their place in the group stage of the CAF Champions League.

The Buccaneers return to home soil with a slender 1-nil advantage after beating Namibian champions African Stars in the first leg.

But with their continental ambitions on the line, Pirates know there is little room for complacency.

The Soweto giants were left disappointed last season after failing to progress to the group stages, and this time around, they are determined not to stumble at the final hurdle.

READ | Pirates confirm Ncikazi exit as Golden Arrows comes calling

“I see that this season Orlando Pirates is a giant in Africa," Orlando Pirates head coach Abdeslam Ouaddou said.

"The fans, the partners, the stakeholders, the club is waiting for us to come back in this big competition. Our players are ready. Our players know the target we have to reach tomorrow."

Defender Tapelo Xoki says last season’s disappointment has provided valuable lessons, with the squad fully focused on getting the job done in this decisive encounter.

“For us, we put all our energy and focus on tomorrow’s game. It’s a big game for the club. We want to take the club to the group stages. We learnt from our lessons from last season. We have a lead, but we are playing at home. For us, it’s all about the energy tomorrow, getting through.”

READ MORE | Nkota returns to Pirates from Al-Ettifaq

Despite holding the aggregate advantage, Pirates expect a difficult challenge against an African Stars side that could adopt a defensive approach in an attempt to frustrate the hosts.

Ouaddou has stressed the importance of patience and intelligent movement as his team looks to break down the opposition.

The Buccaneers’ quest for a second continental star remains alive, but only a disciplined and composed performance will ensure their CAF Champions League ambitions stay on track.

World.title: Local Government Elections 2026: Your guide to special voting
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Local Government Elections are just weeks away, with voters heading to the polls on 4 November 2026.

Special voting will take place on 2 and 3 November, allowing eligible voters whose applications have been approved to cast their ballots ahead of Election Day.

Here is what you need to know if you applied for a special vote.

How does a home visit work?

Voters whose home visit applications have been approved can cast their ballots at home on 2 or 3 November.

This option is intended for voters who cannot travel to their voting stations because of physical infirmity or disability.

How does voting station-based special voting work?

Voters whose applications for voting station-based special votes have been approved must visit their designated voting stations on 2 or 3 November to cast their ballots.

This allows eligible voters who are unable to vote on Election Day to participate in the elections ahead of time.

Can someone assist me to vote?

Voters with physical disabilities, including blindness or visual impairment, may be assisted by a person of their choice.

The person assisting must be at least 18 years old and cannot be a candidate or party agent.

Voters who require assistance should confirm the applicable procedures with the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC).

How many special vote applications have been approved?

The IEC has approved a record 2,655,067 special vote applications for the 2026 Local Government Elections.
