World.title: Liberia: War Victims, Survivors Protest at Court Office, Capitol as House Chairman Pledges to Put Court Bill Before Plenary Tuesday.
World.content:
Some of the protesters at the war crimes court office. Credit: Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

Hundreds of victims, survivors and advocates demonstrated at the war crimes court office, temporarily disrupting operations, before moving to the Capitol Building to demand passage of legislation establishing the court.

Prince Toles, chairman of the House Committee on Claims and Petitions, pledged to bring the matter before plenary Tuesday. Protest organizers said House leaders reinforced that assurance during a subsequent meeting.

The protests came as Liberia approaches its November 2026 target for establishing a National Anti-Corruption Court, while legislation for that court and the War and Economic Crimes Court remains unresolved.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Hundreds of victims and survivors of Liberia’s civil wars, joined by justice advocates, protested Thursday outside the government office overseeing the establishment of a war crimes court, temporarily disrupting operations, before descending on the Capitol Building, where a senior lawmaker pledged to bring long-delayed legislation before the House of Representatives on Tuesday.

The peaceful demonstrations drew people with disabilities, rural women, elderly victims and survivors, young people, and traditional and religious leaders. For hours, protesters gathered outside the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, holding placards demanding justice. One read: “REAL PEACE IS NOT THE SILENCE OF GUNS. REAL PEACE IS DISPENSING JUSTICE AND ENDING IMPUNITY. WE CALL ON THE EXECUTIVE AND LEGISLATURE TO GIVE THE PEOPLE JUSTICE & ACCOUNTABILITY NOW…”



“What’s going on wrong? We are suffering,” said Korpo Dennis, president of the Women in Peacebuilding Network, her voice cracking as tears rolled down her cheeks. Addressing Jallah Barbu, the office’s executive director, Dennis questioned why President Joseph Boakai had not raised the issue at the United Nations General Assembly, as she said he had promised. “He na come, we can hear nothing. We want answer today or else, we will sleep on this street.”

The demonstrations underscored mounting frustration over Liberia’s failure to establish a court to prosecute atrocities committed during its civil wars, more than two decades after the fighting ended. Despite repeated government commitments and extensive consultations, competing bills remain before lawmakers, leaving uncertain when the country will begin prosecuting those accused of some of its worst wartime crimes.

Dennis’s organization was among the women’s peace groups widely credited with helping pressure Liberia’s warring factions to end the conflicts. Her emotional appeal reflected the disappointment of victims and survivors who have spent years campaigning for accountability, only to see successive governments struggle to translate commitments into legislation.

Barbu told the protesters he remained confident that Boakai had not abandoned his commitment to establishing the court. Pressed for answers, he unsuccessfully attempted to reach House Speaker Richard Koon by telephone.

Barbu also contacted James Verdier, the speaker’s chief of staff, who assured the demonstrators that the legislation would be approved. But the assurances failed to satisfy the protesters, who moved to Capitol Hill to press lawmakers directly.

Kula Fofana, Boakai’s press secretary, did not respond to a request for comment on the protesters’ concerns.

At the Capitol, the demonstrators renewed their demand for action, challenging lawmakers over the delays and questioning why the legislation remained unresolved despite years of public campaigning.

“It has taken us too long,” said Jeremiah D. Cooper, a member of the Group of 77, an organization representing people with disabilities. “If these people cannot pass this bill, then my question to you is: Who brought you here? Who made you people come here?The same Liberian people who voted for you are the same Liberian people demanding that you pass certain documents in the interest of the country. You people say you will not do it. Why?”

The protests also included people with disabilities.

But the gathering soon exposed another source of disagreement: whether the proposed court would prosecute both war crimes and economic crimes.

Prescilla A. Cooper, a Montserrado County representative and member of the House Committee on Claims and Petitions, told the protesters that a joint legislative committee tasked with harmonizing the competing bills had agreed to proceed with legislation establishing a war crimes court, leaving economic crimes to be addressed separately.

Prince Toles, chairman of the committee, sought to calm the protesters, assuring them that the legislation would establish a War and Economic Crimes Court. His statement appeared to contradict Cooper’s account of the committee’s decision, leaving its final position unclear.

“We signed it in 2024 (the joint resolution). We signed it 5G. But this one, we will give it 20G,” Toles said, referring to the Legislature’s earlier support for establishing the court. “If people did not rob the system, all of us would have lived better. I want to tell you that we are with you.”

He then made a specific commitment.

“We will bring this matter before plenary,” Toles said. “But if they ask us to bring a paper signed by the different stakeholders, I will just propose that you draft something for us temporarily. Bring it here tomorrow (Friday), then I will put it on the floor on Tuesday.”

Plenary, the full membership of either legislative chamber, is its highest decision-making body. Toles’s pledge does not guarantee a vote or passage of the legislation Tuesday.

After the exchange, House leaders invited protest organizers to a meeting.

Peterson Sonyah, executive director of the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association, one of the country’s leading victims’ and survivors’ organizations, said participants emerged encouraged by the assurances they received.

“We feel a little bit relieved that it will work,” Sonyah said by phone. “We are impressed with the discussion. We are planning to be there on Tuesday.”

The protests came as Liberia approaches a significant deadline in its plans to establish the courts.

Under a 36-page roadmap submitted to President Boakai in July 2025 , the court office projected that the National Anti-Corruption Court would be fully operational by November 2026, followed by the War and Economic Crimes Court in November 2027.

With November approaching and legislation establishing both courts still awaiting approval, the timetable faces uncertainty. The roadmap also envisaged that both courts would conclude their trials by 2031, with the war crimes court subsequently transitioning to a residual mechanism to handle outstanding matters.

The renewed pressure comes as Liberia prepares to assume the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December, a moment justice advocates say will draw fresh international attention to the country’s unfinished efforts to address its wartime past.

In earlier reporting, transitional justice expert Aaron Weah raised concerns about the implications of continued delays for Liberia’s international standing and its efforts to consolidate peace and accountability.

Public opinion surveys have shown substantial support for establishing the court.

A FrontPage Africa/New Narratives survey of 1,150 people across 11 counties found that 91 percent supported establishing the court, while 89 percent said they would not vote for lawmakers who opposed it.

The survey was not conducted using scientific sampling methods. Only 4 percent of respondents said they were aware of consultations by lawmakers on the proposed court.

The legislative process has been complicated by six competing proposals concerning the establishment of the courts.

They include a 2021 War Crimes Court bill submitted by the Liberian National Bar Association ; a separate proposal from a coalition of civil society organizations led by the Independent National Commission on Human Rights ; and two bills introduced by Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah , one for a War Crimes Court and another for a Special Economic and Corruption Crimes Court.

The remaining two bills were prepared by the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court , proposing a War and Economic Crimes Court and a separate National Anti-Corruption Court. President Boakai subsequently forwarded both proposals to the Legislature .

The senators’ proposals drew criticism from leading justice advocates , who warned that provisions concerning the courts’ jurisdiction and appeals procedures could weaken accountability for wartime atrocities.

In June, more than 40 members of the House of Representatives participated in a two-day technical deliberation in Buchanan, Grand Bassa County , organized by the court office and its partners to examine the proposed legislation.

At the gathering, constitutional lawyer Tiawan Gongloe urged lawmakers to prioritize the court , describing accountability for wartime atrocities as an unfinished national obligation.

Separately, the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights, Claims and Petitions began consultations on the six competing bills in June, seeking to resolve disagreements over the appointment of senior court officials, prosecutorial independence and the appeals process.

The Senate committee had outlined a timetable for harmonizing the proposals , with further consultations and hearings planned before the end of the legislative session.

Neither chamber approved the legislation before lawmakers departed for their constituency break.

The Legislature was scheduled to return October 9, but a dispute over lawmakers’ benefits disrupted the House’s reopening. Regular House business resumed October 13.

Thursday’s demonstrations came 13 days after the scheduled return, with victims, survivors and advocates demanding that lawmakers move beyond consultations and assurances to legislative action.

For Sonyah and the other organizers, Tuesday will provide the next test of those assurances. They intend to return to the Capitol to see whether the promised action materializes — and whether the legislation presented will address both war crimes and economic crimes.

World.title: Liberia: House Summons Health Authorities To Comprehensive Briefing On Liberia’s Preparedness, Response Measures Amid Latest Outbreak In Nigeria
World.content:
MONROVIA, October 22, 2026 — The House of Representatives has summoned Liberia’s health authorities to provide a comprehensive briefing on the country’s preparedness and response measures following reports of a confirmed Ebola case in Nigeria and an ongoing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The House voted unanimously on Thursday to summon the Minister of Health, the Director General of the National Public Health Institute of Liberia (NPHIL), and other relevant health officials to appear before its plenary on Tuesday, October 27.



The decision followed a communication from Montserrado County Electoral District #16 Representative Dixon Seboe, who called on the Legislature to obtain detailed information about Liberia’s readiness to prevent and respond to a potential public health emergency.

Seboe’s request comes after the Ministry of Health issued a public notice directing health facilities, border entry points, public buildings and other institutions nationwide to strengthen screening procedures and enforce infection prevention and control measures.

While acknowledging the importance of the preventive measures, Seboe argued that the regional developments require a broader assessment of the country’s preparedness, including the availability of essential medical supplies, trained personnel and emergency response resources.

“Honorable Speaker, as representatives of the Liberian people, we have a constitutional and public responsibility to ensure that the appropriate authorities are taking all necessary measures to safeguard the health and well-being of our citizens,” Seboe stated in his communication.

The lawmaker wants the Minister of Health to brief the Legislature on the government’s overall Ebola preparedness strategy, emergency response arrangements and coordination with regional and international health authorities.

He also requested that the NPHIL Director General provide updates on disease surveillance systems and laboratory testing capacity, including the country’s ability to identify and confirm suspected Ebola cases promptly.

Additionally, Seboe called for representatives of the County Health Teams to explain the level of preparedness across Liberia’s 15 counties, particularly the availability of isolation facilities and other resources needed to manage suspected cases.

The communication further seeks clarification from border and port health authorities on screening procedures at the country’s points of entry and the protocols for handling travelers who exhibit suspected symptoms or report relevant exposure histories.

Emergency Funding, Public Awareness Under Scrutiny

Beyond surveillance and screening, Seboe wants health authorities to account for public awareness campaigns, infection prevention supplies, frontline health worker training and the resources available to enforce the Ministry of Health’s preventive directives.

He also called for information on measures to protect public schools, markets, government institutions, transportation facilities and densely populated communities, particularly in Montserrado County, where population movement and congestion could complicate efforts to contain an outbreak.

The lawmaker emphasized the need for transparency regarding the availability of emergency funding, medical equipment, trained personnel and logistical support.

“The briefing should clarify whether Liberia has adequate emergency funding, medical equipment, trained personnel, and logistical support to respond promptly to any suspected Ebola case, should one arise,” the communication stated.

Seboe maintained that his request was not intended to create public panic but to ensure that the government takes proactive steps to protect the population.

“Early preparation, accurate public information, and effective coordination among relevant institutions are essential to preventing a public health emergency,” he said.

He urged the House to treat the matter with urgency and direct the relevant authorities to provide a full account of the country’s preparedness.

Following the reading and deliberation of the communication, Margibi County Electoral District #2 Representative Ivar K. Jones moved that the health officials appear before the full plenary on Tuesday.

The motion was overwhelmingly approved by lawmakers.

Government Intensifies Preventive Measures

Before the House’s decision, the Ministry of Health had ordered heightened disease surveillance and stricter infection prevention measures at health facilities, border entry points and public institutions nationwide following reports of a confirmed Ebola case in Nigeria.

In a statement issued after the reports emerged, the Ministry said the directive took immediate effect and was intended to strengthen Liberia’s preparedness against the potential spread of Ebola and other infectious diseases.

The planned briefing is expected to give lawmakers an opportunity to assess the implementation of those measures and determine whether additional interventions are necessary to protect public health.

The health authorities had not yet appeared before the House as of Thursday, with their briefing scheduled for October 27.

World.title: Editorial: The Supreme Court Must Speak Clearly On Kolubah, and Soon
World.content:
Six months after the House of Representatives expelled Rep. Yekeh Kolubah while a Supreme Court stay order was pending, the full bench has heard his appeal and reserved its ruling. The case rests on a narrow question: whether the House was properly served with the order. But the answer will decide whether court orders bind Liberia’s Legislature, and whether due process protects elected officials. FrontPageAfrica urges the Court to rule promptly and plainly.

THE SUPREME COURT of Liberia heard arguments on Thursday in the appeal of Yekeh Kolubah, the Montserrado County District #10 lawmaker expelled from the House of Representatives in April. The Court then reserved its ruling. The Court has every right to take time to deliberate. But Liberia cannot afford a ruling that is late, narrow or vague. The case is about more than one outspoken legislator. It tests whether a court order means anything once it reaches the doors of the Capitol.

THE FACTS ARE simple and troubling. On April 16, 2026, Associate Justice Yussif D. Kaba, presiding in Chambers, granted Mr. Kolubah’s petition for a writ of prohibition. He ordered the House leadership to stay all proceedings and summoned them to a conference on April 20. The next day the House voted to expel Mr. Kolubah. Forty-nine members signed the resolution. The House Clerk’s office said it had received no order from the Court. Yet the Court’s Marshal had delivered the writ to the offices of the Speaker and the Chief Clerk, where a receptionist and a computer operator received it.



IN MAY, JUSTICE Kaba dismissed Mr. Kolubah’s Bill of Information. He held that the House had not been lawfully served, because House Rule 26.5 names the Sergeant-at-Arms as the only officer authorized to accept court documents. Without proper service, he reasoned, the House could not be held in contempt. On Thursday, Mr. Kolubah’s lawyer, Cllr. Jonathan Massaquoi, argued that service on the Legislature is governed by the Civil Procedure Law, not by the House’s internal rules. He cited Section 3.38(9), which requires service on a government subdivision to be made on its chief executive. The Speaker’s office, he said, was the right place.

THIS IS THE first lapse the full bench must confront. A body’s internal rule cannot override the law of the land. If the House’s own rulebook decides who may receive a court order, the House effectively decides whether it has been served. Any institution that wants to escape judicial review would need only to keep its designated officer out of reach. No court in a constitutional democracy can accept that result.

THE SECOND LAPSE lies with the Court itself. The Marshal who delivered the writ is the Court’s own officer. If the service was defective, the defect began inside the Temple of Justice, not with the litigant. Yet Mr. Kolubah alone has paid the price, losing his seat while the procedural question was being argued. Justice should not depend on which desk a document happens to land on.

THE THIRD LAPSE concerns notice. The Court’s stay was public knowledge on Capitol Hill before the vote; Liberian newspapers reported it the same day. Justice Kaba correctly stated that contempt requires actual or constructive notice. The full bench should say plainly whether a legislature that reads of a stay order in the morning press, and proceeds anyway, can claim it did not know.

WE DO NOT defend Mr. Kolubah’s conduct. His remarks on the Liberia-Guinea border dispute angered many colleagues and citizens, and in 2021 he was suspended twice over his invective against then-President George Weah. Article 38 of the Constitution gives each House the power to discipline its members, including expulsion by a two-thirds vote of its entire membership. In a 73-member House, 49 votes is exactly that threshold. The House had the power to act. The question is whether it exercised that power lawfully, with due process, and while a court order was pending.

THE CONSTITUTION IS clear on due process. Article 20 forbids depriving any person of a right or privilege except after a hearing consistent with the Constitution and the law. Mr. Kolubah’s lawyers walked out of the committee hearing on April 15 after being denied a five-day extension and access to the evidence against him. That walkout may have been a tactic. But a committee that moves to expel an elected member within a week of the complaint, without giving his counsel time to see the evidence, invites serious constitutional doubt.

THE STAKES REACH far beyond District #10. Tens of thousands of voters have had no representative since April. If the expulsion stands on a technicality, every legislature in Liberia will learn that a stay order can be ignored if it is handed to the wrong clerk. If the Court instead voids the expulsion without addressing the House’s genuine constitutional powers, it risks a standoff between two branches of government. Neither outcome serves a country that has worked hard, since the end of its civil wars, to build institutions people trust.

LIBERIA’S DEMOCRACY HAS earned international respect, including through peaceful transfers of power. That record rests on a basic bargain: those in power obey the courts, even when the ruling is unwelcome. A House that can expel a member while a stay order sits in its own offices, and a Court that cannot say whether its orders were received, both weaken that bargain.

WE THEREFORE URGE the Supreme Court to rule promptly and to answer the questions directly. Who may lawfully receive service on behalf of the Legislature? Does the Civil Procedure Law govern, or the House rulebook? What is the legal effect of an act taken after a stay order was delivered, however imperfectly? And what process does the Constitution require before a member is expelled?

CLEAR ANSWERS WILL protect the next lawmaker, whatever party or district. They will also protect the House, by telling it exactly what the law requires. Silence or a narrow ruling would leave a dangerous precedent. Liberia needs the Court to be clear.

World.title: LSEZA Pitches Liberia’s Investment Potential at Prosperity Africa Conference
World.content:
The Liberia Special Economic Zones Authority (LSEZA) is using the 7th Prosperity Africa Conference in Monrovia to promote Liberia as an emerging destination for investors, highlighting opportunities in industrial development, exports and job creation.

The Authority made its case during the conference, held under the theme “Bridge by Prosperity,” at the EJS Ministerial Complex in Monrovia.

The gathering has brought together investors, government officials, business leaders, financial institutions and chambers of commerce from across Africa and beyond to discuss opportunities for economic growth and business partnerships.



Representing LSEZA, Director for Regulations and Legal Affairs Atty. Ebenezer Wilson outlined the role of Liberia’s Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in driving industrialization and attracting investment.

Wilson said the SEZ framework could help expand economic opportunities, create jobs, increase exports and strengthen Liberia’s competitiveness as an investment destination.

He also highlighted incentives available to businesses operating under the SEZ regime, including tax incentives, access to a youthful workforce, land resources and business support services.

According to LSEZA, the incentives are intended to make it easier for companies seeking to establish new operations or expand existing businesses in Liberia.

Beyond its presentation, LSEZA has set up an exhibition booth at the conference where prospective investors can obtain information about investment opportunities within the country’s Special Economic Zones.

The booth is also providing information on investment entry requirements, application procedures, available incentives and the process for accessing opportunities under Liberia’s SEZ regime.

The Authority said the direct engagement with investors provides an opportunity to demonstrate how Special Economic Zones can support business expansion, value addition, export development and employment creation.

The Prosperity Africa Conference is a biennial business gathering organized by the Pan African Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PACCI), in partnership with the Liberia Chamber of Commerce (LCC).

LSEZA said it remains committed to promoting Special Economic Zones as platforms for investment, industrial growth, trade expansion and sustainable job creation.

The Liberia Special Economic Zones Authority is the statutory body responsible for designating, promoting, developing and managing Special Economic Zones across Liberia, with a mandate to support industrialization, attract investment and create sustainable employment.

World.title: Liberia Study of Rwanda: Tax Administration and Digital cooperation Under the Spotlight
World.content:
KIGALI – Liberia’s Commissioner for Domestic Tax at its Revenue Authority (LRA), Ms. Margrete P. Krote, says the country is committed to advancing its decentralization program and hoped to learn from Rwanda’s experience in using technology to improve revenue collection and public service delivery.

Ms. Krote made the statement on Thursday during a meeting with officials of the Rwanda Revenue Authority in Kigali as Liberia Study Tour of Rwanda.

“Rwanda has evolved significantly over the last decade, especially in technology and transformation. We in Africa are looking up to Rwanda because of the work you are doing,” she maintained.

Ms. Krote acknowledged that Liberia had faced challenges in implementing its decentralization reforms, despite the passage of the Local Government Act in 2018. She said continued engagement with Rwanda could help Liberia identify practical ways to accelerate the process.



She also described the study tour as an opportunity to strengthen cooperation with Rwanda and turn lessons from the East African country would help accelerate practical reforms at home.

Rwanda stresses digital cooperation

Speaking earlier, Rwanda Revenue Authority Commissioner General Hon. Roland Niwenshuti welcomed the Liberian delegation and reaffirmed his institution’s willingness to share its experience in revenue mobilization and decentralized tax administration.

He intimated that digital transformation could not succeed if revenue authorities worked in isolation.

“You can digitalize as a tax administration, but you can never succeed if you are digitalizing alone,” Hon. Niwenshuti stressed.

He explained that effective tax collection, particularly property taxation, depends on accurate information and cooperation among government institutions, land registries, financial institutions and the private sector.

Hon. Niwenshuti said these partnerships help revenue authorities identify taxable properties, improve records and strengthen compliance.

He also highlighted the importance of leadership and coordination between national revenue authorities and local government administrations.

In Rwanda, Hon. Niwenshuti disclosed that the revenue authority works with district leaders and local authorities to support the collection of taxes and fees that contribute to local government financing.

Digital services also under study

Earlier on Thursday, the Liberian delegation visited Irembo, Rwanda’s digital public service platform, which enables citizens to access a range of government services online, including applications for marriage certificates.

The visit formed part of Liberia’s wider effort to understand how digital systems can simplify administrative processes and improve access to public services.

The study tour brings together representatives of Liberian government institutions to examine Rwanda’s experience in decentralization, public financial management, revenue administration and digital service delivery.

Liberia is pursuing decentralization reforms aimed at strengthening local governance, expanding community participation in public decision-making and improving the management of public resources at the county level.

The government is also advancing revenue-sharing arrangements and the deployment of county treasurers in six of Liberia’s 15 counties, with the aim of putting resources in the hands of the locals and bringing government processes closer to communities.

World.title: Mining companies urged to translate mineral wealth into tangible benefits
World.content:
Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Permanent Secretary, Hapenga Kabeta, has urged mining companies in the country to ensure that mineral wealth translates into tangible and lasting benefits for Zambians.

Dr Kabeta says increased mineral production must be accompanied by local value addition, skills development, technology transfer and the growth of local enterprises.

He has advised that mining activities should also protect the environment and improve the welfare of citizens, noting that production targets would be meaningless if they resulted in environmental destruction and left communities without benefits.

The Permanent Secretary was speaking in Lusaka last evening when he officiated at the cultural night gala night held on the sidelines of the 2026 Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka.

He said the Insaka also provides an opportunity for face-to-face engagements that can strengthen professional relationships, generate ideas and facilitate business deals.

Dr Kabeta encouraged participants to establish meaningful partnerships, share experiences and develop strategies that would help unlock Zambia’s mineral potential for the benefit of the people.

He said Zambia needs a productive, innovative, inclusive and responsible mining industry that attracts investment, creates decent jobs, supports local businesses and contributes to long-term economic transformation.

Dr Kabeta noted that the mining sector has continued to attract significant investments in various parts of the country, including the Copperbelt and North-Western Provinces which are contributing to national economic development.

Meanwhile, Dr Kabeta presented awards to organisations recognised for their participation and contribution to the 2026 Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka.

Among the recipients were ZESCO, Konkola Copper Mines, First Quantum Minerals, Anglo American Corporation, Zanaco and Indo-Zambia Bank.

Passing a vote of thanks, Buterla Investment Limited Chief Executive Officer, Happy Mbulo, said the Grow Zambia Agenda can be achieved if mining firms apply themselves.

Mr Mbulo implored the private sector to work closely with government to fully realise their potential in enhancing the production of goods and services associated with the value chain system.

World.title: Mwense man jailed 12 months for theft
World.content:
The Mwense Magistrates court has sentenced a 34-year-old man of Mulundu village to 12 months concurrent imprisonment with hard labour for two counts of theft contrary to section 272 of the penal code Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia.

This is in a matter in which Simon Kunda masquerading as a traditional healer operating as Dr Mwiko is alleged to have obtained money amounting to K 1,500 belonging to Jacob Mwape and Ireen Chisha respectively.

This is after he claimed he would heal their sicknesses.

In the first count, Kunda is said to have Charged Mwape K 1000 on the pretext that he would give him treatment for his ailing feet.

In count two the now convict is alleged to have charged Chisha a K 500 as payment to treat her stomach pains.

The two complainants are said to have paid the money in full respectively after Kunda refused the 50 percent down payment claiming that the spirits being consulted demanded full payments before treatment could be given.

Testifying before Magistrate Fred Mwangala, the two complainants said that Kunda however vanished without offering the required services and was only arrested a few months after he was spotted in public.

In mitigation, Kunda prayed for the court’s leniency saying he was a poor man.

“Am a poor man so I ask the court to forgive me otherwise I have nothing more to say,” Kunda begged.

In sentencing, Magistrate Mwangala noted that the victims from whom the now convict had stolen the money were also not rich.

Magistrate Mwangala ruled that Kunda should be given a custodial sentence at a correctional facility for reformation.

Magistrate Mwangala handed Kunda eight months imprisonment on each count to run concurrently.

However, Magistrate Mwangala immediately increased the sentence to 12 months imprisonment after the convict warned the complainants as he stood down from the dock.

World.title: Lufuma calls on youths to engage in productive activities
World.content:
Kabompo East Member of Parliament (MP) Ambrose Lufuma has called on young people to engage in productive activities that will contribute to the attainment of the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Lufuma says youths should be active participants in national development by becoming producers, innovators, entrepreneurs and job creators rather than relying on formal employment.

Contributing to the Motion of Thanks on the President’s address during the official opening of the First Session of the 14th National Assembly, Mr Lufuma, a former Defence Minister, also called for the upgrading of feeder roads leading to productive areas in Kabompo to gravel standard.

He said the government will continue creating opportunities for young people to acquire practical skills, establish businesses and participate in productive sectors such as agriculture and construction.

In his median speech to the House, the former minister of defense cited the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) grants, loans, empowerment programmes and National Service training as important interventions that can help empower young people.

Mr Lufuma stated that agriculture remains the mainstay of the constituency’s economy, with an estimated 95 percent of the population engaged in farming and related activities.

The MP called for improved access to farming inputs, extension services, appropriate technologies, irrigation, storage facilities, satellite depots and reliable markets to enhance agricultural production and food security.

Mr Lufuma has further urged the government to upgrade township roads in Kabompo to improve connectivity and facilitate economic activities.

Meanwhile, Nkombwa East MP Jairos Simbeye has called for a results-oriented public service, saying effective delivery of government programmes requires commitment, discipline and proper time management.

Mr Simbeye says public officers should focus on delivering tangible results rather than merely reporting for work.

He has commended the National Assembly for promoting professionalism and orderly service delivery, citing the conduct of security personnel and staff as an example of the standards that should be upheld across public institutions.

He stressed that all stakeholders must work together to support President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda and ensure the country achieves its development targets.

The MP cautioned against spreading misinformation about government programmes, particularly the school feeding programme, saying such conduct can discourage beneficiaries from accessing essential services.

On housing, Mr Simbeye encouraged residents to take advantage of land available in rural constituencies such as Nkombwa Constituency to support settlement and development, rather than concentrating on limited plots in urban areas.

He said efficient public service delivery at all levels is essential to restoring public confidence and ensuring that government policies and programmes benefit citizens.

He further called for unity of purpose among public officers and other stakeholders, saying collective efforts are necessary for Zambia to achieve its national development aspirations.

World.title: Government hails public support for energy diversification
World.content:
Government has commended the public for complementing its efforts to reduce the country’s dependence on hydropower.

Speaking during an interview with ZANIS, Ministry of Energy Principal Public Relations Officer, Bob Sianjalika, said the ministry has recorded an increase of Independence Power Producers and Independence Power Traders, which has increased the solar electricity generation.

Mr Sianjalika disclosed that the ministry is still receiving applications from individuals and groups showing interest in being in the Independence Power Producer chain, while others have power purchase agreements with ZESCO.

He further highlighted that the energy sector is now at 4,700 megawatts of collective generation across the country, giving them an assurance of meeting the target of 10,000 megawatts by 2026.

Mr Sianjalika added that about 2,600 megawatts of electricity is expected to be generated from thermal and solar plants alone, from the community.

He also disclosed that the government will be commissioning three solar power plants in three areas before the end of the year.

“We will be commissioning one in Shimabala generating 100 megawatts, one in Chipata generating 100 and the other one in Mumbwa with120 megawatts” he added.

Mr Sianjalika has described the current electricity generation state as comfortable if compared to the 2021 state.

He also revealed that the government intends to generate 1,000 megawatts of electricity before the end of the year 2026.

He has urged Zambians and foreign investors to invest in Zambia’s growing energy sector.

World.title: Police arrest suspect in Chasefu well poisoning
World.content:
Police have arrested a male suspect in the poisoning of a community well in Chasefu district, that affected about 38 people.

Yelemiya Zimba, 28, of Chalotwa Village of Chasefu District, was arrested immediately he was discharged from Lundazi District Hospital where he was being treated after ingesting the same suspected weed killer he had used to contaminate the community well.

Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer, Robertson Mweemba said that the suspect is expected to appear in court soon.

And all the 17 victims of the water poisoning have since been discharged.

Yelemiya Zimba, who stands charged with the offence of maliciously administering poisonous substances into drinking water with intent to harm innocent people, is one of the 17 victims that have been discharged.

“All the 17 victims who were admitted to Lundazi District Hospital have been treated and discharged today,” Mr Mweemba said.

He added that the other 21 people who also drank the same poisoned water within Chalotwa Village and complained of diarrhea and abdominal pains were treated at the local health facility within Chasefu district.

World.title: MoE staff urged to make cleanliness an everyday work culture
World.content:
Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary for Administration, Noriana Muneku, has implored the ministry staff to make cleanliness an everyday work culture rather than limiting it to national commemorations.

Ms Muneku says cleanliness should be embraced as a way of life rather than a temporary activity, stressing that everyone has a role to play in keeping the environment clean.

Speaking during a cleaning exercise at the Ministry’s premises in Lusaka today ahead of Zambia’s 62nd Independence Anniversary, Ms Muneku emphasised that the ministry’s surroundings should remain clean and presentable at all times.

Ms Muneku urged the administration department to take the lead in maintaining high standards of cleanliness, stressing that staff must demonstrate their commitment through consistent action.

And Lusaka Mayor, Chitambala Mwewa, called on members of the public to take responsibility for maintaining cleanliness around their premises and trading in designated market places.

Mr Mwewa expressed concern over the disposal of plastic waste into drainage systems, which he attributed to trading activities conducted in undesignated areas.

He said traders should operate from markets to promote proper waste management and ensure that business activities are conducted in appropriate environments.

Mr Mwewa further called for high standards of cleanliness along the road between the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Finance, saying the area should be spotless.

He urged the public to support efforts to relocate traders to designated markets, emphasising that the initiative represents a permanent change in the way trading and environmental cleanliness are managed.

World.title: Govt. recommits to reforming Zambia’s pension system
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to reforming Zambia’s pension system to expand coverage, strengthen regulatory oversight and improve retirement income security, particularly for workers in the informal sector.

Speaking at the official opening of the 2026 Annual Pension Conference, held under the theme “Building Sustainable Pension Innovation, Governance and Policy Reform,” Ministry of Labour and Social Security Secretary Zachariah Luhanga said pension reforms were essential to safeguarding workers’ contributions, enhancing benefits and positioning pension funds to contribute to national economic development.

Mr Luhanga said government remained committed to building a sustainable pension system that protects members’ savings, provides adequate retirement income and supports families in old age.

“Pension is more than a monthly payment,” the Permanent Secretary said, describing retirement benefits as recognition of workers’ years of service and sacrifice.

Mr Luhanga added that pension funds could also contribute to economic development by directing capital towards productive sectors, including infrastructure, housing and capital markets.

“The true measure of success is when the system protects members, provides adequate retirement benefits and reaches those who need it most,” Mr Luhanga said.

The Permanent Secretary also highlighted government’s ongoing efforts to improve the pension system through legislative reforms.

He further identified digital technology as an important tool for modernising pension administration, reducing operational costs and improving access to information.

Mr Luhanga, however, warned that technological advancement must be accompanied by strong data management, cybersecurity safeguards and adequate protection of members’ personal information.

He reiterated government’s commitment to expanding pension coverage, particularly among workers in the informal sector, many of whom remain outside formal pension arrangements.

Speaking earlier, Pension and Insurance Authority Registrar and Chief Executive Officer, Namakau Ntini, called for stronger governance, greater transparency and expanded pension coverage to ensure a sustainable retirement system capable of protecting contributors and supporting national economic development.

Ms Ntini stressed that pension systems could no longer rely on traditional approaches alone, particularly as demographic changes increase the need for sustainable retirement planning.

On governance, the Registrar emphasised the importance of competence, accountability, effective risk management and transparent investment decisions in protecting contributors’ savings and maintaining public confidence in pension institutions.

She said strengthening governance structures was essential to addressing weaknesses in pension administration and ensuring that the interests of contributors and retirees remained central to industry operations.

And Zambia Association of Pension Funds (ZAPF) Chairperson, Collina Halwampa, urged pension industry to embrace innovation, strengthen member engagement and promote policy dialogue to ensure the long-term sustainability of pension schemes amid changing membership demographics.

Meanwhile, Pan African Fund Managers Association Programme Manager, Oguche Aguda, called for reforms in pension systems to ensure retirement income security, promote sustainable contributions and channel pension funds into investments capable of driving economic growth.

Mr Aguda, said pension administrators and regulators must strike a balance between innovation, investment security and the long-term sustainability of retirement savings.

He also urged stakeholders to pay greater attention to younger workers, saying pension systems must become more relevant and understandable to younger generations to encourage early and consistent contributions.

World.title: Petauke senior citizens, freedom fighters receive hampers
World.content:
Senior citizens and freedom fighters in Petauke District have received assorted hampers from the District National Events Committee (DNEC), with support from Dealer’s Corner Millers. ‎

The gesture, which is part of this year’s Independence celebrations, is an appreciation gesture, also aimed at enabling beneficiaries to share in the country’s Independence celebrations.

The hampers were presented by Petauke District Commissioner Wachepa Phiri, who said the initiative was intended to share the Independence spirit with less privileged members of society.

‎

‎ “To share the Independence celebration with others who are not as privileged as some of us might be,” he said.

‎

Meanwhile, Dealer’s Corner Millers Director Ibrahim Phiri said the donation was part of the company’s Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR).

‎

‎Mr Phiri said he valued the partnership and support from the public, which had contributed to the growth of his business.

‎

‎ “We are a Christian nation, so with the little we have, we thought of sharing,” he said.

‎

‎Meanwhile, 83-year-old Alifat Tembo said the gesture reminded him of the celebrations in the early days of Zambia’s Independence.

‎

‎ “With this parcel you have given me, I am reminded of the old days and reassured that we are still remembered. Government should continue to remember freedom fighters,” he said.

‎

‎Another senior citizen, Esnart Mbewe, thanked the organisers for the gesture and appealed for continued support towards senior citizens and freedom fighters.

‎

‎ “I am grateful that you have helped me during this year’s Independence celebration. As a parent, I feel that you have truly thought of me. The honour and respect you have shown us are greatly appreciated. May this continue,” she said.

The hampers included mealie meal, cooking oil and salt, among other items.

World.title: South Africa: Fuel Retailers Warn Relief Falls Short - South African News Briefs - October 23, 2026
World.content:
press review

Fuel Retailers Say R10bn Relief Offers Little Ease

The Fuel Retailers Association has said that the government's R10 billion fuel levy relief package will cushion consumers against rising fuel prices but offer little relief to retailers, reports EWN. From November 4, petrol prices will be reduced by R1.50 a litre and diesel by R3, before the relief decreases to R1 for petrol and R1.50 for diesel from December 2. Association representative Henry van der Merwe warned that fuel prices could still rise sharply in November, with tensions around the Strait of Hormuz adding uncertainty to global oil markets. Declining fuel sales are also putting pressure on retailers, forcing some rural filling stations to close at night to cut costs, while jobs are increasingly at risk.

KwaZulu-Natal Police Concerned Over Attacks on Foreign Nationals

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

KwaZulu-Natal police have raised concerns about ongoing attacks on foreign nationals in parts of Durban and urged communities to report incidents, reports SABC News. A foreign national was killed after allegedly being assaulted by a crowd of about 50 people in the Durban central business district. Police also received reports of an attack on a foreign national in the Point area, as well as an incident involving a company in Essenwood that assists with permit applications in partnership with the Department of Home Affairs. Police spokesperson Colonel Robert Netshiunda condemned the violence. He said that while people have the right to protest, attacks and killings are criminal offences. Investigations are underway to identify those responsible.

Murder-Accused Woman Awaits Psychiatric Evaluation

The Bellville Magistrate's Court is set to receive an update on the psychiatric evaluation of 63-year-old Aletta Rose, who is accused of murdering her 80-year-old sister in March, reports EWN. Rose allegedly decapitated her sister and dismembered her hands. Her case has been repeatedly postponed because she has been unable to access the district surgeon for a court-mandated forensic psychiatric assessment, despite being referred to Valkenberg Psychiatric Hospital in June. The Western Cape Health and Wellness Department said the hospital, the province's only facility authorised to conduct such evaluations, has 391 beds but just 17 approved for forensic psychiatric observations, including two for female accused. Rose has remained fifth on the waiting list since August, while 416 accused are awaiting forensic assessment across the system.

World.title: Senegal: General Strike Continues Amid Protests Against New Labour Laws
World.content:
Dakar — Senegal's labour unions have called for a 72-hour general strike, from October 21 to 23, 2026. The government disputes the legality of the strike, saying the notice filed by the unions doesn't comply with the procedures. This standoff comes amid ongoing tensions surrounding the reform of the Labor Code and the Social Security Code.

The confrontation between the government and the trade unions has entered a new phase. At the call of the Trade Union Front for the Defense of Labor (FSDT) and the mobilized trade union federations, workers are invited to observe three days of strike action to protest, in particular, against the conditions under which the new labor and social protection laws were adopted.

For several months, unions have been denouncing a process they deem insufficiently consultative. On July 10, the FSDT had already announced a general strike to express its opposition to the approach taken by the authorities. Despite this protest, the two texts were promulgated on September 3, 2026, under laws no. 2026-18 and no. 2026-19, before their publication in the Official Journal on September 18th.

A disagreement over the legality of the movement

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Faced with this new call for mobilization, the Ministry of Public Service, Labor, and Public Service Reform considers the strike order unlawful. According to information reported by PressAfrik, the administration contests the use of a single strike notice to cover the public, semi-public, and private sectors, which are subject to separate procedures.

In the private and semi-public sectors, the Labor Code stipulates that the dispute must be notified to the Labor and Social Security Inspector or the relevant Director General, as applicable. If no agreement is reached, or in the event of partial conciliation, a thirty-day notice period may then be given to the company's management.

For civil servants, the ministry reminds them that written notice must specify the reasons for and duration of the strike, with one month's notice given before the action begins. Local government employees, for their part, must notify the president of the departmental council or the mayor concerned of their strike notice.

The administration warns that failure to comply with these formalities may result in salary deductions for days not worked and disciplinary action. It also mentions potential consequences for the right to compensation and damages in the event of termination of the employment contract.

For more, read the original story in French.

World.title: East Africa: Ruto Hands Comesa Chairmanship to Mnangagwa
World.content:
Nairobi — Africa must take greater responsibility for financing its development by strengthening its own financial institutions, President William Ruto has said.

The President urged African States to show confidence in African institutions, saying they have already demonstrated their capacity by financing Africa's trade, insuring the continent's risks and standing with African States when others stepped back.

He called on African governments to place more of their reserves with African institutions, channel development projects through them and back their bonds and guarantees.

Through the Alliance of African Multilateral Financial Institutions, he explained, African institutions can now pool their strength and act on a continental scale.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"We cannot ask the world to trust African institutions if we do not trust them ourselves. Africa holds more than $4 trillion in domestic financial assets. Yet much of these sit in foreign accounts, earning little while our own projects wait for capital," he said.

President Ruto made the remarks on Thursday during the 25th Summit of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) Heads of State and Government held at the New Parliament Building in Harare, Zimbabwe.

Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema, COMESA Secretary-General Chileshe Mpundu Kapwepwe and AfCFTA Secretary-General Wamkele Mene were among those present.

Kenya, President Ruto pointed out, has increased shareholding in Afreximbank, the Africa Finance Corporation and African Trade and Investment Development Insurance (ATIDI).

"Just for your information, the $16 billion East Africa refinery that will be built in Kenya will be almost wholly funded by African financial institutions. That is the scale of the resources that we have," he said.

He noted that Africa cannot be ambitious in its plans and timid in financing them.

"Every programme we agree upon must be matched by the resources to deliver it. Otherwise, our communiqués will promise what our budgets cannot pay for," he said.

At the summit, President Ruto handed over the chairmanship of COMESA to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

He expressed confidence in President Mnangagwa's leadership to take COMESA forward.

"Under his stewardship, and with the support of every Member State, I trust that we will turn the ambition of One Market, One Future into progress our people can see and feel," he said.

The President said he was proud of the progress made during Kenya's chairmanship, including stronger economic growth, increased intra-regional trade and deeper digital integration.

"When we assumed the Chair, we set one priority: Leveraging digitalisation to deepen regional value chains for sustainable and inclusive growth. Today, that priority is a programme, not a slogan," he said.

As the outgoing chairperson, President Ruto also presented and launched the COMESA 2026-2030 Medium-Term Strategic Plan and the 2025 Annual Report.

The report, he said, outlines the need to accelerate intra-African trade, eliminate non-tariff barriers, improve connectivity and ensure the benefits of integration reach every segment of society.

He noted that as the global order shifts and protectionism rises, Africa's response must be deeper regional integration, stronger value chains and increased trade among African States.

He pointed out that the greatest market for Africa's goods is Africa.

"Regional integration is no longer a dream we discuss. It is an economic and strategic necessity. We must trade more among ourselves, build resilient regional value chains and deepen our productive capacity so that we can withstand the next shock and seize the next opportunity," he said.

The President, therefore, called on the COMESA Secretariat to fast-track the COMESA Market Levy to secure sustainable and predictable financing for regional priorities.

He explained that integration should be measured not by the volume of trade or the strength of institutions alone but by the opportunities created for citizens of the continent.

The President also said Africa seeks a new engagement with its partners, rooted in sovereign equality, built on mutual benefit and measured by shared prosperity.

President Ruto reiterated that the era of extracting Africa's natural resources without corresponding benefits for the continent must give way to mutually beneficial partnerships.

"To every partner who seeks our minerals, our markets and our young workforce, our offer is clear: Invest with us, process with us, build with us. We will be fair in our partnerships, firm in our interests, open in our markets, and reliable in our word," he said.

Close 

He added: "Africa does not come asking for a seat at the edge of the table. We come to help set it."

On his part, President Mnangagwa commended President Ruto for his steadfast leadership during his tenure, steering COMESA with purpose and clarity, particularly in digitalisation and regional value chains.

He called on the summit to advance practical and sustainable solutions that will strengthen resilience, reposition the region to better navigate global shocks and promote the prosperity of the continent.

"With unity of purpose, let us deliver on the promise of shared prosperity, a better life and a better future for the people of Africa," he said.

President Hichilema called on African nations to walk the talk on integration by unlocking the continent's resources for the benefit of its people and the vast African market.

He said that Africans are responsible for developing Africa, noting that others will follow if citizens take the lead.

"We are all saying the right things. We must now take the extra steps to realise this vision. And nobody will do it other than ourselves," he said.

World.title: Malawi: Who Is Running Malawi? Opposition Seeks Answers Over Mutharika's Trip Abroad
World.content:
Questions are mounting over the prolonged absence of President Peter Mutharika from Malawi, as the country struggles with fuel shortages, empty hospital shelves and deepening economic hardship.

The opposition Malawi Congress Party (MCP) has accused the government of leaving anxious citizens in the dark.

Speaking in Lilongwe, MCP campaign director Moses Kunkuyu demanded urgent answers about who is steering the country while the President remains on a private trip abroad.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Kunkuyu said Malawians did not challenge the President's right to attend to personal matters. The problem, he said, was a lack of communication from those in power.

"The issue is not that the President has travelled," he said. "The issue is that people are suffering and want reassurance that somebody is in charge."

Motorists are spending hours in fuel queues, and patients are struggling to obtain essential medicines, Kunkuyu said.

He argued that citizens were entitled to know what action the government was taking to address the crises.

The MCP also directed its criticism at Vice-President Jane Ansah, accusing her of remaining silent as uncertainty grows.

Kunkuyu said she should step forward to assure the nation that the government remains functional and has a clear strategy to resolve the country's problems.

The remarks come amid mounting concern over the economy, as many Malawians face rising living costs and shortages of key goods and services.

The opposition's message is simple: citizens want answers. Until they receive them, questions about the President's absence are unlikely to fade.

World.title: South Africa: Man Beaten to Death in Central Durban
World.content:
50 people murdered the man in broad daylight on Thursday morning

On Thursday morning, an immigrant man was beaten to death by a group of about 50 people.

The man, who has not yet been named by police, was accosted by a group who were marching on Dr Pixley kaSeme Street towards Maud Mfusi Street, according to Colonel Robert Netshiunda, KwaZulu-Natal police spokesperson. A murder case has been opened.

Two men split off from the group and approached the man, said Netshiunda. Then about 50 people assaulted him, leading to his death.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A security guard, who asked to stay anonymous, told GroundUp that the group was out targeting immigrants. He said the man was probably walking to work at around 7am when he was spotted and attacked by the group.

The guard said shop owners and residents in the area have been terrorised for weeks by groups of roaming vigilantes. He said SAPS and metro officers are hardly visible and have done little to intervene.

The guard said that even South African shop owners have begun closing their doors, fearing they may be mistaken for immigrants.

When GroundUp visited the area where the man was fatally assaulted, we saw police and SANDF members.

On Wednesday, a Ugandan man was also assaulted by a mob in Durban.

Anti-immigration protests in Durban reignited after Home Affairs issued a directive on 28 September implementing a Constitutional Court ruling that asylum seekers can't be turned away on technicalities before their claims are heard. Home Affairs withdrew the directive on 9 October.

Violence erupted on Dr Pixley kaSeme Street two weeks ago during a march by hundreds of anti-immigrant protesters.

A group of anti-immigrant protesters was gathering on Che Guevara Road outside the Home Affairs Refugee Reception Centre on Thursday afternoon. It was unclear if they planned to march into the city centre later.

World.title: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night.

The hourlong showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932.

The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall.

Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate.

SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Debate opens with candidates confronted over personal controversies

The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates.

Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills.

"Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric."

Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse.

Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation.

FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO âNOT THAT INFORMEDâ: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS

"I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part."

Marshall says 'President Trump is not always right'

Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week.

"And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd.

Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda.

"No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump.

Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports.

"Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right."

Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate.

Both candidates say there are 'two genders'

The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are.

"There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls."

"There are two genders, male and female," Hamilton responded.

TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR

The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports.

Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females.

"I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight."

Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology."

Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people.

Hamilton calls AI an 'existential threat' â but can't name regulations he'd support

Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons.

"We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said.

But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer.

"You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers.

Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement.

Hamilton pushed back sharply.

"This is an existential â potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best."

BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH

Hamilton calls Biden's border policies a 'disaster'

Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle."

The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed.

"The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders."

"I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle."

Hamilton also reiterated during the debate that he would not support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader if Democrats capture control of the chamber.

World.title: Blanche won't rule out DOJ blocking election certification in 'doomsday' scenario
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to rule out whether the Department of Justice could seek to intervene in states’ midterm election certification processes, saying there are extreme scenarios that could prompt federal action.

Speaking to reporters in Virginia on Thursday, Blanche said it was not his intention to "improperly interfere with elections," but declined to rule out federal involvement if a "doomsday scenario" were to happen.

"Of course there’s scenarios that we can all come up with hypothetically, you know, some doomsday scenario, for example, right?" he said. "So, I don’t think it’s proper to make any kind of conclusory statements about what’s going to happen in the future, because I have no idea what’s happening in the future."

Blanche said he could not say there were no circumstances under which the DOJ would get involved.

NEWSOM SPARS WITH TRUMP-APPOINTED PROSECUTOR OVER 20,000 SUSPECTED NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS

"Of course, I’m not going to say that," he said. "But am I planning my days around the election to be somewhere to not certify? Of course not, no, not at all."

The DOJ's role in elections is limited under the Constitution and federal law, allowing it primarily to safeguard civil rights and prosecute people who violate election law. Federal law does not specifically authorize the department to challenge ballots or delay a state's certification of election results.

Under the Constitution and federal law, U.S. elections are run by state and local officials rather than the federal government.

During a news conference in Norfolk, Blanche was questioned about the DOJ's litigation against states, seeking to force officials to turn over unredacted voter data and halt the counting of ballots cast by thousands of voters the federal government argues are likely noncitizens.

TRUMP ADMIN SUED OVER ALLEGED ILLEGAL COLLECTION OF SENSITIVE VOTER DATA FROM 47 STATES

Blanche said the DOJ was "not trying to create chaos" but wanted to alert officials to potential problems.

"I’m not trying to not have an election certified. Of course not," Blanche said. "What we’re trying to do is guarantee to the American people that the only people that are voting are people that are eligible to vote."

In response to Blanche's comments, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said Senate Democrats "have been preparing for this for months and will be ready" for whatever administration officials try.

"As Trump and his cronies attempt to steal this election, we are fighting them at every turn," Schumer posted on X. "Our elections must always belong to the voters — not Donald Trump."

The administration sued California election officials last week, arguing they failed to act quickly enough to review names the federal government identified as likely noncitizens. The DOJ asked a judge to block the state from counting mail-in ballots from those individuals unless their eligibility could be confirmed.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The California secretary of state's office said it was given only 48 hours to review roughly 20,000 names.

The DOJ was also weighing additional election-related litigation against states, but a federal judge this week temporarily restricted certain election-related field operations and interviews in nine states through Election Day. The judge stayed the order until Friday evening to give the administration an opportunity to appeal.

Earlier this week, Democratic leaders and election groups filed a lawsuit against the administration, accusing it of "threats and intimidation" ahead of Election Day.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly said noncitizen voting poses a serious threat to election integrity, although documented instances of noncitizens casting ballots in federal elections have historically been rare.

World.title: Utah man charged with attempted hate crime after alleged threat to 'blow up' synagogue
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Utah man is facing several charges, including attempting to commit a hate crime, after he allegedly threatened to "blow up" a synagogue.

Skyler AJ Rose, 22, of Ogden, was indicted by a federal grand jury on Wednesday, on multiple federal charges, including possession of an unregistered destructive device, threatening to kill or injure people and destroy a building with an explosive, and attempting to commit a hate crime, among other offenses, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Utah.

"There is no place for hate motivated violence—attempts or otherwise—in our communities. A place of worship should be a refuge of safety, not fear," U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak for the District of Utah said in a statement. "Thanks to the dedicated work of the FBI and the outstanding efforts of our local police partners, these alleged threats were identified and stopped before anyone was harmed. Let these charges serve as a clear warning: if you attack or attempt to attack a place of worship, you will face the full force of the federal government."

On Dec. 23, 2025, Rose allegedly made multiple threatening posts on social media, according to court documents.

PENNSYLVANIA MAN ACCUSED OF PLOTTING ISIS ATTACK ARRESTED WITH RIFLE AND 190 ROUNDS OF AMMUNITION: DOJ

"I wanna blow up a synagogue," one of the posts read, according to prosecutors.

An investigation was launched and authorities learned that the posts were made from an IP address tracing back to Rose's home. The FBI then contacted the Ogden City Police Department to assist, with a home visit where authorities said they confirmed the social media handle belonged to Rose.

Investigators executed a search warrant and recovered six improvised explosive pipe bombs and one inert device, explosive precursors and components that officials say could be used to construct further improvised explosive pipe bombs, a black Samsung cellphone and two rifles with accompanying magazines and ammunition, prosecutors said.

FLORIDA MAN INDICTED FOR ALLEGEDLY PLOTTING MASS SHOOTING TARGETING JEWISH EMPLOYEES AT ADVOCACY ORGANIZATION

A subsequent search of Rose’s cellphone revealed that Rose searched online for a synagogue near him in November 2025.

"Today’s indictment stops in its tracks an alleged plan to carry out a violent attack on a synagogue," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division said in a statement. "The Department of Justice will take decisive action to protect American worshippers from violent threats, no matter where they occur."

Special Agent in Charge Robert Bohls of the Salt Lake City FBI added that "no one should have to fear for their safety because of their faith."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Every person deserves to worship freely, without threats, intimidation, or fear," Bohls said. "The FBI takes every threat seriously. Thanks to the swift, seamless collaboration with our law enforcement partners, we were able to address the threat and protect lives from potential physical harm."

The investigation also allegedly revealed evidence of child sexual abuse material on Rose's cellphone, including hundreds of cached images and screenshots depicting child sexual abuse material, according to prosecutors. Rose was also indicted on charges of receipt and possession of child pornography.

Rose's initial appearance is scheduled for Oct. 23 in federal court in Salt Lake City.

World.title: Rhamondre Stevenson's miraculous 48-yard touchdown stuns Bears as clock expires in first half
World.content:
The final play of the first half between the New England Patriots and Chicago Bears on "Thursday Night Football" was the definition of: "What in the world did we just watch?"

After Luther Burden III scored for the Bears on third-and-17 near the red zone, Chicago went up 20-7 in the waning seconds of the second quarter. With the Bears getting the ball to start the third quarter, it would’ve been the perfect ending to the first half at home.

World.title: Todd Benzinger, who caught the final out of the Reds' 1990 World Series sweep, dead at 63
World.content:
Todd Benzinger, the first baseman who caught the final out of the Cincinnati Reds’ 1990 World Series sweep, died Wednesday at age 63. His cause of death has not been released.

A Cincinnati-area native, Benzinger was drafted out of high school by the Boston Red Sox in 1981. After two seasons in Boston, he was traded to his hometown Reds ahead of the 1989 season. His defining career moment came on Oct. 20, 1990, when he caught the game-ending out in foul territory against the Oakland Athletics, securing Cincinnati's most recent title.

The Reds posted on X:

"The Cincinnati Reds are saddened by the passing of former first baseman and 1990 World Series champion Todd Benzinger. Todd will be remembered with great affection and gratitude for his place in one of the most memorable chapters in Reds history. Our deepest condolences go out to his family, friends, former teammates and all who knew and loved him."

The Reds traded Benzinger to the Kansas City Royals in 1991. He retired after the 1995 season, finishing a nine-year major league career with a .257 batting average, 733 hits, and 376 RBIs over 924 games.

Benzinger stayed active in local baseball after his playing days, managing Cincinnati's Class-A affiliate, the Dayton Dragons, from 2009 to 2010.

"Todd will forever be remembered by Reds fans for catching the final out of the 1990 World Series, but those of us who had the privilege of knowing him will remember so much more," said Rick Walls, executive director of the Reds Hall of Fame and Museum.

World.title: Super Bowl champion Marshall Faulk says he is living with Parkinson's disease
World.content:
Super Bowl champion and Southern University football coach Marshall Faulk is facing a personal battle off the field. The Pro Football Hall of Famer announced Wednesday that he has been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.

Faulk, 53, said during an appearance on "The Caring Neurologist" podcast that medication has helped limit his symptoms to hand rigidity. He added that he believes the rigidity has not worsened during the year and a half he has been dealing with the disease because of his treatment. Faulk also said he has experienced "little tremors."

Faulk told host Dr. Sandeep Thakkar that he hopes speaking publicly about his diagnosis will help others. "I want to help as many people as I can," he said.

Faulk initially dismissed the hand rigidity he experienced while golfing as normal nerves but grew concerned when it continued even when he was not competing.

"I just thought it was normal nerves when putting and stuff like that," he said. "But it started to be times where ... I was playing, but I wasn't in a match, and it would still do that. And I was like, 'Wow, is that something -- is that normal?' And the doctor was -- he literally was like, 'You need to go get checked.'"

FORMER NFL STAR CHRIS JOHNSON SAYS HE'S BEEN DIAGNOSED WITH ALS

Faulk’s outlook was shaped in part by a dinner with Muhammad Ali, who also had Parkinson’s. He left that interaction thinking, "He’s all there," and said the diagnosis did not make him believe his life was over.

Faulk was selected No. 2 overall by the Indianapolis Colts in the 1994 NFL Draft.
