World.title: What is PHP, and how did a flaw in its code lead several websites to go dark this week?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A vulnerability in a critical piece of the internet's infrastructure was exposed this week, sending website operators worldwide scrambling to implement a fix.

The problem resided in part of the PHP coding language — a commonly used software that's "the backbone of the internet," according to Isaac Privett, a senior penetration tester at Toronto-based cybersecurity firm Packetlabs.

And the vulnerability had been there for years, potentially allowing bad actors to access sites, make changes to them and harvest data.

The issue prompted many to take their websites offline while they implemented a fix, causing some websites — including government ones in Canada — to go dark.

Here's what you need to know about the PHP language, how it came to light and how serious the vulnerability is.

What is PHP?

PHP is an open-source computer language — meaning anyone can download and use it for free — that's widely used across the internet. The tech is managed by the non-profit PHP Foundation, with a team of volunteer board members and a handful of developers.

When you visit a website, a lot of pieces of information, such as images, links and what colour a site should appear in, all need to be assembled and displayed correctly to end users, explains technology analyst Carmi Levy. That's the job PHP does, Levy says, pulling those elements together and bringing websites to life.

"PHP is silently working in the background to make sure that websites make it from disjointed data sitting on a server somewhere to a live website that you can interact with on the browser, on the device that is sitting in front of you," said Levy, who's based in London, Ont.

Wiz, one of the cybersecurity firms that helped identify the issue, estimates that about 70 per cent of websites are powered by PHP, while web technology tracker W3Techs puts the figure at 75 per cent.

A programmer works with PHP code at RK Solutions software development company in Guernica, Spain, on Thursday. (Vincent West/Reuters)

That widespread use makes the tech a "foundational" piece of technology for the internet to function, Levy said, and that's why a vulnerability with it can have potentially wide-reaching consequences.

What's the problem, and how was it discovered?

A group of researchers from two cybersecurity companies — Calif and Wiz — released blog posts Wednesday, saying they had found two vulnerabilities in PHP. The researchers had been working as part of an OpenAI program to detect potential vulnerabilities across the internet, including within PHP.

Ryan Austin, a cybersecurity researcher at Calif.io who helped identify the problems, says he was aware of a 2004 security issue with PHP and sent OpenAI's GPT‑5.6 Sol to look in the same part of PHP's code for other potential bugs.

"And then a few days later, we managed to find something pretty serious," Austin said.

The PHP Foundation explained in a Wednesday release that both issues sit in "parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling."

Austin explains that when PHP encounters an error, it leaves behind memory details that can be corrupted and potentially give hackers a way into sites.

Tech analyst Carmi Levy says the fact that PHP is used so widely across the internet is part of what makes a vulnerability with it so concerning. (Submitted by Carmi Levy)

Once inside, hackers would be able to make changes to the websites — potentially installing malware or removing content from the sites — or to read sensitive data such as passwords, according to Levy.

Wiz said the vulnerabilities had existed for more than a decade. PHP Foundation acknowledged that a researcher had theorized this possible exploit in 2024, but no concrete way to enact it was found at the time.

PHP Foundation said the delay in implementing a solution was a "structural failure" caused by a lack of resources and the security team's decision process.

How serious is it?

Levy likens it to if one of the most popular makers of locks for doors discovered a master key was widely available to use.

"So someone could literally walk up to your front door, put that master key in, and they could gain access to your home," Levy said.

He explains security incidents are scored on a scale from zero to 10 using something called the Common Vulnerability Scoring System. These ones ranked as a 9.2, which Levy says means they're quite serious.

WATCH | Websites worldwide taken down amid fears PHP flaw opens door to hackers: Websites around world taken down after flawed code opens them up to hackers | Duration closed caption 1:47 Government and corporate websites around the world were taken down after developers found flaws in the popular PHP code that could open the door to armies of hackers.

"One vulnerability in a technology that almost everybody uses means there's a potential global impact here," Levy said.

From Austin's perspective, it's "probably one of the worst vulnerabilities that I've ever seen."

How is it being fixed?

Cybersecurity experts say the good news is that a solution exists.

PHP Foundation released patches for the vulnerability on Wednesday and urged those who use it in their websites to implement the fix as soon as possible.

Government cybersecurity agencies and government leaders around the world, including in Canada, echoed that call.

Many websites, including government ones from Canada, France and Japan, went dark while the potential security issue was remedied. Provincial sites for Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island were down for the day, for example, but both appeared to be running again on Thursday.

The U.S. National Security Agency's cyber unit called for any organizations that couldn't patch the issue immediately to take their websites offline until the fix could be put in place.

While websites going down caused some panic, Levy says the story has a silver lining. Those sites were taken down temporarily out of an abundance of caution after researchers identified a vulnerability before hackers did, and Levy says that shows the system for flagging these kinds of things is working.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government site was offline on Wednesday after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. (CBC)

Some sites experienced hack attempts after the vulnerability was made public, but those didn't appear to work. Cloudflare's CEO, for example, said on social media that the Cloudflare network experienced tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw within 45 minutes of the announcement being made and "hundreds of thousands" within two hours.

On Wednesday, PHP Foundation told CBC News in an email they hadn't seen any evidence of hackers being able to successfully exploit the vulnerability.

Do I need to take action?

Cybersecurity experts say because the issue affects the back end of websites, the onus is mostly on those who run them — like businesses or other organizations — to make sure they're implementing the fix.

That's fairly straightforward for website operators to do in most cases — somewhat like updating a personal computer, according to Privett from Packetlabs.

"You just have to upgrade to the newest version of PHP, and that seems to handle 99 per cent of your problems," Privett said.

WATCH | How AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter: AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter | Duration closed caption 1:29 A new EY report suggests AI will become a major force behind cybercrime in 2026 as programs help attackers hone their scamming skills.

But because the vulnerability and the fix have been made public for quite some time now, Privett says website owners will need to be on watch for indicators of possible breaches that could have happened before they were able to put the patches in place.

"It's always a good idea that after you patch, just to look for indicators of compromise in case that someone got in your system using that bug," Privett said.

Privett also encourages consumers who have their own websites or apps to double check whether they use PHP to make sure that they're protected.

And for all consumers, Levy says they can protect themselves from any potential kind of data breach by maximizing their own personal digital safety protocols. Practicing good password hygiene — by changing passwords often and not reusing them — and activating two-factor authentication, for example, help ensure that even if hackers were to access your data on a breached website, they wouldn't be as effective at using that information against you.

World.title: 'Agent Layla': A sex assault victim went undercover to bring her abuser to justice. Now he's out on parole
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A woman who went undercover to get a confession from the man who sexually assaulted her says she's "fed up" and "retraumatized" by a parole board decision to release him.

The parole board decision comes as Vienna Luke has received support from people across Canada and abroad who have heard her extraordinary story of going undercover as an RCMP agent in the CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla.

"I feel deflated," said Luke of the decision to release Justin Sewell early. "My story being out there is like, 'Wow, look.' But there's still so much work to be done."

18 years of fighting for justice. 6 months in prison. 7 months in a halfway house.

The parole board made its decision to release Sewell on Oct. 6, citing his low assessed risk to reoffend and his compliance and participation in therapeutic programs during his time in a halfway house.

Justin Sewell (left) was a trusted brother-in-law to Vienna Luke (second from right) and Shawnessy Luke (right). Vienna met him when she was 10 years old. (Submitted by Shawnessy Luke)

As described in the Personally: Agent Layla podcast and in court documents, Sewell drugged, assaulted and photographed Luke in 2007 when she was 20 years old.

After wrestling for years with what really happened the night she was drugged into unconsciousness and assaulted, Luke decided in 2019 to report the assault to police after she and her sister, Shawnessy Luke, recorded a phone conversation with Sewell's ex-lover who said he disclosed putting ketamine in Vienna's drink. In court, Sewell has denied it was ketamine, but a provincial court judge found it was either ketamine or Valium.

RCMP proposed a plan to put Vienna Luke undercover, giving her the code name Agent Layla. They used emails to entice Sewell to meet her face to face at a hotel lounge at the Vancouver International Airport under the premise that him telling the truth might be a path back to family reconciliation.

In the recording from the sting, obtained by CBC and included in Episode 3 of the Agent Layla podcast, Vienna Luke pushes Sewell to describe the specific details of his offence. He admits to drugging and assaulting her, and to watching her through her bedroom window on two separate occasions.

Eventually, Sewell pleaded guilty to sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism.

Sewell was a successful veterinarian in the northern B.C. community of Fort St. John at the time of the assault. (Submitted by Shawnessy Luke)

After what was described in court as an unusually lengthy sentencing hearing in which Sewell took the stand arguing that a self-diagnosed addiction to pornography was the root cause of his offences, a provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to two years less a day of house arrest in April 2025.

Seven months later, a panel of B.C. Court of Appeal judges overturned that decision and imposed a sentence of 33 months less a day to be served in prison.

After serving about six months in a federal institution, Sewell was granted day parole and transferred to a halfway house in April 2026.

Since then, according to notifications provided to his victims and viewed by CBC News, Sewell has been granted permission to leave the halfway house and travel to his home in Fort St. John or to "recreate" in Grande Prairie, Alta., for 70 days over a period of less than seven months.

Discrepancies in 2 Parole Board of Canada decisions made 6 months apart

The Parole Board first considered Sewell's applications to be granted full parole in an April 2026 face-to-face hearing. His case was up for review again six months later in early October. This time he was subject to a paper review, a parole decision-making process that assesses documents written about the offender's behaviour and programs they have completed, but does not interview the offender.

The two boards came to a few markedly different conclusions.

The parole board members in April 2026 found in their decision that Sewell "engaged in considerable rationalizing and minimizing" of his offences. Instead of addressing the "key issues leading to your violence," the board found he focused on "[his] use of pornography and the problems in [his] marriage, as though solving those particular problems was a solution also for the behavioural issues that led to the sexual assault."

"The Board believes that a day or full parole release to your home community is not adequate to the task of protecting the community from your risk."

With support of her sister Shawnessy Luke (left), Vienna Luke went undercover in her own case and obtained a confession. The sisters continue to work together seeking justice in the case. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Six months later, despite letters from Vienna and Shawnessy Luke imploring the board to weigh heavily the findings of the April board members who interviewed Sewell and decided against full parole, the October parole board members found Sewell's "compliance, community adjustment, ongoing therapeutic involvement, and low assessed risk" support a reduction in supervision and that release on full parole "will not present an undue risk to society."

That board granted full parole on Oct. 6. Correctional Service Canada confirmed the end of Sewell's sentence is Jan. 1, 2028. For the 14 months that remain, Sewell is required to report all sexual and non-sexual relationships with females, and he is prohibited from accessing pornography.

'How is [he] allowed the freedoms to go on a recreational hunting trip?'

For Vienna Luke, it has been an intense time. On the one hand, she's received messages from podcast listeners commending her for sharing her story of confronting her abuser, which led to a conviction and prison time. On the other hand, she's found herself still advocating behind the scenes for justice in her case.

"I'm a person that chose to report," she said. "You can understand why people are just like, 'I'm going to move on with my life.'"

In the most recent parole board decision, board members cited a letter from the Luke sisters questioning the 70 days Sewell was allowed to leave the halfway house, including his release "for the purposes of a hunting trip."

Justin Sewell in a photo where he is hunting. This image is from before he faced the courts for his assault on Vienna Luke. Sewell is now under a 10-year prohibition on possessing firearms. (Submitted by Shawnessy Luke)

The sisters say that in September they began to suspect that some of Sewell's trips might be to participate in hunting, an activity he described as an important hobby in court.

Concerned he might be violating a 10-year ban on using firearms, the Luke sisters say they called the Fort St. John RCMP non-emergency line to alert the police. They say the officer on the line told them Sewell had been granted permission to go hunting with an "approved associate."

Vienna Luke said she met with Correctional Service Canada and parole board officials to express her concerns.

"As they talked and continued to justify how they were handling him ... and their allowances to him, I started shaking. I was so upset," she said.

The sisters weren't worried for their personal safety. They live in Vancouver, about 800 kilometres from Fort St. John as the crow flies. Their concern was that the decision to grant him time to participate in a hobby was at odds with the seriousness of the crime.

"We had a hunch he was going hunting, but we didn't think he was approved to go hunting," said Vienna Luke.

"We were livid," said Shawnessy Luke.

CBC News reached out to Correctional Service Canada to confirm the details of Sewell's permission to go hunting. In an email, it says the organization cannot provide details of travel permits because of the Privacy Act.

The statement adds that "[w]hile we cannot talk about specifics of this case due to privacy, please note that if, at any time, an offender's risk increases or there is a change in their behaviour ... we take immediate action."

The Luke sisters' concerns were summarized by the parole board, who wrote in the October decision: "It is also concerning that your index offence involved violence and yet you are requesting to engage in an extended activity which involves weapons."

Vienna Luke wants systemic change

Vienna Luke knows the outcome of her case – a conviction in a historic sexual assault – is rare. But throughout the lengthy process since she first reported the assault seven years ago, she has found herself questioning whether the justice system is working for sexual assault survivors.

"You would think that maybe the fact he went to jail, he went to a halfway house, the justice system is telling me that I should feel grateful. Look at what you got," she said.

"I feel ungrateful. What did we do all this work for?"

Vienna Luke told her story in honour of other women who have told their stories of surviving sexual assault. (Submitted by Vienna Luke)

In interviews for the podcast and elsewhere, Vienna has emphasized she is telling her story to honour sexual assault victims who went before her. She told their stories, including their struggles with the justice system, which gave her strength in the hardest times.

Now she's receiving emails from other women telling her she has become a symbol of strength for them.

"I've come so far," she said. "To be in a place where I can speak about what happened to me, what was done to me publicly, and everything I did in this process is unbelievable and really I just feel so proud."

World.title: Rogers to charge new fee for bills paid by credit card, says practice is 'increasingly common'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Rogers Communications says it will roll out a new fee early next year for customers who pay their bill with a credit card.

The Canadian telecom giant says a 1.6 per cent "processing charge" will apply starting Jan. 17, for both auto-pay and one-time credit card payments.

"The charge applies every time you pay your Rogers bill with a credit card," Rogers says on its website .

"This reflects the fees we are charged by credit card companies."

According to Rogers, the fee is not applicable to customers in Quebec, nor those on certain "specialized plans" and former Shaw Mobile customers who migrated to Rogers when it acquired Shaw Communications in 2023 .

A Rogers spokesperson tells CBC News that its credit card processing costs have increased by nearly 40 per cent since 2020, amounting to about $150 million annually in fees for the company.

WATCH | New fee for some Rogers customers: Rogers adds 1.6% surcharge for credit card payments | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 8:42 Some Rogers customers outside of Quebec will soon see a change on their bills. Starting Jan. 17, 2027, the telecommunications company says customers paying a Rogers bill with a credit card will be charged a 1.6 per cent processing fee. The company says other payment options, including debit cards, are available without the charge.

Other forms of payment are not subject to the new fee. These include direct debt and online banking payments, cheques, Rogers gift cards, prepaid cards, Debit Mastercard and Visa Debit.

"If you choose to pay your bill by credit card, it's increasingly common across many sectors for a credit card fee to apply," Rogers said.

Retail analyst Bruce Winder expects consumers will "grudgingly" swallow the new charge.

"Rogers I'm sure has done some research and surveys with customers to test the waters to see how customers will react, whether they'll leave Rogers, or whether they will just pay it," he said.

"Companies are always looking to either lower cost or increase revenue. One of the easiest ways to increase revenue is on your existing customers."



Rogers is scheduled to report financial results before the stock market opens on Friday. While the company has reported stronger sales in the first half of 2026, its Toronto-listed shares are down more than 10 per cent year-to-date.

Marvin Ryder is an associate professor of marketing at McMaster University's DeGroote School of Business. He says many consumers are probably not aware of the transaction fees that businesses pay to credit card companies.

"That fee can be as high as 3.5 per cent, depending on the benefits you're getting from your credit card," he said on Thursday.

"Some companies are beginning to discover that those fees that they pay to take credit cards are getting bigger and bigger and bigger."

Winder says Rogers is now clearly spelling this out for consumers.

"They can say, 'Look, we're passing this onto you. This isn't our cost. This is the cost we get from the credit card provider.' So, they can sort of deflect a little bit of the blame for the charge to another company, versus if they increase their fees, then that's really on them."

Telus scrapped similar fee

In 2022, rival telecom provider Telus asked the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) for permission to add a 1.5 per cent surcharge to the bills of some landline phone customers who pay their bill using a credit card. The CRTC rejected this request.

However, the regulator's approval was only required for a fee on landline services. Telus rolled out a 1.5 per cent credit card fee for mobile and home internet customers.

Telus scrapped the fee in 2023 , following a settlement between credit card companies and merchants allowing merchants to pass on the cost directly to customers.

Telus did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday.

A Bell spokesperson said it does not currently charge clients a fee for credit card payments.

World.title: Emmy-winning actor Tom Skerritt, with roles in Alien and Top Gun, dies at 93
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tom Skerritt, the Emmy-winning actor who embodied a solid, wry authority figure — whether as a flight instructor in Top Gun, a tough-but-fair sheriff on TV's Picket Fences or the doomed captain of Alien — has died. He was 93.

Skerritt died Wednesday of natural causes, his family said in a statement.

"While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humour, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought into our lives. He cared deeply about imagination, creativity, storytelling, service, veterans, the natural world and helping others find and share their own voices," the statement said.

Skerritt was twice nominated for an Emmy — both for Picket Fences, winning outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 1993. Other career highlights included playing Shirley MacLaine's patient husband in The Turning Point, Sally Field's husband in Steel Magnolias and a scheming opportunist who stands in the way of Jodie Foster's attempt to communicate with extraterrestrial life in Contact.

From left, Tom Skerritt, David E. Kelley, creator of Picket Fences, and actor Kathy Baker after the show won best drama series during the 45th annual Emmy Awards in Pasadena, Calif., on Sept. 19, 1993. (Douglas C. Pizac/AP Photo)

"A writer once described me as a character actor locked in a leading man's body, and I've always loved that. It's a nice compliment. I've been able to walk the line between television and features," he told the Seattle Post-Intelligencer in 1997.

Onstage, he was the narrator in Our Town at Seattle's Intiman Theatre in 2004 and made his Broadway debut in 2013 in an adaptation of John Grisham's A Time to Kill, in which The Associated Press wrote that he "nicely pulls off a charming, disgraced and drunken lawyer."

Skerritt's early life

Skerritt grew up in a middle-class family in Detroit. His father a small businessman and his mother a housewife. He had two brothers; a sister died as a child.

He spent four years in the Air Force, attended Wayne State University and then switched to the University of California, Los Angeles, to study filmmaking, inspired by Citizen Kane.

His performance in a Los Angeles theatre production of The Rainmaker led to his first film role — a supporting part as a sergeant in the scrappy, $250,000 independent Korean War film War Hunt in 1962. The movie marked the debuts of Skerritt, Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola.

Redford and Skerritt had been vying for the same lead role, with Redford winning out. Years later, Redford, now directing, cast Skerritt in A River Runs Through It, as the stern Rev. John Maclean, a minister whose governing passions are his faith and fly-fishing. The New York Times praised his "halting, thoughtful manner."

Redford, who died last year, became a lifelong friend. "There was such a deep connection we made with each other that it matured into a level-headed friendship," Redford told the Seattle Times in 2007. "His values were close to mine, and he kept his integrity."

Alien and Top Gun

The cast of Alien poses on set. From left, actors John Hurt, Veronica Cartwright, Tom Skerritt, Yaphet Kotto, Sigourney Weaver, Harry Dean Stanton and Ian Holm are pictured in 1979. (Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation/Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

After War Hunt, Skerritt struggled for screen time, landing a small role in M*A*S*H and Thieves Like Us for Robert Altman, and a bit part as a motorcycle cop in Harold and Maude for Hal Ashby.

Things changed with The Turning Point, which earned him a National Board of Review award. Then came Alien, with Skerritt playing the beleaguered and doomed captain of the Nostromo, crouched in a dark, claustrophobic duct while hunting the alien with a sputtering flamethrower. He told the Seattle Times that what appealed to him in the script was that the lead actor disappeared and "the woman becomes the hero. I really like that idea."

Then came another memorable role as Tom Cruise's instructor in the landmark Top Gun: "Gentlemen, you are the top one per cent of all Naval aviators. The elite. The best of the best. We'll make you better," he told the students. "This school is about combat. There are no points for second place."

Skerritt achieved perhaps his best notices as the kindly sheriff in Picket Fences, a drama created by David E. Kelley that won 14 Emmy Awards — including one for Skerritt — and a Golden Globe over its four-year run from 1992 to 1996.

Skerritt co-starred opposite Kathy Baker, who played his doctor wife, in the community of Rome, Wisconsin, a place of bizarre happenings, including a robber who left a trail of frogs and the pope becoming the primary witness to a murder.

"It was written by the best writer on television," he told the A.V. Club in 2019. "That was the magic and brilliance of it. Because I wasn't trying to do a series, but then they said Kathy Baker was going to do it, and I thought, 'She's fabulous — what do they want me for?'"

Tom Skerritt with his wife Julie Tokashiki in Geneva, Switzerland in 2012. (Andreas Rentz/Getty Images for IWC)

On the small screen, Skerritt played William Walker on ABC's Brothers & Sisters, Jimmy Ford on TNT's Leverage and the recurring character Evan Drake on Cheers. He starred in the Hallmark movie What the Deaf Man Heard, alongside Matthew Modine, Judith Ivey and James Earl Jones. He also modelled for Guess jeans.



Directing and writing — his initial dream — had been overtaken by a career in front of the camera, though he managed to direct and star in the 1997 television movie Divided by Hate.

"Things happen," he told The Ottawa Citizen in 1992. "You get hired for a film and the roles kept coming for me. I kept telling myself that if I stuck with acting it would be a really good training for what the problems are in directing. Then the family came along and I had to support them. The years flew by and there was a time when I said I would give up acting and really try to get into directing. But it hasn't worked out that way and I have no regrets."

He is survived by his third wife, Julie Tokashiki, and five children.

World.title: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Robert Harold Corbett was sure he was an American citizen until federal agents showed up at his door with an arrest warrant earlier this month.

Corbett was born in Canada, but raised in the United States, he told reporters outside a federal courthouse in Raleigh, N.C.

"I did not find out I was adopted until I was 51 years old," said Corbett, who has been charged with one count of falsely claiming citizenship to vote and one count of voting by an alien. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) says he voted in six elections since 1998.

Corbett is among at least 15 Canadians who have been caught up in a crackdown on non-citizen voting by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

On Wednesday, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa drew a direct connection between those prosecutions and what it described as Canadian interference in American politics.

In a statement, the embassy accused Canadian politicians of openly attempting to influence the U.S. election through trade policy, political campaigning and public remarks. It also singled out Canadians for illegally voting, claiming Canada has the second-highest number of its citizens facing fraudulent or illegal voting charges of any country.

The embassy listed 11 Canadians as having been charged with illegally voting, but CBC has identified two more cases announced by the DOJ not mentioned in the statement.

"All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way. Americans decide America's elections," said the statement, which comes amid heightened tensions between the U.S. and Canada over tariffs and trade.

On Thursday, the DOJ announced charges against two additional Canadians — part of a total of six U.S. permanent residents accused of either illegally voting, or falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to vote, in 2022 and 2024 elections.

WATCH | U.S. ambassador to Canada accuses Canadian politicans of interference: Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. midterms, Joly says | Duration closed caption 1:19 Asked about the United States Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra's comments about watching for Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections, Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly says 'we never do that and we never accept that also being done to us in Canada.' She says her recent visits to the U.S. were 'to attract investments' by American companies and she will continue to do so.

Since late last year, federal prosecutors have charged dozens of non-citizens, many of them longtime U.S. permanent residents, with illegally voting in federal elections. But several of those accused say they didn't know they were breaking the law, with some saying they didn't even know they were registered to vote.

Investigations have consistently found that illegal voting by non-citizens is highly uncommon, said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation and Research.

"This is likely an attempt to sow doubt about the elections in advance of an election in which the president and his administration might fear the voters might reject them," Becker said.

A Reuters investigation published in September found that software glitches and clerical errors across a dozen states could have added more than 30,000 self-declared non-citizens to voter rolls since 2000.

Becker said the DOJ has an "election crimes manual" that cautions prosecutors against taking enforcement actions close to elections because of the potential to influence voters.

"There's no reason these arrests couldn't have been made on Nov. 4 or some time after," he said.

Aaron Cohen, a Florida criminal defence lawyer who represents several non-citizens facing voting-related charges, said some of the confusion among his clients stems from election officials failing to properly verify eligibility when registering voters.

"I feel strongly that it's a policy decision for whatever policy outcomes are that the current administration is seeking," Cohen said of the U.S. efforts to prosecute non-citizens for voter fraud.

Lawyers who spoke with CBC News said U.S. voter registration systems can sometimes catch non-citizens up in errors, and one of them says he has seen an uptick in non-citizens being questioned last month.

Handcuffs, prison time

The DOJ's news release including information about Corbett's arrest features images of people handcuffed with their arms being held by police officers and faces blurred.

A video posted by the department on social media platform X on Tuesday features a COPS-style montage of masked officers and a man in pyjamas being led down a brightly lit hallway, advertising the arrests of 28 people in California for non-citizen voting. Two Canadians were among them.

Corbett told WRAL, a North Carolina NBC affiliate broadcaster, that he spent the night in a crowded and dirty jail cell with "people peeing on the floor." He said he was certain he was a dual citizen of Canada and the U.S.

Paige Adamson, a Canadian citizen who has lived in Point Roberts, Wash., as a U.S. permanent resident for 14 years, was accused by U.S. border agents of illegally voting and questioned for several hours in September, CBC previously reported.

Adamson, who was heading back to the States after a birthday dinner in British Columbia, was told t he Department of Homeland Security (DHS) believes she falsely claimed she was a U.S. citizen in order to vote in Washington state.

The department also alleged Adamson voted in Washington state's 2018 general election and cited those allegations as grounds for removing Adamson from the U.S. Adamson said she has no memory of ever voting in the U.S.

A North Carolina Election Integrity Team sign in Spanish, seen Oct. 25, 2024, in Durham, N.C., warns non-citizens not to vote and that doing so could lead to deportation — a notice that advocacy groups say could intimidate legitimate voters who speak Spanish. (Jonathan Drake/Reuters)

The consequences for the accusations can be serious. The Trump administration has sought to deport non-citizens convicted of voting illegally, and in June, another North Carolina-based Canadian, Denis Bouchard, was sentenced to two months in federal prison.

Others have successfully challenged their charges. In August, a federal judge in Florida acquitted Gaynell Jeffries, a Canadian citizen accused of illegally voting, after she argued that an election official had mistakenly told her permanent residents were eligible to cast ballots.

Broader implications for democracy

Frédérick Gagnon, a political science professor at the Université du Québec à Montréal and the head of the university's Observatory on the U.S., said the prosecutions in the U.S. are unfolding under a climate of fear and uncertainty for immigrants.

"People are worried about profiling. They're worried of getting arrested, and we can see that ICE wants to operate so quickly that sometimes they're proceeding with arrests that aren't justified," Gagnon said.

LISTEN | Political scientist Lucan Way says the U.S. has crossed the line into 'competitive authoritarianism': The Current 16:14 Is the U.S. sliding into competitive authoritarianism? Ever since U.S. President Donald Trump took office for the second time, he's been criticized for eroding democracy and the rule of law. Now, political scientist Lucan Way, argues that the United States has definitively crossed the line into a system of what he calls competitive authoritarianism. Lucan Way, a Distinguished Professor of Democracy in the Department of Political Science at the University of Toronto, explains what that looks like, and whether it can be reversed.

He said Trump's repeated allegations of widespread voter fraud also serve a political purpose by mobilizing his supporters.

Both Becker and Gagnon see no indication Canadians in particular are being singled out.

"They're looking at anybody they can possibly find because they are desperate to make the lie of widespread non-citizen voting look a little better," Becker said.

World.title: 'They destroyed my life': 2 Sask. men imprisoned for exploiting woman from Bangladesh
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Bangladeshi woman who was trafficked and exploited by two men in Saskatchewan — and repeatedly raped by one of them — says she now lives in fear and struggles to trust anyone.

"I can't forget them. They stopped my dream. They destroyed my life. They ruined my honour, my future, my family, my career," the woman wrote in her victim impact statement.

Mohammed (M.D.) Masum, 45, and Sohel Haider, 56, were convicted earlier this year of human trafficking and returned to Saskatoon provincial court on Thursday for their sentencing.

Masum was also found guilty of three counts of sexual assault, for actions that the judge classified "in clearer and simpler layman's language" as rapes. The victim's identity is protected by a court-ordered publication ban.

Even though her name has not been published, she said in her victim impact statement that the gossip in her home community in Bangladesh has affected her family's honour and ruined her siblings' futures.

The woman said she used to be independent and self-sufficient, but now depends on others for support and struggles with that. She questions her decision to come to Canada, where she felt like a product being sold to a customer.

The charges covered a period between Aug. 1, 2022, and March 31, 2023. The woman came to Saskatchewan after being told she would have a job in a restaurant that would help her stay in the country as a temporary foreign worker.

She worked first at a restaurant Haider operated in Gull Lake, then she was sent to Tisdale to work in a restaurant operated by Masum. They did not have the proper work permits for her, but said they were working on it. She was not properly paid and was forced to work long hours, six days a week.

When she finally received a work permit, it was for a different restaurant in Elrose. Shortly after arriving there, the woman fled with the help of some people who had become concerned about her.

Trust violated, Crown argues

Human trafficking carries a mandatory minimum sentence of four years in prison.

Crown prosecutor Leslie Dunning argued that Masum's crimes — one count of human trafficking and three counts of sexual assault — called for a total sentence of 15 years in prison, and Haider should be sentenced to five and a half years for the human trafficking.

Dunning argued both offenders were in positions of trust and authority over the woman, and they violated that trust by controlling "virtually every aspect of her life" after she came to Saskatchewan.

In addition, Masum exploited the woman "for his own sexual gratification" in a series of sexual assaults, including some that involved physical violence, Dunning argued.

Masum's lawyer Zachary Carter argued for a total sentence of seven to nine years, suggesting that is still a "substantial" sentence.

Haider's lawyer Chris Gratton argued for the mandatory minimum of four years, arguing there was an absence of aggravating factors that would push the sentence higher than the minimum, which is itself a significant sentence.

Restitution ordered

Judge Miguel Martinez delivered his sentencing decision late Thursday afternoon.

He agreed with Gratton that Haider should serve the mandatory minimum sentence of four years.

For Masum, the judge imposed a total sentence of 14 years.

He also ordered both men to pay restitution to the victim for wages owed to her. Haider was ordered to pay $5,885.16 and Masum was ordered to pay $12,268.
