Why Chile Is Hesitating

Meganoticias says the doubts concern what the coalition’s forces may do. One fear is lethal force inside other American countries, and Barros is reported to be a sceptic.

In September, when Chile joined the Shield, Barros said it would not compromise sovereignty or create obligations, Meganoticias recalls. Signing the A3C, the channel argues, could open the door to the military component he then ruled out.

BioBioChile adds that the government must also check whether Chilean law allows the commitments. Meganoticias says the Palace has been under strong domestic and foreign pressure to sign.

How Chile Joined the Shield in September

Chile’s foreign ministry announced on Tuesday, 22 September that Chile joined the Shield group, El Dinámo reported. It listed benefits such as intelligence access, data analysis and police training, and said each state acts under its own legal obligations.

Kast joined the Shield meeting hosted by Trump in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, El Dinámo reported. Former presidents Michelle Bachelet and Gabriel Boric later asked him to reconsider Chile’s place in the Shield, Pauta reported.

Foreign Minister Francisco Pérez Mackenna told senators on Wednesday, 7 October the text has no joint forces, bases or troops. He said it states political intentions and creates no legal obligations, Pauta reported.

Washington’s Push and the Domestic Debate

Meganoticias says the US Embassy in Santiago lobbied government-aligned legislators this week to reverse the decision. They include National Renewal senators Manuel José Ossandón and Andrés Longton, and Republican Party president Arturo Squella.

Ossandón, president of the Andean Parliament, told the channel Chile cannot end up like Colombia, Ecuador and Peru with organised crime. He added that any partnership must protect sovereignty.

US executive sources told Meganoticias that joining would not cost sovereignty. They said each military action would need national approval, and that Chile would be the only Shield member not signing.

Refusing the A3C would not by itself remove Chile from the Shield, Meganoticias reports. Palace sources also weigh joining as an observer, which would avoid the full conditions.

Meganoticias says the government awaits Foreign Minister Pérez Mackenna’s return from Europe to decide over the weekend. Esta Pasando repeats that the answer would be communicated on Monday, which would be 26 October.

What It Means for US Readers

Chile’s choice signals how far Washington’s anti-cartel campaign reaches in South America. A refusal would not end cooperation, because Chile could stay in the political Shield and keep sharing intelligence.

Investors and travellers should expect no immediate change, since nothing is signed and no decision date is official. Related moves include Argentina adding the Sinaloa cartel to its terror list and the Guyana defence partnership signed at the Pentagon.

See also Uruguay hosting 10 US agents, Bolivia asking US backing for two police units and the Chile expulsion law. The Chile news hub carries the latest national news.

What Is Not Known

The government has not publicly confirmed the report, and no on-the-record statement from La Moneda or the ministries was found. The story rests on unnamed sources first reported by Meganoticias in a single exclusive, and other outlets repeat it.

It is not known whether Chile will attend the 27 October meeting, send a delegation, or take observer status. The text of the A3C agreement and what exactly signatories commit to were not available.

The US claim that Chile would be the only Shield member not signing is not independently confirmed. Figures also differ, with Meganoticias citing 19 members and observers and BioBioChile expecting 19 to 20 signatories.

What Comes Next

Next week the Defence Ministry is due to assess whether Chilean law allows joining. Meganoticias and Esta Pasando report that the answer would come on Monday, 26 October, before the Tuesday, 27 October meeting.

A no to the coalition would not mean leaving the Shield, and a yes could still come as observer status. Any of these outcomes remains possible until officials speak.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition?

It is a US-led military cooperation initiative against cartels in the Americas, part of the Shield of the Americas. Its agreement is due to be signed on 27 October.

Has Chile decided to stay out?

Not officially. Meganoticias reports the government is preparing to say no, but sources say the decision could change at the last minute.

Would Chile leave the Shield of the Americas?

Not by refusing the coalition alone. Meganoticias says Chile could stay in the political Shield, which covers intelligence sharing and cooperation.

Why is Chile hesitant?

Officials doubt what coalition forces could do, including whether lethal force could be used inside other countries. Chilean law must also allow the commitments.

Who is pressing Chile to sign?

The US Embassy has lobbied government-aligned senators, Meganoticias reports. Washington says joining does not cost sovereignty and every military action needs national approval.

Sources: Meganoticias, 22 October; BioBioChile, 22 October; Esta Pasando, 22 October; El Dinámo, 22 September (foreign ministry statement); Pauta, 7 October (all accessed 23 October 2026).

World.title: Ivory Coast Starts 50MW Katiola Solar Plant
World.content:
RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

IVORY COAST · ENERGY

Key Facts — The country Ivory Coast (Côte d’Ivoire) is a French-speaking West African nation and the world’s top cocoa producer, with Abidjan as its economic capital.

— What happened On Thursday 22 October 2026 Energy Minister Mamadou Sangafowa-Coulibaly laid the first stone of the plant at Lonankaha, near Katiola.

— The plant The plant is rated 50 megawatts-peak (MWp), the maximum output of its panels in full sun.

— The numbers The investment is about 33 billion CFA francs (about US$56 million), per the 2025 announcement, and building should take 15 months.

— Who benefits The developer says the plant will bring electricity to more than 300,000 people in the Hambol region.

— Who pays The state is not paying: the company designs, finances, owns and runs the plant under a 25-year concession.

— Still open Lenders have signed only mandate letters; no buyer contract or exact completion date has been published.

Ivory Coast has started building the Katiola solar plant, a 50MW project in a town in the north of the country. Energy Minister Mamadou Sangafowa-Coulibaly laid the first stone on Thursday 22 October 2026, according to Ivorian outlets including Linfodrome and Koaci.

For US readers, the project shows a West African market where private developers, not the state, put up the money for power plants. American solar firms, equipment makers and lenders looking at Africa can use it as a guide to how such deals are structured.

What Happened at Katiola

The minister laid the first stone of the Katiola solar plant at Lonankaha, a locality of Katiola in the Hambol region of north-central Ivory Coast. Katiola’s mayor, Thomas Camara, and a representative of the developer also spoke, according to Linfodrome and the Ivorian outlet Koaci.

Koaci reports that the minister told the developer to give construction jobs first to young people from Katiola and Lonankaha. The developer expects about 150 direct jobs during building, 350 people at the peak, and around 20 permanent posts.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Côte d’Ivoire Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Is Building the Plant

The developer is Katiola Solar Power, which Ecofin Agency described in 2025 as a subsidiary of the Swiss energy group JC Mont-Fort. The Ivorian outlet APA says Toyota and the French utility EDF also back the project, which the 2025 reports do not mention.

Ivory Coast’s government approved the deal at a Council of Ministers meeting on Wednesday 21 May 2025, after the agreement was signed in December 2024. The concession runs for 25 years, so the company keeps the plant and sells its power for a quarter of a century.

What the Plant Costs and Produces

The investment is about 33 billion CFA francs (about US$56 million at 585 francs to the dollar), according to the 2025 government announcement. The CFA franc is the shared currency of eight West African states and is pegged to the euro.

The Katiola solar plant is expected to produce 85,934 megawatt-hours of electricity a year, the same announcement said. A December 2024 trade report put its net grid feed at 41.4MW, and Koaci says a 1.3-kilometre line will connect it to the national network.

Where Katiola Fits in Ivory Coast’s Solar Push

A similar 50MW plant at Kong, in the north, had its first stone laid in October 2025 by the same minister. PV Magazine says Kong is due in the first quarter of 2027, with 58.2MW of solar in operation and 149MW under construction nationwide.

Ivory Coast wants about 1,044MW of solar power by 2030, up from an earlier goal of 678MW, and 45% of its electricity from renewables. Background on the country is in our guide to Ivory Coast.

What It Means for US Readers

The project is a template for private power in West Africa, with a foreign-linked developer taking the financing risk under a state concession. US developers, panel suppliers and lenders weighing similar projects can study the terms as they emerge.

The backers named so far are Swiss, Japanese and French rather than American, so direct US exposure looks small. Ivory Coast’s wider economy, which this plant helps to power, is covered in our GDP ranking report.

What Is Not Known

The sources do not say who will buy the Katiola solar plant’s electricity or at what price. Koaci and APA report mandate letters with lenders EBRD and Proparco, but financial close on the 33 billion CFA francs (about US$56 million) is pending.

A 2024 report planned commissioning for the fourth quarter of 2026, so the 15 months now announced point to roughly early 2028. No official has given a firm date for the Katiola solar plant to start work or deliver power.

More: Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Katiola solar plant?

The Katiola solar plant is a 50MWp solar power plant being built at Lonankaha, near Katiola in northern Ivory Coast. Its first stone was laid on Thursday 22 October 2026.

Who is paying for the Katiola solar plant?

The developer, Katiola Solar Power, finances the plant itself under a 25-year concession. The government put the private investment at about 33 billion CFA francs (about US$56 million) in 2025.

How many people will the plant serve?

The developer says more than 300,000 people will gain access to electricity. The plant should produce about 85,934 megawatt-hours a year.

When will the Katiola solar plant be finished?

Construction is set to take 15 months from the start of work. No exact opening date has been published.

Can US companies take part in Ivory Coast solar projects?

The power sector uses long private concessions, so foreign firms can join projects, but the sources do not name any American company at Katiola. Interested firms would deal with the Ministry of Mines, Petroleum and Energy.

Sources: Linfodrome (French), Katiola : la première pierre de la centrale solaire photovoltaïque de 50 MWc posée, 22 October 2026; Koaci (French), Katiola, Sangafowa-Coulibaly lance une centrale solaire de 50 MWc et exige des emplois pour les jeunes locaux, 22 October 2026; APA News (French), RCI : top départ d’une centrale solaire de 50 MWc à Katiola, 22 October 2026; AllAfrica / Government of Côte d’Ivoire (French), Le gouvernement annonce la construction d’une centrale solaire à Katiola, 24 May 2025; Ecofin Agency, Côte d’Ivoire approves US$60M solar project in Katiola, 22 May 2025; PV Magazine, Ivory Coast breaks ground on 50 MW solar project, 14 October 2025.

World.title: Argentina Opens Kirchner Trial on 23 October
World.content:
ARGENTINA · COURTS

Key Facts — What is happening Former president Cristina Kirchner and her son Máximo go on trial in Buenos Aires on Friday, 23 October, at 10 a.m. local time (9 a.m. ET), accused of money laundering and running an illicit association.

— Why it matters The trial is a new case for Cristina Kirchner, who serves house arrest in another corruption case, and it opens in the year before Argentina’s 2027 presidential election.

— The numbers Twenty-one defendants face two joined cases opened in 2014 and 2016. Money laundering and illicit association carry three to ten years in prison.

— Who is who Federal Oral Tribunal 5 hears the case, with judges José Michilini, Fernando Machado Pelloni and Adriana Palliotti. Carlos Beraldi leads the defence, and both Kirchners deny the charges.

— What to watch The first hearing reads out the charges, and the Kirchners may follow it on video. Hearings then run on Mondays, Fridays and Saturdays, and defendants must attend in person for questioning.

— Power Index Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in Argentina ranks 4th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 61.2 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you US readers tracking Argentina’s politics get the first full court calendar for the main opposition figure before 2027. The charges are allegations, and no verdict is expected soon.

Cristina Kirchner and her son Máximo go on trial in Buenos Aires on Friday, 23 October. Prosecutors allege a hotel and rental scheme laundered illicit payments.

The Kirchner trial opens in Buenos Aires on Friday, 23 October, at 10 a.m. local time (9 a.m. ET). Former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner and her son Máximo, a congressman, face one joint trial for money laundering and illicit association.

The case, known as Hotesur and Los Sauces, concerns two family companies that managed hotels and rental properties in Santa Cruz province. Prosecutors say the firms were used to launder payments from state contractors, and both Kirchners deny the charges through their lawyers.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Argentina ranks 4th of 14 with 61.2 points. Strongest pillar: future resources (68); weakest: economic relationships (23). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

For US readers, the hearing starts a long court calendar for Argentina’s most prominent opposition figure. It runs in the year before the 2027 presidential election, according to Perfil and El Cronista.

What the Prosecution Alleges

Prosecutors say that between 2003 and 2015, during the presidencies of Néstor Kirchner and Cristina Fernández, the family built a money-laundering circuit. The Cooperativa report, based on an EFE dispatch, says the firms Hotesur and Los Sauces received illicit payments from businessmen.

In Hotesur, the focus is the family hotel company and the Alto Calafate and Las Dunas hotels. Prosecutors say firms tied to contractor Lázaro Báez paid for rooms that, in their view, were not actually used.

In Los Sauces, investigators examine rentals of the family real-estate firm to companies tied to Báez and to the Indalo group. Its leaders, Cristóbal López and Fabián De Sousa, are also defendants.

Cristina Fernández is accused of illicit association as its head, and of money laundering. Máximo Kirchner is accused as an organiser of the alleged association, and of money laundering.

Who Else Is on Trial

The indictment covers 19 other defendants, among them businessmen, provincial officials and people close to the family. They include Carlos Sancho, a former governor of Santa Cruz, and Báez, who has been jailed since 2016 in another case.

Florencia Kirchner, also a daughter of the former president and a shareholder, is not on trial. She was definitively dismissed from the case in 2023, according to the EFE report.

The complaints that opened the investigations came from former congresswoman Margarita Stolbizer of the GEN party. Hotesur began in 2014 and Los Sauces in 2016, and the cases were joined at the cassation level in 2019.

How the Case Reached Trial After Years of Delay

In November 2021, Federal Oral Tribunal 5 dismissed the defendants without holding a trial. An appeals court reversed that in September 2023, and the Supreme Court left a trial standing in December 2024.

In September 2026, the trial court split the case. Los Sauces was to open on 23 October, and Hotesur was set for 19 March 2027, according to NoticiasNQN.

On Tuesday, 20 October, Chamber I of the Federal Criminal Cassation Court reversed the split. Judges Diego Barroetaveña and Daniel Petrone formed the majority, and Judge Alejandro Slokar dissented.

The majority said the trial court had not explained why it departed from the joint handling set years earlier. Prosecutors and the financial intelligence unit, the UIF, had argued that two trials could fragment the evidence.

What Changes for the Defendants on Friday

On Wednesday, 21 October, the trial court let the Kirchners attend the first hearing by video link. That hearing will read out the charges, and the court kept the 10 a.m. start.

Judge Adriana Palliotti dissented and wanted them present from the first day. Questioning of defendants who are called must happen in person, according to Perfil.

Cristina Fernández has served house arrest since 17 June 2025, under a six-year sentence and lifetime office ban in the Vialidad case. She asked to join the first hearing remotely, according to El Cronista.

Hearings are planned for the AMIA room at the Comodoro Py federal courts in Buenos Aires, on Mondays, Fridays and Saturdays. Defence lawyer Carlos Beraldi had argued that changing the format days before the start could harm his clients’ rights.

For context, see earlier coverage of the Hotesur cassation ruling and of Kirchner facing trial. The Argentina hub and the explainer on the 2027 Kicillof and Milei race add the political background.

What It Means for US Readers

The trial puts a former president and leading opposition figure in court as Argentina heads toward its 2027 presidential election. Investors and policy watchers should treat it as one part of the political calendar, not as a market event on its own.

Nothing in the case concerns US companies or the US government, according to the reports reviewed. A conviction would take years, and appeals could follow.

What Is Not Known

The court has not published the trial schedule beyond the first hearing, and no verdict date exists. The length of the trial is unknown, given 21 defendants and a large volume of evidence.

The court’s own notice of the hearing could not be opened, so details rest on Perfil, El Cronista, NoticiasNQN and Cooperativa. The defendants’ written responses to the charges are not public in the reports reviewed.

What Comes Next

The first hearing on Friday, 23 October, reads out the charges. The court will then fix who testifies and when.

The opening does not mean a finding of guilt, and the charges remain allegations until the court rules. The trial court could take months or longer to reach a verdict.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Hotesur and Los Sauces case?

It is a money-laundering and illicit-association case about two Kirchner family firms. Prosecutors say hotel and rental deals with state contractors hid illicit payments, and the defendants deny it.

When does the Kirchner trial start?

The oral trial starts on Friday, 23 October, at 10 a.m. in Buenos Aires (9 a.m. ET). The first hearing reads out the charges.

Will Cristina Kirchner attend in person?

Not on the first day, because the court let her and her son follow the reading of the charges by video. Questioning must be in person.

Who is on trial besides the Kirchners?

Nineteen others, including businessmen Lázaro Báez, Cristóbal López and Fabián De Sousa and former Santa Cruz governor Carlos Sancho. Florencia Kirchner was dismissed in 2023.

What penalty could they face?

Money laundering and illicit association carry three to ten years in prison. Any sentence would follow a verdict and could be appealed.

Sources: Perfil, 21 October 2026; El Cronista, 21 October 2026; NoticiasNQN, 20 October 2026; Cooperativa, citing EFE, 22 October 2026 (all accessed 23 October 2026).

World.title: US Visa Sanctions on Bolivia Judges Explained
World.content:
BOLIVIA · JUSTICE

Key Facts — What is happening On Thursday, 22 October 2026, the US State Department named 15 Bolivians for visa restrictions over alleged corruption and drug trafficking, and Santa Cruz court president Aldo Quezada resigned hours later.

— Why it matters It is the second US visa action on Bolivia in under a month, and it reaches judges, prosecutors, deputies and police officers in the very institutions that guard the rule of law.

— The numbers The statement names 15 people but says it restricts 40 individuals in Bolivia, and it does not explain the gap. The first round on Monday, 28 September, revoked 12 visas and made nine Bolivians ineligible.

— Who is who Quezada led the Santa Cruz Departmental Tribunal of Justice, Julio Nelson Alba Flores sits on it, and Rómer Saucedo, president of the Supreme Court, urged both to resign.

— What to watch Whether Alba Flores steps down, who now leads the Santa Cruz tribunal, and whether Bolivian prosecutors open cases against any of the 15 people named.

— Power Index Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 28.4 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you The measure targets named individuals, not Bolivia’s economy, but it shows Washington will use visa powers against officials in the region, and the State Department calls the mechanism durable.

Washington named 15 Bolivians for visa restrictions on 22 October, and the Santa Cruz court president quit. This guide explains the list and what is not yet known.

The US visa sanctions Bolivia judicial list why it matters question starts on Thursday, 22 October 2026. That day the US State Department named 15 Bolivians, including two Santa Cruz judges, and one of them resigned within hours.

It matters to Americans because Washington is using visa powers, not tariffs, to pressure officials it links to corruption and narcotrafficking. A visa restriction is not a conviction, and no court has found any of the 15 guilty.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Amounts in this guide are in US dollars, so no currency conversion is needed. Related coverage includes the Rio Times news report on the judges resigning and the Rio Times Bolivia page.

What the US List Is

On Thursday, 22 October, Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a statement titled “Additional Visa Restrictions on Bolivian Individuals”. It names 15 Bolivian nationals and says the restrictions also cover their immediate family members.

The State Department says the 15 undermine democratically elected governments in the region through corruption or narcotrafficking. The statement says the administration “stands with the government of Bolivia” against criminal influence in courts, police and the legislature.

The list expands a policy the State Department announced on Monday, 28 September. The US Embassy in Bolivia posted that first statement, which covered Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru.

How Visa Sanctions Work

The legal basis is Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the US Immigration and Nationality Act. It lets the Secretary of State refuse a visa on reasonable grounds that entry would seriously harm US foreign policy.

In the first round, existing visas of 12 Bolivians were revoked, and nine more Bolivians without visas were made generally ineligible. The State Department described the tool as one it can use quickly as evidence develops.

A second tool, Section 7031(c) of the State Department appropriations act, was used on 28 September against then Attorney General Roger Mariaca. It publicly designates an official for significant corruption and makes him and his immediate family generally ineligible for US entry.

The 22 October statement itself rests on Section 212(a)(3)(C). It announces entry restrictions only, with no asset freeze, no charges and no evidence for individual people.

Who Is on the List

The 15 names cover the justice system, the legislature, the police and migration services. Two are sitting judges of the Santa Cruz departmental court.

Judges: Aldo Ismael Quezada Cerruti, president of the Santa Cruz Departmental Tribunal of Justice, and Julio Nelson Alba Flores, a judge on it. José Ayaviri Siles, a former criminal court judge.

Aldo Ismael Quezada Cerruti, president of the Santa Cruz Departmental Tribunal of Justice, and Julio Nelson Alba Flores, a judge on it. José Ayaviri Siles, a former criminal court judge. Prosecutors: Juan Lanchipa Ponce, former attorney general, and Julio César Porras Velarde, who coordinates controlled-substances prosecutors in Santa Cruz. Félix Gerardo Balderas Arteaga and Armando Rojas Toledo are former prosecutors.

Juan Lanchipa Ponce, former attorney general, and Julio César Porras Velarde, who coordinates controlled-substances prosecutors in Santa Cruz. Félix Gerardo Balderas Arteaga and Armando Rojas Toledo are former prosecutors. Deputies: Rafael Darío López Mercado and Rolando Santos Pacheco Chávez, both national deputies from Santa Cruz.

Rafael Darío López Mercado and Rolando Santos Pacheco Chávez, both national deputies from Santa Cruz. Others: Diego Alejandro Barboza Zeballos, former head of the financial investigations unit, and Tarija police commander Freddy Bismarck Pereira Molina. The list also names former migration chief Katherine Calderón Valle and three others, among them a private citizen.

The Resignation in Santa Cruz

Quezada resigned on Thursday as tribunal president and as judge of its second constitutional chamber, El Deber reported. La Patria quotes his letter as an “irrevocable” resignation dated 22 October.

Saucedo, president of the Supreme Court, urged Quezada and Alba Flores to resign and face investigations without the privileges of judicial office. He said the named citizens “no longer enjoy the credibility necessary” to run the departmental judiciary, in El Deber’s wording.

Neither article reports a statement from Quezada beyond his letter. Alba Flores had not been reported as resigning when those reports appeared.

US Visa Sanctions Bolivia Judicial List Why It Matters for Washington and La Paz

The list reaches the justice system itself, so it tests how far Bolivia’s courts can police their own members. Saucedo’s public call for resignations shows the Supreme Court president did not defend the two judges.

For US-Bolivia relations, the statement presents the sanctions as support for the government of President Rodrigo Paz. It ties them to commitments from the Doral Summit in March and the Shield of the Americas leaders’ statement of 22 September.

Jurist reported that Bolivia confirmed Mariaca’s arrest on Thursday, 1 October, but the sources do not link the list to it. Correo del Sur reported a court ordered him six months of preventive detention on Saturday, 3 October.

Prosecutors allege Mariaca protected the trafficker Sebastián Marset, and he has not been convicted. Jurist reported that he denies the US allegations and calls them political pressure, and his lawyer asked for due process.

Earlier coverage of the 28 September round is in the Rio Times report on the visa bans. The Rio Times report on the attorney general case follows Mariaca, and the Bolivia power guide names who holds office.

What It Means for You

For US travellers and investors, nothing in the statement restricts trade, flights or the Bolivian state. It targets named individuals and their families, so the effect is felt by those people and by anyone who deals with them.

For US policy watchers, it is another case of visa power used as a quick tool against officials in the region. The State Department calls the mechanism durable and able to act quickly as evidence develops.

What Is Not Known

The State Department says 40 people in Bolivia are restricted, but names only 15, and the sources do not explain the gap. The 22 October statement also gives no conduct or evidence for each person.

It is not known whether Alba Flores will resign, or who will lead the Santa Cruz tribunal. The reports reviewed carry no response from the other named people, and no statement from the Bolivian government.

No court has charged or convicted any of the 15 over the US allegations, as far as the sources show. Whether Bolivian prosecutors will open cases is also open.

What Comes Next

Saucedo asked the tribunal’s full chamber to address its leadership within hours, so the court must now settle who leads it. Further US lists are possible, because the State Department called the 28 September policy a durable mechanism.

It does not mean that any of the 15 has been convicted, in Bolivia or in the United States. It also does not change Bolivia’s own judicial process, which stays with Bolivian courts.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are US visa sanctions on Bolivian officials?

They are restrictions on entering the United States, imposed by the State Department under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Existing visas can be revoked, and family members are covered.

Who is on the list of 22 October 2026?

The State Department named 15 Bolivians, including two Santa Cruz judges, a former attorney general, two deputies, prosecutors and a police commander. Aldo Quezada, the Santa Cruz court president, resigned the same day.

Is a visa restriction a criminal conviction?

No, it is an administrative decision on entry to the United States. No court has found any of the 15 people guilty of the US allegations.

Why did the Bolivian judge resign?

Aldo Quezada resigned hours after the list appeared, and the Supreme Court president had urged him to step aside and face investigation. His letter, quoted by La Patria, calls the resignation irrevocable.

Does this affect US travellers or investors in Bolivia?

The statement restricts named individuals and their families, not trade, travel or the Bolivian state. It matters mainly as a signal of how Washington is using visa powers in the region.

Sources: US State Department, Additional Visa Restrictions on Bolivian Individuals (22 October 2026); US Embassy in Bolivia, 28 September statement; El Deber; La Patria; Brújula Digital; Correo del Sur; Jurist (all accessed 23 October 2026).

World.title: Equatorial Guinea Fire Kills 6 in a Family
World.content:

EQUATORIAL GUINEA · SOCIETY

Key Facts — The country Equatorial Guinea is a small oil-producing nation in Central Africa, ruled since 1979 by President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo. Malabo, on Bioko island, is its former capital.

— What happened A fire in the Semu-Salomé neighbourhood of Malabo killed six members of one family on Wednesday 21 October 2026, AhoraEG reported.

— Who died The wife of Salvador Nsue Nguema, three of his children and two grandchildren died, and Nsue Nguema survived with burns and was in hospital.

— Suspected cause Early hypotheses point to a candle, used for light while a power cut hit much of the city.

— Why escape was hard AhoraEG says bars on the doors and windows blocked access to the house, and the home had no second exit.

— What it means for you Visitors and US energy staff in Malabo face thin emergency cover, as ambulance services are not available throughout the country.

— Still open No official has spoken publicly, and the cause, the victims’ ages and the fire service’s role have not been confirmed.

An Equatorial Guinea fire in Malabo killed six members of one family on Wednesday 21 October 2026, according to the local news site AhoraEG. The blaze hit the Semu-Salomé neighbourhood while a power cut had left much of the city dark.

The story matters beyond the family because it shows how thin the safety net is in an oil-rich state where US companies work. Barred doors, candles and a shaky power grid together turned one house fire into a mass tragedy for a single family.

What Happened in the Malabo Fire

The Equatorial Guinea fire broke out in the afternoon of Wednesday 21 October, AhoraEG reported on Thursday 22 October. Six people from one household died: the wife of Salvador Nsue Nguema, three of his children and two grandchildren.

Nsue Nguema is the only survivor and was being treated in hospital for burns when the report appeared. He has asked the public for help, because the fire destroyed the family’s belongings.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Africa Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Candle and a City Without Power

AhoraEG says the family was using candles for light because a power cut had hit much of Malabo. The first hypothesis is that one of the candles started the Equatorial Guinea fire, and the report treats that as unconfirmed.

The report quotes only the survivor and cites no official or fire service. Malabo lies on Bioko island, off the coast of the African mainland.

Bars on the Doors and No Second Exit

AhoraEG says bars fitted on the doors and windows made it hard to get into the house. With no second exit, escape and rescue were harder still.

The outlet does not name any fire crew, police unit or hospital in its account of the Equatorial Guinea fire. It only speaks of rescue work, so how quickly help arrived is still unclear.

A City Where the Lights Keep Failing

Equatorial Guinea’s electricity company, SEGESA, has been under government review since September 2025 over power cuts and missing spare parts. On 14 October the vice president, a son of the president, gave the power ministry one week to act, as our SEGESA report describes.

The World Bank says 24% of the country’s people have no electricity at all, and when the grid fails, candles are the fallback. Nothing in the fire report blames SEGESA, and no statement from the utility is cited.

Not the First Family Tragedy This Year

AhoraEG recalls that months earlier, in the Acrópolis neighbourhood of Malabo, a retaining wall collapsed onto a home. Cosme Nguema Ondo lost his pregnant wife, Andrea Nguema Nguema, and their six children in that collapse.

The same outlet has reported other house fires in Malabo since December 2025, some leaving families homeless. It also reported a blaze that hit stalls in the Central Market in April.

Oil Wealth, Thin Safety Net

Oil still pays most of the state’s bills, about 73% of revenue in the 2027 budget, which totals 1,119.7 billion FCFA (about US$1.91 billion). The World Bank says 61% of people lived below the poverty line in 2025, and our budget report has the detail.

That gap between oil income and daily life shows in small details, from candles during blackouts to missing ambulance cover. Our country guide sets out how the economy has shrunk as the oil fields age.

What It Means for US Readers

US-listed firms such as ConocoPhillips and Vaalco Energy hold gas and oil interests in Equatorial Guinea. The Equatorial Guinea fire is a reminder for such firms to check housing, power backup and emergency plans for staff.

The US State Department tells travellers to exercise increased caution in Equatorial Guinea because of crime and health. It adds that ambulance services are not available throughout the country and that there are no adequate trauma services.

What Is Not Known

No official statement on the Equatorial Guinea fire has been published, and its cause is still only a hypothesis. The ages of the six victims, the name of the hospital and the exact time of the blaze are not public.

It is also not known whether the authorities will open an inquiry or offer help to Nsue Nguema. No one has said whether the power was back on at the time of the fire or how long the cut lasted.

More: Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Malabo on 21 October 2026?

An Equatorial Guinea fire in the Semu-Salomé neighbourhood killed six members of one family, according to the local news site AhoraEG. The sole survivor, Salvador Nsue Nguema, was in hospital with burns.

What caused the fire?

The first hypothesis is that a candle started the Equatorial Guinea fire, as the family used candles during a power cut. No official has confirmed the cause.

Why could the family not get out?

AhoraEG reports that bars on the doors and windows hindered access to the house and that there was no second exit. That made both escape and rescue harder.

Is Malabo still the capital of Equatorial Guinea?

A January 2026 decree named Ciudad de la Paz, a mainland city, the new capital and gave state bodies a year to move. Malabo, on Bioko island, is the former capital, and many ministries still work there.

Should US travellers be concerned?

The State Department advises increased caution in Equatorial Guinea and warns that ambulance services are not available throughout the country. Visitors should plan for thin emergency cover and for power cuts.

Sources: AhoraEG, Un incendio acaba con la vida de seis personas de una familia en el barrio Semu-Salomé de Malabo, 22 October 2026; World Bank, Equatorial Guinea overview, 23 October 2026; US State Department, Equatorial Guinea travel advisory, 23 October 2026.

World.title: Punta Peuco Prison Chile Human Rights Crimes Controversy
World.content:
CHILE · JUSTICE

Key Facts — What is happening Chile’s Justice Minister Fernando Rabat confirmed on Thursday, 22 October 2026, that he signed decrees cutting the sentences of two inmates at Punta Peuco, the prison for ex-military convicted of dictatorship-era crimes.

— Why it matters The cuts reached convicts of kidnapping and torture under conservative President José Antonio Kast, and they landed amid a separate row over 56 reductions for child sex offenders.

— The numbers Two Punta Peuco inmates received reductions, one for aggravated kidnapping and one for torture. The prison held 139 men in April 2025, against a capacity of 130 in 2017.

— Who is who Rabat is Justice and Human Rights Minister in the Kast cabinet. Punta Peuco, in Tiltil near Santiago, is run by Gendarmería, Chile’s prison service, and opened in 1995 for dictatorship-era convicts.

— What to watch Whether Congress passes the bills the government says it will fast-track, and whether opposition deputies file the constitutional accusation against Rabat that Christian Democrats are weighing.

— Power Index Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in Chile ranks 3rd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 63.6 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you There is no direct effect on travel or on copper and lithium investments, but the row tests how Kast’s government handles human rights and Congress, which investors in Chile follow.

Two ex-military inmates convicted of kidnapping and torture had their sentences cut. This guide explains the prison and the dispute.

The Punta Peuco prison Chile human rights crimes controversy grew on Thursday, 22 October 2026. Justice Minister Fernando Rabat confirmed that two inmates there received sentence reductions.

Punta Peuco holds former military and police convicted of crimes under the 1973 to 1990 dictatorship. The cuts matter to foreigners because Chile, a US trade partner, is testing how far a conservative government goes.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Chile uses the peso, and this guide contains no money amounts. Related coverage includes the Rio Times news report on the sentence cuts and the Rio Times Chile page.

What Rabat Confirmed on 22 October

Asked on T13 Radio whether he signed two decrees reducing sentences at Punta Peuco, Rabat said “es cierto”, T13 and BioBioChile reported. The Ministry of Justice and Human Rights gave the reductions to one inmate convicted of aggravated kidnapping and one convicted of torture.

The Clinic says both crimes were committed under the military regime. Interferencia identified the decisions through two exempt decrees, and Rabat said the benefits follow the law.

Rabat said similar benefits to military convicts were granted in each of the last 20 years under governments of different politics. He said, if his memory served, that only ex-president Gabriel Boric rejected every request.

He added that the Supreme Court overturned at least four refusals, a claim El Mostrador says did not identify the rulings. The sources reviewed do not confirm it.
