World.title: Who really writes the budget?
World.content:
Andy Burnham has promised Britain can “hope again”. But with inflation rising, borrowing costs soaring and trillions of pounds of national debt, how much room does Chancellor John Healey actually have to deliver in the budget on Oct. 28?

This week, Pat and Sascha speak to Treasury insiders to find out who really calls the shots when a Chancellor puts together a budget. First, they hear from Matt Pound, one of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves’ closest advisers, about the tough choices facing Healey, the dangers of leaks and U-turns, and why keeping the bond markets onside matters more than politicians might like to admit.

Then, Cameron Brown and Simon Finkelstein, two former Treasury officials who lived through the turmoil of the Liz Truss era, reveal just how obsessed Westminster is with the bond markets. And POLITICO’s Financial Services Editor Fiona Maxwell gives her predictions for what Healey might have in store on budget day.

World.title: Can Europe save the world’s war crimes court from Trump?
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has the world’s war crimes court in his crosshairs.

By sanctioning the entire International Criminal Court, his administration is threatening its ability to function. Europe has rushed to the court’s defense — but can it actually protect it from American financial power? And how far is the European Union willing to go to confront Washington when it still relies so heavily on the U.S. for its own security?

Host Sarah Wheaton is joined by European Parliament lawmaker Dirk Gotink and Atlantic Council sanctions expert Lize de Kruijf to discuss Europe’s options, its dependence on the U.S. dollar and American technology and whether the EU can stand up for international justice.

If you have any questions or comments, send us a message on our WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

World.title: ‘Andy Time’: Why Burnham’s budget isn’t going to deliver a revolution
World.content:
There will also be a “fiscal devolution roadmap” on budget day, setting out terms of how regional mayors can get more power and money and drawn up partly by Burnham’s new Manchester outpost, No. 10 North. Legislation to let them impose tourist taxes will be published in the coming weeks. And officials have talked behind the scenes about procurement and boosting Britain’s heavy industries; the budget needs to find almost £5 billion to plug a hole in a defense investment plan unveiled under Starmer.

Targeted cost-of-living measures appear likely to include scrapping “standing charges” on domestic gas bills, which cost the average household just over £100 a year. Burnham said Wednesday that he had asked Healey to look at the issue — though any help could be eclipsed by a predicted £276 rise in domestic bills this January.

The other message will be that the Treasury can do big, consequential things without raising taxes. Healey will make “a political argument that actually there are other types of budgets that you can have,” said the first government official quoted above, “busting through some of that sludge and ripping up a lot of that red tape.” Cash-strapped chancellors have reached for regulatory reform before, with mixed success.

MPs are looking closely at cost-of-living support. One backbencher in an affluent seat said any help had to be significant, because even their well-off constituents were struggling to take the holidays they wanted. Defense, by contrast, barely comes up on the doorstep: “There are hardly any votes in it, but it’s just something we have to do.”

There has been heavy engagement with Labour MPs, whose detachment from No. 10 helped force Starmer out in July. Treasury ministers Torsten Bell and James Murray are among those engaging while Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds handles tricky negotiations with Cabinet ministers, alongside No. 10 chief of staff James Purnell.

Healey has negotiated with Cabinet ministers and spoken to union leaders, banks and MPs — though not lobbyists. “No one can get to Healey,” said one. “It’s very smart. Let him do his job.”

World.title: Europe has a big cheese problem
World.content:
France has been having a bad time of late, and it’s not just because of riots, fires and looting — incidentally, if anyone wants 250 slightly singed Paris Saint-Germain football jerseys and several dozen boxes of apéricubes, please look for me on eBay.

The droughts and heat waves that battered Europe mean strict production rules for some of France’s most famous cheeses were loosened. Comté, Beaufort and Abondance — not a French kids TV series about three dairy-loving glove puppets but rather cheeses made out of milk from cows that graze in the mountains and carry the appellation d’origine protégée label — all suffered because of a lack of suitable grazing land, so farmers were allowed to temporarily change the diet of their cows (perhaps to Diet Coke and Mars bars).

And it’s not just France that’s having cheese problems.

Readers over the age of four may remember Italy as Europe’s version of the fun uncle who isn’t an actual uncle; wonderfully entertaining but also disturbingly unstable. Though Italy has been a bastion of calm of late (relatively speaking).

That appears to be coming to an end now, as a truckers’ strike has wreaked havoc on the production of buffalo mozzarella. The war in Iran has caused the cost of fuel to soar, so the truck drivers have pulled over to the side of the road, which means buffalo milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region, and the cheese cannot reach customers.

Italians, who never have any strong opinions on food (!!!!!!), are furious and hungry in equal measure, with an estimated €3 million of cheesy, milky goodness lost in just 24 hours.

World.title: Spain wins landmark victory in decades-long dispute over lost energy subsidies
World.content:
The dispute dates back to 2013, in the middle of the European debt crisis, when cash-strapped Spain, then under a new conservative government, decided to remove subsidies for renewable energy. Investors who had poured money into Spanish renewables said this was a breach, as they had invested on the understanding they would receive the subsidies.

The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes ruled that Spain must pay the money, but the European Commission has told Spain doing so would constitute unlawful state aid.

The standoff has played out all over the world, with investors attempting to freeze Spanish assets in multiple jurisdictions. In June, U.S. investment fund Blasket Renewable Investments LLC issued subpoenas demanding documents from Adidas, Hilton Hotels, and other entities involved in Spain’s Football World Cup participation to help with its bid to freeze Spanish assets.

In the end, the team went back home with its assets intact, along with the World Cup.

Spain also has cases going on in courts in Australia, Germany and the U.S.

In 2023, a British court ordered an embargo on an international school in London owned by the Spanish state. The Belgian court’s original decision was one of the few examples where investors were successful, and the decision this week to overturn it will set a precedent for other challenges.

World.title: Serbia’s protesting students mount serious challenge to Vučić’s power
World.content:
The largest protest movement in modern Serbian history began in November 2024, when a freshly renovated railway station awning collapsed in Novi Sad, killing 16 people, including two young children.

Vigils for the dead turned into mass protests, fueled by government denials of wrongdoing that forced out the previous prime minister. Demonstrations drew huge crowds, peaking with a March 2025 rally attended by more than 325,000 people in Belgrade. Student protesters have been demanding early elections ever since.

A fraught campaign

New Serbian Political Thought’s editor Đorđe Vukadinović cautioned that the polling figures released by his outlet are a snapshot, not a projection, adding that he had considered not publishing the results at all given what he called “near-hysterical” attacks and reactions from the government to its previous findings.

Pro-government tabloids and senior Progressive Party figures have spent the election campaign tearing into independent pollsters, branding them “fake researchers.”

But for the Student List, the polling reflects months of concerted door-to-door canvassing to reach every corner of the country, as well as something Serbia’s established opposition parties may be short of after more than a decade of fighting SNS’s omnipresence in the country: the stubborn persistence of youth.

“We have the energy. We refused to accept that this was a lost cause or accept there were pro-SNS dead zones that we didn’t reach out to,” Golubović said, explaining that the Progressive Party was the only party that previously had the capacity to mount nationwide campaigns.

World.title: This summer’s heat was Europe’s deadliest on record, scientists say
World.content:
“I think we can be quite confident in stating that the summer of 2026 is likely to have been the worst on record for heat-related mortality across much of Europe,” said study lead author Clair Barnes, an extreme weather researcher at Imperial College London.

“These numbers are a stark reminder that our hotter, more extreme summers are having an increasingly severe impact on public health. Behind these statistics are real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them,” she added.

Scientists from Imperial College and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine examined 854 cities in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Norway and Switzerland, home to about 40% of the 30 countries’ population.

The first study, published earlier this month, looked at climate-linked mortality between 2000 and 2025, while the second study, released on Friday, focused on 2026.

Both papers estimated heat-related excess deaths by analyzing temperature records and historical heat-mortality models, a method the researchers say has consistently produced results mirroring official statistics later released by governments.

To isolate the role of climate change, the scientists then compared the actual weather seen in these cities to a temperature model representing a world without global warming.

World.title: A Budapest reset, and a scramble to get Ukraine peace talks back on track
World.content:
Brussels-Budapest reset: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa will join a commemoration of the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 anti-Soviet uprising in Budapest today, with von der Leyen expected to deliver a speech in parliament alongside Prime Minister Péter Magyar. It’s arguably one of the clearest signals yet of the new chapter in EU-Hungary relations, our Hungarian correspondent Sándor Zsiros writes this morning.

 

Major turning point: The thaw in relations between Brussels and Budapest comes after years of acrimony under Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orbán – with von der Leyen’s speech likely to capture a moment of change, Sándor reports.

In the past, von der Leyen was portrayed on billboards in Hungary as a public enemy. She is set to address the same parliament where just a few months ago Orbán lashed out at the EU.

The commemoration is the first big international event for Magyar since he took office in May.

He had extended an invitation to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as first reported by Euronews, but the Ukrainian leader is unlikely to attend. Diplomatic ties between Ukraine and Hungary have improved dramatically since Magyar’s election in April. Yet, Budapest surprised EU diplomats earlier this week by blocking the next steps in Ukraine’s EU accession talks, despite Kyiv meeting its previous demands.

French President Emmanuel Macron was also set to take part, but cancelled the trip in the wake of riots in France. Moldovan President Maia Sandu and Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze are both expected to attend.

Ukraine latest: Meanwhile, Vladimir Putin has offered another remarkable explanation of Russia's war against Ukraine: Moscow doesn't want to fight its neighbour. It is Ukraine, apparently, that insists on fighting Russia.

The Russian president also declared that Russians and Ukrainians are effectively "one people" – an argument Moscow has repeatedly invoked to justify its invasion and occupation of Ukrainian territory – and expressed confidence that the two countries could reach an agreement, provided it served Russia's imperialist interests, my colleague Sasha Vakulina writes.

And what if Ukraine doesn't agree?: "Well, then it will be otherwise," Putin said, promising that Russia would achieve all the "objectives" of its all-out war against Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy is awaiting a briefing from US envoy Steve Witkoff on Friday, followed by further consultations between Ukrainian, American and European teams. As diplomacy hangs in the balance, Moscow continues to pound Ukraine.

Overnight on Thursday, Russia launched ballistic missiles carrying cluster warheads at Kyiv, targeting the historic city centre and damaging monastery buildings, homes, shops and cafés.

Maximum alarm: Meanwhile, Europe continues to grapple with Donald Trump’s embrace of Vladimir Putin, which has revived long-gestating fears that the two presidents will secretly thrash out a deal that ends in Ukraine’s capitulation.

Moscow’s pitch for a summit between Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping has further fuelled the impression that Europe’s security architecture is hanging by a thread, my colleague Jorge Liboreiro reports this morning.

“It’s very disturbing. It’s terrifying,” a senior official said. “We’re simply not built to operate in this kind of ruthless transactional environment.”

Jorge Liboreiro, Sasha Vakulina and Shona Murray have this must-read story depicting a continent on edge.

Chin up: Despite the alarming circumstances, European officials insist that engagement with the Trump administration must continue to ensure the European point of view is reflected in the peace process. For Ukraine, European presence is fundamental to counter Washington’s transactional approach.

Russia has indicated it’s prepared to resume trilateral talks at the technical level with the US and Ukraine in mid-November. Brussels hopes the format can expand into multilateral talks to include European representatives as well, although it’s far from guaranteed that Moscow would agree.

PHP security flaw: Why websites across Europe went dark and what it means for you

AI models have uncovered what OpenAI calls "one of the most impactful" security bugs in recent memory, hidden in PHP, a programming language that quietly powers most of the internet. It’s sent organisations worldwide scrambling to shut down websites before hackers can exploit them.

The bugs sat undetected in PHP’s code for more than a decade. It took cutting-edge AI models from OpenAI and Google to turn a long-suspected weakness into a working attack — and now the race is on to close the door.

The Dutch government pulled its DigiD digital identity system, the Overheid.nl government portal and the website of the lower house of parliament, with the Port of Rotterdam, hospitals and the country’s five largest political parties following suit.

Even the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre took its own site down.

Finland’s state IT provider Valtori switched off government web services wholesale “as a precautionary measure,” France’s Interior Ministry put local administration sites into maintenance mode and Germany’s federal IT service ITZBund took down several portals.

CERT-EU, the cybersecurity service for the EU institutions, went further than most, telling any organisation unable to patch immediately to take its websites offline rather than risk being hacked.

The European Commission, ENISA, CERT-EU, Europol and the EU’s network of national cyber response teams also issued a joint statement urging organisations to act immediately, prioritising systems exposed to the internet.

Una Hajdari has more.

More from our newsrooms

EU Parliament awards Sakharov Prize to ICC in rebuke of US sanctions. The European Parliament has awarded the Sakharov Prize to the International Criminal Court in a show of support after the US imposed sanctions on the court. The abstention of the far-right Patriots for Europe group was decisive in breaking the deadlock over the final choice. Vincenzo Genovese has the details.

Italy and Spain to end border checks, easing tensions after Ceuta migrant row. Rome and Madrid have agreed to end temporary border checks, in a sign of de-escalation after weeks of tension over the Ceuta migrant crisis. The decision follows a phone call between the countries’ interior ministers, after prime ministers Giorgia Meloni and Pedro Sánchez signalled their intention to end the checks in Brussels last week. Fortunato Pinto has the story.

Gulf nations brace for possible return to all-out war between US and Iran. The volatility around the Israeli and US midterm elections is fueling fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran in a short and intensive military campaign to push Tehran into concessions, with Iran vowing a devastating response against the Gulf nations. Peter Barabas and the Euronews Doha bureau have more.

We’re also keeping an eye on

EU trade ministers gather for informal talks in Dublin, Ireland

Hungary holds a commemoration of the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution of 1956. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa to attend.

That’s it for today. Jorge Liboreiro, Sándor Zsiros, Sasha Vakulina and Vincenzo Genovese contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: Could lab-made gold crash prices like diamonds? US start-up says it turned mercury into gold
World.content:
Marathon Fusion, a small fusion energy company in San Francisco, announced on Wednesday that it had transmuted, or converted, mercury into stable gold last month, beating a record set by CERN tenfold. The Geneva-based organisation runs the world's largest particle physics laboratory.

 

The claim, which has not been independently verified, revives an alchemist's dream and a market fear that lab-made gold could do to bullion what lab-grown precious stones did to diamonds.

Founded in 2023 by Kyle Schiller and Adam Rutkowski, a former SpaceX engineer, Marathon develops fuel systems for future fusion power plants, which aim to generate electricity by fusing atoms together, as the sun does.

It lists the US Department of Energy as a partner on its website and won a 2023 award from ARPA-E, the department's agency for high-risk energy research.

Its backers include Breakthrough Energy, the climate technology network founded by Bill Gates, and Anglo American, the mining group that owns De Beers, the world's leading natural diamond company behind the "A diamond is forever" slogan.

In its announcement, the company said it had turned "mercury into real, stable gold, beating CERN's record by a factor of 10".

In 2025, CERN said its Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's most powerful particle accelerator, had created about 29 picograms, or 29 trillionths of a gram, of gold during its 2015–2018 run. That amounted to around 86 billion gold nuclei, or atomic cores, which existed for only a tiny fraction of a second before being destroyed in collisions with accelerator equipment.

Marathon's method fires neutrons from fusion reactions at mercury, turning it into an unstable isotope, or form of the metal, that decays into gold.

It also claims to have broken a 40-year-old Soviet record with its plasma centrifuge, a machine that spins electrically charged gas at high speed to separate isotopes used in fusion fuel.

It says it is now building a reactor in San Francisco to achieve record power density, meaning the most power produced for its size.

The gold claim has not been independently verified, and the material available does not establish how much gold was produced or at what cost.

What happened to diamonds?

Lab-grown diamonds are chemically identical to mined stones.

Although specialists can tell them apart, factories churned them out and sold them for a fraction of the price.

Wholesale prices for lab-grown stones fell 90% to 95% from their 2015 levels, diamond industry analyst Paul Zimnisky said last year, while competition from lab-grown stones also weighed on mined diamond prices.

De Beers launched its own lab-grown brand, Lightbox, in 2018 at $800 (€712) a carat. However, it shut it down in 2025 to focus on natural diamonds.

De Beers made an underlying loss of $511 million (€455mn) in 2025, and Anglo American is in talks to sell its 85% stake for about $1 billion (€890mn) to a group led by former De Beers boss Gareth Penny, according to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.

Swiss luxury group Richemont, which owns Cartier, and US jeweller Signet, which owns Kay and Zales, are reportedly also in talks to join the group.

Why gold is different

Gold is a far bigger market.

Mines produced 3,672 tonnes in 2025, and about 222,600 tonnes have been mined throughout history, according to the World Gold Council.

Central banks also hold it in their reserves as a safe store of value, and many have been buying heavily in recent years, including those of China and Poland.

Gold traded at $4,062 (€3,617) an ounce on Thursday, more than 27% below its record high of $5,598 (€4,985) in January.

Marathon's own 2025 study estimated that a fusion plant could make about 5 tonnes of gold a year per gigawatt of electricity, roughly the output of a large nuclear reactor.

On that basis, 100 such plants would add an estimated 500 tonnes a year, roughly 14% of last year's mine output.

However, no fusion plant yet sells electricity, and the first commercial ones are still years away. The gold could also contain radioactive isotopes and might need to be stored for up to 18 years before it could be sold, the company has said.

There are currently no public plans to attempt to produce and commercialise the product, but unlike lab-grown diamonds, transmuted gold, once its radioactivity fades, would be impossible to tell apart from the mined kind.

World.title: Europe Today: France braces for fresh protests as EU leaders seek Hungary reset
World.content:
On today's show:

 

Sándor Zsíros, Euronews' Hungarian EU correspondent, examines the significance of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa visiting Budapest to mark the 70th anniversary of Hungary's 1956 uprising against Soviet rule. The visit, hosted by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, signals a potential reset in relations between Hungary and the EU after years of tensions under Viktor Orbán.

Estelle Nilsson-Julien reports live from Paris as France prepares for another round of mass demonstrations on Saturday. Following last weekend's violence and looting, the government has announced heightened security measures, while protesters remain determined to take to the streets.

Alice de Brito, vice president of France's main student union UNEF, joins us to discuss why students are protesting, the challenges they face and whether the upcoming presidential election offers hope for change.

Polish Deputy Interior Minister Maciej Duszczyk speaks to us about the growing divisions between EU leaders over migration following the unrest in France. We discuss Emmanuel Macron’s response to foreign leaders commenting on France’s protests, Poland’s demands for tougher migration rules and the tensions between Donald Tusk and Pedro Sánchez over the EU’s Migration Pact.

Berta López Domènech, analyst at the European Policy Centre, examines Serbia’s upcoming snap parliamentary election, where a student-led movement hopes to challenge President Aleksandar Vučić after two years of demonstrations. With concerns mounting over electoral irregularities and the country’s democratic direction, we ask whether the opposition can bring political change.

When and where to watch Europe Today?

You can join Euronews’ chief anchor Méabh Mc Mahon and our EU editor Maria Tadeo live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am Brussels time.

In just 20 minutes, our new format brings you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. It's also available as a newsletter and podcast.

World.title: EU-Canada 'love story' needs more than warm words, senior MEP warns
World.content:
The EU must turn its offer of “associate membership” to Canada into a meaningful partnership that goes well beyond trade, Tobias Cremer, the European Parliament's standing rapporteur on Canada, told Euronews.

 

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the EU's first “associate member” in September, but gave little indication of what the unprecedented status would mean in practice.

The offer comes as geopolitical upheaval draws Brussels and Ottawa closer together. Canada is embroiled in a trade war with its traditional US ally, while the EU is struggling to keep Washington on its side over Ukraine.

The two sides are due to meet at a summit in Montreal at the end of next week, with agreements expected in several areas, including critical raw materials and digital cooperation.

“For the last couple of months, we've been great, Canada and Europe, at writing each other love letters and saying how much we really want to work together,” said Cremer, a German socialist MEP. “But I think now is really the time to start to get serious and turn that love story into concrete commitments.”

He added that “associate membership” must mean the “closest possible partnership that the EU can offer to a non-European country and since Canada is probably the most European of non-European countries that should be very close.”

Beyond trade deals

Cremer insisted that the relationship must amount to more than “a trade deal ‘plus’”.

“There must be a new quality to the relation.”

He called for a “pragmatic approach,” involving sectoral agreements covering trade, defence, digital cooperation, the Arctic and students, but also going further.

“We should go a step further and start embedding all of these great initiatives into something more enduring, into a common institutional framework of coordination and cooperation.”

Cremer suggested that Canada could participate “as an observer” in the Council of the EU, where national ministers meet, and called for the creation of a formal parliamentary partnership assembly.

Such a body could follow the model of the existing EU-UK Parliamentary Partnership Assembly, which brings together 35 members from each side twice a year for sessions that can focus on specific policy areas.

Regarding the UK, however, the MEP described it as a European country for which, “if it wishes so,” the ambition “should not be associate membership, but full membership.”

His comments came as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently floated the idea of rejoining the EU, with polls showing that a majority of Britons want to return to the bloc.

But Cremer also argued for closer cooperation not only with the UK and Canada, but also with countries such as Australia and South Korea.

“I think it is of our interest to bring all of these actors together and say 'hold on, actually the majority of the world wants to play 21st century politics which is focused on collective security, on shared interests, on mutual respect rather than might is right.'”

World.title: Oil prices climb above $113 as AI sell-off rattles stocks and investors buy bonds
World.content:
Asian shares were mostly lower on Friday after the latest sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks weighed on markets around the world, giving the benchmark S&P 500 its worst day since July.

 

Oil prices were hovering at their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran, with Brent crude trading at $113.73 per barrel early Friday, up 0.5% after a 4% jump in the previous session. Brent settled at $113.17 on Thursday. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude rose 0.6% to $100.08 per barrel.

Oil rallied on Thursday as deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia fuelled concerns that a full-scale regional conflict could further choke off global energy supplies.

On top of the risk premium, soaring shipping costs are adding to the cost of delivering oil.

By mid-October, the cost of shipping crude from the Middle East Gulf to Asia on a large tanker had climbed to over $37 per barrel, more than five times its level before the war began, according to MarketWatch.

Gas prices jumped, too. November futures for the European benchmark, Dutch TTF, traded above €90 per megawatt-hour on Thursday.

Concerns about AI build-out hit stock markets

On Thursday, in the US, the S&P 500 fell 1.2%, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness in tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength elsewhere in the US market, where the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added less than 0.1%.

AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it has become to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips. Investors fear share prices shot too high during a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.

Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it would introduce a new class of non-voting shares, giving it another way to fund AI investments and other expenses while preserving existing shareholders’ voting power.

Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting third-quarter profit above analysts’ expectations, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.

The global sell-off in AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by market value, movements in its stock carry more weight in the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single biggest drag on the index.

CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips and rent out access to them through its cloud services, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.

Technology stocks face fresh tests next week when Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet report their earnings. The Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision is also due next week, on Wednesday, 28 October.

Bond market worries

Bond market worries

Worries about big government debt loads and strained budgets are hanging over many developed economies. Protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.

France's 10-year government bond yield stood at around 5.07% late Thursday, compared with Germany’s 3.34%, putting the gap at about 173 basis points. Italy’s 10-year yield was around 4.61%.

Debt and inflation fears had helped drive a major global bond sell-off, pushing US Treasury yields to their highest levels in decades.

But US yields fell sharply on Thursday as investors bought US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. The 16-basis-point daily fall was a sharp move for the benchmark yield.

Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. New applications for unemployment benefits fell by 6,000 to 194,000 last week, their lowest level since July, suggesting layoffs remained low.

Investors will also watch Friday’s preliminary business activity surveys for the eurozone, the UK and the US for signs of how higher energy prices and borrowing costs are affecting growth.

In other dealings early Friday, the US dollar rose to 156.93 Japanese yen from 156.77 yen. The euro was unchanged at $1.1215. Sterling traded at $1.3391.

Gold futures fell nearly 1% to $4,020.20 an ounce.

World.title: Europe just had its deadliest summer. Which country was hit the hardest by extreme heat?
World.content:
Europe’s sweltering summer is estimated to have claimed more than 50,000 lives in urban areas, making it the “worst on record”, according to a new report.

 

Researchers are clear on the cause: climate change – primarily from the burning of fossil fuels – was responsible for about two-thirds of these excess heat deaths.

The figure far outstrips the previous highest figures of about 29,000 deaths in the summer of 2022 and 28,000 in 2003 across the area modelled.

It’s a testament to the extreme heat faced by the world’s fastest-warming continent between June and August this year. A succession of heatwaves saw temperatures in Western Europe soar 2.9°C above the 1991-2020 average – even rising by as much as 12°C on some days – often hitting countries that are neither used to nor prepared for such highs.

“These numbers are a stark reminder that our hotter, more extreme summers are having an increasingly severe impact on public health,” says study co-author Dr Clair Barnes, an extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College London.

“Behind these statistics are real people whose lives were lost and real families who grieve for them.”

Nearly one-third of deaths estimated occurred during the particularly intense heatwave between 17 June and 1 July, when temperatures were on average 5.3°C above the norm.

How were summer heat deaths estimated?

The study used modelling to estimate the number of heat-related excess deaths during summers dating back to the start of the century.

“The true burden of mortality, in fact, due to heat is not directly observed or measured,” says study co-author Dr Malcolm Mistry, assistant professor in climate and geospatial modelling at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM).

“Heat is therefore often commonly referred to as a ‘silent killer’, with the death toll underreported in several regions globally.”

The scientists used temperature records and modelling based on the historical relationship between heat and mortality to estimate the number of casualties in summer 2026. They took geographic and environmental features, socioeconomic factors, availability of health services, and age-specific temperature-mortality links into account.

The modelling was applied to 854 urban areas across the EU, UK, Norway and Switzerland – areas that make up around 40 per cent of the population of the 30 countries studied.

A separate attribution study covering the summers of 2000 to 2025 was used for comparison, with results for these years proving broadly consistent with official statistics released by national health authorities. Many European countries are yet to release final figures for summer 2026.

Researchers then compared the actual temperatures with those that would have been expected without warming from climate change to estimate the additional deaths caused.

Overall, 65 per cent of heat-related excess deaths – or around 32,000 – in summer 2026 were attributed to human-induced climate change. Earlier in the century it was estimated to be responsible for about 40 per cent of heat-related deaths.

“It is yet another reminder both of the imperative of rolling out targeted interventions to protect those who are most vulnerable to this increasingly extreme heat, and of the growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming,” says Dr Barnes.

The thermometer of a drugstore shows the temperature of 38 degrees Celsius as temperatures reached record highs, in Rome, June 24, 2026. AP Photo/Andrew Medichini

Who is most at risk from extreme heat?

Vulnerable people are most exposed to the dangers of extreme heat, including those suffering from disease; elderly or very young people; and those unable to move away from the heat – either for physical or socioeconomic reasons.

In the summer 2026 study, people aged 85 and over accounted for roughly half of the estimated deaths. But younger adults were also affected: there were an estimated 800 excess deaths among people aged between 20 and 44, and a total of around 6,000 people under the age of 65.

The researchers also found geographical variations, with Southern Europe experiencing significantly more deaths linked to high temperatures than Northern Europe.

This is primarily due to the higher temperatures faced by countries further south, although other vulnerabilities also came into play.

“For example, factors such as increased air pollution levels, limited green space infrastructure, accessibility to health systems and heat alerts,” explains study co-author Dr Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, assistant professor at ICL’s Grantham Institute.

Europe’s unprecedented summer: Which country was worst hit?

The public health risks of Europe’s scorching summer were immense, with several governments issuing heat warnings and real-time estimates of heat-related mortality.

According to the summer 2026 report, Italy is estimated to have suffered the highest number of heat-related excess deaths: a total of 13,303. Next was France at 7,268, followed by Spain at 6,824.

Traditionally-cooler countries also struggled in the heat, which was made more dangerous by infrastructure designed for a different climate and citizens unaccustomed to such highs.

Germany faced an estimated 6,340 excess deaths and the UK 4,354.

“In the UK, the summer is historically the quietest time for our health service. This summer, however, saw demand and strain that was akin to a really bad winter virus season,” says Andrew Hartle, Professor of Practice of Anaesthesia at Imperial College Healthcare.

The accuracy of the modelling means it has the potential to allow health services to prepare for extreme events before they hit.

Besides cutting greenhouse gas emissions to limit future warming, cities can invest in adding green-blue spaces, which come with the cobenefits of reducing temperatures and improving air quality.

Northern and Western Europe should look to the south for solutions that are already well established, the study’s authors say.

These include investing in climate shelters; retrofitting buildings to better withstand the heat, such as by adding external shades or blinds; and promoting behavioural changes like checking in on vulnerable neighbours, not going out in the midday sun, taking heat advisory warnings seriously, seeking shade, and drinking plenty of water.

World.title: Drones, AI and cybersecurity on display as Milipol Qatar brings together firms from 33 countries
World.content:
Security companies from 33 countries gathered in Doha this week for Milipol Qatar, displaying drones, robots and AI systems as the country reviews its defences following the Iran war.

 

The three-day exhibition, which ended Thursday, covered equipment for policing, emergency response and industrial safety, along with discussions on cybersecurity and protecting essential services.

Alexandros Lakatamitis, general manager of West Bay Petroleum, which brought drones to the exhibition, said government and industry customers were taking security more seriously.

“The security bubble that we’ve enjoyed for so long is no longer there,” he told Euronews.

Lakatamitis, who grew up in Qatar, said security had become a more pressing consideration across government and business, including among the customers his company speaks to daily.

Around 280 companies participated in the exhibition at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Center, according to Major Khalid Saadon Al-Kuwari, a member of the Milipol organising committee. About 70% came from outside Qatar.

Major Al-Kuwari said the event brought together “solutions for whatever challenges that different governments and different countries are facing”.

He said it gave governments an opportunity to examine systems already tested in other countries and consider how they could be used at home.

The exhibition took place during a week of security discussions in Doha.

On Monday, Qatar’s Defence Minister Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said the country was drawing on lessons from the Iran war to improve protection against ballistic missiles, drones and cyberattacks.

He also outlined plans for a local defence production hub and closer cooperation with regional and international partners.

Sending machines into danger

On the exhibition floor, companies also presented equipment intended for civilian emergencies and hazardous industrial work.

Lakatamitis described how drones could search large areas for missing people. Photographs collected during a flight can be analysed by software to identify possible signs of a person, helping rescuers decide where to concentrate their efforts, he said.

He also pointed to industrial inspections, where a drone fitted with gas-detection equipment could investigate a suspected leak without sending someone into a potentially dangerous location.

Those applications were part of a broader discussion about using AI in security. The second Doha International Conference on AI & Security ran alongside Milipol, with sessions on responsible AI use, autonomous systems and the protection of critical infrastructure.

At a cybersecurity seminar on Thursday, officials discussed how to keep essential services operating during an attack.

Khalid Al Nasr, assistant director of the information security department at Qatar’s National Cyber Security Agency, said the response needed to extend beyond restoring IT infrastructure to ensuring vital government services continued or were restored within an acceptable timeframe.

At the discussion, Al Nasr called for cybersecurity to be incorporated into disaster recovery and crisis management plans, with clear responsibilities to reduce confusion during an incident.

The exhibition also saw fresh international security agreements. Qatar and France signed a cooperation plan between their interior ministries covering 2027–2030, aimed at strengthening coordination and exchanges of expertise.

A joint statement following French President Emmanuel Macron’s visit to Doha said the expanded partnership covered homeland security and civil protection.

On Thursday, Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani launched the sixth Watan exercise during a visit to Milipol. The exercise brings together security, military, and civilian agencies to rehearse emergency responses.

World.title: Musk's Starshield system 'back' in Ukraine, says Trump
World.content:
Trump said that he did not want to comment on who called for capping Starshield for Ukraine, but that Musk had "put it back."

The Starshield military communications system — the military-grade version of satellite-based communication network Starlink — is "back" in Ukraine, US President Donald Trump said on Thursday.

His announcement comes after the Wall Street Journal reported that the US president asked tech billionaire Elon Musk to restore the service vital to Ukraine's defense against Russia's invasion.

What did Trump say about uncapping Starshield for Ukraine?

"I don't want to comment on it, you know, whether I called or whether somebody else called — doesn't make any difference," Trump told journalists when asked about the report.

"I guess the bottom line, he put it back," Trump said, referring to Musk.

Kyiv is yet to confirm if the throttling has been lifted.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have been increasingly tense of late after Trump called for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced after he criticized a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.

Meanwhile, Kyiv has questioned Washington's support over intelligence sharing and speculation that the White House may have ordered the restrictions on Starshield.

The unsolved mystery of who throttled Starshield

Earlier this week the Journal reported that Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network. The move rendered some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless, it added.

Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The report, citing two unnamed sources, said Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public. One person claimed that Musk spoke with multiple senior administration officials, including Trump, before imposing the speed cap.

In response to that report, Musk had said that "any limits to speed or usage" of Starshied, operated by his company SpaceX, were "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Both Trump and then Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the Pentagon had not directed any changes.

Ukraine has not recieved a clear official explanation of who ordered the restrictions or why, a senior European official familiar with the matter told AP on Thursday.

US Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal on Thursday said he had opened an inquiry into the matter.

World.title: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
World.content:
Names are central to our identity, so what happens when that name is a source of ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name — or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection, as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

How do names shape first impressions

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness.



For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.



What do Nigerians think of bullying? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Weirdness': Why people react negatively to some names

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 41, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

How humor helps — and harms — as a coping mechanism

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

How an embarassing name can also offer a sense of belonging

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point," she said.

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message" and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

Superpower laughter — how humor makes us strong , To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."



Edited by: Richard Connor

World.title: India news: Thousands of Indian pilgrims stranded in Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks disrupt flights, government facilitating return
World.content:
10/23/2026 October 23, 2026 Hindu nationalist group to protest Elon Musk's Starlink in Delhi

An organization affiliated with India's Hindu nationalist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) movement will hold a protest march in New Delhi on Friday against SpaceX founder Elon Musk's Starlink, citing national security and digital sovereignty concerns.

The Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM) said the march would begin at 11 a.m. (0530 GMT) in the capital's Chanakyapuri area.

It has urged the government to block Starlink's commercial satellite broadband launch, arguing that its network could complicate internet shutdowns and lawful interception during security emergencies.

The campaign follows Musk’s criticism of regulatory delays facing Starlink in India and his accusation that Reliance Industries, led by Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani, is using its market power to block foreign competitors.

In a tweet addressing Ambani as the Prime Minister of India and the "real boss of India," Musk accused the tycoon of "monopolistic exploitation" of Indians and keeping Starlink out of the market.

Reliance has rejected the allegations.

"It is unfortunate that instead of responding to the information requested from his company on national security grounds, Elon Musk chose to indirectly accuse Indian businesses and the government," the SJM said in a statement on its website.

The SJM highlighted Starlink in Ukraine as a case study for national security. According to a Wall Street Journal report, the trillionaire ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Kyiv relies on.

Separately, in a sign of Musk's plummeting popularity in India, recently, controversial Dussehra posters displayed in the northern Lucknow city depicted Musk and other international figures, including US Senator Ilhan Omar, as the ten faces of Ravana, portraying them as opponents of India's interests.

During the Hindu Dussehra festival effigies of Ravana are traditionally burned symbolizing the victory of good over evil.

World.title: Serbia: Tens of thousands rally ahead of elections
World.content:
After two years of student-led protests, Serbia will soon vote in what observers describe as a referendum-like snap election pitting strongman Aleksandar Vucic against the student movement.

Over a hundred thousand of Serbians took to the streets in support of Serbia's protesting youth movement on Thursday, in what was the final campaign rally ahead of a pivotal election challenge to the Balkan nation's populist strongman, Aleksandar Vucic.

Crowds poured into Belgrade's central square from all directions and filled up several blocks around the area. Independent crowd-monitoring group Archive of Public Gatherings estimated about 150,000 people were at the rally.

Protesters filled Belgrade's Slavija square and its surrounding streets Image: Marko Djurica/REUTERS

The optimistic crowds chanted "victory" ahead of Sunday's crunch vote which comes after two years of student-led protests against Vucic. It was triggered by a 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station which killed 16 people.

The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, has since snowballed from demands for an independent investigation into the incident, into calls for early elections.

The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What happened at the protest?

The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, is the veteran leader's biggest threat.

Thousands supporting it flocked to Belgrade's streets on Thursday.

"I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country," 47-year-old Marija Nedeljkovic Radic told the French AFP news agency as she arrived for the students' rally.

"Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible," she said.

The Students List's election ticket is polling neck and neck with Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party Image: DW

"We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours," university professor Jugoslav Gasic, one of 250 candidates on the Student List, told the crowd who chanted "Victory, victory!"

"You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!"

How has Vucic responded?

Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade now, either as prime minister or president of the Balkan country.

As pressure from the protests mounted, he announced a snap election last month. He has resigned as president, but many argue it is a tactical move so that he could run for prime minister.

This is now the biggest electoral challenge his party, the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), has faced since it was elected into power in 2012.

The leader, meanwhile, has regularly accused the students movement of being a foreign-funded coup.

"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it," Vucic said to a sports hall full of supporters on Thursday. "Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!"

Serbia's student revolt: Will it bring about change? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Worries of post-result unrest

Days before the vote, Serbian civil societies warned that conditions for "free and fair election" were lacking.

"This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government," a joint statement by 24 organisations said, arguing it was supported by documented findings.

Analysts warn that a close election result could lead to post-election instability, if both sides declare victory. Vucic, who controls the Serbian police, has said he would quash any unrest after the vote.

While several minor parties are also in the race for premiership, observers say that there is a referendum-like atmosphere between Vucic and the students' movement which could sideline other parties in the 250-member parliament.

World.title: Airbnb scraps guest checkout chores such as cleaning
World.content:
Under new rules, guests will no longer have to do tasks that cleaners would normally handle. Hosts can now only make "reasonable" requests, such as leaving dirty dishes in the sink and sorting trash from recycling.

Chores such as washing dishes, stripping beds and taking out the trash at the end of your Airbnb stay will soon be a thing of the past.

Under new rules unveiled this week , the short-term rental platform says hosts should only make "reasonable" requests of guests.

Airbnb said hosts are generally not allowed to "ask guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes."

'Unreasonable' demands like changing the sheets are being scrapped Image: Sviatlana Barysenka/Zoonar/picture alliance

Why did Airbnb introduce the new rules?

Checkout chores have been a contentious issue for guests, especially in cases where they are also charged cleaning fees.

Airbnb has previously admitted that such fees can create confusion between guests and hosts.

"Guests expect checkout to be relatively simple, and most want to avoid unexpected chores," Airbnb said in a message to hosts on the platform.

"Asking them to do things a cleaner should handle can negatively affect their stay and your reviews."

Guests will still be expected to leave dirty dishes in the sink or dishwasher Image: Thomas Trutschel/photothek/picture alliance

The new rules come amid growing protests against housing shortages in many European cities, with protesters arguing that short-term rentals such as Airbnb have pushed them out of their own cities.

In September, the European Commission proposed more restrictions on Airbnb and other short-term rental companies in tourist hubs.

What else do the new Airbnb rules for hosts say?

Guests can still be asked to leave dirty dishes in the sink, to gather used towels and separate trash and recyclables, for example.

Hosts can also require guests to put trash in animal-proof containers areas where bears are active or ask them to "limit shower time due to local drought-related water restrictions."

But hosts will no longer be allowed to ban guests from using amenities listed in the property description, such as air conditioners, nor will they be allowed to fine guests.

Instead, hosts must seek compensation for any damage from insurance that the platform provides.

The new policy applies to bookings starting on November 20.

World.title: Tibet earthquake kills at least 16 people, injures dozens: state media
World.content:
A powerful magnitude 7 earthquake has struck Tibet in southwestern China, official media reported. Chinese state TV said it's the strongest quake to hit the remote Himalayan region in five years.

A strong earthquake struck Tibet in southwestern China on Thursday night, killing at least 16 people and injuring 65 others, Chinese state media reported.

Hundreds of homes in the remote Himalayan region collapsed due to the magnitude 7.0 quake, Xinhua reported.

China's President Xi Jinpinghas ordered "all-out search and rescue efforts" to locate missing people, provide "prompt medical treatment for the injured" and called for "every effort to minimize casualties," Xinhua said.

The earthquake is the strongest to hit the region in the past five years, broadcaster CCTV said, and the most powerful to hit China since January 2024.

Firefighters have been deployed to help with disaster relief efforts Image: Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

How severe was the earthquake in Tibet?

At least 339 residential buildings and 20 livestock sheds have collapsed, local government officials said, according to state media.

Of the 65 injured, 11 were in serious condition, the local media office said.

Disaster relief efforts were ongoing as officials assess the scale of the damage, the state news agency added.

Xinhua reported that power and communication lines to the area were also disrupted.

Over 1,600 people from the local county have been deployed to assist with relief efforts.

More ⁠than ​12,000 people have been relocated, ​state media said.

Some 3,000 tents and folding beds have been provided for quake victims Image: Xinhua/dpa/picture alliance

What do we know about the area where the earthquake struck?

The earthquake's epicenter is around 190 kilometers (120 miles) northeast of Nagqu, a city around 300 kilometers north of the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, the US Geological Survey said.

The mountainous area is sparsely populated.

The quake struck at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.

How often do earthquakes hit China?

Earthquakes are relatively common in China.

In January 2025, a quake near Mount Everest in Tibet's Tingri region killed at least 126 people.

In 2010, at least 2,698 people were killed when a magnitude 7.1 quake hit Qinghai province, which neighbors Tibet.

World.title: Poland: Thousands protest for more abortion rights
World.content:
Thousands rallied across Poland to demand abortion rights six years after a landmark court ruling tightened restrictions. The country has one of the strictest abortion rules in all of Europe.

Thousands of people took part in abortion-rights demonstrations across Poland on Thursday, including in the capital Warsaw and more than 20 other cities.

Abortion is legal in Poland only when the pregnancy is the result of a criminal act like rape or incest, or when it endangers the life or health of the mother. As a result, most abortions are carried out secretly.

The protesters held placards with slogans such as "Women's hell continues” and “Men of quality don't fear equality."

Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power in 2023 after pledging to loosen Poland's abortion restrictions. But disagreements among members of his governing coalition have hampered efforts to change the law, and protesters have accused the government of breaking its promise.

What is the current legal framework?

Abortion has been legal in the overwhelmingly Catholic country since 1993, but only in cases involving a threat to the mother's life or health, a pregnancy resulting from rape or incest, or severe fetal abnormalities.

In 2020, under the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, abortion laws were tightened even further, and abortions in cases of fetal abnormalities were banned.

Activists say tens of thousands of abortions take place outside hospitals each year.

Women who undergo secret abortions, for instance by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility. However, people who help them, including doctors and family members, can potentially be prosecuted and face up to three years in prison.

Thousands braved the rain to call for the decriminalisation of abortion Image: Mladen Antonov/AFP

Activists question government’s reform push

The protests on Thursday came just days after Poland’s parliament passed two bills that would ease abortion restrictions but which are expected to be vetoed by the country’s President Karol Nawrocki, a politician with the backing of the conservative PiS opposition.

"These are breadcrumbs," Kinga Jelinska, director of the Women Help Women Foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, told news agency AFP.

The activists said that passing the draft laws one year before the next parliamentary election was a token gesture with no chance of passing into law.

They accused the liberal Tusk government of merely creating the impression of taking action because it needed women's votes in the upcoming election.
