World.title: Albania's student protests are only getting bigger
World.content:
As police try to suppress anti-corruption protests by young Albanians, Prime Minister Edi Rama is claiming that "antifa" is behind the unrest. Few are buying that explanation.

The fallout from the October 13 protests was still visible when students and faculty from the University of Tirana gathered outside the Education Ministry in Albania's capital on Tuesday to express their continued discontent. Smashed windows have yet to be replaced; the walls are still black with soot from fires that broke out during the protests.

Albania has seen nearly five months of peaceful anti-government protests, sparked initially when plans were made public that Jared Kushner — a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump — and associates intended to build a luxury hotel complex within a nature reserve.

Since then, anti-government and anti-corruption protests have escalated. Now, college and high school students clash with police forces almost daily, with the fiercest clashes so far occurring last week.

Why Albania's political crisis is deepening To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Protesters denounce corruption, mismanaged universities and the rising cost of education in Albania — and call for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in office since 2013.

Wearing a black hooded jacket and a scarf across her face to conceal her identity, a woman who asked to be called Sara because she fears repercussions for speaking to the press told DW that protesters "communicate via text messages — that's the only way."

She cut the interview short as some protesters began flinging stones at the Education Ministry. Police pushed demonstrators and journalists out of the way, using water cannons to disperse the crowd.

"Social media is the most important public space today — more so than physical spaces," Besmir Semanaj, a prominent Albanian cybersecurity advocate told DW. "Young Albanians no longer organize through traditional structures such as political parties, associations or public appeals. Instead, they organize themselves where they spend much of their daily lives: on their cellphones."

"The most important communication channels include Instagram, WhatsApp groups for academic-year cohorts, departments and dormitories, Telegram channels for general announcements, and TikTok for sharing videos," Semanaj said. He added that people who are especially concerned with security use the Signal messaging app.

"This is a horizontal organizational structure, without individual 'leaders' and without a central command structure," Semanaj said. "That is exactly why the government is having such a hard time understanding and controlling the situation."

Semanaj said the Telegram messenger app had proven particularly useful for protesters. "Telegram channels allow you to reach tens of thousands of people at once," he said. "Notifications are sent out within seconds, and external control is more difficult to establish than on traditional platforms."

Anti-corruption protester "Sara" says communication occurs online Image: Kristi Çavo/DW

Rama: 'Hybrid war'

Rama has called the youth uprising a "hybrid war." He said protesters thought they could "make Albania a better country through TikTok and without even being able to string together more than seven coherent words." Though not all are terrorists, he said, he believes that "they are hostages to a certain mindset, a new ideology that has only one goal: to destroy, to turn everything upside down, to raze everything to the ground."

Over nearly five months, Rama has accused various "true" masterminds of organizing the anti-government and anti-corruption protests. He has alleged that the governments of Greece, Russia and Iran are stirring up dissent.

Most recently, Rama said it was "antifa" — or a decentralized movement of global antifascists — that had stoked anti-government and anti-corruption sentiments in Albania. "These are young people who have been radicalized and ideologically indoctrinated and who are acting under the pressure or influence of a new, dark force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, a force that the President of the United States has designated as a terrorist organization: Antifa," Rama claimed.

A protester hurls back a tear gas canister fired at students by police Image: Florion Goga/REUTERS

Redion Qirjazi, a security affairs researcher who focuses on violence prevention and conflict resolution, told DW that Rama's claim was not likely to prove true. "That is a serious accusation — one that requires equally compelling evidence," Qirjazi said. "To date, no verifiable evidence has been presented to prove the existence of an organized Antifa structure in Albania, let alone its involvement in coordinating the protests."

Qirjazi said Rama's reference to Trump's calling antifa a terror group was problematic. "Antifa is not a unified international organization with a centralized structure or leadership," he said, "but rather an umbrella term for various movements and groups united by the fact that they are, at their core, anti-fascist."

Sara said she rejected the "terrorist" label that Rama had attempted to slap on her and her fellow protesters. "There are groups that are willing to use violence — that's true — but I have nothing to do with them," she said. "As soon as I see violence, I walk away; I'm against it."

Is Rama deflecting?

Arlind Qori, the chairman of the Together Movement, a social-democratic opposition party with just one seat in Albania's parliament, said youths had taken to the streets out of dissatisfaction with the status quo rather than any particular ideology. "Young Albanians are outraged by the current socioeconomic conditions: the poverty, the fact that many of their parents have emigrated because they couldn't support their families, the decline of the education system, the lack of postgraduation prospects," Qori said. The students' central demand is for Rama to resign, he added "not a socialist revolution."

Arlind Qori says the protesters are voicing legitimate demands Image: Kristi Çavo/DW

"People aren't demanding anything radical," Qori said. "They merely want a corrupt head of government to resign — that's a fundamental and moderate demand. But Edi Rama continues to meet this demand with police violence and arrogance."

Qirjazi said Rama's allegations of foreign interference could be a strategy. "When a government faces protests and public discontent, linking demonstrators to extremism and foreign influence may serve to divert attention away from the actual causes and toward a national security narrative," he said.

"This can serve several political purposes: to delegitimize the protesters, to weaken their support among the public, and to justify a tougher crackdown in the name of law and order," Qirjazi said.

Semanaj said this was a common pattern in governments' efforts to dismiss dissent. "Protests are portrayed as acts of violence," he said. "Young people are cast as manipulated, and their legitimate concerns — conditions at universities, tuition fees, corruption and a lack of prospects — vanish from the news agenda."

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Feijóo se refuerza en el Congreso: portavoces de la línea dura, veteranos y experiencia de gestión con miras al Gobierno
World.content:
Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha decidido llevar a cabo una renovación profunda de las listas del Partido Popular al Congreso para las elecciones del próximo 29 de noviembre con la vista puesta en un futuro Gobierno de la derecha. El PP va poco a poco desvelando las candidaturas y el resultado hasta ahora es un cambio de calado en los cuadros del partido. El líder del PP se refuerza en el Parlamento con portavoces de la línea dura, como Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo y Xavier García Albiol, pero también con perfiles de gestión, como consejeros de Gobiernos autonómicos y alcaldes, lo que está obligando a remodelaciones en las comunidades autónomas. Y con más veteranos, algunos de los cuales saltan del Senado al Congreso. Se trata de construir “un grupo parlamentario sólido”, apuntan en Génova, del que saldrán muchos cargos gubernamentales si Feijóo llega al poder.

Feijóo ha apostado por una reestructuración a fondo de las listas en las que incorpora a perfiles con “experiencia de gestión y de solvencia” procedentes del amplio poder territorial del PP y que en el partido se da por hecho que, si alcanza La Moncloa, irán a un futuro Gobierno como directores generales, secretarios de Estado o en su caso ministros. Varios de ellos salen de los Gobiernos autonómicos presididos por el PP y obligan por tanto a los barones populares a acometer remodelaciones de sus Ejecutivos, porque se trata de consejeros que se integran en las candidaturas del PP al Congreso y, por tanto, dimitirán de sus responsabilidades de gestión autonómica, según informan fuentes de Génova.

Es el caso, hasta ahora, de la consejera de Política Social de la Xunta de Galicia, Fabiola García, que irá como dos por A Coruña; de la consejera de Educación de Castilla y León, María Pardo, que encabeza la lista por Valladolid; y de la consejera de Presidencia, Justicia, Seguridad y Simplificación Administrativa del Gobierno de Cantabria, Isabel Urrutia, que encabeza por Cantabria. Todas ellas serán relevadas en los Ejecutivos autonómicos. Pero habrá más consejeros que salgan de los Gobiernos autonómicos en dirección al Congreso a petición de Génova, porque todavía faltan por desvelarse las listas al completo en territorios como Andalucía o la Comunidad Valenciana.

Algunos barones han tenido que frenar más salidas de sus Ejecutivos, según fuentes de los territorios, porque la dirección quería llevarse a más perfiles. “Quieren a los mejores, con experiencia para un futuro Gobierno y también con tirón electoral y con capacidad de aglutinar sensibilidades en el partido, pero tampoco pueden llevarse a todos”, cuenta una fuente territorial del PP, que interpreta que Feijóo también quiere vincularse a los Gobiernos populares para reforzar la imagen del PP como partido gestor.

De Galicia, su tierra, Feijóo se lleva en la lista al Congreso también al exconsejero de Sanidad Julio García Comesaña (que fue el responsable de Sanidad durante la pandemia con el líder del PP cuando era el presidente de la Xunta) y a Miguel Santalices, el presidente del Parlamento de Galicia. Y ya incorporó en 2023 y repite en las listas el exconsejero de Economía y exvicepresidente primero y segundo de la Xunta Francisco Conde, a quien muchos en el PP ven como un posible ministro del área económica de un eventual Gobierno de Feijóo.

Génova ha incorporado también a varios alcaldes a las candidaturas, como el de Toledo, Carlos Velázquez, o la de Santander, Gema Igual, que concurre al Senado. “Queremos a gente solvente en el Congreso para que los debates no le resulten fáciles al PSOE. Es gente que no viene a improvisar, buscamos un grupo que no vaya con la L de prácticas”, apuntan fuentes de la cúpula del PP.

Feijóo se ha rodeado también de portavoces duros para competir con un Vox al alza. Génova confirmó ayer que Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo irá como número dos, tras Feijóo, en la lista por Madrid, como quería el PP de Isabel Díaz Ayuso, mientras que Xavier García Albiol encabezará por Barcelona. El líder del PP mantiene como número tres por Madrid a Borja Sémper, la principal figura del ala más moderada del partido, y puede reivindicar así que ha integrado a las diferentes sensibilidades. Sin embargo, es Álvarez de Toledo la novedad y quien escala en la lista, porque en las últimas elecciones iba en el puesto seis, y en cambio su número dos fue la ex dirigente de Ciudadanos Marta Rivera de la Cruz.

Feijóo ha elegido ahora como número dos a una política con la que ha tenido diferencias estratégicas y de estilo desde mucho antes de llegar a la presidencia nacional del PP. Cuando Álvarez de Toledo ejerció como portavoz parlamentaria de Pablo Casado, la acusó incluso de haber “perdido los papeles” en un debate con Pablo Iglesias. Ella, por su parte, reconoció sus “diferencias” con Feijóo por la política territorial. “Eso del ‘constitucionalismo catalanista’ me parece una gallegada”, declaró en una entrevista en El Español. Pero poco a poco, tras su aterrizaje a Madrid como presidente del PP, el político gallego fue integrándola en su círculo pese a sus reticencias de partida. “Feijóo ha sido listo al aupar a Cayetana, porque ella representa a un sector importante de la derecha”, opina un dirigente del ala moderada, resignado al ascenso de los duros.

Las listas del PP reflejan también un refuerzo del Congreso con veteranos que saltan desde el Senado, como el excoordinador general del PP Fernando Martínez Maíllo. “Génova tiene que reforzar mucho el grupo en el Congreso, porque cuando se gobierna un tercio de los diputados desaparece en quince días porque se va a cargos gubernamentales. Además, sería un Gobierno sin mayoría absoluta del PP, obligado a negociar permanentemente con Vox”, analiza un dirigente que da por hecho que el PP llegará a La Moncloa. La veteranía es un grado también en el nuevo presidente de la Fundación del PP Reformismo 21, el exalto cargo del Gobierno de José María Aznar Gabriel Elorriaga.

Los miembros del comité de dirección de Feijóo repetirán en puestos de salida por sus circunscripciones de origen, aunque todavía falta por conocer cómo queda el encaje del resto de la lista por Madrid, en la que irán también los vicesecretarios Alma Ezcurra, Jaime de los Santos y Alberto Nadal, y Feijóo incluyó en las últimas elecciones a su jefa de gabinete, Marta Varela, y a su coordinadora de imagen, Mar Sánchez.

La nota atípica entre los gestores, los duros y los veteranos que ganan posiciones en el PP es Jon Echeverría, un joven de 22 años que todavía es estudiante y que encabezará la lista por Gipuzkoa, con el objetivo de conseguir un escaño que el PP no logra desde hace quince años.

World.title: Alquilé mi vivienda en 2019 y el contrato se prorrogó tres años más. ¿Podrá el casero echarme en 2027?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. Alquilé mi vivienda en julio de 2019 por cinco años, hasta julio de 2024. El contrato se prorrogó tres años más, hasta julio de 2027, debido a que la propiedad no me avisó con cuatro meses de antelación de que quería rescindir el contrato. ¿Puede el propietario rescindir el contrato de alquiler en 2027 con los nuevos decretos de vivienda? Eduard.

Respuesta. Efectivamente, se encuentra disfrutando de la prórroga de tres años prevista en el artículo 10 de la Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos (LAU). Al vencimiento del octavo año, el arrendador puede decidir no renovar el contrato, siempre que lo comunique con un preaviso mínimo de 30 días.

Si el arrendador realiza dicho preaviso en tiempo y forma, el artículo 10.3 de la LAU contempla dos supuestos en los que el arrendatario puede solicitar una prórroga:

Si el arrendatario acredita encontrarse en situación de vulnerabilidad económica , podrá solicitar una prórroga extraordinaria por un plazo máximo de un año, durante el cual se mantendrán los mismos términos y condiciones del contrato vigente. Para ello, deberá aportar un informe o certificado emitido en el último año por los servicios sociales municipales o autonómicos que acredite su situación de vulnerabilidad social y económica. Esta prórroga será obligatoria para el arrendador cuando tenga la condición de gran tenedor y siempre que las partes no hayan suscrito un nuevo contrato de arrendamiento.

Si la vivienda se encuentra en una zona declarada como mercado residencial tensionado y dicha declaración sigue vigente, el arrendatario podrá solicitar una prórroga extraordinaria por periodos anuales, hasta un máximo de tres años. Durante ese tiempo se mantendrán los términos y condiciones del contrato en vigor, salvo que las partes acuerden otras condiciones, se firme un nuevo contrato con las limitaciones de renta que correspondan o el arrendador necesite la vivienda para uso propio.

No obstante, si no concurre ninguna de las circunstancias anteriores, la disposición final quinta del Real Decreto-ley 29/2026, de 6 de octubre, permite solicitar una prórroga extraordinaria de hasta dos años adicionales, renovable año a año, manteniendo las mismas condiciones del contrato vigente. Esta medida resulta aplicable a los contratos cuyo vencimiento se produzca antes del 31 de diciembre de 2028.

Para acceder a esta prórroga, el arrendatario debe encontrarse al corriente de pago y haber mantenido esa situación durante los ocho meses anteriores. La solicitud deberá ser aceptada por el arrendador, salvo que exista un acuerdo distinto entre las partes, se formalice un nuevo contrato, se acepte un nuevo arrendamiento con una reducción de la renta de al menos un 5% o el arrendador necesite la vivienda para sí o para familiares de primer grado, siempre que acredite una necesidad real y lo comunique dentro del plazo legalmente establecido, aunque esta facultad no figure expresamente en el contrato.

Por último, debe tenerse en cuenta que esta prórroga extraordinaria de hasta dos años no es acumulable a la prórroga extraordinaria prevista en el artículo 10.3 de la LAU, que tiene carácter preferente.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

Unions FNV and CNV have suspended their weekly strikes in regional public transport for two weeks after employers made new commitments on a collective labour agreement, broadcaster NOS reported on Wednesday.

The suspension means Thursday’s planned strike did not go ahead, the unions said in a press release.

The unions announced in early October they would strike one day a week after talks broke down. Staff at operators including Arriva, Keolis and Qbuzz walked out for the first time last week, cancelling many buses and regional trains across the country.

The unions are demanding a 9.5% pay rise over two years and better conditions for older staff.

World.title: Gambling regulator hits illegal casino with record €37m fine
World.content:
The Dutch gambling regulator KSA has issued a record fine of €37 million on a company for running a dozen unlicensed online casinos.

EOD Code SRL, which says it is registered in Costa Rica, offered games to players in the Netherlands through sites including Instantcasino and Skyhills without a Dutch licence, KSA said on Thursday.

KSA inspectors were able to register and gamble on the sites with no measures in place to stop people in the Netherlands using them. Several of the sites had no visible age checks and accepted cryptocurrency and other anonymous payment methods.

The investigation began with Instantcasino and later uncovered 11 more sites run by the same company. The KSA based the fine on an estimate of the company’s Dutch revenue.

Online gambling was legalised in October 2021, with the government arguing a regulated market would draw players away from illegal sites. But the KSA estimated last year that more money goes to unlicensed sites than to legal ones.

In August, radio station BNR found that illegal operators were targeting Facebook and Instagram ads at people on Cruks, the national register that bars them from gambling. The cabinet set out plans in June to ban online gambling advertising and bonuses.

If you are concerned about your own or someone else’s use of alcohol, drugs, or gambling, the Jellinek addiction helpline can be reached on 088 505 1220 or at jellinek.nl. The line is staffed in Dutch and English on weekdays, 1pm to 5pm.

World.title: Airbnb to hosts: no more asking guests to wash the dishes
World.content:
In addition to increasingly strict rules for hosts renting out their homes on Airbnb – including limits on the number of nights, guest caps and permit fees – there are now new rules to abide by: they can’t ask their guests to do the dishes or remove bed sheets.

Airbnb introduced a new policy on house rules earlier this week that will go into effect on November 20, 2026. Among them are what the company considers “reasonable requests”, which Airbnb defines per chore.

“You may not ask guests to wash everything and store the dishes, but you may ask them to put the dishes in the sink,” says the site.

“You may not ask guests to pick up the bed linen or put the laundry in the washing machine, but you may ask them to collect used towels.”

And: “You may not ask guests to take the garbage and dispose of it elsewhere, but you may ask them to separate their residual waste and recyclable waste in the designated waste bins in the accommodation.”

But “reasonable” appears to be a relative term. Airbnb will let hosts, for example, ask guests to put their garbage in animal-resistant containers if there are bears in the area.

“It’s ridiculous,” said one former Airbnb host who doesn’t want to be named. “The rules were changing all the time, getting more restrictive, which made it increasingly hard to make any money at all. I’m glad I got out of it before I can’t tell my guests to clean up after themselves. What’s next? Will we have to provide sunbeds for them?”

According to the booking website, the world’s largest for private stays, landlords already charge their guests a cleaning fee. Making them clean more is unfair, says Airbnb, and leads to guest dissatisfaction.

Airbnb has faced criticism for years in many cities where it operates, with detractors saying it leads to higher rents, less housing for locals and less livable neighbourhoods, especially in smaller cities with huge tourist populations like Amsterdam and Barcelona.

World.title: Get help with careers, homes and more at IamExpat Fair The Hague
World.content:
The IamExpat Fair is returning to the Grote Kerk in The Hague on Saturday November 7 with more exhibitors than ever, three international centres from across South Holland and large sections for families and health.

The IamExpat Fair, now in its 24th edition, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, from housing and careers to schooling and leisure, including special offers only available for attendees. Tickets go for €6 online, or €10 at the door.

“We have an exciting lineup of exhibitors and workshops this year in The Hague,” says events manager Claire Leunissen.

“From exhibitors specialised in preparing newcomers for the inburgering exams, to career coaches experienced in advising expats, and stocking the health & leisure section with physical and mental resources, we’re confident that services at the IamExpat Fair will help internationals thrive. ”

Workshops, presentations and centres

Experts will run workshops throughout the day on topics including buying a house and securing a mortgage, job hunting and help with lifestyle and health. Places are limited, so make sure to book your chosen sessions in advance – you can sign up here.

The Hague International Centre will have a large stand, joined by representatives from across the province, including Leiden International Centre and the Rotterdam International Center, to answer practical questions about settling in the region.

Learning Dutch and finding work

For newcomers working toward the inburgering exams, there are resources from Inburgering Online and Easy Dutch, alongside language schools including Language Institute Regina Coeli, and Bart de Pau.

Career stands and coaches include recruitment agency Undutchables and Work & Worth Coaching, while Work in South Holland will explain the state of the labour market across the region’s main industries.

Families and health

The Family & Kids section brings together several international schools, including the International School of The Hague, The British School in the Netherlands, International School Delft and Optimist International School. There is also kids’ area where families can play games together.

The Health & Leisure section is one of the largest at the fair, with exhibitors ranging from mental health services to dentists and chiropractors.

The IamExpat Fair The Hague takes place in the Grote Kerk on Saturday November 7 from 10am to 5pm. Free tickets are available online while they last; after that, entry costs €6 in advance or €10 at the door. The first 1,000 visitors receive a free tote bag.

World.title: Police shut 30 webshops linked to counterfeit pill deaths
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Thirty websites were taken offline and three men arrested earlier this week in connection to sites that sold counterfeit pills that led to the deaths of three people.

The suspects – a 35-year-old man from Kwintsheul, a 39-year-old man from Rotterdam and a 66-year-old male from The Hague – are suspected of “offering, selling and supplying illegal drugs”, including sedatives, sleeping pills and painkillers like oxycodone, which contained extremely potent synthetic opioids known as nitazenes.

Nitazenes can be many times stronger than morphine and more lethal than fentanyl.

Police say the victims bought the prescription-only pills on websites Slaappillen.net or regionapp.net shortly before they died, and are holding the suspects responsible for running them.

Whack-a-mole

Even though Slaappillen.net was taken down last year, police say the men continued to sell the counterfeit drugs through other websites, which kept popping up as soon as others were taken down.

But according to police, this time they not only took the web shops offline, but confiscated the servers they ran on.

“We have taken down the entire technology behind the websites,” Ron van Brussel told NOS. He is responsible for tackling serious organized crime at the National Investigation and Interventions Unit. “This makes it more difficult to make a restart.”

Both the servers and data have been seized for investigation, and more arrests have not been ruled out.

The police searches were carried out in five locations, including homes and a storage box in The Hague. Crypto wallets, cash and valuables were seized.

With this week’s arrests, police say the main players from the group are now in custody. But, they add, the sale of illegal drugs is far from over.

“There are several criminal groups that keep these types of sites online,” said Van Brussel.

World.title: Are you financially fit for your life in the Netherlands?
World.content:
New to the Netherlands or a longer-term resident looking to get your finances organised to make the most of your Dutch life? A little planning, a few local habits and some expert coaching will soon have you in the best financial shape.

The foundation of any fitness plan is the basics, so first of all you need to establish what your monthly costs are likely to be. Alongside your rent or mortgage repayments, you’ll have to pay for health insurance, council taxes, public transport, gas and electricity, and perhaps a gym membership.

“If you are financially fit, you are able to meet all your monthly and annual payments, save some money and live the life you would like to have at that moment,” says Ame Pots, a financial health coach with ABN Amro who helps expats make the most of their money.

What costs can you expect?

ABN Amro is hosting a free webinar on October 28 to explain how to get financially fit in the Netherlands.

You will have to pay for insurance. Health insurance, for example, will cost you upwards of €160 a month from next year, and you will have to pay the first €400 of insured treatment. You can cut the monthly premium by around €25 if you raise your voluntary deductible by €500, but that means you’ll need to increase your savings so you can pay if you do fall ill. If you want supplementary insurance, such as dental coverage or extra physiotherapy, you will pay more.

By the way, the six-week window for changing health insurer kicks off in mid-November, so now might be a good time to start shopping around for a better deal.

You’ll also have to pay your local authority for waste collection and the water board for water usage. How much you pay depends on the size of your home and how many people live there, but between €250 and €450 a year is the norm in most places. If you are a homeowner, you will pay slightly more. These bills often arrive at the same time of year, in the spring, so you’ll need to make sure you have enough savings to cover them as well.

“We rarely use credit cards, and this surprises a lot of people,” Ame says.

Some bills are monthly, others come once a year

If you live in rented accommodation, you may have to pay service costs, which can range from around €50 to over €250 a month if you live in a building with a lift and lots of amenities such as co-working spaces or a gym. The monthly service fee is an estimate, and you will get a final invoice once a year. Rents also go up once a year, usually in July, by a percentage set by the government. For 2027, the increase in the non-rent-controlled sector, where most expats live, will be 4.4%.

You can keep an eye on your gas and electricity bills if you have a smart meter. If you pay too little to cover your usage, you will be invoiced for the extra costs and your monthly payment is likely to increase. If you pay too much, you’ll get the difference back.

“All this means that you need to really plan out your spending over the year,” says ABN Amro expert Ame. “For example, if you have the 30% ruling, will you still be able to meet your payments when it ends in five years’ time?”

Once you understand the costs you face, create a budget that includes fixed spending, savings and fun stuff. Remember to adjust it if your financial situation changes.

Why is banking in the Netherlands different?

“It’s important to explain to new arrivals how the financial system works in the Netherlands, because it may be very different to back home,” says Ame. “For example, we rarely use credit cards, and this surprises a lot of people from countries where they use a credit card as part of their regular spending.”

You’ll need a Dutch bank account for your salary, your rent and pretty much everything else. The Netherlands runs on digital payments, with debit cards, internet payments and payment request apps dominating how the Dutch spend their money.

“If I ask people how much they spend on rent or groceries, they often give a round number – €100 or €200 – but in practice it is more than that,” says Ame. “Once you are aware of what is really happening in your finances, you will understand how much you can actually spend each month.”

How can you improve your financial fitness?

What to know more about how to stay financially fit in the Netherlands. Join ABN Amro’s free webinar on Wednesday, 28 October, 12:00–13:00 CET. Register now

World.title: Afghans washed up on Texel were human smuggling victims
World.content:
Two Afghan men whose body parts washed ashore on Texel in 2023 were victims of a vast human smuggling network led by infamous migrant smuggler Idriss Ghazi Kareem, according to an investigation by regional broadcaster NH and investigative TV programme Zembla.

The Afghan refugees, Samiullah (20) and Ahmad Jan (27), were only identified this summer. They had boarded a rubber dinghy on the night of August 12, 2023, along with 66 others just north of Calais, in an attempt to cross the English Channel. The boat’s engine failed and, after an explosion, the vessel tore apart.

Although 60 men survived, six were declared dead when found. Samiullah and Ahmad Jan, though, had gone missing.

Two months later, a single foot still in a shoe and a torso washed up on Texel. Dutch detective Fetze Venema worked with the Red Cross to identify the remains, including tracking down the relatives of the missing men in Afghanistan for DNA testing.

Idriss Ghazi Kareem

Following the incident, French authorities dismantled a huge human-trafficking network led by Idriss Ghazi Kareem. He was tried with eight others in Paris last year and sentenced to 15 years in prison for, among other things, procuring boats and other equipment for migrants to cross the English Channel.

The court found he earned hundreds of thousands of euros a year from his people-smuggling operations, which he continued to organise from prison.

Kareem had visited the Netherlands several times, including just three days before the fatal accident. The Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border control, says the country plays a key role in people-smuggling.

“It involves the import, transit, and storage of nautical equipment that is transported to the French coast, where it is then used to ferry migrants across to Great Britain.”

The Marechaussee has not commented on the latest media investigation, saying it “may be part of an ongoing investigation”.

Additional research by NH and Zembla found that at least 26 people, including eight women and two children, have died this year attempting to cross the English Channel in unseaworthy boats.

“Floating coffins”

Much of the equipment – from the rubber boat to its motor and life vests – was substandard. “These rubber boats are not seaworthy and generally originate from China,” national public prosecutor for migration-related crime Petra Hoekstra told Zembla. “They are imported into the Netherlands via Turkey.”

And, he said, the smugglers knew that. “For us, that is an aggravating circumstance. They believe that the money outweighs a human life. And that means they are deliberately placing people in floating coffins.”

World.title: Rotterdam police arrest AI scammers over €400k thefts
World.content:
Police in Rotterdam have rounded up a gang who ran a sophisticated phishing scam using a fake banking app that stole nearly €400,000 from 170 victims.

The gang set up a bogus bank helpdesk service that targeted customers by phone and asked them to download an app that could read the NFC chip on their bank card.

Police arrested the two men behind the operation, a 23-year-old man from Vaassen, and a 25-year-old man from Ede, on October 4. On Tuesday they appeared in court, where a magistrate extended their detention for 90 days.

The fraudsters made the scam more plausible by using AI-generated voices to read out messages telling their victims to check if Google Pay had been installed on their phones by their bank.

When they saw it had not, they were told to press 1, which connected them straight to the fake helpdesk.

The victims were told to install the app and hold their card to their phone, allowing the criminals to download their details. At the same time accomplices would try to hack into the account using the card’s PIN.

Ruben van Well, head of the Rotterdam cybercrime team, said the victims ranged in age from their twenties to their eighties. “We found a lot of young people had been defrauded,” he said. “The victims also came from all over the country.”

Police confiscated hundreds of thousands of euros in cryptocurrency following the arrests and took the fake app and server offline. “We are not ruling out further arrests,” said Van Well.

World.title: Poland charges second Georgian man over murder of Russian dissident
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year. The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself. Warto przypomnieć: ▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości. ▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026 Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin. He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons. After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused. On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then. Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week. "Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway. The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban. Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN. The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”. Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty. A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”. However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026 The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”. In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations. Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia. Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states. World.title: Poland and India aim to double trade by 2030 as PMs meet in New Delhi
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies. Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades. During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”. Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies. Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20. “The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said. Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.” Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market. Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”. “Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.” However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals. The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible". "Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility. To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations. Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people. The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations. Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War. “In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”. The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year. World.title: How will recent scandals affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did. They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises. The hospital scandal Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk. In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients. Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue. Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services. KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors. Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens. The cryptocurrency scandal The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds. However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro. The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto). For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations. The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026 PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation. Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive. The diminishing impact of scandals It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape. For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party. A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force. Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions. The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland. Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence. Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage. Scandal-neutralising structural shifts This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics. Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy. Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative. Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023 This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage. Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines. In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media. So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high. Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now. How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment. Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity. They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues. Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments. Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence. The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote. In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day. Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections. We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed. Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them. Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote. So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation. World.title: Court acquits Polish soldier who accidentally shot Syrian refugee at Belarus border

A Polish soldier who accidentally shot a Syrian refugee who had entered Poland over the border from Belarus has been acquitted of negligent use of a weapon. The Syrian man had been seeking 50,000 zloty (€11,500) in compensation from the soldier. The verdict was welcomed by defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, whose ministry had supported the soldier’s legal defence. ❗Podporucznik Wojska Polskiego został dziś uniewinniony przez Wojskowy Sąd Garnizonowy w Warszawie. Nie udowodniono mu żadnych zaniedbań w czasie służby na granicy z Białorusią. W listopadzie 2023 r. przypadkowo postrzelił on migranta. Od początku zapewniliśmy mu pomoc prawną… pic.twitter.com/RS2p2WsQ7Z — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 21, 2026 The incident in question took place in November 2023 in Poland’s northeastern Podlasie province. The soldier, named only as Adam Ł. under Polish privacy law and who holds the rank of second lieutenant, had only recently received his first posting to the border, reports legal news service Prawo.pl. Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging, assisting and in some cases coercing tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to cross into Poland. Among those who make it over the border, most head westwards to Germany, while some have sought to claim international protection in Poland. In response, Poland has posted thousands of soldiers to the border, where they provide support to the border guard and police. Officers have at times faced violence from migrants trying to cross. In one case, in June 2023, a Polish soldier died after being stabbed. Poland has named a Moroccan man, Mohamed Addamrou, as the suspect in the 2024 murder of a Polish soldier, Mateusz Sitek, who was fatally stabbed while trying to stop a group of migrants from forcing their way through the border from Belarus to Poland https://t.co/mw8JuOPwcE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 10, 2026 A few months after that tragedy, Adam Ł. took part in an operation to apprehend a group of migrants who had crossed from Belarus and were around 2 kilometres from the border. After the soldiers called on the migrants to stop, one of them, a 23-year-old Syrian man, began to flee. As Adam Ł. chased him, the soldier slipped and fell, resulting in his gun, a PM-98 Glauberyt submachine gun, accidentally discharging two rounds. One bullet hit the Syrian man in the back, close to his spine. The soldier immediately began providing him with first aid, before the Syrian was taken to hospital. He was discharged a few weeks later and, in May 2024, was granted asylum in Poland. Initially, when it appeared possible that the Syrian could suffer partial paralysis, military prosecutors considered charging Adam Ł. with negligent use of a weapon resulting in serious injury, a crime carrying a prison sentence of up to eight years. In the end, that was downgraded to a lower charge of negligent use of a weapon causing impairment or a health disorder, which is punishable by up to three years in prison. The defence ministry provided the soldier with legal counsel from a special team set up in 2024 to defend military personnel. They advised him not to plead guilty. Eventually, prosecutors asked only that the court impose an indemnity of 2,000 zloty on Adam Ł., to be paid to the Syrian. The Syrian’s lawyer, meanwhile, sought 50,000 zloty for his client. The president has signed into law new rules removing criminal liability from officers who use firearms while serving on the border. The measures were passed in response to a surge in aggression from some migrants seeking to cross the border from Belarus https://t.co/sBMaoYhoCw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 16, 2024 In a ruling announced on Wednesday, a military court in Warsaw fully acquitted Adam Ł. Judge Michał Żak said that it remained unclear how the incident unfolded. He also pointed to expert evidence commissioned by the court that found the soldier’s gun could have had defects that caused it to fire when it hit the ground. Those doubts, and a lack of convincing evidence to support the prosecutor’s version of events, meant the charge of negligence could not be proven, found Żak. The verdict can still be appealed. The Syrian’s lawyer said they would wait for the judge’s full written justification before deciding whether to appeal. Kosiniak-Kamysz, meanwhile, welcomed the ruling in a social media post. “From the very beginning, we provided him with legal assistance,” wrote the defence minister. “A soldier who carries out his duties cannot be left alone, even in a difficult situation.” In May this year, another soldier was acquitted over an incident in which he fired shots towards a group of migrants who had illegally crossed the Belarussian border. The judge found that, in fact, the soldier had been fulfilling his obligation to defend the Polish border. A Polish soldier who fired shots towards migrants who had illegally crossed the border from Belarus has been acquitted of abusing his powers and threatening the lives of others The military judge found he had been fulfilling his duty to protect the border https://t.co/ugxq5tkdFV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026 In 2024, Poland’s government introduced a new law making it easier for soldiers and other uniformed officers serving at the border to use firearms. They now no longer face criminal liability for employing their weapons in certain cases. Since then, the government has also further strengthened physical border barriers and banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly from Belarus. That has been followed by a significant drop in attempted crossings by migrants from Belarus: in the first half of this year, only 250 attempts were recorded, down from 15,500 in the same period of 2025 – a 98% drop. Poland also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do manage to cross. World.title: Poland condemns Ukrainian region for honouring figures associated with WWII massacres of Poles
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has condemned a decision by the Lviv region in Ukraine to declare 2027 a year honouring the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led the massacre of Poles during World War Two, and one of its leaders, Roman Shukhevych. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the decision “suicidal”, saying that it harms Ukraine by making it harder for the country’s friends to support it. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski announced that the local official responsible for pushing through the commemorations in Lviv has been banned from entering Poland. Decyzja Lwowskiej Rady Obwodowej, by 2027 rok był rokiem UPA i Szuchewycza, jest nieakceptowalna. Taka decyzja nie buduje wzajemnego zaufania między narodami, lecz wzmacnia podziały. Konieczne jest odcięcie się władz Ukrainy od tego stanowiska. — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 20, 2026 On Tuesday, the Lviv regional council adopted resolutions proclaiming 2027 the year of the UPA, of Shukhevych, and of Oleh Olzhych, a poet and leading figure in the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN). Sviatoslav Sheremeta, chair of the region’s committee on culture, said the decisions will pave the way for “large-scale events” to commemorate the UPA, Shukhevych and Olzhych. “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honour their memory,” he added, quoted by local news service Sokal Voice. The OUN was a nationalist organisation that sought Ukrainian independence. The UPA, a partisan formation, emerged in 1942 from a more radical faction of the OUN, with Shukhevych serving as its military commander. While the UPA is still remembered positively by some in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which the UPA led the slaughter of around 100,000 Poles, mostly women and children. Poland has previously condemned official commemorations in Ukraine of Shukhevych and other figures associated with the UPA. And the resolutions adopted by the Lviv region on Tuesday likewise prompted a swift response from Warsaw. “Glorifying the UPA and criminal figures is contrary to European values ​​and the strategic and good-neighbourly nature of relations between Poland and Ukraine,” foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór told news website Wirtualna Polska. “Shukhevych is a criminal stained with the blood of thousands of innocent victims, people who were murdered simply because they were Poles,” he added, also noting that the UPA’s victims included Jews, Czechs, Armenians and Ukrainians themselves. Wewiór warned that, while the Ukrainian and Polish governments have recently made progress towards reconciliation over historical issues, “irresponsible local activists are damaging these relations by honouring people clearly responsible for crimes and collaborating with the Nazis”. The European Parliament has criticised Ukraine's @ZelenskyyUa for naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII, calling it an "unprovoked escalation" that is “not in line with European values” and "disregards Polish sensitivities" https://t.co/54rbPSrs9S — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 On Wednesday, Tusk said that such decisions “harm Ukraine” by “making the work of Ukraine’s friends and supporters of closer cooperation very difficult”. By contrast, the “Russians always rub their hands in glee in situations like these”, added Tusk, quoted by Polsat News. Meanwhile, Sikorski announced that he had signed a motion to place Sheremeta, who has led the efforts to commemorate the UPA and Shukhevych in Lviv, on Poland’s “list of undesirable persons”. Wirtualna Polska reports that Sheremeta was previously banned from entry in 2017, under Poland’s former government, for his actions in blocking the exhumation and commemoration of Polish massacre victims buried in Ukraine. Podpisałem wniosek o wpisanie na listę osób niepożądanych w RP radnego obwodu lwowskiego S. Szeremeta, rekonstruktora Galizien Waffen-SS, autora pomysłu ustanowienia 2027 rokiem R.Szuchewycza, dowódcy UPA, który wydawał rozkazy wysiedlania i mordowania Polaków.… — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 21, 2026 Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) also condemned the resolutions. It called Shukhevych “an architect of the genocide in Volhynia” as well as the “co-founder of collaborationist units operating alongside Germany”. It quoted an order issued by Shukhevych in which he wrote: “Cut them down to the last man. Burn villages inhabited exclusively by Poles; in mixed villages, eliminate only the Polish population.” However, the IPN noted that Olzhych – whom Lviv is also honouring next year – was the head of a group that condemned the crimes committed by the more radical faction of the OUN. The Lviv Regional Council has designated 2027 in the Lviv region as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, an architect of the genocide in Volhynia, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), and Oleh Olzhych, a leader of the OUN-M. Among those being commemorated, Roman Shukhevych stands out as… pic.twitter.com/Bge2muwjHz — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) October 21, 2026 Polish leaders have previously warned that the honouring of the UPA and figures associated with it would harm Ukraine’s chances of joining the European Union. Poland, like all other member states, can veto accession. However, there have also been recent signs of progress on issues of historical memory. Last year, in a diplomatic breakthrough, Ukraine lifted a ban on exhuming the remains of Volhynia massacre victims on its territory. But this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky triggered a diplomatic crisis when he approved the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. Since then, tensions have calmed, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan that includes approving more exhumations. This month, the head of the IPN and its Ukrainian counterpart held their first meeting since 2018.
