World.title: Red flags in 2027 agri budget: Coordinates at sea, ‘overpriced’ infra projects
World.content:
HEARING. Senators and officials of the Department of Agriculture (DA) review the proposed 2027 budget of the DA and its attached agencies and corporations, on October 21, 2026. Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program, the DA is set to receive ₱198.4 billion, an 8 percent decrease from its ₱215.7-billion budget in 2026.

Coordinates for farm-to-market roads allegedly point to the Celebes Sea or waters near Brunei

MANILA, Philippines – The civil society group People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) raised several red flags during the Senate finance committee hearing on the proposed budget of the Department of Agriculture (DA) for 2027.

At the center of the group’s report are farm-to-market (FMR) and irrigation projects. Following the flood control scandal, the DA launched a portal for FMR projects to monitor the standard and completion of farm-to-market roads worth millions of pesos.

Here are the issues that the PBC raised during the hearing:

No publicly available documents on insertions

The group flagged P15 billion worth of FMR and irrigation projects that do not have publicly-posted project attachments. They alleged these projects are insertions made in the House of Representatives.

Kenneth Isaiah Abante, co-convenor of the PBC, said the House inserted 355 FMR projects not originally included in the National Expenditure Program and the DA’s proposal.

“We are not sure if these are connected to the national highway network or connected to their resorts,” Abante said.

In addition, Abante alleged that the House also inserted 319 irrigation projects worth P9.4 billion without proper documents.

Coordinates of farm-to-market roads end up at sea

Coordinates of some FMR projects are erroneous as well, according to citizen-led mapping of 18,000 projects in the House’s general appropriations bill. (READ: House passes P7.2-trillion 2027 budget amid pork barrel concerns)

A P23-million FMR project in Nueva Ecija had coordinates that point to the sea near Benham Rise, said Abante. A project that is supposed to be in Cebu appeared in Celebes Sea. Coordinates of a P55-million project appeared in the waters near Brunei.

Likely overpriced roads and irrigation

The group also flagged costings that it alleged were way over the market price. The standard cost per kilometer of a farm-to-market road is P15 million, but some projects allegedly showed costs of P6 million to P19 million per meter.

“If we take the budget as is, there will likely be overpriced projects in the DA,” said Abante.

The group also said instruments for solar irrigation pump systems were likely overpriced. Abante questioned the P50 million to P200 million price tags for solar panel systems, noting that individual 600- to 700-watt panels cost around P7,000.

The cost of solar materials has risen amid the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which has fueled fears of power outages and higher electricity bills. (READ: ‘Solar rush’: Surge in solar demand overwhelms local industry)

MARKET. People buy basic commodities at the Paco Market in Manila on March 11, 2026.

Watchdogs and civil society groups like the People’s Budget Coalition are given the floor to present recommendations and red flags in the proposed 2027 budget.

This is part of an effort to make the budget process more transparent and participative after the public uproar over the flood control scandal.

The DA accepted PBC’s offer to mobilize their volunteers in verifying the progress of existing FMR projects.

“We welcome initiatives that empower citizens to hold public spending accountable and ensure that funds go where they are intended and deliver real benefits to the people, from agricultural workers to ordinary residents whose lives are improved by these infrastructure projects,” Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel said.

The DA took over FMR projects from the Department of Public Works and Highways after the latter faced public scrutiny over allegations of massive corruption. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No reports link Sandro Marcos, Romualdez to Laos drug bust
World.content:
Remulla rejected claims linking Sandro Marcos to the intercepted drug shipment; there are also no PNP or PDEA statements about the two officials' alleged involvement

Claim: A Filipino suspect in the drug shipment intercepted in Laos, who was reportedly a former employee of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, identified presidential son and Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative Sandro Marcos as the alleged mastermind behind the operation.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook post by “Nimfa Ambasan Oranio,” published on October 16, bears the claim.

Its caption reads, “Agoy paano yan kumanta na ang Pilipino na nahulihan ng dr*ga sa Thailand.”

(Oh no, what now, the Filipino caught with drugs in Thailand has already spoken.)

The accompanying graphic asks, “Mastermind si Sandro Narcos?” (Is Sandro ‘Narcos’ the mastermind?) and claims that the Filipino arrested in Laos and Thailand was a Romualdez employee who pointed to the presidential son as the alleged mastermind of the attempted trafficking of 521 kilograms of shabu from Laos.

As of writing, the post has received 645 reactions, 278 comments, and 902 shares.

The facts: Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla rejected claims linking Marcos to the drug shipment. In an interview on October 19, he said there was “no grain of truth” to the allegations and that investigators found no evidence connecting the presidential son to the operation or its alleged financier, former Bangsamoro Transition Authority parliament member Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang.

The Filipino arrested in the Laos case was identified as Fahad Mulok Dibarosan. Laotian authorities detained him on October 1 at Luang Prabang International Airport after intercepting 521 kilograms of suspected shabu aboard a chartered Learjet bound for the Philippines. As of October 21, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) had sent a letter to Lao authorities as part of their probe.

There is no credible report or official statement showing that Dibarosan named Marcos as the mastermind or that he worked for Romualdez. The post offers only an unverified social media comment to support the alleged employment link.

There are also no statements from the Philippine National Police or the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) about the alleged involvement of Marcos or Romualdez.

The misleading post also conflates the Laos drug seizure with a separate incident in Thailand. In early October, Thai authorities intercepted about 1,178 kilograms of suspected shabu aboard a fishing vessel in the Gulf of Thailand en route to the Philippines, but PDEA chief Isagani Nerez later said that there was no evidence indicating that the shipment was bound for the country.

The Laos shipment probe: On October 16, Remulla identified 11 persons of interest in the drug seizure investigation, including Rimbang, whom he named as the alleged financier; former commercial pilot Rioklyn “Boyet” Toledo, who allegedly procured the aircraft; and Police Executive Master Sergeant Aileen Mendoza, who allegedly arranged arrival permits and hangar access in Manila.

The Criminal Investigation and Detection Group has issued 40 subpoenas as part of its investigation into the case. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: A decade later, threat of Kidapawan unrest looms again as El Niño ravages farms
World.content:
FARMING. Members of the Kababayen-ang Banikanhon Isip Lig-ong Nibarog ug Nagkahiusa (KABILIN), an assisted women's group of the Department of Agriculture- Central Visayas (DA7) from Barangay Obat, in Sta. Catalina town, Negros Oriental participated a training program on Ginger/Turmeric Production held in May.

The Department of Agriculture estimates damage in the sector hitting P20 billion, affecting millions of farmers and fisherfolk

MANILA, Philippines – Ten years after the Kidapawan protests, the unrest remains a reminder of what happens when severe El Niño pushes farmers and communities to the brink.

The bloodshed that transpired on April 1, 2016, was briefly mentioned in the almost two-hour press conference of representatives of United Nations agencies and the Philippine government. Officials emphasized that with a great deal of preparation, the strong El Niño need not result in a humanitarian crisis.

“The Office of Civil Defense (OCD) is mandated to ensure that if ever that happens we are still able to manage the situation before we allow the military to take in,” said Jose Harry Barber on Thursday, October 22.

But there are no red flags yet of civil unrest, said Barber. Anticipating such is only part of “template planning.”

“During the 2016 El Niño, [there was a] Kidapawan civil unrest,” added Ana Liza Solis, chief of PAGASA’s climate monitoring and prediction section, to reporters’ queries on the gravity of the situation and possible worst-case scenarios.

“That was quite difficult because of El Niño during that time,” said Solis. “It was also one of the strong El Nino episodes.”

The government warned of “intensifying very strong El Niño” that will persist midway through 2027. Already, agricultural losses reached P8.57 billion due to El Niño. Over 200,000 farmers are currently affected.

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said during the Senate budget hearing on October 21 they were expecting agricultural damage to hit P20 billion. Up to 4.6 million farmers and fisherfolk may be affected, according to Tiu Laurel. (READ: Food supply sufficient for Super El Niño, P45-B aid coming for farmers – DA)

In early October, farmers camped outside the Department of Agrarian Reform with an array of demands, among them, support for the worse months ahead due to a very strong El Niño. Journalist Ernest Cruz, who was covering the campout, was assaulted by police.

“Our message today is that climate shocks do not have to become a humanitarian crisis,” Tristan Burnett of the International Organisation for Migration told reporters. “We have the science, we have the forecasts, we have the knowledge, and we have the tools to act early.”

An imminent disaster

More than a hundred towns and provinces across the country already declared a state of calamity. Nine provinces are already experiencing drought, according to PAGASA.

There is now a call to declare an imminent disaster supposedly to open up funds for anticipatory action.

During the hearing on the Department of Agriculture’s budget, Senator Francis Pangilinan and Tiu Laurel were in agreement that a declaration of sorts is needed.

A state of imminent disaster is declared before the disaster or impact occurs, based on forecasts and data on previous experience (as opposed to a state of calamity where it is declared after the fact).

As such, funds would be disbursed ahead of the anticipated disaster to help communities prepare.

The hitch comes from unfinished operational guidelines of the law that backs such declaration. It was only last September that government agencies tried to develop drought triggers, according to Solis, following the recent release of the law’s implementing rules and regulations.

“We have to work hard with these triggers and thresholds, and when to activate, when is the readiness, and activate [anticipatory action] at the ground,” said Solis. “There’s still ongoing effort with the national government.”

LINE. Residents queue to collect water from a tanker, following a prolonged outage caused by a damaged pipeline that disrupted supply in several barangays in Sampaloc, Manila, on June 17, 2026.

The timing of release of funds is crucial in planning and responding to severe climate shocks.

“Unfortunately, this El Nino event is coming at a time where perhaps that setup is not fully established,” said Regis Chapman of the World Food Programme Philippines in the same briefing.

Ten years ago, farmers and indigenous people blocked the Davao-Cotabato Highway in Kidapawan City demanding the release of calamity funds and rice stocks. It ended in bloodshed – two protesters were killed.

‘Balde’ and what science says

The World Meteorological Organization has sounded the alarm that El Niño may reach unprecedented strength by December, according to its latest report. It is not the strongest on record but stronger than the historic 2015-2016 El Niño that pushed farmers to march to the streets and protest in Kidapawan. The ongoing El Niño now could be “literally off the monitoring charts.”

For the Philippines this may mean higher heat index than previously recorded, more farms ravaged, and water stress.

Tiu Laurel said the country needs P1.2 trillion to irrigate farmlands across the country and P50 billion more for post-harvest facilities and mechanization.

Expecting less rainfall, the government is urging people to conserve water while supply is still stable.

“This is part of anticipatory [action] wherein we need to properly manage our water and properly use our water,” said Solis. “That’s why balde (bucket) is totoo (real). We still have rain so we need to catch the rain using our balde.”

The reference to “balde” stems from public criticisms against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s advice collect rainwater in buckets. Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian has also demonstrated the use of a water filtration system using plain, old buckets.

The environment department estimated 34% of barangays nationwide as priority intervention zones for water supply.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Stewardship not leadership: Chief justice aspirant Caguioa’s plans for the judiciary
World.content:
'The law doesn't mean anything if it does not impact a life positively,' Supreme Court Associate Justice Benjamin Caguioa says in his Judicial and Bar Council interview

MANILA, Philippines – Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa, the second aspiring chief justice to face the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) on Thursday, October 22, gave a short message to begin his interview.

“The position never makes the man. The man justifies the position,” said Caguioa.

Caguioa said his father told him the quote, and that he shared the same phrase when he took his oath in 2016 as the Supreme Court’s (SC) 174th associate justice before then-chief justice Ma. Lourdes Sereno.

Caguioa is one of the two remaining SC appointees of former president Benigno Aquino III, alongside Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, who is also a chief justice candidate.

He expressed hope that whoever becomes the chief justice, “he listens to that message, that the position of chief justice does not make the man; the man justifies the position.”

“I’m looking at more applied law. And when I say applied law, it’s towards dispensation of justice. So I’m not a fan of this sophomoric thinking in the air…. The law doesn’t mean anything if it does not impact a life positively,” Caguioa said.

The JBC kicked off the public interviews on Thursday as part of its screening process to nominate to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. the possible contenders for the country’s 28th chief justice. There are five candidates who will face the JBC for the interviews.

Afterwards, the JBC will send a short list to Marcos, and the latter will pick his appointee from that list. The judiciary is independent, but it is still the sitting president who has the power to appoint judges and justices to the courts.

Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo will retire on November 6, after reaching the mandatory retirement age of 70.

‘Show by example’

If appointed, Caguioa said he will maintain his core principle that the judiciary is an independent institution that cannot be swayed by money or politics.

“We have to show by example,” he said. “I really don’t like the word ‘leadership.’ I prefer the word ‘stewardship.'”

Caguioa acknowledged that some people do not have full trust in the judiciary. “Maybe that’s why they go to radio stations to complain,” he said.

If he were to be appointed chief justice, he would strive to change this mindset so that people “can trust the judiciary; can trust it to dispense justice.”

“That’s the whole thrust you know…to change the mindset, and in the things I’m going to want to do if I get appointed chief justice…is towards changing that mindset, towards altering that view of the people. That the people can trust the judiciary,” he said.

“They know I’m straight…. I simply follow the law. I don’t deviate…. They can expect me to be the same [if appointed as chief magistrate],” Caguioa said.

Play Video

Focus on judges, review case proportions

If he is picked as chief magistrate, Caguioa said he will still focus on the country’s trial court judges.

“My focus now really are the trial judges because they’re the face of the judiciary,” said the associate justice.

As of December 31, 2024, SC data showed that there are 2,245 trial court judges in the country and 2,579 courts. Majority or 1,260 of trial court judges are women while 985 are men.

During the interview, JBC member and Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville Luistro asked Caguioa, if there was an independent body that will assess the judiciary, what are the issues that it should look into?

Caguioa said it should assess the level of compensation within the judiciary because “corruption breeds when [people] don’t have money,” adding that if the government would “want to address that, compensation comes in.”

Caguioa also believes that to protect the integrity of judges, the JBC’s vetting process should be more stringent. The council, according to him, needs to have a good appreciation of the applicants’ vulnerabilities.

He was also asked about corruption issues, such as the multi-billion flood control mess, that continue to hound the country. Caguioa said he recognizes that “there’s something wrong in our society,” but refuses to believe that they are solely the judiciary’s problem.

“So it’s a whole-of-nation approach in that sense. So that’s where exactly maybe the judiciary, the executive, and the legislature, we actually sit down and find ways to how do we do this,” said the justice.

“And I pray everybody finds…the courage. We don’t talk about courage too much anymore, but we have to have the courage to do simply what is right,” he added.

The overwhelming number of cases in courts that clog dockets was also asked during the interviews. Caguioa said he was not certain if additional courtrooms are the answer to this, but he believed that this could be addressed by using a more rational apportionment ratio in raffling or assigning cases to courts.

Caguioa was also asked about the Unified Legal Aid Service or the mandatory legal aid service of lawyers for indigent Filipinos. He chairs the judiciary’s ULAS board.

He said that they are open to changing the rules to accommodate more clients in specific situations. “Of course, the whole point is to serve the Filipino. That’s the whole point,” he said, adding that the aim is to “engrain the concept of service” among Filipino lawyers.

Play Video

If he were to become chief justice, how would Caguioa want to be remembered?

“I don’t think in terms of legacy — that’s not me,” he said. “[I want to be remembered as] just a decent guy. Sorry, I have my own idea about positions. Even if I don’t get this position, doesn’t really matter. I’ll continue to do what I do.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Taiwan shuts down ahead of typhoon, hundreds of flights canceled
World.content:
THREAT. Typhoon Champi swirls over the Philippine Sea, as seen from space on October 22, 2026 in this screengrab taken from a handout GIF image.

The storm's forecast track shows it will pass just off northeastern Taiwan, turn north toward the Chinese coast and eventually move into southern Japan

YILAN, Taiwan – Almost all of Taiwan shut down on Friday, October 23, ahead of the arrival of Typhoon Champi, which is forecast to bring strong winds and torrential rain, though the storm is weakening and is not expected to make direct landfall on the island.

At one point a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of around 191 kph near its center, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).

The storm was about 320 km east of Taiwan’s southern tip, the CWA said. The storm’s forecast track shows it will pass just off northeastern Taiwan, turn north toward the Chinese coast and eventually move into southern Japan.

One person was killed and 94 were injured in Taiwan, where the government said almost 1,300 people had been evacuated from mountainous areas.

Coastal towns received mobile phone alerts warning of gusts exceeding 150 kph and urging residents to seek immediate shelter, while nearly 3 feet of rain was forecast for northern mountain areas, including around Taipei.

In the northeastern county of Yilan, where strong winds and heavy showers were intensifying and the typhoon was forecast to pass close by later on Friday, authorities distributed sandbags and put amphibious vehicles and inflatable rescue boats on standby.

“When necessary, the military will come in to help people, including using amphibious vehicles for evacuations or disaster relief,” said Lee Ming-chen, head of the port town of Suao, which was badly flooded in previous typhoons.

Huge radius

Taiwan forecasters said the storm’s radius was around 320 km, large enough to cover most of Taiwan, and weather experts said its impact could last nearly two days.

Taiwan’s financial markets also closed on Friday, while only the Taiwan-controlled Kinmen islands, which sit next to the Chinese coast, will open schools and offices as normal.

The transport ministry said all 262 domestic flights were canceled for Friday, along with 669 international ones. The north-south high-speed rail service was operating as usual.

In the capital Taipei there were squally showers, but public transport including the subway was working, albeit with reduced service.

Taiwan is generally very well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike in autumn too.

The typhoon is forecast to first pass over Japan’s westernmost inhabited island, Yonaguni, in Okinawa Prefecture. – Rappler.com

World.title: Will PMA be a gentler, kinder academy with a female commandant at the helm?
World.content:
COMMANDANT OF CADETS. Colonel Leah Lorenzo-Santiago is flanked by her female classmates at the PMA. With them is outgoing PMA commandant of cadets Colonel Eugene Henry Cabugao.

PMA’s first female commandant brings a tough record to the academy, challenging assumptions that women in charge will make military training gentler. She looks ahead to a reunion with her classmates.

BAGUIO, Philippines – Philippine Military Academy Superintendent Lieutenant General Michael Logico answered my question before Colonel Leah Lorenzo-Santiago could react.

“Definitely not. That’s why I got her in the first place,” he said.

“No. Not gentler,” Santiago said.

If there is one thing I remember about Leah from when I met her 29 years ago, it is that she was anything but fragile or dainty.

She was small and thin at the time, but you could tell she was tough. Her female mistahs were sporting the Demi Moore haircut then, but not her. The hairstyle she had during her installation as the first female commandant of cadets at the PMA was the same one she had when she graduated third in the PMA Kalasag-Lahi Class of 1997.

Right after graduation, she was sent to the battlefield in Mindanao. I remember that she belonged to a team that infiltrated the Abu Sayyaf. For a woman doing that at the time, spying on the group was a life-and-death undertaking. Her exploits caught the attention of the Army chief then, retired general Roy Cimatu, who included her among his aides when he became chief of staff.

Now Santiago is on the path to follow suit. Only the signature of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is needed to make her the first female PMA graduate to become a general.

The announcement of her appointment as commandant of cadets was made on September 26, giving Santiago time to prepare.

One thoughtful gesture was her invitation to all her female classmates.

There were 17 of them when they entered Fort del Pilar in April 1993. They were called the Rasul Ladies, after the late senator Santanina Rasul and Republic Act 7192, or the Women in Development and Nation Building Act of 1992.

The PMA built separate barracks for women and added female tactical officers, but these measures were not enough to keep all of them. Some were wooed by their upperclassmen and eventually decided to leave the academy.

‘Magnificent 7’

Over the next four years, only seven remained.

I can’t recall who first called them the “Magnificent 7,” but the name stuck.

Last Saturday, October 17, two of them joined Santiago at Yap Hall.

MEMORY LANE. The ‘Magnificent 7,’ which includes Colonel Leah Lorenzo-Santiago. courtesy of Andy Zapata

Maria Victoria Blancaflor-Agoncillo remained in the Philippine Army and became a tank commander. In 2000, she took part in an operation that overran the Moro Islamic Liberation Front‘s Camp Rajamuda, earning the Gold Cross Medal.

She later rose to lead the National Capital Region’s Regional Community Defense Group. Vicky is also an aspiring writer. Last month, she even made time to fangirl over Jessica Zafra.

Marissa Arlene Andres-Martinez remained in the Philippine Navy. By 2022, she was serving as assistant chief of fleet staff for plans (F-5) of the Philippine Fleet. She also serves as a Navy spokesperson.

Santiago also invited about 100 female military officers to the photo opportunity. There are now about 800 female military officers considered part of the Rasul Ladies.

Santiago said she plans to bring together all the “Magnificent 7.”

The other members have taken different paths since their days at the academy.

Ma. Consuelo “Bon” Nunag-Castillo remained in the Philippine Air Force and became the first female pilot of the 205th Tactical Helicopter Wing. She later flew with the Presidential Airlift Wing and held senior positions in the defense establishment and the Air Force.

Aireen Somera became a PAF pilot but resigned because of health issues. She married a pilot classmate who also left the military for commercial aviation.

Sheryl Jane Uy-Cabasang suffered serious injuries in a vehicular accident shortly after graduation and was placed on complete disability discharge.

Santiago said Jane was paralyzed from the neck down and is still undergoing rehabilitation. Somera developed arthritis, which forced her to give up flying.

Arlene Orejana-Trillanes resigned from the service and later became dean of a computer college at the National University. She is married to former senator Antonio Trillanes IV.

It would be nice if their reunion happened at the PMA, where their roller-coaster journey began. – Rappler.com

World.title: Typhoon Rosal still bringing moderate to heavy rain to Batanes
World.content:
ROSAL. Satellite image of Typhoon Rosal (Champi) as of October 23, 2026, 4 am.

Typhoon Rosal (Champi) is last spotted 275 kilometers east northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, at 4 am on Friday, October 23

MANILA, Philippines – Typhoon Rosal (Champi) continued to affect Batanes and other parts of Northern Luzon on Friday, October 23, even though it has spared the Philippines from landfall.

Rosal was last spotted 275 kilometers east northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, as of 4 am on Friday. The typhoon is moving northwest at only 15 kilometers per hour (km/h).

Its maximum sustained winds had weakened to 155 km/h on Thursday evening, October 22, while its gustiness eased to 190 km/h.

At its peak, Rosal was a super typhoon with maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in a bulletin issued at 5 am on Friday that Rosal is still bringing moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters) to Batanes in the coming hours.

Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan, and Isabela may also continue to experience rain with gusty winds due to Rosal on Friday, while the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, the rest of Cagayan Valley, Ilocos Sur, La Union, and Aurora are likely to see scattered rain and thunderstorms caused by the typhoon.

PAGASA added that Rosal’s trough or extension is affecting Masbate, Palawan, the Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Basilan, and Tawi-Tawi. These areas could have scattered rain and thunderstorms as well.

Tropical cyclone wind signals also remain in effect in the following areas as of 5 am on Friday:

Signal No. 2

Gale-force winds (62 to 88 km/h), minor to moderate threat to life and property

Batanes

northeastern part of Babuyan Islands (Babuyan Island, Panuitan Island, Calayan Island, Camiguin Island)

Signal No. 1

Strong winds (39 to 61 km/h), minimal to minor threat to life and property

rest of Babuyan Islands

mainland Cagayan

northeastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Santa Maria, Cabagan, San Pablo, Palanan)

Ilocos Norte

Apayao

PAGASA no longer sees Signal No. 3 as a possibility.

The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to these areas:

Friday, October 23

most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Camiguin, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Saturday, October 24

Batanes, Babuyan Islands, Ilocos Norte, Polillo Islands, Bicol, Romblon, Capiz, Iloilo, Negros Occidental

Sunday, October 25

Batanes, Babuyan Islands

Warnings for seaboards affected by Rosal have yet to be lifted. These are the updated coastal conditions for Friday:

Up to very rough, high, or very high seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Northern and eastern seaboards of Batanes – waves up to 12 meters high

Remaining seaboards of Batanes – waves up to 9 meters high

Northern and eastern seaboards of Babuyan Islands; northeastern seaboard of mainland Cagayan – waves up to 8 meters high

Remaining seaboards of Babuyan Islands and mainland Cagayan; seaboard of northern Isabela; northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 6 meters high

Remaining seaboard of Isabela – waves up to 5.5 meters high

Remaining seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 5 meters high

Seaboards of northern Ilocos Sur and northern Aurora; northern seaboards of Camarines Sur and Camarines Norte; northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands and Catanduanes – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Seaboard of northern La Union; remaining seaboards of Aurora and Ilocos Sur; eastern seaboard of Northern Samar; northeastern seaboard of Eastern Samar; western seaboard of Pangasinan – waves up to 4 meters high

Eastern seaboards of Albay and Sorsogon; northern seaboard of Northern Samar; remaining eastern seaboard of Eastern Samar – waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboard of Zambales; eastern seaboards of Dinagat Islands and Siargao-Bucas Grande Islands – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Western seaboards of Bataan and Lubang Islands; seaboard of Surigao del Sur; remaining seaboards of La Union, Pangasinan, and Catanduanes; northern seaboard of Kalayaan Islands – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Western seaboards of Batangas, Cavite, Occidental Mindoro, and Palawan including Calamian Islands; eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining seaboards of Lubang and Kalayaan Islands – waves up to 2 meters high

ALSO ON RAPPLER

Rosal may exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility by early Saturday morning, October 24. It entered PAR on Tuesday, October 20.

After leaving PAR, Rosal is likely to be downgraded to a severe tropical storm by Saturday morning, then weaken further into a tropical storm by Saturday evening.

Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Market Rider] SEC’s market maker push and how it can boost PH stock trading
World.content:
SEC Chairman Francis Lim spearheads a daring undertaking into the realm of market making, in a bid to boost stock market trading in the Philippines

A quote from the legendary Gus Levy of Goldman Sachs perfectly captures what could be the operational and psychological framework of a market maker.

Play Video

During his time as senior partner, Levy revolutionized Wall Street trading by turning Goldman Sachs into a primary market maker, for in the ’60s and earlier when an institutional investor wanted to sell a massive block of stock when normal daily volume was comparatively too small, the stock price would tank. Levy turned Goldman Sachs into a primary market maker that would use its own cash to buy those massive blocks instantly, taking the risk into its own balance sheet.

As the story goes, a junior trader at Goldman Sachs bought a massive block of stock from a client. Feeling sure he’ll make a profit, he decided to hold on to the position. Gus Levy noticed the giant unhedged position sitting on the books. He looked down at the young trader and said a line that would become the absolute mantra for market makers in the industry: “Young man, you misunderstand our job. We are in the moving business, not the storage business!”

Among those very happy to welcome this daring undertaking into the realm of market making in the Philippine capital market, spearheaded by no less than the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Francis Ed. Lim, are three of the country’s highly respected financial and stock market personalities. They are: Presidential Legislative Liaison Office (PLLO) Secretary Jose Ma. Clemente “Joey” Salceda, Edward “Edward” K. Lee, and Paulino “Paul” S. Soo.

Salceda has an extensive background in the Philippine financial and stock markets as a top-tier equity analyst and research director prior to entering politics. Lee is the founder and chairman of the country’s largest online stock brokerage firm, COL Financial, while Soo is the chairman and CEO of First Abacus Financial Holdings Corp. and also serves as chairman and president of Abacus Securities Corporation along with its online trading platform, MyTrade PH.

“We have many fundamentally sound Philippine companies trading at attractive valuations. What we lack is liquidity. Now is the time to unlock their value,” Salceda said.

Likewise, Lee is confident that our capital market is vibrant enough for the plan of the SEC to succeed considering developments in the country’s structural architecture on ease of doing business and liberal regulation that is now generally attractive for risk takers.

Truly a longtime proponent for the development of the stock market, he gave these passionate words: “It’s been 30 years. Francis is our only hope.”

A bit more cautious but certainly in about the plan, Soo suggested a careful consideration. He said, “I would be interested to see how the pros and cons are.” He also wondered if there are enough people knowledgeable on how the plan will work.

A seasoned participant of the market, Soo admitted that he has only basic knowledge, not to mention the fact that that has been ages ago, with this deeply truthful message, “I spent one month in New York in the T-Bills market; too long ago.”

Core rules and regulations

The official source for the rules on market making is SEC Memorandum Circular No. 28, Series of 2026, issued on October 15, 2026.

Its stated main purpose is “to establish a formal regulatory framework for market making to improve secondary market liquidity, enhance price discovery, and support capital formation.”

For trading participants applying to act as market makers, capital requirement is set to as low as P150 million minimum unimpaired paid-up capital.

Applicants must also show adequate operational capacity, a satisfactory track record, and designate at least one specialist with a minimum of three years of relevant experience in securities trading or market making.

Financial instruments covered in the rule applies only to equity and fixed-income securities either listed, traded, or enrolled on an exchange under the jurisdiction of the SEC. It does not cover government securities governed by the Bureau of the Treasury’s Primary Dealer framework unless extended.

Incentives are to be extended to participating firms which includes “reduced transaction fees, liquidity rebates, and access to enhanced trading facilities.”

Market makers are to provide continuous quoting services for buy and sell prices of select securities, the submission of quarterly performance reports, and compliance with the provisions for incentive and/or rebate.

Existing market makers have six months to comply and the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) must submit implementation guidelines within 30 days.

Feedback and evaluations

Also glad about the new development but has some questions about the plan is the president and chief trader of Eagle Equities Inc., Joseph “Joey” Roxas. His main concern is how the market maker will exactly make a profit considering the various costs involved.

Roxas is referring to the prescribed rules in the market maker’s quoting obligations, spread thresholds, minimum quote sizes, and other related matters in the trading of the related securities.

Supposedly, the entire business model of market making is to keep assets moving like buying at the “bid side,” and immediately selling at the “ask side,” and capturing the tiny difference — the spread — as many times a day as possible. To Roxas, this is not always possible all the time.

For this, “incentives will be a big factor,” Roxas said. In this regard, he would like to know “if it is the stock exchange that would be partially subsidizing liquidity, through what is mentioned as “liquidity rebates.”

As far as he could see, the rebate that may come from the stock exchange could be “the PSE fees based on turnover, which he said is only equivalent to just 0.00001 of the cost of total transaction.

“I hope the implementation guidelines are not so complicated as to turn off prospective market makers, just like what happened in the Securities Borrowing and Lending (SBL) policy of the short selling program of the PSE,” Roxas added.

Another market veteran is H.E. Bennett Securities Inc.’s market strategist and chief trader, Joel de la Peña. He finds the P150 million capital requirement may be too small for a market maker. In the market heydays of the past, he said “I know about a group of traders has a budget on hand of P1 billion to day trade.”

De la Peña also suggested that the SEC and PSE control the “manipulative” acts of listed companies that may derail and imperil the financial health of market makers. As to how, De la Peña says, “For one, just look back at the delisting stories in the market.”

Not a silver bullet

On the overall, the plan is without a doubt welcome. This is captured by the enthusiastic proffered comment of Andro Leo “Andoy” I. Beltran, vice president of First Metro Securities Brokerage Corporation (FirstMetroSec): “This is a welcome development for the Philippine stock market and one that we at FirstMetroSec can relate to from firsthand experience. This is a positive step toward developing a deeper, more liquid, and more efficient capital market, especially as the PSE introduces new products.”

“Market making has been allowed in the Philippine stock market since 2013, when the ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund) framework was introduced. Since the launch of the then First Metro Philippine Equity Exchange-Traded Fund (FMETF), now ATR FAMI ETF (AETF), FirstMetroSec has served as its market maker. What is new now is the expansion of market making beyond ETFs to other eligible securities and products, including Global Philippine Depositary Receipts (GPDRs).

“Some securities may not naturally attract enough buyers and sellers, especially when they are newly introduced or their markets are still developing. Market makers can help bridge this gap, and effectively give investors greater assurance that they can enter or exit positions freely.

“Of course, market making is not a silver bullet. But this is one that may help build a Philippine stock market where investors can transact more efficiently, companies can access capital more effectively, and more Filipinos can participate in long-term wealth creation.”

Edward Lee offered the wisdom of the following quote as to calm the fears on the adverse effects the plan may present: “If you try to protect your investors too much from bad companies, from failing investments, and from horrible mistakes, it may not lead you to a vibrant market. You have to allow for mistakes. You have to allow people to deal with the consequences. Do not rush in to bail them out from their overreach.”

In short, “it’s education, not protection” should be our attitude toward the proposed plan, Lee added. – Rappler.com

A veteran stock market analyst, Den Somera has long years of professional experience in investment banking and stockbroking and founder-convenor of The Monday Circle. You may reach the writer at kapitaltek@gmail.com

World.title: A Fitting Conclusion to an Intellectual Life: James C. Scott on the Irrawaddy
World.content:
James C. Scott (2025). In Praise of Floods: The Untamed River and the Life Brings. Yale University Press. 220 pp.

In Praise of Floods, puts the Irrawaddy River itself—not generals, kings, peasants or revolutionaries—at the center of Myanmar’s history, and in doing so establishes principles for how river basins are best understood.

James C. Scott (Shwe Yoe) was one of the most important social scientists of the last 50 years. He began his international career in Burma in 1958 but was unable to return after Ne Win’s 1962 coup until 2012. His affection for Myanmar, however, did not diminish, and he then went back regularly until 2021. He was even known to give lectures in Burmese in the 2010s. He died at the age of 87 in 2024, and In Praise of Floods is his final book.

What Scott is most famous for is descriptions of how farmers resisted exploitation by feudal lords and politicians who sent armies and police to tax them. His research led to provocative books like The Moral Economy of the Peasant, Weapons of the Weak and The Art of Not Being Governed. Their creative tension was always between the cunning of the “weak” peasantries and the simplifications powerful governing elites make to squeeze surpluses from them.

In Praise of Floods is a departure in focusing instead on rivers and floods. Scott believes that they are “alive” in the sense that they are born, develop and shrink across millennia. In the Irrawaddy’s case, it created the fertile plains of central Burma at the end of the last Ice Age 12,500 years ago.

Scott’s point is that rivers emerge at particular times, support different types of life, shift channels and courses, and eventually disappear. He calls this process the river’s “pulse.” For the Irrawaddy, the low-water point is usually in February, and as the rains resume, about eight times as much water flows out of the highlands above Mandalay by September, bursting out of the meandering channels formed in previous years.

For thousands of years, perhaps from 10,000 BCE until about 5000 BCE, this meant that migratory people avoided the floods by annually moving their camps to higher ground. Life came from the rich topsoil the floodwaters laid down across the flat plains stretching from Mandalay, which is only 80 m above sea level, to the Andaman Sea some 1,000 km to the south. Early humans harvested the bounty of the river by fishing, netting birds, hunting game, collecting mussels, and gathering fruit and roots. The flood pulses determined what the people ate, and where they lived and settled.

By about 3000 BCE people began creating new ways to use the temperamental river and sought to bend the Irrawaddy’s surges to their own needs. They started by scattering seeds along the shoreline as the flood waters receded. After tending the crop of grain for a few months they could harvest more food than ever before, but this type of food needed to be processed and stored in granaries, to be eaten while waiting for the next harvest to mature.

This is also when they began managing water flows with weirs, fish traps, drainage canals and dikes, and eventually developed the engineering capacity to flatten fields with animal-drawn plows and other tools needed to harvest paddy rice. Human societies came to see the living river as a tamable resource, whose annual surges could be engineered, so people confidently settled into permanent villages near the rivers. There, the arts, markets, religion, literature, architecture and other human pursuits flourished. By about 2,200 years ago, the Pyu states began to emerge, building permanent cities, markets and worship centers.

And when the river behaved as planned, it was a great thing and populations flourished. But there were new dangers too for people living in fixed villages and cities, because the river pulses did not always rise and fall as humans intended—after all, Scott writes, the river was also alive, and perhaps even had a mind of its own. So when the monsoons arrived late or not at all, there would be a drought. Or when they arrived early and in force, there were floods.

Humans and the rest

A particularly creative touch in Scott’s book is his concluding chapters about non-human life, which includes fish, animals and plants, as well as the ubiquitous Burmese spirits, the Nats. A charismatic character, the Irrawaddy river dolphin organizes the other creatures of the river to comment on the algae, molluscs, worms, larvae, zooplankton and microbes, most of which are ignored by homo sapiens, who is only interested in the river as it applies to human endeavors.

As Scott admits, these chapters fit awkwardly with the overall tone of the book. But surely in his final book he can be given some leeway. He is correct, moreover, that social science needs to acknowledge the spiritual life that is important to the ecology of places like the Irrawaddy valley and delta.

Flooding is a catastrophe for humans, but the “infrastructure” of non-human life, including plants, fish, mammals, birds, and of course the river itself are perhaps more ambivalent, or at least have a different perspective on the river pulses. So, for that matter perhaps do the Nats.

Scott’s emphasis on these spirits reflects stories that his research associates Maung Maung Oo and Naing Tun Lin collected while travelling along the Irrawaddy seeking to understand what locals knew. They travelled from the headwaters of Kachin State through the dry zone of Magwe and Sagaing. The spirits must be placated because they are believed to cause both those disastrous floods and the good fortunes of farmers, fishers and hunters. And then there are the dangers of the surrounding forests, which are also effected by the Nats.

Scott soon segues into more modern descriptions of the Irrawaddy watershed, in which the hydrodynamics of the water surges are highlighted in the context of modern social problems like deforestation, mining, and rebellion. All such activities disturb the ecological balance, and the capacity of humans to manage the Irrawaddy.

Full circle

Scott’s lifetime of creative scholarship is impressive. He started in Burma, studied in Vietnam, went to Malaysia, and ended up studying the economics, politics and psychology of the oppressed, and how highlanders respond to attempts to control them. In Praise of Floods brings this career full circle; he is back in Burma and writing about geography. As he writes in his preface, he planned two more years of field research, following the stories of farmers, river dolphins, spirits and flooding himself, but was prevented by the 2021 coup. His own public activism supporting the Spring Revolution made a return even less likely.

But even without these field data, the book pushes social scientists yet again to consider the perspectives of beings they typically ignore. Scott spent a lifetime searching for what he once called “hidden transcripts“—the voices of people overlooked by rulers and states. In this final book he tries something still more audacious: hidden transcripts of dolphins, spirits, forests, floods and the river itself. It is an appropriately unruly ending to the provocative intellectual life of James C. Scott.

Tony Waters is a professor of sociology at Leuphana University, Germany. His most recent book is The Socio-Political Systems of Highland Burma and the Art of Governance.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Pushes on Four Fronts in Southern Chin State
World.content:
Thousands of regime troops are advancing on four fronts across southern Chin State as they push to seize the gateway to Rakhine State, according to resistance sources.

On Wednesday, the military claimed its forces had secured Hlaingdoke and nearby villages in Kanpetlet Township along the Rakhine border after clearance operations along the Laung She-Hlaingdoke-Kyindwe road.

The regime’s counteroffensive to retake Chin resistance strongholds spans from Magwe Region’s Tilin and Saw townships, across the border into Mindat, Kanpetlet and Kyindwe townships.

Intense clashes have erupted in Magwe’s border villages of Shweaungthar and Kyee as regime forces advance to cut off supply lines to Mindat, according to resistance sources.

“The regime has deployed roughly 3,000 troops across all the fronts,” Yaw Meng, spokesperson for the Chin People’s Army (CPA), told The Irrawaddy.

Regime forces began massing for a southward push five months ago after securing the northern Chin towns of Tonzang, Falam, and Thantlang. The southern Chin campaign launched in May, when around 1,500 troops advanced on Kanpetlet and Mindat from Magwe’s Saw and Kyaukhtu townships respectively, according to the CPA.

“During five months of clashes, resistance forces repelled regime troops and defended the Chin State and its people,” Yaw Meng wrote in an October 20 Facebook post.

He declined to comment on the current battlefield situation in southern Chin, where the regime’s ground offensive is accompanied by indiscriminate airstrikes.

On Sunday, a bomb struck the Paletwa jetty, killing nine civilians including a six-month-old child and injuring four others. A regime airstrike on the same site killed another person the following day, according to the Chin People’s Union, the CPA’s political wing.

World.title: Myanmar Ranks Worst in World for Internet Freedom
World.content:
Myanmar has scored just 9 out of 100 on the Internet Freedom Index for the third consecutive year in 2026, making it the world’s worst environment for internet users as the military regime continues its aggressive crackdown on media freedom and online expression, U.S.-based rights group Freedom House said.

Under the group’s rankings, Myanmar has long been categorized as “Not Free” for internet freedom, but its score dropped significantly from 36 in 2019 to 17 in 2021 after the military staged a coup, and finally to 9 from 2024 onward.

It said the military maintains control over all major service providers to enforce mass censorship, localized shutdowns and digital surveillance.

Following the coup, the Myanmar military regime stepped up suppression of internet freedom and digital rights by enforcing shutdowns, blocking social media and news platforms, and criminalizing virtual private network (VPN) use to crack down on political dissent.

As a result, Myanmar netizens have lost access to information and had their freedom of expression curtailed.

During December-January elections, authorities intensified the blocking of news platforms and the use of anti-censorship tools while arresting individuals for online expression under restrictive new laws.

“This is a very concerning situation,” Thit Nyan, a digital rights analyst from the Myanmar Internet Project, told The Irrawaddy. “This is a life-and-death matter for the public.”

He added that the people of Myanmar, whose lives are seriously affected by conflict, rely heavily on mobile and internet connections for information about airstrikes and to facilitate basic services such as health, education and money transfers.

Myanmar internet users require digital literacy for their own safety, he said.

More than 2,000 netizens have been detained as of September since the 2021 coup for sharing posts or comments criticizing the regime and supporting anti-regime movements, mostly on Facebook, according to Data for Myanmar, a monitoring group.

The regime relies mostly on the Penal Code’s Section 505A outlawing “incitement”, the counter-terrorism law, and the telecommunications law to arrest online critics, including artists and celebrities.

Data for Myanmar said, however, that in 2026 the regime has expanded its scope of action to target individuals who merely express their political views online, rather than just those who are deemed to pose a security threat.

At the same time, experts point out the regime has shut down or restricted mobile and internet networks to control information flow, in an effort to prevent military information from leaking and to conceal its human rights violations.

A total of 140 out of 358 monitored townships are facing communication shutdowns, according to Athan, a group that focuses on freedom of expression. Most of the affected townships are experiencing fighting between regime and anti-regime groups.

Meanwhile, users require VPNs, whose use the regime has criminalized, to access the most-used social platforms such as Facebook.

“I have to swallow my own feelings and control myself not to share them online,” a Yangon netizen told The Irrawaddy. He said he was using his real name for his social account and was aware of many people in major cities who had been arrested for sharing their views in favor of the anti-regime resistance.

“This is a violation of our rights to express ourselves freely and to live safely,” he said.

World.title: China’s Myanmar Policy—Consistent but Fundamentally Flawed
World.content:
Observers are often baffled by China’s outright support for Myanmar’s criminal military regime in the face of global opprobrium. But Beijing has been remarkably consistent in terms of where it believes its interests lie. During a visit to Naypyitaw in August 2024 that followed the Myanmar military’s unprecedented battlefield defeats in northern Shan, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi outlined what he called Beijing’s “three bottom lines”. Myanmar must not descend into civil strife, drift away from the ASEAN family, or be infiltrated or interfered with by external forces.

The position, in other words, was support for resolving Myanmar crisis within the ASEAN framework, with a warning that escalating civil war, state collapse, or intervention by other countries—especially of course Western countries—would directly harm Chinese interests. Stability comes before everything else.

Military first

China’s Myanmar policy has consistently centered on the Myanmar military. Since the late 1990s, Beijing has treated Myanmar military as the decisive force in stabilizing the country.

After the popular pro-democracy uprising in 1988 toppled the then-regime and the China‑backed Communist Party of Burma collapsed the following year, Myanmar’s military broke with the Western powers. With that, the assistance they had given it under the pretext of a counter‑narcotics campaign came to an end. Facing sanctions, the military turned instead to China and became Beijing’s trusted partner in assuring border security.

Beijing concluded that only the military could hold the country together. Despite its brutality, China viewed it as the sole practical guarantor of the status quo, aligning with Chinese interests and counterbalancing Western hostility.

Strategic energy interests

In 2003–2004, then President Hu Jintao highlighted the risks posed by great‑power competition over the Malacca Strait to China’s energy security. To reduce dependence on that chokepoint, Beijing proposed building oil and gas pipelines across Myanmar into Yunnan. Than Shwe’s regime obliged, and relations improved as a result.

Through these pipelines, China now imports about 22 million tons of crude oil annually—worth roughly US$16 billion—bypassing the Malacca Strait. Beijing’s recognition of Than Shwe as a trusted ally further entrenched its military‑centric policy.

The position today

China continues to prioritize the Myanmar military, treating ethnic armed groups along the border as secondary entities it must keep in check and largely ignoring forces farther afield such as the National Unity Government (NUG), People’s Defense Forces (PDF) and Spring Revolution alliances.

It was only natural, then, that when the military was on the verge of collapse after losing the northern Shan capital of Lashio in 2024, Beijing propped it up rather than let it fall.

To be sure, China’s policy on Myanmar has delivered some success, leading to the junta’s bogus elections and cosmetic transformation into a civilian government, and now ASEAN governments’ re-engagement with Myanmar. Their dealings with the putschist regime are motivated not only by trade, migration, drug trade and online scam concerns, but also by China’s political and economic influence.

It is an entirely pragmatic, interest‑driven diplomacy, prioritizing national interest over moral principles, and of course that is not unique to China. The U.S. is increasingly open about the transactional nature of its own international policies, and ASEAN has been taking note.

Drawbacks

Yet the core problems remain unresolved. The war has not abated. Myanmar is not stable. Min Aung Hlaing’s elections led to worsening airstrikes and intensified military campaigns, mass killings and war crimes.

Unlike the Thein Sein government, the rebranded regime has offered no political reforms of any kind. It rejects inclusive peace, aiming instead to divide resistance forces.

In practice, the regime remains keen on military solutions alone—retaking lost territory with Chinese backing. Since China intervened, hostilities ceased in northern Shan but the regime escalated fighting in the rest of the country, forcibly recruiting 100,000 young people under Conscription Law since 2024 for use as cannon fodder. The resulting brain drain has left the country poorer in human resources than ever.

Two years of heavy Chinese support have only allowed the regime to recapture 21 townships out of more than 100 lost. Over 80 remain under resistance control. And now its gains are slowing dramatically, with rural areas and key routes beyond its control.

China’s goal of stability in Myanmar, in other words, is further out of reach than ever. By trusting the military to deliver it, Beijing has handcuffed itself to failure. Is it too late to change course?

Thet Htar Maung is a political analyst.

World.title: Son of Aung San Suu Kyi Says He Has First Call With Her in 5 Years
World.content:
YANGON—The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi said he spoke Thursday to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.

“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook.

Aung San Suu Kyi is detained at a “designated residence” in the capital, Naypyitaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

AFP could not immediately reach Aris—who lives in the United Kingdom—and it was not clear how he spoke to his mother, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring democracy to Myanmar.

However, images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show him standing outside the Myanmar Embassy in London.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” Aris wrote.

“But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”

Myanmar’s military held Aung San Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy.

But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.

On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles III, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.

Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.

Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyitaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.

After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing—who ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup—was earlier this year installed as civilian president.

Analysts describe the election putting him in elected office as a charade, and say he may be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in a bid to court international legitimacy.

World.title: Japan’s Sasakawa Renews Myanmar Peace Pledge as Regime Battles Arakan Army
World.content:
Yohei Sasakawa, honorary chairman of Japan’s Nippon Foundation, met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Monday, pledging once again to assist Myanmar’s “internal peace process.”

Sasakawa made a similar promise during his last visit in August. This time, regime media said only that he offered to help strengthen Myanmar’s “human resources,” without elaborating on what that would entail. No details were released on what progress had been made since his earlier pledge to support peace efforts.

Sasakawa’s latest visit comes amid fierce fighting in Rakhine, where the regime is struggling to defend the state capital, Sittwe, from the ethnic Arakan Army (AA)’s attacks. Sasakawa previously mediated a ceasefire between the Myanmar military and the AA in 2021, though fighting resumed in late 2023 after Operation 1027. The regime has since lost 14 of 17 townships in Rakhine.

The regime claims to be open to peace talks with ethnic armed organizations (EAOs), but has excluded the AA from talks so far. It has demanded that the People’s Defense Force, the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government, surrender.

Sasakawa’s latest meeting follows the regime’s self-styled “peace talks” with several EAOs that were not actively fighting the regime, having maintained earlier ceasefire deals with the Myanmar military even after the 2021 coup—an event that led other EAOs to resume fighting.

Separately, two EAOs that had been fighting the regime—the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army—agreed to ceasefires with the regime under direct pressure from China.

The regime insists that EAOs, after signing ceasefires, must transform themselves into Border Guard Forces under the Myanmar military’s command or disarm.

The Nippon Foundation on Wednesday declined to comment on the details of Sasakawa’s latest meeting with Min Aung Hlaing. The organization believes the most useful contribution it can make in Myanmar is through “quiet, practical engagement rather than public commentary,” its executive director, Takashi Arikawa, told The Irrawaddy.

“It is not helpful to discuss the substance of ongoing efforts before there are results that can be shared publicly,” he said.

Political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye noted that multiple countries and organizations are currently exploring ways to address Myanmar’s crisis, including attempts to open dialogue between the regime and resistance forces.

“Japan and Sasakawa may be among those countries and organizations. But they haven’t released details about their plans, so it is hard to gauge what measures they will take and what impacts they could have,” he said.

In recent weeks, Japanese lawmakers Hiromichi Watanabe and Shunsuke Takei visited Naypyitaw and met with Lower House Speaker Khin Yi. Meanwhile, Tokyo hosted meetings between U.S. officials and Myanmar regime representatives this month, leading to speculation that Tokyo is considering a shift in its policy toward engagement.

Japan suspended official development assistance to Myanmar after the 2021 coup. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi reiterated in July that relations would only improve if the junta halts violence, releases detainees including jailed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi, and pursues genuine political dialogue.

Months ago, the regime publicly appealed for previously agreed aid to be restored.

World.title: Buying Gas or Buying Surveillance? Gas-Rich Myanmar’s Deal With Russia
World.content:
Anyone who still thinks Russia is simply bankrolling Myanmar has the direction of money backwards. In this arrangement, Myanmar is the customer. It is preparing to buy Russian gas and, in doing so, send money into a Russian economy still financing the war in Ukraine. Russia, meanwhile, is offering technology in return: satellite navigation, communications, Earth observation and aerospace cooperation. In other words, Myanmar is not being paid to stand with Russia. Myanmar is paying Russia, while Russia trades technology for access to a new market.

In August 2026, Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing traveled to Moscow for an official visit and met Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin. The visit produced 12 agreements and memoranda covering everything from energy and culture to competition policy and space technology. Four of them are particularly interesting because the technologies involved have obvious civilian applications, but equally obvious military ones.

The four were:

Memorandum Memorandum on information and communication technologies; Memorandum satellite navigation, human spaceflight Memorandum between the Myanmar Space Agency and Bauman Moscow State Technical University on technological and aerospace cooperation.

At roughly the same time, Russia and Myanmar were also negotiating something much less futuristic: liquefied natural gas.

The interesting part is that Myanmar was not discussed only as the final customer. According to the Myanmar President’s Office, the talks also covered onward supplies of Russian LNG to China and Thailand. That changes the scale of the arrangement considerably. Russia is not simply looking for another buyer. Myanmar is being considered as a possible regional distribution point for Russian LNG into Southeast Asia.

That is where the arrangement starts to look slightly extravagant.

Myanmar already has substantial natural-gas reserves and remains a major gas exporter. Recent estimates put its proven reserves at around 22.5 trillion cubic feet, while a large share of its production is exported. It certainly does not suffer from a geological shortage of natural gas.

So why import Russian LNG?

Part of the answer may simply be infrastructure, contracts and energy shortages. Having gas underground is not the same thing as having sufficient gas available in the right place, at the right time and in the right form. But the Russian side has another obvious problem: it needs markets.

Western sanctions and the war in Ukraine have placed sustained pressure on Russia’s traditional energy relationships. Russia’s finances are under considerably more pressure than before the war. The liquid part of the National Wealth Fund on September 1, 2026, was lower than ever, at 13,194.88 billion rubles (US$159.94 billion). Russia therefore has every reason to find new buyers for what it still has in abundance. And what Russia has in abundance is natural resources.

Myanmar offers access to the Southeast Asian market. Russia offers LNG. So far, fairly conventional.

The LNG story did not begin in August. In April, Russian Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilev and Myanmar Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin were already discussing supplies of Russian LNG, petroleum products and crude oil. Myanmar’s Ministry of Electricity and Energy was quite specific about what it wanted: favorable prices, quality guarantees, secure transportation and long-term supply. The same visit produced a Memorandum of Cooperation between the Ministry of Electricity and Energy and RC-Investments. The framework was designed with Russia identifying suppliers and partners and Myanmar facilitating Russian hydrocarbon and petrochemical deliveries.

Myanmar’s LNG import system already exists. Imports resumed in late 2025 after a four-year break, with LNG loaded at the Bintulu LNG complex in Malaysia and delivered to the Thilawa floating storage unit near Yangon. So, Russia is effectively trying to insert itself into an existing supply chain. Kpler expected Myanmar to import around 0.4 million tonnes of LNG in 2026, mainly to supply the Thanlyin and Thaketa power plants. Myanmar’s own Ministry of Information confirms that LNG imports are now feeding around 500 MW of generation in Yangon.

What Russia appears prepared to provide alongside it is considerably more interesting.

The Roscosmos agreement includes satellite-navigation measurement stations, access to navigation data, a COSPAS-SARSAT ground station and an ASPOS opto-electronic telescope station. Russia will also help select and train Myanmar astronauts. According to the Myanmar Space Agency (which already took the announcement down from their website), the stated purposes include economic development, search and rescue, scientific research and monitoring hazardous objects in space. All very peaceful.

Then the cooperation expanded further. On August 19, Min Aung Hlaing met Roscosmos Director General Dmitry Bakanov. Their discussions included Earth-observation satellite imagery, a satellite-navigation measuring station, the Rassvet low-orbit communications system, nano-satellites and continued Russian assistance in developing Myanmar’s space capabilities.

None of these technologies is inherently military. That is precisely the point. They do not need to be. Remember the Chinese balloon incident in 2023? A Chinese high-altitude balloon crossed the United States before being shot down by an F-22 off the coast of South Carolina on February 4. Beijing insisted that it was a civilian airship used mainly for meteorological research which had simply been blown off course. The U.S. State Department had a rather different interpretation. A U-2 surveillance aircraft examined the balloon while it was still in the air and confirmed that it carried intelligence-collection capabilities. The U.S. government later described it as part of a broader Chinese military-linked aerial surveillance program.

Earth-observation technology works on exactly the same uncomfortable boundary between civilian and military use. The same satellite imagery that monitors forests, floods, agriculture or climate can also show roads, buildings, camps, vehicles and changes on the ground. Optical satellites provide detailed imagery; synthetic-aperture radar can observe through cloud and at night; repeated passes over the same area show what has moved, appeared or disappeared. Communications systems can connect remote communities. They can also support command and control. Radio-electronic technology can support industry. It can also support surveillance and electronic warfare. Calling the technology civilian therefore tells us very little about what it can actually be used for. A satellite looking for deforestation can look at a military base just as easily.

Below is the kind of imagery Russia can produce. These are examples from Russian Resurs-P and Canopus-V satellites:

Resurs-P4 and P5 can produce panchromatic imagery at about 1 m resolution and multispectral imagery at roughly 3-4 m. As for the Canopus-V imagery, you can clearly distinguish agricultural plots, settlements, roads and terrain. Russian Space Systems explicitly lists infrastructure monitoring among the applications of these Earth-observation systems.

And what about Rassvet? It is essentially Russia’s answer to Starlink, a low-Earth-orbit broadband communications network being built by Bureau 1440, part of Russia’s X Holding. Bureau 1440 describes the satellites themselves as “5G base stations in orbit”. The target orbit is around 800 km, with advertised speeds of up to 1 Gbit/s and latency below 70 milliseconds. The satellites communicate with each other through laser links, while user terminals can be installed on fixed sites as well as cars, ships, aircraft and trains.

Militarily, the potential is obvious. What it can potentially do is provide broadband communications in places where terrestrial networks are absent or unreliable. That could support communication between command posts, mobile units, aircraft or unmanned systems. It could also transmit satellite imagery and other intelligence quickly from one location to another.

Myanmar is an unusually important place to make that distinction.

Myanmar’s civil war is nearly as old as the country itself. Armed conflict between the central state and ethnic organizations began almost immediately after independence in 1948. The Karen conflict started in 1949, while other ethnic insurgencies developed across Kachin, Shan and other border regions. These were not temporary rebellions. They became long-running territorial conflicts over autonomy, federalism, political control and, in some cases, independence.

The Myanmar military has never been particularly effective in many of these areas. Geography is one reason. Ethnic armed organizations operate in mountains, jungles and forests along the borders with Thailand, China and India. They know the terrain, move in small units, use ambushes and landmines and often operate among populations with which they have close local connections. The Myanmar military has traditionally been much stronger in towns, on major roads and around fixed military positions.

The military is therefore not acquiring these capabilities in an abstract security environment. It is fighting an actual war.

Better Earth observation means better information about what is happening on the ground. Better satellite navigation means better positioning. Better communications mean better coordination. Better mapping means a clearer picture of roads, settlements, bases and infrastructure in territories that the military has historically struggled to control.

Russia does not need to sign a memorandum saying that it will help Myanmar locate ethnic armed organizations. No government writes agreements like that. It only needs to provide the infrastructure that makes locating them easier.

Ana Brown is a nuclear lawyer, academic and intelligence analyst specialising in defence economics, and an ALM candidate at Harvard University.

World.title: ‘They’re Definitely Afraid of Her’: Aung San Suu Kyi’s Son Speaks Out
World.content:
Kim Aris would much rather stay out of the spotlight. But when his mother Aung San Suu Kyi was once again imprisoned after Myanmar’s military coup in 2021, he realised he could no longer remain silent. As a part of his mission to draw attention to his mother’s plight and the continuing struggle of the people of Myanmar, he came to Prague last week.

There he attended the democratic Forum 2000 Conference to remind the world that wars raging closer to home have not brought an end to those that have been devastating countries thousands of miles away for years.

His mother is now 81 and her family do not know exactly where she is being held or in what conditions. In an interview with Chechia’s Seznam Zpravy daily, he asks: if he, as her own son, does not stand up for his mother, how can he expect anyone else to do so?

When you look at Myanmar today, more than five years after the coup, what kind of country do you see?

I see a country torn apart by civil war, with people on the ground facing a very, very desperate situation. The military continues to bomb civilians regularly and refuses to stop its brutality against the population despite international pressure.

And yet, despite all this, I don’t think the situation is quite as straightforward as the rest of the world tends to portray it.

The people of Burma have shown incredible strength over the past five years, and the military is nowhere near as strong as it would like the rest of the world to believe. In fact, I would say the country is more united today than it has been for decades. It’s just very difficult for the outside world to see that at the moment.

We are witnessing something of a diplomatic rehabilitation of regime leader Min Aung Hlaing. He was warmly received in Malaysia, and the United States has begun direct talks with his government. What do you think of these developments?

I think those who are now trying to negotiate with the military are going to be very disappointed when they realise that the military is making promises it simply cannot keep.

Are you referring, for example, to American efforts to gain access to Myanmar’s rare earth mineral deposits?

Yes. But those minerals are not being mined in areas controlled by the military. Many of the promises the military is making concern things it simply cannot deliver. And even if it could deliver them, we’ve known for decades that the military frequently breaks its promises.

When was the last time you heard from your mother directly?

I’ve received just one letter from her in the past five years. That must have been about three years ago now.

This summer, photographs finally emerged showing her meeting representatives of the Red Cross. When you first saw those pictures, did they reassure you, or did they raise even more questions?

At first, I wasn’t even sure whether to believe that the meeting had actually taken place. After all, over the past five years, the military has put out a great deal of false information about my mother’s health and whereabouts.

For example, they claimed she had been transferred to house arrest, and we know that isn’t true. But when I found out that the photograph was genuine—or at least that one of them was—it gave me some hope that she was, at least, still alive.

Do you think the military is afraid of Aung San Suu Kyi herself or of what she continues to represent?

They’re definitely afraid of her. Why else would they keep her locked up?
