World.title: Kazakhstan’s bitumen makers to end 100/130-grade output from Nov. 1
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. Kazakhstan’s two major bitumen producers - the CASPI BITUM plant in Aktau and the Pavlodar Oil Chemistry Refinery (POCR) - will discontinue production of 100/130-grade road petroleum bitumen from November 1, 2026, according to KazMunayGas.

Both facilities will switch to producing grades of road petroleum bitumen tailored to the climatic conditions of Kazakhstan’s regions, in line with directives issued by the country’s government.

Under the revised production policy, 70/100-grade bitumen will be produced for the northern and central regions, while 50/70-grade bitumen will be designated for the southern regions.

Both plants play an important role in supplying Kazakhstan’s road construction sector with domestically produced bitumen. CASPI BITUM has an annual production capacity of 750,000 tons, while POCR can produce approximately 500,000 tons per year.

Together, the two facilities have a combined annual production capacity of 1.25 million tons, compared with Kazakhstan’s estimated annual road bitumen demand of 1.2 million tons.

According to KazMunayGas (KMG), CASPI BITUM produced 221,000 tonnes of road bitumen in January-August 2026, nearly 50% more than in the same period last year. The company increased shipments to 220,000 tonnes from 147,000 tonnes in January-August 2025, also representing growth of approximately 50%.

World.title: Azerbaijan plans no 2027 budget transfers to its 67 cities, districts
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. No additional state budget transfers are planned for any of Azerbaijan’s 67 cities and districts to cover local expenditures in 2027.

This was stipulated in the draft law on Azerbaijan’s state budget for next year.

According to the draft, total revenues of Azerbaijan’s cities and districts are projected to reach 18.43 billion manat ($10.84 billion) next year, while local budget expenditures are projected at 735.57 million manat ($432.69 million).

Thus, the minimum amount of revenues exceeding local expenditures and allocated to centralized budget revenues has been set at 17.69 billion manat ($10.41 billion).

According to the projections, Baku’s revenues are expected to reach nearly 16.65 billion manat ($9.79 billion), while local expenditures are projected at 326.78 million manat ($192.23 million). The amount of the capital’s projected revenues exceeding local expenditures is estimated at 16.32 billion manat ($9.6 billion).

Among other cities, revenues for Sumqayit are projected at 288.3 million manat ($169.59 million), with local expenditures of 25.38 million manat ($14.93 million), while revenues for Ganja are estimated at 152.35 million manat ($89.62 million), with local expenditures of nearly 28.91 million manat ($17.01 million).

Among the districts, Absheron is expected to be among those with the highest revenues. The district’s revenues are projected at 133.5 million manat ($78.53 million), while local expenditures are estimated at about 11.44 million manat ($6.73 million).

According to Article 10 of the draft law, when the revenues of cities and districts do not cover their local expenditures, transfers from the state budget of up to 10 percent of their expenditures may be allocated. However, the 2027 projections indicate that all 67 cities and districts will be able to cover their local expenditures through their own revenues.

State budget revenues next year are expected to reach 39.25 billion manat ($23.09 billion), while expenditures are projected at 42.4 billion manat ($24.94 billion).

World.title: Uzbekistan, Georgia seek to boost trade, and transport ties
World.content:
Photo: The telegram channel of the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Uzbekistanra

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. Uzbekistan and Georgia are seeking to expand trade, investment and transport cooperation following the establishment of a strategic partnership, Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov said.

This was announced by FM Saidov on his Telegram channel following his meeting with Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze in Batumi on October 22.

In a post shared on social media, Saidov stated that, in a meeting, he conveyed the greetings and best wishes of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev to PM Kobakhidze.

He noted that Kobakhidze’s official visit to Uzbekistan in March 2025 and Mirziyoyev’s state visit to Georgia in July 2026 had elevated bilateral relations to a new level. The signing of a Declaration on Strategic Partnership during Mirziyoyev’s visit marked a milestone in bilateral cooperation, Saidov said.

The meeting focused on expanding trade, economic and investment ties, increasing bilateral trade turnover and advancing joint projects in transport and logistics. The officials also exchanged views on regional and international issues.

During his visit to Batumi, Saidov also met with Zurab Pataradze, chairman of the government of Georgia’s Autonomous Republic of Adjara.

Saidov reaffirmed Uzbekistan’s commitment to strengthening its strategic partnership with Georgia and advancing new practical initiatives to deepen bilateral cooperation.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s parliament receives draft state budget for 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. Azerbaijan's state budget revenues for 2027 are projected at 39.25 billion manat ($23.09 billion), while expenditures are projected at 42.4 billion manat ($24.94 billion).

This was stipulated in the draft law on Azerbaijan's state budget for next year.

The main sources of budget revenue include taxes, customs duties, receipts from state property, dividends from state enterprises, and transfers to the state budget.

The largest shares of state budget revenue for 2027 are expected to come from value-added tax (VAT), at nearly 9.39 billion manat ($5.52 billion); corporate income tax, at 6.98 billion manat ($4.11 billion); and personal income tax, at 3.07 billion manat ($1.81 billion). The upper limit of the transfer to the state budget from the relevant institution is set at 11.9 billion manat ($7 billion).

The main areas of budget spending include economic activity, defense and national security, education, general public services, social protection and social security, and healthcare. The budget allocates about 8.91 billion manat ($5.24 billion) to economic activity, roughly 8.82 billion manat ($5.19 billion) to defense and national security, 5.52 billion manat ($3.25 billion) to general public services, 5.99 billion manat ($3.52 billion) to education, 4.9 billion manat ($2.9 billion) to social protection and social security, and 2.8 billion manat ($1.6 billion) to healthcare.

Of the education expenditure, 2.18 billion manat ($1.29 billion) will be allocated to general education, 434.8 million manat ($255.76 million) to preschool education, and 240.6 million manat ($141.53 million) to higher education. In healthcare, 1.1 billion manat ($647.06 million) is earmarked for the Compulsory Health Insurance Fund. A transfer of 1.6 billion manat ($941.18 million) from the state budget is allocated to balance the budget of the State Social Protection Fund.

Under economic activity, 6.4 billion manat ($3.76 billion) will be allocated to construction and urban planning, including 5.3 billion manat ($3.1 billion) for public capital investment. Furthermore, about 1.38 billion manat ($811.47 million) is earmarked for agriculture, 438.6 million manat ($258 million) for environmental protection, and 335.2 million manat ($197.18 million) for housing and communal services.

The ceiling on public debt servicing expenditure is set at 772.5 million manat ($454.41 million) for domestic debt and approximately 1.43 billion manat ($839.7 million) for external debt. These amounts include interest payments of 635.3 million manat ($373.71 million) and 364 million manat ($214 million), respectively.

In 2027, the ceiling on domestic government borrowing is set at 2.5 billion manat ($1.47 billion), while the ceiling on external government borrowing is set at 6 billion manat ($3.53 billion). The ceiling on state guarantees to be issued during the year is also set at 6 billion manat.

The state budget deficit of nearly 3.15 billion manat ($1.85 billion) is planned to be financed through privatization receipts, domestic and external borrowing, and the unspent balance in the single Treasury account as of January 1, 2027.

For 2027, the ceiling on total consolidated budget expenditure is set at about 50.38 billion manat ($29.63 billion), while the ceiling on the consolidated budget deficit, excluding revenues of the relevant state institution, is set at approximately 16.7 billion manat ($9.8 billion).

According to the draft law, the 2027 state budget law will enter into force on January 1, 2027.

World.title: Methane cuts could open EU market to Turkmen gas - expert
World.content:
ASHGABAT, Turkmenistan, October 23. Reducing methane emissions during gas extraction and production could open up opportunities for Turkmenistan to export natural gas to the European Union (EU) market, given the tightening of environmental requirements for imported fuel, Associate on energy and climate regulation at Correggio Consulting, Enri Gjondrekaj said, Trend's special correspondent reports.

Gjondrekaj made the remark on the third day of the OGT 2026 conference in Ashgabat on October 23.

“I believe that in a few years, especially by 2030, which marks the end of this period, this figure will decrease and meet EU requirements. This will allow the European Union to become a potential buyer of Turkmen gas in the future,” he said.

According to the expert, gas producers must take into account European regulatory requirements, which provide for the phased introduction of obligations for importers of oil, gas, and coal from countries outside the EU. These obligations pertain to the disclosure of information on the origin of fuel and measures to reduce methane emissions, as well as the monitoring, reporting, and verification of emissions data.

“This regulation establishes obligations for gas producers both in Europe and beyond. The main provisions stipulate that importers into the EU who supply gas, oil, or coal from countries outside the European Union must comply with certain requirements,” Gjondrekaj explained.

He noted that one of the key criteria going forward will be methane intensity, defined as the ratio of methane emissions to the total volume of fuel sold. According to the current EU regulatory timeline, methane intensity requirements are to apply to relevant fuel import contracts concluded or renewed after August 5, 2030.

“In 2030, the European Union will set a cap on methane intensity. This indicator is calculated as the ratio of methane emissions to the total volume of gas sold on the market. The limit will be enshrined in the regulations, and gas exports to the European Union will have to comply with the established limit. We do not yet know what this limit will be,” the expert said.

At the same time, Gjondrekaj pointed out the possibility of revising the deadlines for implementing certain requirements. According to him, on October 22, the European Parliament supported a three-year postponement of a number of obligations regarding the monitoring, reporting, and verification of methane emissions for importers and producers. However, this proposal still needs to be agreed upon by the Council of the EU and has not yet changed the current deadlines.

“Today is October 23. Yesterday, October 22, the European Parliament adopted a series of amendments providing for a three-year postponement of two deadlines – August 2028 and August 2030. However, these amendments have not yet been approved and have not entered into force. Tripartite negotiations between the relevant legislative bodies are now pending,” he noted.

Speaking about practical measures to reduce emissions, the expert emphasized the importance of a clear division of responsibilities at production facilities. It is necessary to determine who is responsible for identifying leaks, eliminating them, and documenting the work performed. Satellite technology offers additional capabilities, allowing for the detection of large emissions and the prompt transmission of relevant information to government agencies.

As an example of progress in this area, Gjondrekaj cited data from the International Energy Agency (IEA) on methane intensity in Turkmenistan.

“The International Energy Agency conducted an analysis according to which the methane intensity in Turkmenistan appears to be 7 percent. At the same time, this figure is gradually decreasing,” he said.

The expert expressed the view that a further reduction in methane intensity and the development of monitoring systems will help Turkmenistan bring the oil and gas sector’s performance closer to the requirements of the European market. He also emphasized that regulation in this area continues to evolve, so producers need to keep track of changes in the regulatory framework.

Meanwhile, the final day of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan” (OGT 2026) is underway in Ashgabat.

On the third day, participants are discussing ways to reduce methane emissions, improve environmental and energy efficiency, and the role of natural gas in ensuring a balanced and sustainable energy future.

Participants are exploring opportunities for international exchange of expertise and technologies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions and improving the environmental performance of the oil and gas industry. In addition, the role of natural gas in shaping a balanced energy system is being discussed.

World.title: Bruce Lehrmann's rape trial postponed to allow time to find barrister
World.content:
The looming rape trial of former Liberal Party staffer Bruce Lehrmann has been postponed amid a bitter courtroom clash between lawyers.

Mr Lehrmann had been scheduled to face trial on November 2 this year on two counts of rape alleged to have occurred in Toowoomba, west of Brisbane, in October 2021.

He has indicated he will plead not guilty, but the Brisbane District Court on Friday heard that his solicitor Zali Burrows had encountered difficulty locking down a barrister to represent him for the trial and an adjournment was required.

The argument was accepted by Judge David Kent, saying the short time before a trial meant the interests of justice would be served by adjourning the case to allow time for suitably qualified counsel to be prepared.

"The adjournment should certainly not be regarded as open-ended. The defendant must now act promptly," Justice Kent said.

Crown prosecutor Caroline Marco had argued against the adjournment, pointing out the length of time in the whole matter and complaining of a paucity of evidence from Ms Burrows about contacting barristers to defend Mr Lehrmann.

"We have not a great deal of evidence to show what efforts have been made but for an affidavit of one barrister who hasn't been produced for cross-examination, who was never briefed, never accepted the brief," Ms Marco said.

"We don't know what other counsel, if any, have been approached to take on the matter."

"It is a realistic possibility that at a future trial listing that Mr Lehrmann will continue to be represented solely by Ms Burrows."

Defence lawyer Zali Burrows, pictured in August last year, represented Mr Lehrmann with the hearing conducted largely with the lawyers online. (ABC News: Brandon Long)

Ms Marco complained of a "continual drip feeding of applications to the court by Ms Burrows" and argued it would be preferable if the defence would have an understanding of a time by which all applications should be made.

"This is unsatisfactory for the complainant. The interest of justice goes both ways," Ms Marco said.

Ms Burrows fired back at the prosecutor's argument.

"I do take umbrage with the submissions Ms Marco's made," Ms Burrows said.

She argued she had been "verballed" and "the Crown have drip-fed the defence material".

"From the very first instance of coming involved in this matter, it was a bit of a struggle in trying to make sure that we were getting all the material that was in the brief."

Ms Burrows said if case management directions were given, then the prosecution should "go and disclose everything that is disclosable (sic), especially if its exculpatory material".

"It's not up to them to decide, what is relevant to the defence case or not."

The hearing on Friday was conducted largely with the lawyers online, and Justice Kent at one stage halting proceedings because of a constant whooshing sound that he said seemed like emails were being sent.

"It could probably be an iMessage of Mr Lehrmann sending messages to my computer and I stopped that," Ms Burrows said. "I apologise."

Any trial date is yet to be locked in, with a next mention scheduled for November 2.

Prosecutors estimated the trial could take about a week, while the defence estimated two weeks.

World.title: Man jailed for six years for killing friend in drunk driving crash
World.content:
A man who drove drunk and killed his close friend in a crash on the New South Wales Far South Coast has been jailed for six years.

Edward James McCoid, 34, was sentenced by Bega District Court Judge Andrew Haesler today, after pleading guilty to aggravated dangerous driving occasioning death.

Ritchie Faulkner, a 46-year-old grandfather and former high school teacher, died from his injuries after the car they were in crashed at Tura Beach, north of Merimbula, on June 21 last year.

Police alleged that McCoid's blood alcohol concentration could have been as high as 0.25 when he was behind the wheel.

McCoid lost control while overtaking a car towing a boat, sending the car airborne before it rolled for more than 60 metres along the roadside.

He was flown to Canberra Hospital, while Mr Faulkner died later that night from cardiac arrest after being taken to Bega's South East Regional Hospital with severe injuries.

The crash occurred on Sapphire Coast Drive at Tura Beach. (ABC South East NSW: Lisa Markham)

Family shattered

Outside court, Mr Faulkner's sister, Valley Mein, described her brother as fun-loving, outgoing and non-judgemental.

"He was a friend to everyone because he was very open," she said.

In her victim impact statement, Ms Mein described her brother as the "glue" that held their family together.

"Losing him has shattered our foundation," she told the court.

" This offender has given us a life sentence of trauma and profound grief. "

Ritchie Faulkner died in hospital from his injuries. (ABC South East NSW: Lisa Markham)

Jack Faulkner told the court he had lost not only his father but also his "best mate".

"He was the first person I called every time I achieved something," he said.

"Not a day will go past where he isn't missed."

In her victim impact statement, Mr Faulkner's daughter, Kaylah Harlow, said she often wondered what her father's final moments had been like.

"I cry in the car when I hear a song that reminds me of him," she told the court.

"I cry when I listen to his voicemails every week."

An 'incomprehensible betrayal'

During sentencing, Judge Haesler read a letter from McCoid, who appeared via video link from custody with his head bowed for much of the hearing.

In the letter, McCoid expressed remorse and sorrow towards Mr Faulkner's family and friends.

"These thoughts will haunt me for the rest of my life," the letter read.

The judge described the events of that night as "tragic" and an "incomprehensible betrayal by a friend".

The court heard McCoid continued to drink heavily after being discharged from rehabilitation following the crash, and at one point suffered an alcohol withdrawal seizure that required hospitalisation.

McCoid was sentenced to six years in jail. (ABC South East NSW: Adriane Reardon)

"The community has to be protected from him," the judge told the court.

" Jails are not holiday camps, they are nasty, violent places. "

McCoid was disqualified from driving for two years and will be eligible for parole in May 2030.

World.title: Teen jailed for sexually assaulting jogger while on bail
World.content:
A teenage boy who sexually assaulted a jogger in Canberra’s north has been jailed for more than six years.

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

The woman, aged 60, was running down Oak Hill on the Centenary Trail in Bonner just after 10am on May 26 last year, when the then-15-year-old grabbed her from behind.

The boy strangled the woman, causing her to pass out briefly.

When she regained consciousness, she was able to break free and scream, but the teenager grabbed her legs and pulled her back — striking her in the head several times and saying "shush, just shush".

He then pulled her head back with such force that she thought he was going to break her neck.

The boy indecently assaulted her before she was able to push him off. He took her phone and ran away.

The woman got up and ran until she found another woman, who called triple zero.

Police found the boy a short time later, and he was arrested.

'I was in so much fear'

The woman told the ACT Supreme Court the incident turned her world "upside down".

"I truly felt that I was going to die on that hill that day," she said.

"I was in so much fear that I could not feel the physical pain of what was happening to me."

At the time of the attack, the boy was on bail for sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl he met while she was out with friends a few months earlier.

He offered to go with the girl to buy alcohol and told her he knew a shortcut to a nearby bottle shop, but he instead led her into a park.

There he forced himself on her, despite her repeated protests and attempts to push him away.

In a victim impact statement, the girl said she was "still suffering with the haunting thoughts held from the event".

"I miss being able to leave the house freely and live in the moment without fear," she told the court.

The boy pleaded guilty to charges including sexual assault in the third degree; committing acts of indecency, choking, strangling or suffocating another person and theft.

Judge commends victims' courage

In sentencing, Justice Louise Taylor noted the boy — now 17 — has a severe neurodevelopmental disorder and had had a difficult childhood but said ultimately, he knew what he was doing was wrong.

"The offending was brazen," Justice Taylor said.

"He could only have known that in each case the victim was not consenting."

The woman was jogging down Oak Hill on the Centenary Trail in Bonner. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Justice Taylor was satisfied the boy was remorseful and ashamed of his offending, and had made positive changes during his time in custody.

And while she said his inevitable return to the community meant rehabilitation was critical, she acknowledged his sentence had to reflect the "irrevocable harm" suffered by the victims and the impact of sexual violence has on the community — predominantly women and girls.

"The insidious harm caused by sexual violence does not discriminate," Justice Taylor said

"The hope that both victims had, for their perhaps quite different futures, has been shattered.

"I commend their courage and hope for their healing"

The boy was sentenced to serve six years and six months' imprisonment, including time already served, at Bimberi Youth Justice Centre.

That sentence is to be suspended from May 2028 on entering into a good behaviour order and accepting supervision conditions.

World.title: Fortnite returns to Apple's Australian app stores after landmark case
World.content:
The Federal Court has ordered Apple to open up its devices to other app stores, as part of a landmark finding that the tech giant violated Australian competition law.

It's a fundamental shift for an estimated 15 million Australian Apple users, who will soon be able to download apps from the open web as well as rival app stores as a result.

The company has until March 2027 to make the changes, Federal Court Justice Jonathan Beach ruled on Thursday.

It's the latest chapter in a six-year anti-trust legal battle between Apple and the game developer behind Fortnite, Epic Games, spanning Europe, UK, the US and Australia.

The long-awaited judgement sets out the consequences of the Federal Court's decision in August last year in which both Apple and Google were found to have misused their market power in how their app stores were run.

Apple and Google lose landmark court case The federal court has today ruled against tech giants Apple and Google in a major win for consumers, finding that the companies engaged in anti-competitive conduct.

Epic Games, and lawyers in a parallel class action, had long alleged Apple and Google were running illegal monopolies, by effectively banning other app stores from their devices and forcing apps to use their payment platform, where they collect between 15 and 30 per cent in fees.

The iPhone maker had cited security and intellectual property concerns in its defence throughout the case.

Now, as a result of yesterday's decision Apple will also have to permit the use of alternative payment methods, as well as allowing alternative app stores.

Consumer advocates are hopeful the changes will result in increased competition and lower prices for millions of Apple users.

In publishing his reasons, Justice Beach said Apple had contravened the Competition and Consumer Act with an "intricate web of terms and technical measures", and ordered the company to pay 85 per cent of Epic Games' legal costs from the months-long trial.

The decision signals the immediate return of one of the world's most popular games, Fortnite, to Apple's Australian app store from today, after a six-year hiatus.

Apple told Reuters it disagreed with many of the court's findings and would seek to challenge ​them.

"We will request a stay and appeal ​the outcome to seek a resolution that respects our ‌intellectual ⁠property and protects the safe, secure experience that consumers and developers expect from the App Store," an Apple spokesperson said.

World.title: Premier Coal gives employees redundancy forms ahead of move to close night shifts
World.content:
The Western Australian government says it is disappointed that one of the state's last remaining coalmines will shift to day operations only.

The ABC has received confirmation from the government about Premier Coal's decision to reduce operating hours.

The government is seeking more information on the matter.

Transitioning to day shift operations would result in job losses at the mine in Collie, 200 kilometres south of Perth.

The ABC understands Premier Coal has told workers night shifts will end in the coming months and there will be a three-week planned shutdown over summer.

WA Premier Roger Cook speaks on ABC radio on Thursday. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"Premier Coal's decision to move its operational workforce to day shift is very disappointing," a state government spokesperson said.

" The government has sought urgent clarity from Premier Coal on the impact these changes will have on its workforce. "

Premier Coal did not respond to questions from the ABC.

Unions said the move would mean the axing of about 40 per cent of the workforce, or about 150 jobs.

Management today handed out forms for workers to nominate for voluntary redundancies.

A form asking for voluntary redundancies was handed out at Premier Coal in Collie. (Supplied: AMWU)

The decision comes as owner Yancoal has been embroiled in a tumultuous period of enterprise bargaining with workers as they try to negotiate their final agreement before the government's planned shutdown of coal-fired power generation by 2030.

The workforce, which is more than 90 per cent unionised, has taken several hours of strike action since July, including refusing to load coal onto trains.

Unions say the proposed offer from Premier Coal could leave workers tens of thousands of dollars worse off each year. (ABC South West WA: Neve Brissenden)

Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union Secretary Steve McCartney said the impacts of the decision were not just about staffing.

"It looks like about a 40 per cent reduction in workers," he said.

"That's a lot of people that would be looking for a job where there isn't one at the moment.

" But more importantly, the redundancies will all be paid out on day shift rates and the night shift component will be taken out … that's 45 per cent of their money going missing when they're leaving. "

In April, Premier Coal announced the loss of between 70 and 100 jobs at the Collie mine site.

No power blackouts expected

Energy analyst Tim Buckley, from Climate Energy Finance, said the night operations shutdown would not cause rolling blackouts.

Premier Coal's open pit is near Collie in WA's South West. (ABC News: Anthony Pancia)

"Customers of WA can be confident there's not going to be significant impacts to the energy grid from this," he said.

Coal generated 24 per cent of all electricity in WA in the past 12 months, while renewables contributed about 40 per cent.

Mr Buckley said the decision by Premier Coal came sooner than the government was prepared for, but renewable projects across the state were steaming ahead.

In a statement, the state government said it was confident Premier Coal's decision would not affect the state's power supply.

Workforce in transition

Taxpayer money has been pouring into Collie since the government made the announcement about shutting coal production in 2022.

The WA government's $230 million Collie Industrial Transition Fund has laid the groundwork for several new industries, but few have reached a final investment decision.

Last month, $58 million in funding was announced for rehabilitation, road infrastructure and workforce transition initiatives in Collie, including targeted voluntary redundancy measures.

In May, the WA government also flagged Collie as a potential home for a new manufacturing defence hub.

World.title: NSW's second-largest national park created to protect koalas
World.content:
After a marathon parliamentary debate, the state government has established New South Wales's second-largest national park.

The Great Koala National Park (GKNP) will take in 478,000 hectares of land between Kempsey and Grafton on the Mid North Coast, following a key promise from Labor during the 2023 state election.

It will comprise a patchwork of existing national parks and more than 178,000 hectares of state forest and Crown Land.

The Great Koala National Park covers land between Kempsey and Grafton. (Supplied: NPWS)

The legislation passed today after more than 14 hours of debate in the Legislative Council, which considered approximately 160 amendments.

NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe hailed the GKNP as a win for the environment that would protect more than 100 species of flora and fauna.

"This is a defining moment for conservation in NSW," she said in a statement.

"After more than a decade of campaigning and years of detailed assessments, consultation and planning, we have cleared the final hurdles to delivering our biggest environmental commitment.

"We are protecting extraordinary forests … while ensuring future generations can enjoy these incredible places."

Penny Sharpe welcomes the passing of the legislation to create the national park. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

For conservationist Ashley Love, the park's creation is the culmination of more than a decade of campaigning to protect koalas and their habitat along the Mid North Coast.

"We're extremely grateful that the government has decided to protect native forest," he said.

"Its nature is quite fragmented, and there are gaps and connectivity issues between sections of it, but it is a big step forward."

A long journey

Mr Love began lobbying for what would become the Great Koala National Park after hearing multiple reports from residents that koalas in the region were not as common as they once were.

"It became too much to ignore," he said.

"We proposed a reserve over the Crown land covering [the region], and that was a basis for the proposal for the Great Koala National Park."

Ashley Love helped lobby for the Great Koala National Park for more than a decade. (ABC News: Emma Rennie)

The NSW Labor Party unsuccessfully took the proposal to the 2015 and 2019 state elections, before winning government in 2023.

Mr Love said despite the passing of the legislation, he would continue to push for more areas of the surrounding forest to be protected.

"We still have to keep working on those elements that were not included," he said.

Logging industry deflated

Key to the establishment of the park was the approval from the federal government to generate carbon credits for ending native forest logging in the park's state forest areas.

On Thursday, the federal Clean Energy Regulator announced it had registered the project, with more than 117,000 hectares designated for carbon protection.

A moratorium on logging on the proposed area of the GKNP was introduced last year, and a transition package was offered to affected workers.

Andrew Hurford says many mills now have no wood to process in the region. (ABC Landline: Cameron Lang)

Timber New South Wales president Andrew Hurford said the logging ban has had a "creeping impact" for the industry along the Mid North Coast.

"Staff have been laid off; engineering firms that provide support to those companies have no forward orders … downstream people supplying tyres, fuel, trucking, transport, engineering.

"All of those things are gradually becoming slower and quieter."

In July, state forest manager the Forestry Corporation of NSW (FCNSW) announced it would cut more than 30 jobs in Coffs Harbour related to the impacts of the GKNP.

The government said impacted FCNSW staff would be appointed to suitable roles with the National Parks and Wildlife Service.

World.title: Former cop found guilty of cold case murder of Warrnambool man
World.content:
A Supreme Court jury has found an elderly former police officer guilty of murdering Warrnambool father Christopher Jarvis more than 20 years ago.

Mr Jarvis, who was 38, has not been seen since he disappeared from his Wangoom home near Warrnambool on June 13, 2006.

During the 21-day trial in Warrnambool, the court heard that Steven Frederick Johnson, 74, orchestrated a violent attack on Mr Jarvis, his tenant, over $2,210 in unpaid rent.

Johnson murdered Mr Jarvis with a baseball bat before dumping his body in bushland.

Mr Jarvis's car was later found burnt out at a tourist lookout on the coast near Warrnambool.

His body has never been found.

Members of Mr Jarvis's family cheered and celebrated in court when the verdict was delivered, while Johnson's family members sat in shock.

Christopher Jarvis has not been seen since 2006. (Supplied: Australian Missing Persons Register)

Johnson, 74, had pleaded not guilty to one charge of murder over the disappearance.

The jury deliberated for four days before returning a guilty verdict.

No bail application was made, and Johnson will return to court for a plea hearing on December 14.

Speaking outside court, Mr Jarvis's family spoke of their relief at the guilty verdict.

"It's been the longest 20 years to finally get what we've wanted — a little bit of closure, so we can hopefully move on," his daughter, Bree, said.

Mr Jarvis's son, Cale, said he hoped Johnson "rots in his dirty little cell for the rest of his life, and thinks about his actions".

A long time coming

The murder was initially treated as a missing person case, before police began reinvestigating and arrested Johnson in 2022.

The Supreme Court, sitting in Warrnambool, heard Johnson fired a starter pistol in Mr Jarvis's ear on the day of the attack before bundling him into his own car.

He then drove the man to the nearby Framlingham Forest, where Johnson killed Mr Jarvis by hitting him over the head with a baseball bat and buried him in a shallow grave.

Prosecutors believe Christopher Jarvis's body is somewhere in Framlingham Forest, near Warrnambool. (ABC News: Jean Bell)

The murder was carried out the day before the men were due to appear at a contested hearing in the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) over the rental dispute.

World.title: Courtney Act immortalised with dismembered Barbies, sequins and beer can
World.content:
Discarded fingernails, sequins, a pair of high heels, a beer can, and a dismembered Barbie doll have been used to capture the likeness of Australia's most celebrated drag queen.

A glittering new portrait of Courtney Act has been unveiled at the National Portrait Gallery in Canberra.

The large mosaic by artist Paul Yore is an eclectic assemblage of thousands of objects, each meticulously placed with tweezers, to pay tribute to the queer icon.

"I sent Paul a bag of my old fingernails and eyelashes and broken jewellery, and so I knew that it was going to be made of found objects and mixed media, but to see it hanging on the wall is absolutely amazing," Act said.

Courtney Act's portrait features found items, including a football. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Courtney Act has spent more than two decades in the public eye and is an internationally celebrated drag performer, queer advocate and television personality.

She is the alter ego of Queensland-born Shane Janek, who never felt like he fit into masculine norms growing up.

"Imagine beaming back to 14-year-old me, listening to the Spice Girls, wearing my platform buffalo boots to school," Act said.

"In Brisbane in the 90s there was certainly nobody like me around and not anybody like me portrayed in the media.

"So when an institution like the National Portrait Gallery commissions a portrait of you, it feels very validating."

Australian queen of drag, Courtney Act and artist Paul Yore. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

'Get that off my face'

Among the objects used in the portrait is an old Nokia phone — the same model used by a young Shane Janek to come out to his parents.

There is also a statue of Aphrodite, an array of Australian iconography, and a football — something Act admits she has never played.

Artist Paul Yore said he was initially intimidated when he was approached by the gallery to create the portrait.

"I've obviously followed Courtney's career for decades now and idolise her as an icon as so many of us in the queer community do," he said.

Yore's mosaic portrait of Act has been unveiled at the National Portrait Gallery. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

The process took him about a year, and Yore said he felt a great sense of responsibility to "get it right".

"It was one of the most challenging things I've ever had to make," he said.

"At different times, I did hear Courtney's voice in my head being like, 'Oi, what are you doing? Why are you putting that there? Get that off my face!'"

'Monument to queer culture'

Growing up queer in a Catholic household, Yore said he took inspiration from illuminated icons — including the Virgin Mary — to make the portrait.

National Portrait Gallery director Bree Pickering described the artwork as a "monument to queer culture".

"At a distance, this is a glossy likeness of Courtney, yet up close thousands of small details tell another story, about a big life lived without apology," she said.

Act's portrait mosaic features glitter and a beer can. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

The portrait is now the first artwork you see when you walk into the gallery.

"Well, they say that you should always open with a strong number," Act said.

"I think that when people turn in, and they see this, they're just going to have a smile on their face.

"There's a sense of joy about it.

"I'm very grateful that this portrait has been created of me and that it celebrates drag and queerness in all of its sparkle."

World.title: Why these HSC students were grinning about a 2000-year-old public notice
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC Why these HSC students were grinning about a 2000-year-old public notice Emily Kowal October 23, 2026 — 5:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What does a 2000-year-old public notice banning the dumping of human faeces near water fountains reveal about political life in Pompeii and Herculaneum? It’s the four-mark question that had Parramatta Marist high school student Daniel Barletta grinning on Friday as he tackled his ancient history HSC exam. “There’s something comedic about people dumping waste in the street ... how they are declaring that you must stop doing this because it’s such a problem,” the 18-year-old said. “It brings a smile to your face.” Parramatta Marist College ancient history HSC students Daniel Barletta, Lachlan Doan-Vance, Marcus Khadi, Mark Ghostine and Christopher Nehme after the exam. Wolter Peeters Over three hours, 7755 students tackled short-answer questions about Pompeii and Herculaneum, as well as three other in-depth topics of choice. At Parramatta Marist, students studied Sparta, Hatshepsut of Egypt, and New Kingdom Egypt to the Death of Thutmose IV. The students said a string of coincidences left them in good shape.



At the end of year 11, the class visited a Pompeii exhibition in Canberra. As they stared at the plaster casts of the voids left by victims killed in the 79AD eruption of Mt Vesuvius, they had no idea that, almost a year later, the exhibition would feature in their HSC exam. “It was pretty neat, it goes full circle,” student Lachlan Doan-Vance said. The exam question: Should the display of human remains from Pompeii and Herculaneum be stopped? It referenced an article written about the Canberra exhibition. Doan-Vance said it helped to have seen the exhibition in person. Related Article HSC Teachers are meant to avoid controversy. In this HSC subject, it’s the main event “I talked about the source and how while it does still show the horrific remains, [the museum] partially obscured them,” he said. “It brought to this greater idea of while there is an inherent human dignity to each of the victims of Pompeii, there’s also value in their study, in that they should be preserved.” Barletta agreed: “Witnessing firsthand how they display [remains] with the warnings on the walls, and putting them in a separate area because it can be disturbing to some to see ... ethically we have come a long way.”



Ancient-history teacher Grace Harley described the exam as very fair and was excited about the Canberra coincidence. “It’s such an interesting subject, but a hard subject. I love it,” she said. She pitches ancient history as a “puzzle with less of the pieces”. “With modern [history] you have all the pieces – more than you want and that can be overwhelming – whereas with ancient, a lot of it comes from interpretation and analysis,” Harley said. “Where does the source come from? Why are there gaps in the sources? That can be really fun for kids to fill the blanks in.” Asked why they enjoyed studying ancient history, the students pointed to their teacher, Harley.



“Whenever we had a substitute [teacher], it never felt the same. We didn’t have that charismatic character in the room teaching us,” Barletta said. The HSC continues until November 5. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.content:

Most weeks open with a flicker of hope right now. Not because markets are suddenly looking rosy, but because fear has become the dominant trade. The unending Middle East conflict has punters too rattled to hold stocks over the weekend, preferring to sell on Friday and buy back on Monday rather than cop another gut-punch from the world news in between. In much the same fashion, Wall Street fired up to start the week, with better-than-expected results from SpaceX giving the AI trade another sugar hit. Revenue surged 161 per cent to US$14.6 billion, with a US$4.4 billion profit comfortably beating expectations and helping chip stocks and technology names lead the early charge. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Energy Technologies. That was about where the good news ended. The Middle East, oil prices, inflation, interest rates and the looming US midterm elections became too much to ignore, combining to build a wall of worry that even the AI bulls are struggling to climb. Houthi attacks on Saudi targets sent crude surging above US$113 a barrel, reviving fears that another energy shock could reignite inflation just as markets are hoping for interest-rate relief.



Then came the AI sell-down. Early-week optimism evaporated as the Nasdaq surrendered more than 2.5 per cent, with investors suddenly looking less enamoured with the eye-watering cost of the AI arms race. Meta beat earnings expectations but still took a beating as investors baulked at its enormous AI spending bill. The question is no longer whether AI will transform the world, but whether the mountains of future debt will serve the greater good. A fresh wave of AI incidents marred the powerful technology this week in what is being called “Black October”, after China-aligned hackers used AI agents to target hundreds of organisations worldwide, in some cases gaining privileged access to cloud infrastructure. Meanwhile, critical flaws in the language behind millions of websites have triggered a global scramble to patch up the internet and exploit attempts have surged into the millions after the vulnerabilities became public. And with the UK now urging households to stockpile three days’ worth of food and water in case of emergency, the prospect of digital disruptions is spilling into the real world. Across the channel, the political tinderbox is looking even more primed to blow.



France endured a week of “student” rioting, looting and arson that left thousands of businesses devastated and historic landmarks in ruins . With estimates of a million in protesters littering the streets and billions of dollars in damages across France, the damage bill continues to soar. Before the dust could settle, the unrest spilled across the border into Italy. The historically left-leaning citizens of Milan clearly weren’t about to let Paris hog the protest spotlight, with demonstrations of their own turning violent as hooded protesters clashed with police. The financial fallout is just as ugly. France’s 10-year government bond yield surged above 5 per cent, while the gap between French and German 10-year borrowing costs ballooned to nearly 1.8 percentage points — leaving France paying more than 50 per cent above Germany’s yield. That is the widest spread since the 2011 Eurozone debt crisis, as investors demand a much fatter return to lend to a country increasingly beset by fiscal strain, political paralysis and civil unrest. The problem is that France’s already enormous debt pile is becoming even more expensive to service, leaving less room to manoeuvre and making another Eurozone debt crisis look harder to dismiss. France spends around 30 per cent of GDP on social programs and carries one of Europe’s heaviest tax burdens.



Taxing your people into oblivion, pile on the govt spending and cripple small businesses. Sound familiar? Welcome to Albo’s Australia, where the looming capital-gains tax changes are already crippling investment and the ASX Emerging Companies index (XEC). The XEC has puked its guts out this week, losing more than five per cent in five days and down some 15 per cent over the last month. Australia’s AI industry and its supportive cheer squad have also been wetting the bed following Firmus’ spectacular failure to launch. The proposed $44 billion valuation behind the data-centre hopeful’s planned float proved too much for public markets to swallow, as its Aussie compatriot NEXTDC was next in the firing line this week. The data-centre giant shed 42 per cent on Wednesday, wiping roughly $3 billion from its worth after delays to electricity network upgrades at its West Footscray site forced it to slash forecasts and put new developments on ice. With small caps taking another hiding, this week’s Runners list is predictably a short affair. Top spot went once again to an Israeli technology angle, with Aussie tech hopeful inking a deal with Israeli heavyweight SYNCH that could pave the way for up to US$10 million in purchase orders for its next-generation smart glasses.



Energy Technologies’ Cogenic subsidiary is targeting frontline personnel with its next-generation laser smart glasses. ENERGY TECHNOLOGIES LTD (ASX: EGY) Up 315% (2c – 8.3c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is smart-wearable player Energy Technologies, after its wholly owned Cogenic subsidiary signed a binding heads of agreement with Israeli tech outfit SYNCH, opening the door to a potential US$10 million (A$14.25 million) order for its next-generation smart glasses. SYNCH is a wholly owned subsidiary of defence heavyweight Elbit Systems, a major supplier of land equipment and unmanned aerial vehicles to the Israeli military, so this is a foot in the door of the defence and frontline communications market.



The one-year framework kicks off with a paid US$250,000 proof-of-concept involving 10 field-operational units and if the trial goes well, SYNCH can place orders worth up to US$10 million over the following year. Cogenic’s tech is targeting the “overloaded operator”, frontline personnel juggling a radio, tablet, body camera and data terminal while struggling to keep their eyes on the action. Its lightweight wearable packs a heads-up display, two-way comms and body-worn video into one package. The clever bit is the proprietary laser beam-scanning and MEMS technology, which delivers a display readable in direct sunlight without draining the battery, keeping information in front of your eyes and hands free for soldiers, police, and emergency crews alike. Cogenic already earns a five per cent royalty through its master licence agreement with Amalgamated Vision on retinal display technology supplied to programs with the US Air Force and NASA; however, the SYNCH deal is direct hardware sales, a step from collecting royalties to supplying its own kit at scale. The end customer is staying under wraps for commercial reasons, but applications stretch across homeland security, law enforcement, medical first response and military operations.



Cogenic reckons it can build the first 10 trial units within 12 weeks of receiving final specs, and ramp to as many as 1,000 units every 10 days at full capacity if orders flow. Management puts an illustrative addressable market at around US$42 billion, though turning a slice of that into revenue depends on successful trials and further orders. The market liked what it saw, sending shares up as much as 315 per cent on the week, a price not seen since 2022. The trial still has to deliver, but for now Energy Technologies has shareholders looking through rose-coloured glasses. RAS TECHNOLOGY HOLDINGS (ASX: RTH) Up 133% (0.6c – 1.2c) Snagging silver on the week was global racing and wagering leader RAS Technology Holdings, after it inked a binding scheme implementation deed to be acquired for $1.04 in cash by UK-based The Press Association Limited.



The operator and data provider Racing and Sports has agreed to a $49.8 million cash takeover by UK-based The Press Association, a subsidiary of PA Media Group. The Press Association proposes to acquire every issued RAS share under a binding scheme implementation deed, with completion expected in February 2027. The proposed acquisition offers shareholders $1.04 per share, or a valuation of nearly $50 million, representing a 93 per cent premium to the company’s trading price. RAS co-founders Gary Crispe and Robert Vilkaitis, who together hold or control approximately 34 per cent of the company, have confirmed their intention to support the deal subject to the same qualifications applying to the board. It also fits neatly with what RAS does best. The operator of Racing and Sports provides racing data and wagering technology. The Press Association brings more than forty years of racing heritage and a long record of working with rights holders to promote the sport.



The two businesses’ strengths and global reach are complementary, so customers get a wider range of data, deeper wagering knowledge and coverage across more of the markets each operates in. The Press Association’s racing heritage spans more than forty years, with a long-standing history of working closely with rights holders to promote horse racing. With the Cox Plate heading to Flemington for the first time in its more than 100-year history, there’s no shortage of high-stakes action on and off the track this week. And while the thoroughbreds battle for racing’s big prize, the ASX has a little fight left in it for backing winners and taking a Blind Raise on the next big thing. Tambourah Metals’ Bryah basin gold project north of Meekatharra in Western Australia. TAMBOURAH METALS LTD (ASX: TMB)



Up 81% (3.1c – 5.6c) Taking out the final place on the podium was plucky junior goldie Tambourah Metals, after a fresh round of assays from its Bryah gold projects in WA returned spectacular high-grade hits at the Baxters South prospect. Drilling at Baxters South returned 4m at 41.7g/t gold from 55m in the weathered zone, including a jaw-dropping 1m at 146.5g/t. Then came the sting, with a promising primary discovery in fresh rock of 3m at 35.5g/t from 169m - seemingly directly below the shallower hit. Shallow gold is nice, but gold in fresh rock makes an explorer’s ears prick up, hinting the system goes deeper. Nobody knows yet which way it’s pointing, but that’s the kind of problem explorers love. For a company built around gold exploration, it’s the right kind of surprise. Baxters South sits within the 467 square kilometre Bryah project in WA’s Murchison region, about 160km north of Meekatharra and handy to the Harmony gold deposit.



Beatty Park South, the flagship that previously produced 6m at 25.8g/t, including 1m at 126g/t, was the quieter sibling this time, and the company’s East Pilbara project near Marble Bar covers the historical Tambourah goldfield. Meanwhile, Tambourah is in the middle of a $2.2 million non-renounceable entitlement offer at 3.5c, with a free 6c option for every two new shares subscribed. Convenient timing, then. A great week for the share price and an even better one for a company that’s currently passing the hat around. And with the 250,000-ounce Harmony only 4.3km up the road, the market can be forgiven for dreaming. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.content:
Updated SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby From ‘brushed’ to bolter: The rollercoaster ride of Teddy Wilson’s Wallabies call-up Iain Payten Updated October 23, 2026 — 5:33pm ,first published 2:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Twenty-seven years after his old man helped Australia win its last Rugby World Cup – and 12 days after he feared he’d fallen entirely out of favour with Les Kiss – rising Waratahs halfback Teddy Wilson has been named in his first Wallabies squad. Wilson, the son of former Wallabies flanker David Wilson, was included in a 33-man squad named by Kiss ahead of the Wallabies’ four-Test spring tour. Teddy Wilson posing at Easts’ home ground in Sydney after being named in the Wallabies spring tour squad. Sitthixay Ditthavong The 24-year-old halfback and loosehead prop Tom Lambert were the only two uncapped players in a squad update otherwise dominated by the return of some important cavalry who missed the recent Bledisloe Cup series losses via injury, suspension or overseas club duty. Wilson’s inclusion comes after years of being touted as a future Wallaby, following strong junior careers in both rugby and league, captaincy of the Junior Wallabies in 2023 and a Super Rugby debut at age 20.



But the pugnacious halfback, who has also since played for Australia A and the Aussie sevens side, was left crestfallen on Sunday last week when players were informed of their selections for the Australia A tour of the USA. Wilson had enjoyed strong Super Rugby and Super Rugby AUS seasons, and his dominant form helped Easts win a Shute Shield as well. He’d even been placed on standby to travel to Argentina last month as injury cover for the Wallabies. But after missing Wallabies squad selection for the Bledisloe series, Wilson did not get a call with news of selection in the Australia A squad either. The gutted halfback turned up at Waratahs training on Monday worried about his future, only to eventually learn the omission was, in fact, good news. Wilson would be going on the spring tour with the Wallabies instead. “Les [Kiss] called me while I was running on a Monday morning at the Tahs, and it was a great moment. It was very special and something I’ll remember for a long time,” Wilson recalled on Friday. “It’s a very special feeling. It’s a special moment for myself and my family. Growing up this is definitely the team that you want to play for and aspire to get into, so it’s special.”



Teddy Wilson on his way to the try line for the Waratahs against the Crusaders. Getty Images After a lengthy wait to make a squad, Wilson may even find himself in the mix for a quickfire Test debut in November, in which the Wallabies will play England, Scotland and Wales, and a yet-to-be-determined Six Nations rival in the Nation Championship finals on the last weekend. Tate McDermott has been named in the Wallabies squad as one of three halfbacks, but he is on standby to return to Australia to be with his wife at the birth of their first child. Kalani Thomas, who made his Test debut last weekend in Sydney, has filled the role of third halfback behind Ryan Lonergan and McDermott this year. But the Reds No.9 is on tour is with Australia A, and will join the spring tour if required. David Wilson (left) holding the William Webb Ellis trophy after winning the 1999 Rugby World Cup. Getty Images



Many kids grow up dreaming of pulling on a Wallabies jersey, but most don’t have the added impetus of a few game-worn gold jerseys hanging up in the family home. David Wilson played 79 Tests for the Wallabies between 1992 and 2000, and even captained the side. Wilson said he was motivated to make his dad and mum Nicole proud, but said his father never put pressure on himself or brother Harry, who is a former Waratahs centre now in the Australian sevens squad. “He’s been there and done that obviously,” Wilson said. “He definitely tells me a few things and helps me a lot. He doesn’t put pressure on myself. He just lets me play my game. “The biggest [advice] is just working hard. He’s always been that type of player when he was playing. Wilson has been in dominant form in NSW rugby this year. Sitthixay Ditthavong



“He was a flanker, he was a hard worker, training hard, if he knew we were slacking off when I was younger, he’d get us down to the oval, do some extras.” Related Article Australian rugby ‘Cheat code’: Wilson cleared to play in Shute Shield decider after Wallabies standby call Lambert’s inclusion came at the expense of Reds prop Aidan Ross, who has been left out just a few days after starting at loosehead in the Wallabies’ loss to the All Blacks at the weekend. Lambert is currently on tour with Australia A and will play against a USA XV in Nashville on Sunday morning. He and lock Miles Amatosero will both join the Wallabies in London. Star five-eighth Carter Gordon has been named after overcoming a broken leg, suffered in Argentina, and he’ll join a No.10 stable including Declan Meredith and Ben Donaldson, who is fit again after missing the Sydney Bledisloe with a groin injury.



Key midfielders Len Ikitau [concussion] and Hunter Paisami [suspension] have both been named, and overseas-based stars Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper have returned to the squad, after missing the two clashes with New Zealand given, there is no player release mandate covering October. Nick Champion De Crespigny and Jock Campbell were also left out.

World.title: ‘I served this state’: Former police officer indignant after jury convicts him of murder over $2000
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts ‘I served this state’: Former police officer indignant after jury convicts him of murder over $2000 Tara Cosoleto and and Erin Pearson October 23, 2026 — 5:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A former police officer declared he had “served the state” and its people as he was found guilty of a cold case murder in the state’s south-west. Steven Frederick Johnson, 74, was the landlord of missing Warrnambool man Christopher Jarvis when the father vanished from his home in June 2006. Steven Johnson outside court at a hearing in October last year. AAPIMAGE The Warrnambool Supreme Court heard Jarvis’ burnt-out car was found at a popular seaside lookout in the regional town, but his body had never been located. Police believe he was dumped in a shallow grave in the Framlingham Forest shortly after he was killed over a dispute about $2000 in unpaid rent.



Johnson had pleaded not guilty, arguing another man was responsible for Jarvis’ death. After a jury returned a guilty verdict late on Friday, Johnson’s bail was revoked. Christopher Jarvis was last seen alive in June 2006. His car was found on fire near the Warrnambool coast. Family members sitting in the public gallery burst into sobs while other shook hands after the verdict was delivered. When asked to state his name, age and occupation, Johnson stood before Justice Andrew Tinney and said: “I was a police officer for 15 years. I served this state, I served the people,” before staff intervened.



He appeared to try to speak to the victim’s distraught family seated nearby. Three of them were heard yelling back “do not speak to me” as security guards moved between the two groups. One woman thanked Tinney before they were all ushered out. Christopher Jarvis’ stepdaughter Nicole Raitt and son Cale Jarvis outside the Supreme Court at an earlier hearing. Joe Armao After serving in the police force, Johnson ran a tip at Wangoom. The jury was told Jarvis was attacked in his driveway by Johnson and another man as he tried to leave for work on June 13, 2006.



Johnson struck Jarvis to the back of the head with a starter pistol, held him down on the ground while he yelled for help, and then shot him in the ear, the court heard. Jarvis was bleeding from the head when Johnson and the other man dragged him into the boot of his car and drove to the remote forest. The court heard Johnson then grabbed a baseball bat from the car and struck Jarvis with force, killing him. He and the other man then dug a shallow grave and buried Jarvis before leaving the scene.



The two men dumped Jarvis’s car at Thunder Point in Warrnambool and set fire to the vehicle, the jury was told. Johnson and his tenant had been fighting over $2210 in rent Jarvis allegedly owed, senior Crown prosecutor Mark Gibson, KC, said. Johnson had filed for Jarvis to vacate the Wangoom property and pay the outstanding funds, with a court hearing listed for the day after the alleged murder. Christopher Jarvis went missing in 2006. His body has not been found. Gibson argued the dispute was Johnson’s motive to kill Jarvis.



“It’s no coincidence that Chris Jarvis went missing the day before that court case,” he said in his closing address. “Johnson knew he had a fight on his hands.” Defence barrister Patrick Doyle had argued his client had been happy for the court to sort out the dispute. Doyle instead argued it was Johnson’s co-accused who was responsible for Jarvis’ death. The man, who cannot be identified, gave evidence in the trial but repeatedly lied about Johnson’s involvement in the killing, Doyle said.



“All you have to go on is the word of a man who is a practised liar with an overwhelming incentive to stick to his story ... to get him off a murder charge,” he said. Johnson, who was charged in March 2025, was remanded in custody before a pre-sentence hearing on December 14. NationalQueenslandAnimal attacks Council withdraws destruction order for dogs involved in Chermside attack Dominique Tassell October 23, 2026 — 5:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The destruction order for two dogs involved in the mauling of a real estate agent in Brisbane’s north were withdrawn earlier this week, and a new dangerous dog declaration under state laws proposed. Ajay Malik, 37, suffered serious injuries to his arms, legs and face about 6pm on October 16 when he was set upon by two bulldog-crosses during a run through Chermside’s 7th Brigade Park. Louise and Ruby, who mauled a man at 7th Brigade Park in Chermside on Friday night. Nine News Brisbane City Council announced late on Friday afternoon that a destruction order was no longer in place. The dogs were seized following the attack and remain at a council animal facility, but the destruction orders issued on Saturday were withdrawn on Wednesday.



It instead now proposed to declare both dogs dangerous under state laws, and owner Layla Evans has until November 4 to respond. Council can still decide to issue new destruction orders, which Evans would then have another 14 days to respond to. Layla Evans is arrested after her two dogs mauled a man at 7th Brigade Park in Chermside on October 16, 2026. Nine News Evans was arrested on unrelated charges on Saturday and held in the Brisbane Watchhouse for several days. Before she was arrested on Saturday, she told Nine News the dogs were protective of her but had never been aggressive, and had escaped from the tent she lived in. The dangerous dog declaration would come with stronger penalties if violated, and could incur penalties of up to $120,890 or two years’ imprisonment. Previously, the local laws came with a maximum fine of $51,810.



Under the state laws, the dogs would have to be implanted with microchips, wear identifying collars, be muzzled if away from their registered address and be kept in an enclosure at that address. Both dogs are registered to a Wavell Heights address. Real estate agent Ajay Malik pictured in hospital after he was attacked by two dogs while jogging in Chermside, in Brisbane’s north. Councillor Sarah Hutton said the park attack was horrific and the seriousness of it demanded the strongest possible response. “We know people want swift action and so do we, but we must follow the State Government’s strict legal processes,” she said.



“We’re also working closely with Queensland Police and the progress of our enforcement action will depend on their ongoing investigations. “We will use every power available to us to protect residents and hold irresponsible dog owners to account.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mental health is often forgotten until violence shatters the peace
World.content:
NationalMental health Editorial Mental health is often forgotten until violence shatters the peace The Herald's View Editorial October 23, 2026 — 5:16pm

October 23, 2026 — 5:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Before politics, Helen Haines spent decades working around hospitals in her federal seat of Indi and captured the local mental health crisis with her trademark gentle decency that a few years later echoes with bittersweet poignancy. “Everywhere I travel in Indi, people talk to me about mental health. About the challenges they face in getting help for themselves or their loved ones when facing mental ill-health, and about the impact it has on them and their communities,” she said. “I’ve spent 35 years working in the hospitals of North East Victoria. I know what it looks like when we fail to properly fund our mental health services.” The federal member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines. Marija Ercegovac On Monday, Haines was allegedly attacked by a man driving a Toyota Landcruiser while unpacking her car outside her Wangaratta electorate office. She lost both legs and remains in a Melbourne hospital. No clear motive for the attack has emerged. Brendan Nugent is before the courts.



In the hours afterwards, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced a multi-agency response – involving Victoria Police , the AFP , ASIO and the Joint Counter-Terrorism Team – prompting a Petri dish of paranoia in the media that conflated terrorism, antisemitism and left-wing and right-wing musings and rants. Then, in the days that followed, many MPs revealed the fetid standard of political debate in Australia was behind an increasingly hostile political discourse and surging threats against elected leaders. Senior government and opposition figures moved to reassure anxious colleagues. Security arrangements were reconsidered. Meanwhile, Nugent, the man charged with attacking Haines, reportedly received treatment at psychiatric facilities, including a 20-bed acute adult mental health in-patient facility in Wangaratta, and had lived alone outside town for some 10 years. We don’t know the details of Nugent’s health history. But Wangaratta has echoes of the Bondi Junction tragedy when a homeless Queenslander with a history of mental illness, Joel Cauchi, 40, was shot dead by NSW Police after he rampaged through Westfield shopping centre and stabbed 16 people in April 2024. Six died. A coronial inquest determined that Cauchi, who suffered schizophrenia, was psychotic that day. The thrust of the coroner’s recommendations urged government to do better in housing and caring for the mentally unwell. The Minns government accepted most of the coroner’s recommendations and announced a new health-led response model for mental health emergencies but, admitting its reforms were not enough, baulked on providing short- and long-term accommodation services.



Last week, the Herald reported on a confidential ministerial briefing note that warned $600 million a year would be needed to fix the state’s shortfall of frontline public mental health staff. Police are also concerned that mental illness is increasing within the community, and they are relied upon as primary responders to emotional distress and mental health crises. Related Article Opinion

Haines attack What do Jacqui Lambie, Helen Haines and Queen Victoria have in common? Far too much Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author No one wants to stigmatise those living with mental health problems. But across Australia, there is no escaping the higher risk that comes with a parlous state of our mental health services, lack of support and misplaced priorities. The links between homelessness, isolation and mental health have been an ongoing and worsening issue, yet a crisis seems to be the only time this is openly discussed. The attack on Haines is another reminder that Australia must get serious about mental health. It must be tackled as a matter of urgency – to look after sufferers, and to protect the rest of the community. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.content:
