Argonaut secured roles in $225m of gold raisings as Wiluna shares plunged 22.3%. Brokers pocketed hefty fees and options, while eight of ten Cap Raise Crucible stocks traded below issue price. The capital-raising circus has rolled through another busy fortnight, with gold companies chasing serious money, brokers collecting plum mandates and two small IPOs producing extraordinary rewards for the corporate hounds who got them away. At the top of the broking tree, Argonaut Securities continued its particularly productive run. The Perth broker joined Barrenjoey Markets on Wiluna Mining’s monster $180 million float before teaming up with Canaccord Genuity on Ballard Mining’s $45 million placement, leaving its fingerprints on $225 million of gold-sector fundraising. CommSec appeared on both tickets. Taylor Collison secured Maronan Metals’ $20 million mandate, while Euroz Hartleys joined Canaccord on Torque Metals’ $25 million placement.



Across the Pacific, Baird and Lake Street Capital Markets helped Amaero International raise US$20 million (A$28.7 million), collecting US$1.4 million in underwriting commissions. Further down the food chain, Aesir Corporate, GBA Capital, Veritas Securities, Prenzler Group, Morgans and Ord Minnett joined the action. However, the smaller transactions produced some of the meatiest broker arithmetic, with cash-and-options packages approaching eye-watering percentages of the money raised. The aftermarket told a different story by 10am Perth time on Friday. Just two of the ten stocks examined were trading above their issue prices, while eight were underwater, including one placement still awaiting shareholder approval. A few punters were celebrating spectacular gains. Most discovered that an IPO or discounted placement could become an even bigger bargain once trading began.



Welcome back to the Crucible. Wiluna Mining’s gold operations near the town of Wiluna,940 kilometres northeast of Perth in the northern goldfields region of Western Australia. WILUNA MINING (ASX: WMC) Raised: $180 million

Issue price: 65c

Friday morning price: 50.5c

Return against issue: −22.3% Wiluna Mining supplied the heavyweight transaction, with Barrenjoey and Argonaut sharing joint lead-manager duties on the 7.1-million-ounce gold company’s $180 million return to the ASX.



CommSec joined as co-manager, giving the non-underwritten float a formidable broking line-up. Wiluna’s return offered investors yet another crack at one of Western Australia’s better-known goldfields, with fresh capital providing financial muscle for its next chapter. While the brokers had plenty to celebrate, Wiluna’s new shareholders were calling for the nurse. The stock closed its first session at 56 cents, a bruising 13.8 per cent below its 65-cent IPO price, before sliding to 50.5 cents in Friday morning trading. That left the company’s hard-bitten thrill seekers in intensive care, cradling a painful 22.3 per cent paper loss barely out of the starting blocks.



Wiluna strikes again! That’s an uncomfortable contrast against $8.5 million in budgeted joint lead-manager fees, including third-party advisers, and 5.24 million three-year broker options exercisable at 84.5 cents. The options may be well out of the money, but the cash-fee budget makes uncomfortably short reading alongside the much longer list of injured punters. BALLARD MINING (ASX: BM1) Raised: $45 million

Issue price: 66c

Discount: 7.7%

Friday morning price: 60.5c

Return against issue: −8.3%



Argonaut backed up its Wiluna assignment by joining Canaccord as joint lead manager and bookrunner on Ballard Mining’s $45 million placement, with CommSec again co-managing. The trio placed 68.2 million shares at 66 cents, a 7.7 per cent discount to the previous close and a hefty 16.2 per cent haircut to the 10-day volume-weighted average price. The proceeds are slated to advance Ballard’s 1.84-million-ounce Mt Ida gold project in Western Australia, funding studies, early works and infrastructure planning. An accompanying share purchase plan (SPP) targeted another $5 million, with scope for $5 million in oversubscriptions. Ballard estimated its bank balance could reach a tidy $94.1 million if the targeted SPP proceeds jumped into the tin. But while the brokers filled the book, the aftermarket was less accommodating.



By Friday morning, Ballard had slipped to 60.5 cents, leaving applicants with their noses 8.3 per cent below the waterline. Argonaut and Canaccord no doubt celebrated their success. However, the market has yet to see the champagne corks popping. AMAERO INTERNATIONAL (ASX: 3DA) Raised: US$20 million (A$28.7M)

Offer price: US$4.25 per US share, equivalent to 15.22c per ASX CDI

Discount: 1.8%

Friday morning ASX price: 19c

Return against offer: +24.8% Amaero International took its capital-raising ambitions to Wall Street, with Baird leading a US$20 million (A$28.7M) public offering and Lake Street joining as additional bookrunner.



And the American brokers were hardly working for loose change. Underwriting discounts and commissions totalled US$1.4 million, seven per cent of gross proceeds, or about A$2 million at the original exchange rate. The underwriters also secured a 30-day option to purchase another 705,882 offer shares, potentially adding another US$3 million (A$4.3 million) before expenses. That’s an option to buy additional shares, not free broker oppies. Amaero issued 4.71 million US common shares at US$4.25 each, equivalent to 15.22 Australian cents per ASX CDI using a 40-to-one conversion. Up to US$10 million is earmarked for manufacturing equipment, with the balance available for working capital and research.



Unlike Ballard and Wiluna, Amaero’s investors weren’t looking for something stronger than Nurofen or intensive care. The CDIs traded at 19 cents on Friday morning, putting subscribers 24.8 per cent ahead. A healthy underwriting commission and a positive return for investors. Everyone gets a slice of cake. Back home, Canaccord and Euroz joined forces on Torque Metals’ $25 million placement, with Morgans co-managing. The trio placed shares at 19 cents, a 7.3 per cent discount, to fund Torque’s Ritz gold project southeast of Kalgoorlie.



Unfortunately, the shares had slipped to 16.5 cents by Friday morning, leaving gold bugs 13.2 per cent underwater and needing a Bex and a lie-down. Drill rig in action at Maronan Metals’ Cloncurry silver-lead-copper-gold project in northwest Queensland. Taylor Collison, meanwhile, secured the lead-manager chair on Maronan Metals’ $20 million placement at 40 cents, a tight 2.3 per cent discount to the five-day VWAP. Major shareholder Kinterra Capital lifted its holding to 22.99 per cent, with proceeds earmarked for drilling, engineering and permitting at Maronan’s Cloncurry silver-lead-copper-gold project. There is a catch. The placement requires shareholder approval on November 4, making the $20 million a conditional commitment rather than a completed fundraising.



With Maronan trading at 38.5 cents, its proposed issue price sat 3.8 per cent above market, leaving punters twisting in the warm wind of uncertainty. As usual, the most eye-catching broker rewards were tucked away in the smaller floats. Identifai Genetics raised $10 million at 20 cents for its October ASX debut, with Aesir Corporate as lead manager. Aesir secured a six per cent cash fee worth $600,000, plus 10,154,970 April 2029 options exercisable at 25 cents, valued in the prospectus at a staggering $899,000. Yep, you read it right!



Combined, the cash commission and estimated option value approached $1.5 million, roughly 15 per cent of IPO proceeds—hats off to the Aesir corporate department for bagging that one. Not all cash, of course. The options’ ultimate value depends on the share price, but it was still a mighty sweet package. And the punters were celebrating too. At 10am Friday, Identifai traded at 49 cents, putting subscribers an astonishing 145 per cent ahead on their 20-cent bets; that’s some serious aftermarket fireworks. Grab a calculator and do the maths on Aesir’s take, with the shares trading significantly — and I mean significantly — above Aesir’s option exercise price. If you thought Aesir set a new benchmark for broker fees, Europa Metals demonstrated how a smaller float could produce even bigger percentages.



Europa joined the ASX on October 16 after raising $4 million at 20 cents, with GBA Capital as lead manager. GBA collected a six per cent cash fee worth $240,000 and five million broker options exercisable at 30 cents and expiring in October 2028, valued in the prospectus at around $561,000. Together, the cash fee and estimated option value reached $801,000, equivalent to 20 per cent of IPO proceeds. Get me the manager! Again, option valuations are not cash in the bank. Europa traded at 19.5 cents on Friday morning, leaving subscribers 2.5 per cent underwater and GBA’s options out of the money.



One float delivered a 145 per cent investor gain, while the other slipped below issue price. Yet both brokers secured eye-watering packages. The Crucible wonders whether this might become the new norm? Cooper Metals Colet copper-gold project on Negros Island in the Philippines. Veritas and Prenzler shared joint lead-manager duties on Cooper Metals’ $2.15 million placement, collecting a six per cent fee and four million broker options. Veritas also fully underwrote the $2.7 million entitlement issue for another six per cent, six million options and six million facilitation shares worth $450,000 at the 7.5-cent issue price.



All up, that’s more than $290,000 in cash fees and $450,000 in facilitation-share value, plus 10 million broker options exercisable at 15 cents over three years. The facilitation shares carry 12 months’ escrow and the securities packages require shareholder approval. That’s a cash-and-share remuneration package valued at about $741,000 using the issue price, before putting a value on the options — a staggering potential payday for arranging a raising worth less than $5 million. Let’s see if it gets waived through. The money will support Cooper’s Philippine Colet copper-gold project, although its 7.2-cent Friday morning price left placees four per cent underwater. Not every company needed a conventional brokered book.



Azzuro Resources secured $3.06 million through a strategic placement to Hong Kong-based Kerry Resources Logistics at 1.5 cents per CDI, a seven per cent premium to the previous close. Not a fee in sight. Kerry is expected to emerge holding about 19.9 per cent, with a potential board nomination. But Azzuro’s 1.4-cent Friday price left the investment 6.7 per cent worse off. Recharge Metals took the conventional route, with Canaccord and Ord Minnett jointly managing a $4.13 million placement at 3.6 cents, carrying broker fees of up to five per cent. The issue price represented a 2.5 per cent discount to the pre-halt 10-day VWAP, with funds supporting the Sunset Well gold and Brandy Hill South copper-tungsten projects.



Recharge traded at 3.2 cents on Friday morning, leaving thrill seekers 11.1 per cent in the red. And that neatly captured the fortnight. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Why these HSC students were grinning about a 2000-year-old public notice
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC Why these HSC students were grinning about a 2000-year-old public notice Emily Kowal October 23, 2026 — 5:43pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What does a 2000-year-old public notice banning the dumping of human faeces near water fountains reveal about political life in Pompeii and Herculaneum? It’s the four-mark question that had Parramatta Marist high school student Daniel Barletta grinning on Friday as he tackled his ancient history HSC exam. “There’s something comedic about people dumping waste in the street ... how they are declaring that you must stop doing this because it’s such a problem,” the 18-year-old said. “It brings a smile to your face.” Parramatta Marist College ancient history HSC students Daniel Barletta, Lachlan Doan-Vance, Marcus Khadi, Mark Ghostine and Christopher Nehme after the exam. Wolter Peeters Over three hours, 7755 students tackled short-answer questions about Pompeii and Herculaneum, as well as three other in-depth topics of choice. At Parramatta Marist, students studied Sparta, Hatshepsut of Egypt, and New Kingdom Egypt to the Death of Thutmose IV. The students said a string of coincidences left them in good shape.



At the end of year 11, the class visited a Pompeii exhibition in Canberra. As they stared at the plaster casts of the voids left by victims killed in the 79AD eruption of Mt Vesuvius, they had no idea that, almost a year later, the exhibition would feature in their HSC exam. “It was pretty neat, it goes full circle,” student Lachlan Doan-Vance said. The exam question: Should the display of human remains from Pompeii and Herculaneum be stopped? It referenced an article written about the Canberra exhibition. Doan-Vance said it helped to have seen the exhibition in person. Related Article HSC Teachers are meant to avoid controversy. In this HSC subject, it’s the main event “I talked about the source and how while it does still show the horrific remains, [the museum] partially obscured them,” he said. “It brought to this greater idea of while there is an inherent human dignity to each of the victims of Pompeii, there’s also value in their study, in that they should be preserved.” Barletta agreed: “Witnessing firsthand how they display [remains] with the warnings on the walls, and putting them in a separate area because it can be disturbing to some to see ... ethically we have come a long way.”



Ancient-history teacher Grace Harley described the exam as very fair and was excited about the Canberra coincidence. “It’s such an interesting subject, but a hard subject. I love it,” she said. She pitches ancient history as a “puzzle with less of the pieces”. “With modern [history] you have all the pieces – more than you want and that can be overwhelming – whereas with ancient, a lot of it comes from interpretation and analysis,” Harley said. “Where does the source come from? Why are there gaps in the sources? That can be really fun for kids to fill the blanks in.” Asked why they enjoyed studying ancient history, the students pointed to their teacher, Harley.



“Whenever we had a substitute [teacher], it never felt the same. We didn’t have that charismatic character in the room teaching us,” Barletta said. The HSC continues until November 5. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ASX Runners of the Week: Energy Technologies, RAS Tech & Tambourah
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears ASX Runners of the Week: Energy Technologies, RAS Tech & Tambourah Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd October 23, 2026 — 5:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Most weeks open with a flicker of hope right now. Not because markets are suddenly looking rosy, but because fear has become the dominant trade. The unending Middle East conflict has punters too rattled to hold stocks over the weekend, preferring to sell on Friday and buy back on Monday rather than cop another gut-punch from the world news in between. In much the same fashion, Wall Street fired up to start the week, with better-than-expected results from SpaceX giving the AI trade another sugar hit. Revenue surged 161 per cent to US$14.6 billion, with a US$4.4 billion profit comfortably beating expectations and helping chip stocks and technology names lead the early charge. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Energy Technologies. That was about where the good news ended. The Middle East, oil prices, inflation, interest rates and the looming US midterm elections became too much to ignore, combining to build a wall of worry that even the AI bulls are struggling to climb. Houthi attacks on Saudi targets sent crude surging above US$113 a barrel, reviving fears that another energy shock could reignite inflation just as markets are hoping for interest-rate relief.



Then came the AI sell-down. Early-week optimism evaporated as the Nasdaq surrendered more than 2.5 per cent, with investors suddenly looking less enamoured with the eye-watering cost of the AI arms race. Meta beat earnings expectations but still took a beating as investors baulked at its enormous AI spending bill. The question is no longer whether AI will transform the world, but whether the mountains of future debt will serve the greater good. A fresh wave of AI incidents marred the powerful technology this week in what is being called “Black October”, after China-aligned hackers used AI agents to target hundreds of organisations worldwide, in some cases gaining privileged access to cloud infrastructure. Meanwhile, critical flaws in the language behind millions of websites have triggered a global scramble to patch up the internet and exploit attempts have surged into the millions after the vulnerabilities became public. And with the UK now urging households to stockpile three days’ worth of food and water in case of emergency, the prospect of digital disruptions is spilling into the real world. Across the channel, the political tinderbox is looking even more primed to blow.



France endured a week of “student” rioting, looting and arson that left thousands of businesses devastated and historic landmarks in ruins . With estimates of a million in protesters littering the streets and billions of dollars in damages across France, the damage bill continues to soar. Before the dust could settle, the unrest spilled across the border into Italy. The historically left-leaning citizens of Milan clearly weren’t about to let Paris hog the protest spotlight, with demonstrations of their own turning violent as hooded protesters clashed with police. The financial fallout is just as ugly. France’s 10-year government bond yield surged above 5 per cent, while the gap between French and German 10-year borrowing costs ballooned to nearly 1.8 percentage points — leaving France paying more than 50 per cent above Germany’s yield. That is the widest spread since the 2011 Eurozone debt crisis, as investors demand a much fatter return to lend to a country increasingly beset by fiscal strain, political paralysis and civil unrest. The problem is that France’s already enormous debt pile is becoming even more expensive to service, leaving less room to manoeuvre and making another Eurozone debt crisis look harder to dismiss. France spends around 30 per cent of GDP on social programs and carries one of Europe’s heaviest tax burdens.



Taxing your people into oblivion, pile on the govt spending and cripple small businesses. Sound familiar? Welcome to Albo’s Australia, where the looming capital-gains tax changes are already crippling investment and the ASX Emerging Companies index (XEC). The XEC has puked its guts out this week, losing more than five per cent in five days and down some 15 per cent over the last month. Australia’s AI industry and its supportive cheer squad have also been wetting the bed following Firmus’ spectacular failure to launch. The proposed $44 billion valuation behind the data-centre hopeful’s planned float proved too much for public markets to swallow, as its Aussie compatriot NEXTDC was next in the firing line this week. The data-centre giant shed 42 per cent on Wednesday, wiping roughly $3 billion from its worth after delays to electricity network upgrades at its West Footscray site forced it to slash forecasts and put new developments on ice. With small caps taking another hiding, this week’s Runners list is predictably a short affair. Top spot went once again to an Israeli technology angle, with Aussie tech hopeful inking a deal with Israeli heavyweight SYNCH that could pave the way for up to US$10 million in purchase orders for its next-generation smart glasses.



Energy Technologies’ Cogenic subsidiary is targeting frontline personnel with its next-generation laser smart glasses. ENERGY TECHNOLOGIES LTD (ASX: EGY) Up 315% (2c – 8.3c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is smart-wearable player Energy Technologies, after its wholly owned Cogenic subsidiary signed a binding heads of agreement with Israeli tech outfit SYNCH, opening the door to a potential US$10 million (A$14.25 million) order for its next-generation smart glasses. SYNCH is a wholly owned subsidiary of defence heavyweight Elbit Systems, a major supplier of land equipment and unmanned aerial vehicles to the Israeli military, so this is a foot in the door of the defence and frontline communications market.



The one-year framework kicks off with a paid US$250,000 proof-of-concept involving 10 field-operational units and if the trial goes well, SYNCH can place orders worth up to US$10 million over the following year. Cogenic’s tech is targeting the “overloaded operator”, frontline personnel juggling a radio, tablet, body camera and data terminal while struggling to keep their eyes on the action. Its lightweight wearable packs a heads-up display, two-way comms and body-worn video into one package. The clever bit is the proprietary laser beam-scanning and MEMS technology, which delivers a display readable in direct sunlight without draining the battery, keeping information in front of your eyes and hands free for soldiers, police, and emergency crews alike. Cogenic already earns a five per cent royalty through its master licence agreement with Amalgamated Vision on retinal display technology supplied to programs with the US Air Force and NASA; however, the SYNCH deal is direct hardware sales, a step from collecting royalties to supplying its own kit at scale. The end customer is staying under wraps for commercial reasons, but applications stretch across homeland security, law enforcement, medical first response and military operations.



Cogenic reckons it can build the first 10 trial units within 12 weeks of receiving final specs, and ramp to as many as 1,000 units every 10 days at full capacity if orders flow. Management puts an illustrative addressable market at around US$42 billion, though turning a slice of that into revenue depends on successful trials and further orders. The market liked what it saw, sending shares up as much as 315 per cent on the week, a price not seen since 2022. The trial still has to deliver, but for now Energy Technologies has shareholders looking through rose-coloured glasses. RAS TECHNOLOGY HOLDINGS (ASX: RTH) Up 133% (0.6c – 1.2c) Snagging silver on the week was global racing and wagering leader RAS Technology Holdings, after it inked a binding scheme implementation deed to be acquired for $1.04 in cash by UK-based The Press Association Limited.



The operator and data provider Racing and Sports has agreed to a $49.8 million cash takeover by UK-based The Press Association, a subsidiary of PA Media Group. The Press Association proposes to acquire every issued RAS share under a binding scheme implementation deed, with completion expected in February 2027. The proposed acquisition offers shareholders $1.04 per share, or a valuation of nearly $50 million, representing a 93 per cent premium to the company’s trading price. RAS co-founders Gary Crispe and Robert Vilkaitis, who together hold or control approximately 34 per cent of the company, have confirmed their intention to support the deal subject to the same qualifications applying to the board. It also fits neatly with what RAS does best. The operator of Racing and Sports provides racing data and wagering technology. The Press Association brings more than forty years of racing heritage and a long record of working with rights holders to promote the sport.



The two businesses’ strengths and global reach are complementary, so customers get a wider range of data, deeper wagering knowledge and coverage across more of the markets each operates in. The Press Association’s racing heritage spans more than forty years, with a long-standing history of working closely with rights holders to promote horse racing. With the Cox Plate heading to Flemington for the first time in its more than 100-year history, there’s no shortage of high-stakes action on and off the track this week. And while the thoroughbreds battle for racing’s big prize, the ASX has a little fight left in it for backing winners and taking a Blind Raise on the next big thing. Tambourah Metals’ Bryah basin gold project north of Meekatharra in Western Australia. TAMBOURAH METALS LTD (ASX: TMB)



Up 81% (3.1c – 5.6c) Taking out the final place on the podium was plucky junior goldie Tambourah Metals, after a fresh round of assays from its Bryah gold projects in WA returned spectacular high-grade hits at the Baxters South prospect. Drilling at Baxters South returned 4m at 41.7g/t gold from 55m in the weathered zone, including a jaw-dropping 1m at 146.5g/t. Then came the sting, with a promising primary discovery in fresh rock of 3m at 35.5g/t from 169m - seemingly directly below the shallower hit. Shallow gold is nice, but gold in fresh rock makes an explorer’s ears prick up, hinting the system goes deeper. Nobody knows yet which way it’s pointing, but that’s the kind of problem explorers love. For a company built around gold exploration, it’s the right kind of surprise. Baxters South sits within the 467 square kilometre Bryah project in WA’s Murchison region, about 160km north of Meekatharra and handy to the Harmony gold deposit.



Beatty Park South, the flagship that previously produced 6m at 25.8g/t, including 1m at 126g/t, was the quieter sibling this time, and the company’s East Pilbara project near Marble Bar covers the historical Tambourah goldfield. Meanwhile, Tambourah is in the middle of a $2.2 million non-renounceable entitlement offer at 3.5c, with a free 6c option for every two new shares subscribed. Convenient timing, then. A great week for the share price and an even better one for a company that’s currently passing the hat around. And with the 250,000-ounce Harmony only 4.3km up the road, the market can be forgiven for dreaming. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: From ‘brushed’ to bolter: The rollercoaster ride of Teddy Wilson’s Wallabies call-up
World.content:
Updated SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby From ‘brushed’ to bolter: The rollercoaster ride of Teddy Wilson’s Wallabies call-up Iain Payten Updated October 23, 2026 — 5:33pm ,first published 2:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Twenty-seven years after his old man helped Australia win its last Rugby World Cup – and 12 days after he feared he’d fallen entirely out of favour with Les Kiss – rising Waratahs halfback Teddy Wilson has been named in his first Wallabies squad. Wilson, the son of former Wallabies flanker David Wilson, was included in a 33-man squad named by Kiss ahead of the Wallabies’ four-Test spring tour. Teddy Wilson posing at Easts’ home ground in Sydney after being named in the Wallabies spring tour squad. Sitthixay Ditthavong The 24-year-old halfback and loosehead prop Tom Lambert were the only two uncapped players in a squad update otherwise dominated by the return of some important cavalry who missed the recent Bledisloe Cup series losses via injury, suspension or overseas club duty. Wilson’s inclusion comes after years of being touted as a future Wallaby, following strong junior careers in both rugby and league, captaincy of the Junior Wallabies in 2023 and a Super Rugby debut at age 20.



But the pugnacious halfback, who has also since played for Australia A and the Aussie sevens side, was left crestfallen on Sunday last week when players were informed of their selections for the Australia A tour of the USA. Wilson had enjoyed strong Super Rugby and Super Rugby AUS seasons, and his dominant form helped Easts win a Shute Shield as well. He’d even been placed on standby to travel to Argentina last month as injury cover for the Wallabies. But after missing Wallabies squad selection for the Bledisloe series, Wilson did not get a call with news of selection in the Australia A squad either. The gutted halfback turned up at Waratahs training on Monday worried about his future, only to eventually learn the omission was, in fact, good news. Wilson would be going on the spring tour with the Wallabies instead. “Les [Kiss] called me while I was running on a Monday morning at the Tahs, and it was a great moment. It was very special and something I’ll remember for a long time,” Wilson recalled on Friday. “It’s a very special feeling. It’s a special moment for myself and my family. Growing up this is definitely the team that you want to play for and aspire to get into, so it’s special.”



Teddy Wilson on his way to the try line for the Waratahs against the Crusaders. Getty Images After a lengthy wait to make a squad, Wilson may even find himself in the mix for a quickfire Test debut in November, in which the Wallabies will play England, Scotland and Wales, and a yet-to-be-determined Six Nations rival in the Nation Championship finals on the last weekend. Tate McDermott has been named in the Wallabies squad as one of three halfbacks, but he is on standby to return to Australia to be with his wife at the birth of their first child. Kalani Thomas, who made his Test debut last weekend in Sydney, has filled the role of third halfback behind Ryan Lonergan and McDermott this year. But the Reds No.9 is on tour is with Australia A, and will join the spring tour if required. David Wilson (left) holding the William Webb Ellis trophy after winning the 1999 Rugby World Cup. Getty Images



Many kids grow up dreaming of pulling on a Wallabies jersey, but most don’t have the added impetus of a few game-worn gold jerseys hanging up in the family home. David Wilson played 79 Tests for the Wallabies between 1992 and 2000, and even captained the side. Wilson said he was motivated to make his dad and mum Nicole proud, but said his father never put pressure on himself or brother Harry, who is a former Waratahs centre now in the Australian sevens squad. “He’s been there and done that obviously,” Wilson said. “He definitely tells me a few things and helps me a lot. He doesn’t put pressure on myself. He just lets me play my game. “The biggest [advice] is just working hard. He’s always been that type of player when he was playing. Wilson has been in dominant form in NSW rugby this year. Sitthixay Ditthavong



“He was a flanker, he was a hard worker, training hard, if he knew we were slacking off when I was younger, he’d get us down to the oval, do some extras.” Related Article Australian rugby ‘Cheat code’: Wilson cleared to play in Shute Shield decider after Wallabies standby call Lambert’s inclusion came at the expense of Reds prop Aidan Ross, who has been left out just a few days after starting at loosehead in the Wallabies’ loss to the All Blacks at the weekend. Lambert is currently on tour with Australia A and will play against a USA XV in Nashville on Sunday morning. He and lock Miles Amatosero will both join the Wallabies in London. Star five-eighth Carter Gordon has been named after overcoming a broken leg, suffered in Argentina, and he’ll join a No.10 stable including Declan Meredith and Ben Donaldson, who is fit again after missing the Sydney Bledisloe with a groin injury.



Key midfielders Len Ikitau [concussion] and Hunter Paisami [suspension] have both been named, and overseas-based stars Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper have returned to the squad, after missing the two clashes with New Zealand given, there is no player release mandate covering October. Nick Champion De Crespigny and Jock Campbell were also left out.

World.title: ‘I served this state’: Former police officer indignant after jury convicts him of murder over $2000
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts ‘I served this state’: Former police officer indignant after jury convicts him of murder over $2000 Tara Cosoleto and and Erin Pearson October 23, 2026 — 5:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A former police officer declared he had “served the state” and its people as he was found guilty of a cold case murder in the state’s south-west. Steven Frederick Johnson, 74, was the landlord of missing Warrnambool man Christopher Jarvis when the father vanished from his home in June 2006. Steven Johnson outside court at a hearing in October last year. AAPIMAGE The Warrnambool Supreme Court heard Jarvis’ burnt-out car was found at a popular seaside lookout in the regional town, but his body had never been located. Police believe he was dumped in a shallow grave in the Framlingham Forest shortly after he was killed over a dispute about $2000 in unpaid rent.



Johnson had pleaded not guilty, arguing another man was responsible for Jarvis’ death. After a jury returned a guilty verdict late on Friday, Johnson’s bail was revoked. Christopher Jarvis was last seen alive in June 2006. His car was found on fire near the Warrnambool coast. Family members sitting in the public gallery burst into sobs while other shook hands after the verdict was delivered. When asked to state his name, age and occupation, Johnson stood before Justice Andrew Tinney and said: “I was a police officer for 15 years. I served this state, I served the people,” before staff intervened.



He appeared to try to speak to the victim’s distraught family seated nearby. Three of them were heard yelling back “do not speak to me” as security guards moved between the two groups. One woman thanked Tinney before they were all ushered out. Christopher Jarvis’ stepdaughter Nicole Raitt and son Cale Jarvis outside the Supreme Court at an earlier hearing. Joe Armao After serving in the police force, Johnson ran a tip at Wangoom. The jury was told Jarvis was attacked in his driveway by Johnson and another man as he tried to leave for work on June 13, 2006.



Johnson struck Jarvis to the back of the head with a starter pistol, held him down on the ground while he yelled for help, and then shot him in the ear, the court heard. Jarvis was bleeding from the head when Johnson and the other man dragged him into the boot of his car and drove to the remote forest. The court heard Johnson then grabbed a baseball bat from the car and struck Jarvis with force, killing him. He and the other man then dug a shallow grave and buried Jarvis before leaving the scene.



The two men dumped Jarvis’s car at Thunder Point in Warrnambool and set fire to the vehicle, the jury was told. Johnson and his tenant had been fighting over $2210 in rent Jarvis allegedly owed, senior Crown prosecutor Mark Gibson, KC, said. Johnson had filed for Jarvis to vacate the Wangoom property and pay the outstanding funds, with a court hearing listed for the day after the alleged murder. Christopher Jarvis went missing in 2006. His body has not been found. Gibson argued the dispute was Johnson’s motive to kill Jarvis.



“It’s no coincidence that Chris Jarvis went missing the day before that court case,” he said in his closing address. “Johnson knew he had a fight on his hands.” Defence barrister Patrick Doyle had argued his client had been happy for the court to sort out the dispute. Doyle instead argued it was Johnson’s co-accused who was responsible for Jarvis’ death. The man, who cannot be identified, gave evidence in the trial but repeatedly lied about Johnson’s involvement in the killing, Doyle said.



“All you have to go on is the word of a man who is a practised liar with an overwhelming incentive to stick to his story ... to get him off a murder charge,” he said. Johnson, who was charged in March 2025, was remanded in custody before a pre-sentence hearing on December 14. World.title: Council withdraws destruction order for dogs involved in Chermside attack
World.content:
NationalQueenslandAnimal attacks Council withdraws destruction order for dogs involved in Chermside attack Dominique Tassell October 23, 2026 — 5:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The destruction order for two dogs involved in the mauling of a real estate agent in Brisbane’s north were withdrawn earlier this week, and a new dangerous dog declaration under state laws proposed. Ajay Malik, 37, suffered serious injuries to his arms, legs and face about 6pm on October 16 when he was set upon by two bulldog-crosses during a run through Chermside’s 7th Brigade Park. Louise and Ruby, who mauled a man at 7th Brigade Park in Chermside on Friday night. Nine News Brisbane City Council announced late on Friday afternoon that a destruction order was no longer in place. The dogs were seized following the attack and remain at a council animal facility, but the destruction orders issued on Saturday were withdrawn on Wednesday.



It instead now proposed to declare both dogs dangerous under state laws, and owner Layla Evans has until November 4 to respond. Council can still decide to issue new destruction orders, which Evans would then have another 14 days to respond to. Layla Evans is arrested after her two dogs mauled a man at 7th Brigade Park in Chermside on October 16, 2026. Nine News Evans was arrested on unrelated charges on Saturday and held in the Brisbane Watchhouse for several days. Before she was arrested on Saturday, she told Nine News the dogs were protective of her but had never been aggressive, and had escaped from the tent she lived in. The dangerous dog declaration would come with stronger penalties if violated, and could incur penalties of up to $120,890 or two years’ imprisonment. Previously, the local laws came with a maximum fine of $51,810.



Under the state laws, the dogs would have to be implanted with microchips, wear identifying collars, be muzzled if away from their registered address and be kept in an enclosure at that address. Both dogs are registered to a Wavell Heights address. Real estate agent Ajay Malik pictured in hospital after he was attacked by two dogs while jogging in Chermside, in Brisbane’s north. Councillor Sarah Hutton said the park attack was horrific and the seriousness of it demanded the strongest possible response. “We know people want swift action and so do we, but we must follow the State Government’s strict legal processes,” she said.



“We’re also working closely with Queensland Police and the progress of our enforcement action will depend on their ongoing investigations. “We will use every power available to us to protect residents and hold irresponsible dog owners to account.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Cap Raise Crucible: Gold books, big fees and bruised punters
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Cap Raise Crucible: Gold books, big fees and bruised punters Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 23, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Argonaut secured roles in $225m of gold raisings as Wiluna shares plunged 22.3%. Brokers pocketed hefty fees and options, while eight of ten Cap Raise Crucible stocks traded below issue price. The capital-raising circus has rolled through another busy fortnight, with gold companies chasing serious money, brokers collecting plum mandates and two small IPOs producing extraordinary rewards for the corporate hounds who got them away. At the top of the broking tree, Argonaut Securities continued its particularly productive run. The Perth broker joined Barrenjoey Markets on Wiluna Mining’s monster $180 million float before teaming up with Canaccord Genuity on Ballard Mining’s $45 million placement, leaving its fingerprints on $225 million of gold-sector fundraising. CommSec appeared on both tickets. Taylor Collison secured Maronan Metals’ $20 million mandate, while Euroz Hartleys joined Canaccord on Torque Metals’ $25 million placement.



Across the Pacific, Baird and Lake Street Capital Markets helped Amaero International raise US$20 million (A$28.7 million), collecting US$1.4 million in underwriting commissions. Further down the food chain, Aesir Corporate, GBA Capital, Veritas Securities, Prenzler Group, Morgans and Ord Minnett joined the action. However, the smaller transactions produced some of the meatiest broker arithmetic, with cash-and-options packages approaching eye-watering percentages of the money raised. The aftermarket told a different story by 10am Perth time on Friday. Just two of the ten stocks examined were trading above their issue prices, while eight were underwater, including one placement still awaiting shareholder approval. A few punters were celebrating spectacular gains. Most discovered that an IPO or discounted placement could become an even bigger bargain once trading began.



Welcome back to the Crucible. Wiluna Mining’s gold operations near the town of Wiluna,940 kilometres northeast of Perth in the northern goldfields region of Western Australia. WILUNA MINING (ASX: WMC) Raised: $180 million

Issue price: 65c

Friday morning price: 50.5c

Return against issue: −22.3% Wiluna Mining supplied the heavyweight transaction, with Barrenjoey and Argonaut sharing joint lead-manager duties on the 7.1-million-ounce gold company’s $180 million return to the ASX.



CommSec joined as co-manager, giving the non-underwritten float a formidable broking line-up. Wiluna’s return offered investors yet another crack at one of Western Australia’s better-known goldfields, with fresh capital providing financial muscle for its next chapter. While the brokers had plenty to celebrate, Wiluna’s new shareholders were calling for the nurse. The stock closed its first session at 56 cents, a bruising 13.8 per cent below its 65-cent IPO price, before sliding to 50.5 cents in Friday morning trading. That left the company’s hard-bitten thrill seekers in intensive care, cradling a painful 22.3 per cent paper loss barely out of the starting blocks.



Wiluna strikes again! That’s an uncomfortable contrast against $8.5 million in budgeted joint lead-manager fees, including third-party advisers, and 5.24 million three-year broker options exercisable at 84.5 cents. The options may be well out of the money, but the cash-fee budget makes uncomfortably short reading alongside the much longer list of injured punters. BALLARD MINING (ASX: BM1) Raised: $45 million

Issue price: 66c

Discount: 7.7%

Friday morning price: 60.5c

Return against issue: −8.3%



Argonaut backed up its Wiluna assignment by joining Canaccord as joint lead manager and bookrunner on Ballard Mining’s $45 million placement, with CommSec again co-managing. The trio placed 68.2 million shares at 66 cents, a 7.7 per cent discount to the previous close and a hefty 16.2 per cent haircut to the 10-day volume-weighted average price. The proceeds are slated to advance Ballard’s 1.84-million-ounce Mt Ida gold project in Western Australia, funding studies, early works and infrastructure planning. An accompanying share purchase plan (SPP) targeted another $5 million, with scope for $5 million in oversubscriptions. Ballard estimated its bank balance could reach a tidy $94.1 million if the targeted SPP proceeds jumped into the tin. But while the brokers filled the book, the aftermarket was less accommodating.



By Friday morning, Ballard had slipped to 60.5 cents, leaving applicants with their noses 8.3 per cent below the waterline. Argonaut and Canaccord no doubt celebrated their success. However, the market has yet to see the champagne corks popping. AMAERO INTERNATIONAL (ASX: 3DA) Raised: US$20 million (A$28.7M)

Offer price: US$4.25 per US share, equivalent to 15.22c per ASX CDI

Discount: 1.8%

Friday morning ASX price: 19c

Return against offer: +24.8% Amaero International took its capital-raising ambitions to Wall Street, with Baird leading a US$20 million (A$28.7M) public offering and Lake Street joining as additional bookrunner.



And the American brokers were hardly working for loose change. Underwriting discounts and commissions totalled US$1.4 million, seven per cent of gross proceeds, or about A$2 million at the original exchange rate. The underwriters also secured a 30-day option to purchase another 705,882 offer shares, potentially adding another US$3 million (A$4.3 million) before expenses. That’s an option to buy additional shares, not free broker oppies. Amaero issued 4.71 million US common shares at US$4.25 each, equivalent to 15.22 Australian cents per ASX CDI using a 40-to-one conversion. Up to US$10 million is earmarked for manufacturing equipment, with the balance available for working capital and research.



Unlike Ballard and Wiluna, Amaero’s investors weren’t looking for something stronger than Nurofen or intensive care. The CDIs traded at 19 cents on Friday morning, putting subscribers 24.8 per cent ahead. A healthy underwriting commission and a positive return for investors. Everyone gets a slice of cake. Back home, Canaccord and Euroz joined forces on Torque Metals’ $25 million placement, with Morgans co-managing. The trio placed shares at 19 cents, a 7.3 per cent discount, to fund Torque’s Ritz gold project southeast of Kalgoorlie.



Unfortunately, the shares had slipped to 16.5 cents by Friday morning, leaving gold bugs 13.2 per cent underwater and needing a Bex and a lie-down. Drill rig in action at Maronan Metals’ Cloncurry silver-lead-copper-gold project in northwest Queensland. Taylor Collison, meanwhile, secured the lead-manager chair on Maronan Metals’ $20 million placement at 40 cents, a tight 2.3 per cent discount to the five-day VWAP. Major shareholder Kinterra Capital lifted its holding to 22.99 per cent, with proceeds earmarked for drilling, engineering and permitting at Maronan’s Cloncurry silver-lead-copper-gold project. There is a catch. The placement requires shareholder approval on November 4, making the $20 million a conditional commitment rather than a completed fundraising.



With Maronan trading at 38.5 cents, its proposed issue price sat 3.8 per cent above market, leaving punters twisting in the warm wind of uncertainty. As usual, the most eye-catching broker rewards were tucked away in the smaller floats. Identifai Genetics raised $10 million at 20 cents for its October ASX debut, with Aesir Corporate as lead manager. Aesir secured a six per cent cash fee worth $600,000, plus 10,154,970 April 2029 options exercisable at 25 cents, valued in the prospectus at a staggering $899,000. Yep, you read it right!



Combined, the cash commission and estimated option value approached $1.5 million, roughly 15 per cent of IPO proceeds—hats off to the Aesir corporate department for bagging that one. Not all cash, of course. The options’ ultimate value depends on the share price, but it was still a mighty sweet package. And the punters were celebrating too. At 10am Friday, Identifai traded at 49 cents, putting subscribers an astonishing 145 per cent ahead on their 20-cent bets; that’s some serious aftermarket fireworks. Grab a calculator and do the maths on Aesir’s take, with the shares trading significantly — and I mean significantly — above Aesir’s option exercise price. If you thought Aesir set a new benchmark for broker fees, Europa Metals demonstrated how a smaller float could produce even bigger percentages.



Europa joined the ASX on October 16 after raising $4 million at 20 cents, with GBA Capital as lead manager. GBA collected a six per cent cash fee worth $240,000 and five million broker options exercisable at 30 cents and expiring in October 2028, valued in the prospectus at around $561,000. Together, the cash fee and estimated option value reached $801,000, equivalent to 20 per cent of IPO proceeds. Get me the manager! Again, option valuations are not cash in the bank. Europa traded at 19.5 cents on Friday morning, leaving subscribers 2.5 per cent underwater and GBA’s options out of the money.



One float delivered a 145 per cent investor gain, while the other slipped below issue price. Yet both brokers secured eye-watering packages. The Crucible wonders whether this might become the new norm? Cooper Metals Colet copper-gold project on Negros Island in the Philippines. Veritas and Prenzler shared joint lead-manager duties on Cooper Metals’ $2.15 million placement, collecting a six per cent fee and four million broker options. Veritas also fully underwrote the $2.7 million entitlement issue for another six per cent, six million options and six million facilitation shares worth $450,000 at the 7.5-cent issue price.



All up, that’s more than $290,000 in cash fees and $450,000 in facilitation-share value, plus 10 million broker options exercisable at 15 cents over three years. The facilitation shares carry 12 months’ escrow and the securities packages require shareholder approval. That’s a cash-and-share remuneration package valued at about $741,000 using the issue price, before putting a value on the options — a staggering potential payday for arranging a raising worth less than $5 million. Let’s see if it gets waived through. The money will support Cooper’s Philippine Colet copper-gold project, although its 7.2-cent Friday morning price left placees four per cent underwater. Not every company needed a conventional brokered book.



Azzuro Resources secured $3.06 million through a strategic placement to Hong Kong-based Kerry Resources Logistics at 1.5 cents per CDI, a seven per cent premium to the previous close. Not a fee in sight. Kerry is expected to emerge holding about 19.9 per cent, with a potential board nomination. But Azzuro’s 1.4-cent Friday price left the investment 6.7 per cent worse off. Recharge Metals took the conventional route, with Canaccord and Ord Minnett jointly managing a $4.13 million placement at 3.6 cents, carrying broker fees of up to five per cent. The issue price represented a 2.5 per cent discount to the pre-halt 10-day VWAP, with funds supporting the Sunset Well gold and Brandy Hill South copper-tungsten projects.



Recharge traded at 3.2 cents on Friday morning, leaving thrill seekers 11.1 per cent in the red. And that neatly captured the fortnight. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Big Hits: Rapid Critical Metals, Benz Mining, Encounter Resources Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright October 23, 2026 — 4:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Big Hits looks at standout drill intercepts reported to the ASX this week, with Rapid Critical Metals stealing the show in NSW with a whopping 4m hit grading more than 2000g/t silver. WA explorers Benz Mining and Encounter Resources rounded out the podium with impressive strikes of their own. Let’s dig in. Bulls N’ Bears Big Hits looks at notable drill intercepts reported this week to the ASX. RAPID CRITICAL METALS LTD (ASX: RCM) Project: Webbs silver project, New South Wales

Hit: 4m at 2089g/t silver from 24m downhole Shallow exploration triumphs which immediately break open existing resource boundaries are the lifeblood of junior resource players and this week, Rapid Critical Metals claimed the top step on the podium after turning an ongoing reverse circulation (RC) drilling campaign into a spectacular high-grade silver revelation.



Undertaking a targeted verification program across its highly prospective terrain in northern New South Wales, the company delivered a monumental, multi-kilogram bedrock silver intercept from a remarkably shallow depth. Punched into the northern part of the existing Webbs resource area, the headline RC hole carved through an intensely mineralised zone and returned an exceptional four metres assaying 2089 grams per tonne (g/t) silver - for 2334g/t silver equivalent - from a depth of just 24m downhole. Highlighting the robust grade distribution and absolute metallic tenor operating within the core of this system, the single continuous interval contained an extraordinary higher-grade pocket that peaked with a blistering two-metre assay roaring up to 3950g/t silver – comprising an exceptional 4353g/t silver equivalent - from just 24 metres downhole. The genuine bonanza nature of that discovery was reinforced by an included one-metre chunk assaying 6060g/t silver from 25m - or 6596g/t silver equivalent - the highest silver grade recorded from the company’s drilling to date. What makes this performance globally significant is that the silver mineralisation appears remarkably dense, broad, and continuous beyond the historical limits of the deposit. By successfully demonstrating that the high-grade architecture extends well past the known resource outline at both ends, the result is expected to immediately upgrade geological confidence ahead of a potential inventory expansion.



The commercial and strategic appeal of the project is heavily underscored by its position within the famous Webbs silver district, a premier geological province historically renowned for hosting some of Australia’s highest-grade unmined silver assets. Furthermore, the project benefits from an enviable operational straightaway; recent soil sampling has uncovered a previously unrecognised northwest-trending structure along an estimated untested strike distance of 600 metres. That structure returns the same geochemical strength as the soils sitting directly over the main resource, pointing to an immense exploration runway for future discovery campaigns. With assays pending for several subsequent holes and a four-rig program now being locked down across the project area, the latest breakthrough results represent only the opening shots in a bigger resource growth campaign. The upcoming data will feed directly into updated geological modelling, paving Rapid Critical Metals’ path towards delivering an expanded, high-value mineral resource estimate for the project.



BENZ MINING LTD (ASX: BNZ)

Project: Glenburgh Gold Project, Icon mineralised system, Western Australia

Hit: 46m at 6.5g/t gold from 454m downhole Bulk-tonnage scale combined with high-grade integrity is a rare feat in precious metal exploration; however, runner-up Benz Mining has confidently asserted its presence by revealing a massive gold broadside at its flagship Glenburgh project in Western Australia. Benz’ reverse circulation (RC) drilling targeting extensions of thick gold mineralisation and stacked high-grade lenses has successfully defined a world-class mineralised architecture that continues to grow rapidly. One reverse circulation (RC) hole delivered the headline performance, drilling through a tightly folded structural domain to return a standout 46-metre intercept assaying 6.5g/t gold from a depth of 454m downhole. Reinforcing the camp’s extensive, stacked nature, another hole delivered multiple broad intercepts in a single section, including 42m assaying 3g/t gold from 337m, followed by a lower lens returning 39m at 3.1g/t gold from 388m depth.



Geologically, those results – combined with 12 more long runs ranging between 12m and an astonishing 87m in length - are profoundly significant. The company’s massive 68-hole, 25,776-metre RC drilling campaign has now formally outlined a 100m-to-200m wide mineralised system across the first kilometre of a known three-kilometre-long trend. Remarkably, mineralisation has also been defined to more than 500m vertical depth. Individual lenses within the stacked package average a robust 30m to 50m wide and are enclosed and interconnected by a substantial mineralised halo. With the company’s drilling fleet resources now strategically concentrated on the Icon camp, Benz’ first-pass testing across the remaining two-kilometre trend is nearing completion and the company is set to feed the new data directly into an upcoming maiden resource estimate, slated for completion in the first quarter of 2027. Encounter Resources’ diamond drill core from 32.32 to 32.59m depth showing spectacular copper oxide mineralisation.



ENCOUNTER RESOURCES LTD (ASX: ENR)

Project: Yeneena Copper Project, Parbo System, Western Australia

Hit: 44m at 1.7 per cent copper from 8.1m downhole Western Australia’s Paterson Province continues to solidify its reputation as a premier tier-one mineral hotspot, and Encounter Resources has securely locked down the third place on the Big Hits podium after turning its first drilling campaign at the Tyrell prospect since 2014 into an exceptional high-grade copper revelation. Spearing straight through the highly prospective Broadhurst Formation, the company’s diamond drilling program has successfully validated a major structural corridor while unlocking outstanding near-surface grade potential. The standout diamond drill hole punched through weathered shale and returned a massive downhole width of 44 metres at 1.7 per cent copper from a shallow depth of just 8.1m. Highlighting a potent core within that geological system, that broad interval was anchored by a 12.7-metre bonanza zone at 4.9 per cent copper from 25.75m downhole, generating a copper grade more than double the project’s current average inferred resource grade.



A new structural interpretation has significantly enhanced the commercial profile of Encounter’s 8km-long Parbo system along the McKay Fault, outlining a prominent three-kilometre-long, northeast-trending corridor that bounds the high-grade zones between the Tyrell and Maitland zones and opens a major new search space for copper sulphides down-dip. Encounter is already progressing a comprehensive strategic review of its copper assets alongside rapid sighter metallurgical leach testing of oxide samples from the Parbo copper oxide blankets. With further drilling being planned to aggressively test the Tyrell–Maitland corridor, the latest thick, near-surface copper intercepts will likely provide the definitive technical foundation to expand Encounter’s footprint.
