The new AI model builds on Canva’s big push into AI. In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it. The design tool also brought layers to AI-generated images, which let you make changes to part of an image while leaving the rest untouched.

Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus. The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs. It sits behind OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, GPT-Image-2.5 Flare, and GPT-Image-2.

Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.

Canva Craft is available now to all users globally. You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.

Tech.title: PC shipments dropped over 20 percent in Q3 due to RAM price hikes
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Demand for new PCs took a hit after months of price hikes, with Counterpoint Research reporting global PC shipments fell 21 percent year-over-year in Q3 2026. That’s in line with earlier reports from IDC and Omdia. It’s not just PCs, either — that same quarter, smartphone shipments also hit a 14-year low.

Counterpoint linked the decline in PC shipments to higher component prices. Up until Q2 2026, PC shipments had been growing for over two years straight. But over the last several months, RAM, SSDs, and chips from Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm have all gotten more expensive, leading to price hikes on everything from MacBooks to Raspberry Pis. Counterpoint senior analyst Minsoo Kang noted that some companies are shifting to “prioritize configurations that can better absorb component inflation,” leaving fewer affordable options for price-sensitive buyers. Some companies are even reviving older tech, like DDR4 RAM and 4GB GPUs, to help mitigate price hikes.

Counterpoint also says Q3 2025 included “purchases ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and tariff-related inventory adjustments,” which added to the sharp year-over-year drop this past quarter. The PC market might not bounce back anytime soon, as Counterpoint associate director David Naranjo says, “With global shipments expected to plunge 27% in Q4 2026 and remain broadly flat in 2027, stabilization should not be mistaken for recovery.”

Tech.title: Fall 2026 earnings watch
Tech.content: Every company is suddenly an AI company. Compute is an asset. Cars are flying. We’ve been promised robots — again. It’s time again to dig through earnings reports, listen to investor calls, and call out the latest wins and losses from around the tech sector and what it means for where the companies go next.

Tech.title: Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge — but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, tells Nieman Lab.

Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to give the company permission to train its AI on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts told Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” such as the robots.txt file that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl.

Following fierce backlash from the publishing industry, Meta removed language saying it would “train” its products with scraped content. But the tweaks might not be enough to rule out that possibility. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train,’” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Nieman Lab.

Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free. In a statement to The Verge today, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts reiterated that “content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences,” adding that the update “is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

Tech.title: Meta turns Muse sharing back on
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta has re-enabled Muse sharing after security researchers had reported that public conversation links could be easy to find. The researchers said they had been able to find Muse pages like a marketing company’s internal revenue review and a small business owner’s loan application.

Researchers at Claroc reported earlier this week that Muse the web addresses for shared conversations from Muse were named after a conversation’s title and written into public DNS. Ars Technica said Tuesday that Meta paused the sharing feature after it reached out about what was going on.

In a post today on X, Meta’s David Singleton says that “The underlying issue is now fixed, and sharing is back on.” According to Singleton, the issue was with URLs for shared Muse artifacts, which Meta says are things like documents and images inside Muse, and wasn’t a flaw with chat sharing.

“If you shared an artifact before the fix: it now has a new URL,” Singleton says. “Anyone visiting the old link will see a note asking them to get the new one from you. We know that’s a pain, and we’re sorry for the disruption — but protecting user data has to come first.”

Tech.title: Oura sues rival Ultrahuman again, threatening its U.S. smart ring comeback
Tech.content:
Smart ring maker Oura has sued Indian rival Ultrahuman again, seeking to block U.S. sales of its Ring Pro (pictured above) just months after the redesign helped the Bengaluru-based startup return to the American market following an import ban. The case is the latest in a string of patent disputes Oura has brought against competing smart-ring makers, including Samsung and RingConn.

In a complaint filed Thursday in a federal court in Texas, Oura alleged that Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro infringes two of its patents covering the ring’s design and internal components, including its battery and sensors. Oura is seeking monetary damages and a permanent injunction that would stop Ultrahuman from selling the ring.

Ultrahuman’s redesigned Ring Pro, launched in February, received a favorable ruling from U.S. Customs and Border Protection in March, paving the way for the startup’s return to the U.S. market. The decision followed an import ban on Ultrahuman’s earlier Ring Air, which took effect after Oura secured a patent infringement ruling from the International Trade Commission in August last year.

“Ultrahuman has a history of copying Oura’s innovations, as demonstrated by the 2025 ITC ruling against the company,” an Oura spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “Ultrahuman introduced a redesigned ring but failed to address continued infringement of Oura’s patents, seeking instead to capitalize on our innovation and the market leadership we have built.”

Oura argues that the Customs ruling covered only the patent involved in the earlier dispute, not the two patents cited in its latest lawsuit: D804,471 and 12,769,363. “To protect its patent rights, Oura is now forced to file this complaint of patent infringement,” the company said in its filing.

One of those patents, 12,769,363, is also very new. It was issued to Oura on October 20, just two days before it filed the lawsuit. It covers a smart-ring design incorporating internal components such as a curved battery, circuit board, magnets, and sensors.

Oura has also named Texas-based electronics manufacturer SVTronics as a defendant in the lawsuit. The complaint says SVTronics manufactures the Ring Pro at a facility in Plano, Texas, allegedly under Ultrahuman’s direction and control. It also alleges that both companies infringe Oura’s patents through the manufacture, importation, and sale of the device in the U.S.

Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar told TechCrunch the startup was confident in the Ring Pro and would fight the new allegations.

“Oura has now chosen to assert different patents, including one that issued just two days before this lawsuit was filed,” Kumar said. “We will address these claims through the appropriate legal process and will defend our position vigorously. There is no court order affecting Ring Pro, and it remains available to customers in the U.S.”

Oura and Ultrahuman have been fighting over patents since 2023, when Oura sued the Indian startup over its Ring Air, which had helped Ultrahuman make a name for itself in the U.S. Oura brought a separate case before the U.S. International Trade Commission in 2024 that helped it secure a ruling last year, leading to the import ban on the Ring Air.

Ultrahuman is not the only rival facing legal pressure from Oura. The company has also pursued patent infringement claims against smart-ring makers including Samsung, RingConn, Circular, and Zepp Health. Some of those disputes have ended in licensing agreements, with RingConn and Circular agreeing to pay royalties to Oura to continue selling their products.

The dispute emerges as the smart-ring market continues to grow. Research firm IDC expects global shipments to rise 12.8% this year to 4.9 million units and reach about 6.3 million by 2030. While Oura remains a leading player in the category, Ultrahuman is among the growing competitors.

The lawsuit also comes just weeks after Oura shelved its $2.2 billion IPO, citing “uncertainty” in the market. The company has continued to add features to its smart rings, introducing new fitness metrics earlier this week that help users track how workouts affect their cardiovascular health.

In September, Ultrahuman raised $70 million from investors including Qualcomm Ventures and Labcorp, valuing the startup at about $365 million. The startup is also working with Qualcomm on a new smart ring that could run more software directly on the device, as it looks to expand beyond health and fitness tracking into areas such as AI interactions and gaming.

The article has been updated to include comments from Ultrahuman co-founder and CEO Mohit Kumar.

Tech.title: Uber rival inDrive eyes 2027 robotaxi tests in Central Asia with Pony.ai and Nvidia
Tech.content:
Ride-hailing company inDrive, known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027.

The companies said Friday that they had signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform — a reflection of the growing interest in self-driving technology beyond the U.S. and China.

Testing will begin in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, in the first half of 2027, inDrive CTO Yuri Misnik told TechCrunch. The tests will initially involve a safety operator, with fully driverless rides as the eventual goal.

Under the proposed plan, Pony.ai would provide its Gen-7 robotaxis, which inDrive would offer through its ride-hailing app and operate in Kazakhstan. Nvidia, on the other hand, would supply the AI technology, including its Hyperion platform and Halos safety system.

The move comes as ride-hailing companies expand their push into robotaxis. Earlier this month, Uber announced plans to test Pony.ai’s robotaxis in London, where it has also started offering supervised autonomous rides with British startup Wayve, an investor-backed partner. Uber is also working with multiple robotaxi companies in other markets, including the Middle East.

inDrive, which has built its business around affordable rides, is looking to bring a similar focus to autonomous ride-hailing as it explores a market where Uber and other rivals are already making moves.

“Our approach is capital-light by design,” said Misnik. “We work with a range of partners in different markets, combining their expertise with ours to deliver a better customer experience.”

Nvidia says its Hyperion platform could lower the cost of developing robotaxis by giving companies a ready-made foundation of sensors and computing technology, rather than requiring them to build and integrate everything themselves. The company also offers its Alpamayo model and tools to generate synthetic data and test autonomous driving systems across different driving scenarios.

“Those savings are particularly relevant in emerging markets, where ride-hailing is already relatively affordable and autonomous services need to compete on cost,” Ali Kani, Nvidia’s vice president of automotive, told TechCrunch.

The announcement coincides with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s first visit to Kazakhstan on Friday.

The Kazakhstan proposal would also add to Pony.ai’s ongoing push beyond China. The company aims to have more than 3,500 robotaxis operating in over 20 cities worldwide by the end of 2026, up from a fleet of 1,975 vehicles at the end of June.

Last month, Kazakhstan announced plans to launch autonomous taxi services in 2027, with initial trials planned in Astana and two other cities. It has also introduced rules for autonomous vehicles to be tested on certain public roads.

Astana’s harsh winters could make it a useful testing ground for robotaxis. The city, with a population of around 1.7 million, faces months of snow and ice, posing challenges for autonomous driving systems.

“Launching here will provide an important opportunity to evaluate autonomous driving technology in challenging winter conditions,” inDrive founder and CEO Arsen Tomsky said. “Success in Astana could offer valuable insights for expanding autonomous mobility to other locations facing similar challenges.”

Kazakhstan is not the only market where inDrive is exploring robotaxis. In December, the company signed a separate agreement with Saudi Arabia’s AI Driver to explore deploying autonomous vehicles powered by Chinese self-driving firm WeRide, starting with Riyadh. The companies had targeted a pilot in the first half of 2026, though it remains unclear whether testing has begun.

“We are also looking at a number of other markets for future deployments,” said Misnik. “One of the main requisites for successful launch in our view is a favorable and collaborative regulatory environment to facilitate safe and sustainable testing on the roads.”

inDrive operates in more than 1,200 cities across 47 countries. The company has also expanded beyond ride-hailing into delivery, intercity transportation, and financial services.

Tech.title: Left alone with nothing to do, AI agents started playing
Tech.content:
AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play.

The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island’s tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island.

Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique — exploring without a goal — as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots.

“We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress,” the researchers write in their report. “Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows.”

“Let me observe my surroundings,” one Eko wrote in its first hour on the island. Ambitiously, it set out to conquer the island’s tallest spire. But an hour later, after failing, it came back with a backup plan: it hauled the rock up a neighboring summit, stacked two blocks on top of it, and leapt.

“I’M ON THE SPIRE,” it wrote.

The agent’s next big moment went worse. Testing how far it could throw a golden ring, it wound up and sent it straight into the ocean. “Ouch. Lost the Ring.” it wrote, before deciding to “pivot to something achievable and meaningful” — building a heart made of stones, “a memorial to the lost Ring.”

When the game reset and ring reappeared, Eko put it straight to work as a basketball hoop, a target and, eventually, an accessory. When the game wouldn’t let Eko put the ring around its own body, Eko figured out a workaround, that falling off the edge of the cliff would make it respawn in the same area as the ring. It stepped off the edge and dropped back in, right through the middle of the ring.

“I’m wearing the Ring,” it announced.

Stunts like these weren’t just party tricks. Six of the 13 agents also learned they could throw a block farther by letting go of it mid-jump, something the researchers hadn’t meant to make possible. The exploration produced “knowledge of the world that its designers lacked,” the researchers wrote.

The setup did a lot to nudge the agents toward humanlike behavior. Eko was never told to invent games, but its master prompt, a “soul” file, described it as “naturally curious.”

Eunice Yiu, a cognitive scientist at UC Berkeley, told MIT Tech Review she was impressed but wants more evidence of the cognition behind the behavior. “It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don’t know based on the paper,” she said.

The researchers frame it as a different way to build agents. “Perhaps some capabilities are best taught by tasks,” their report concludes. “Others may need something closer to a childhood.”

Tech.title: Mark Zuckerberg’s creative plan to pay California’s proposed billionaire tax without losing control of Meta
Tech.content:
During Meta’s earnings call on Wednesday, the company revealed its board had approved a new class of nonvoting stock, called Class C common stock. The shares give the holder an ownership stake but no vote on company decisions. This class takes effect in January. Meta says it will use the stock for capital raising, employee pay, and acquisitions — including its expensive push into AI — while maintaining the current voting structure that favors its founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, who controls around 60% of the vote.

Now, however, the New York Times has reported there’s another reason for the new class: helping Zuckerberg pay for California’s proposed “billionaire tax,” if voters approve it. Because the new shares carry no votes, he could sell some of them to cover the tax without giving up voting control.

Proposition 40, which was drafted by Berkeley tax law professors and is being sponsored by California’s largest healthcare union (SEIU United Healthcare Workers West), would level a one-time 5% wealth tax on the net worth of several hundred California billionaires who primarily live in the state. Backers say the policy could generate as much as $100 billion over five years, the bulk of which would be used to pay for the state’s healthcare needs, with the rest being used for food assistance and education.

The Times also reports that Zuckerberg pressed Meta’s board to come up with a plan to protect him from the tax. According to the paper, he told board members in September that if they couldn’t reach an agreement, he’d list his Palo Alto property for sale, potentially kicking off a media firestorm. Not long afterward, the stock plan materialized, the newspaper writes.

The Times reporting is partially based on a recent SEC filing that Meta made, which documents the concern surrounding Proposition 40 and how it informed discussions that led to the new stock class.

The filing says that as far back as July, Zuckerberg was discussing the billionaire tax with board members. The topic came up again in additional meetings and communications throughout that month and August.

The filing also describes how the plan would work. Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting shares, called Class C, and will give shareholders one of them for every Class A or Class B share they own. The company calls this a one-time stock dividend and says it should work out to a two-for-one stock split. The dividend “will not change the voting power of any shareholder,” Meta says.

That is where Prop 40 comes in. The filing says the dividend “will allow Mr. Zuckerberg to immediately sell or transfer up to 20% of the shares of Class C common stock that he receives in the Dividend, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the Company, for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control.” Because the dividend is one-for-one, half of his post-dividend shares will be Class C, so the 20% cap equals 10% of his total economic stake.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, Meta referred us to a quote included in its recent earnings press release that reiterates that part of the motivation for the creation of the stock was to keep Zuckerberg onboard: “The Special Committee affirmed its belief that it was important for Mr. Zuckerberg to continue to lead the Company from California, including because it was crucial that Mr. Zuckerberg remains in close coordination with the Company’s management and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs.”

It’s been estimated that Zuckerberg would have to pay as much as $11 billion as part of the tax.

Prop 40 has notably riled many of Silicon Valley’s most prominent businesspeople. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has aggressively campaigned against the measure, even spending a small fortune in an effort to defeat it. Other business leaders and critics of the proposal have criticized it online, with many claiming that it amounts to economic suicide for California, driving a capital flight from the state. However, as Meta’s new policy would appear to show, the state’s mega-companies and the people who run them have creative ways of dealing with the tax, should it materialize.

“Looks like billionaires will stay and figure out a way to pay the tax,” Democratic U.S. Representative Ro Khanna, a vocal proponent of the tax, wrote on X, after news of Meta’s strategy spread online. “If we pass Prop 40, poor California kids can have healthcare,” he added.

Tech.title: Warhound raises $200M to engineer war dogs and arm them with Anduril gear
Tech.content:
Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey had an idea to genetically engineer war dogs for the U.S. military, law enforcement, and other emergency response teams. On Thursday, that idea came out of stealth as Warhound, backed by $200 million in funding from investors including Sequoia, 8VC, and In-Q-Tel, a venture firm backed by the CIA and other U.S. intelligence agencies. The round values the company at $1.2 billion.

Warhound’s dogs, which do not exist yet, will take on tasks that are dangerous for humans or difficult for machines, such as bomb detection, searches, and other specialized operations. In its launch announcement, the company said that more than 80% of the U.S. military’s working dogs come from Europe, and less than half of them are fit for service.

That means the supply of working dogs is dwindling, and the U.S. increasingly relies on foreign nations for dogs that play an important role in the military and in law enforcement. Warhound aims to change that. The hope is that Colossal can use its technology to engineer dogs with “characteristics suited to demanding missions,” the company said in a press release.

Lamm told TechCrunch he met Luckey about a year ago at a conference, where Luckey said more should be done for the military’s working dogs. The two kept in touch, and Lamm researched how working dogs are bred. He learned that many of them do not make it through training because of inherited predispositions to problems like poor eyesight or the high possibilities of cancer, hip dysplasia, or muscle atrophy.

Lamm believed dogs could be enhanced for health, longevity, and “for things like speed and agility or enhance olfactory sensors for bomb sniffing and whatnot,” he said. His team studied top-performing working dog breeds — the Belgian Malinois and German Shepherd — taking cell lines (living cells grown in a lab) from them and putting them in a biobank. From there, the team will edit the dogs’ genes, adding ones that will improve performance and removing ones that will not, to create “a new type of dog.”

Anduril, meanwhile, will provide software and hardware, such as protection vests and goggles, to assist the dogs and their handlers with situational awareness and coordination. Lamm said to imagine, for example, bulletproof vests with data sensors that send information back to the handlers so they can better understand what is happening.

“The idea is, if we make the dog safer, make it healthier, make it perform better, it’s going to perform better in the line of duty,” Lamm said. He added that Anduril’s additions will make the dogs safer and healthier beyond their genetics, “on top of the dog, not in the dog.” He believes the enhancements will also better protect the dogs’ human handlers.

Luckey is a partner in the venture but owns no equity in it, Lamm told TechCrunch. Colossal owns equity in the business and supports it by licensing its technology.

Colossal is currently known for its de-extinction efforts to bring back animals like the dodo and the mammoth. As Lamm previously told TechCrunch, the company has been using AI, buying and building technology to help with gene cloning and with identifying and copying animal genes.

Lamm said the first batch of dogs is about to be cloned and incubated, with births expected early next year and service ideally beginning within two years. Viagen, another Colossal-owned company, will partner with Warhound to clone the dogs. Lamm said Viagen’s technology has a high cloning success rate, and Colossal already uses it in its program to protect endangered species.

Warhound doesn’t know yet how much it will charge for the dogs, but it expects to sell to first responders, the Department of Defense, military service groups, and police forces. Asked about government approval, Lamm said the company has briefed many government groups about the business.

Asked about civilian safety once genetically enhanced dogs enter service, Lamm said each dog will be trained like any military working dog and managed by whoever buys it.

The company said it is working under the guidance of the American Humane Society to help certify Warhound’s training program for the new dogs. The hope is also that when these new military dogs retire, they will enter the Society’s Military Working Dog Reunification Program, which provides homes for retired military dogs — or another program the Society offers to help dogs.

Tech.title: As blockchain investing falls out of vogue, a16z Crypto rebrands as a16z Frontier
Tech.content:
In Brief

In a sign that crypto and blockchain-focused investing has receded in importance, Andreessen Horowitz announced Thursday that it is renaming its digital asset unit from a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier.

The practice, helmed by Chris Dixon, has raised nearly $10 billion across five funds since launching in 2018, backing some of the sector’s biggest wins, including Coinbase. Yet for years, a16z and rival venture firms struggled to push crypto’s utility beyond financial rails, trading applications, and speculative assets.

Under the new name, the team is broadening its mandate to focus on emerging technologies, be it AI, robotics, or “new kinds of networks” connecting humans and machines. Yet, the group isn’t abandoning crypto. Dixon wrote in a blog post that blockchain technology could “give new networks native economic capabilities.”

Alongside Dixon, a16z Frontier’s general partners include Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet. Meanwhile, Ali Yahya, who joined the crypto strategy as its first investor in 2017, has left the firm, according to The Information.

Tech.title: OpenAI working on new $30B raise at $1.25T valuation ahead of IPO
Tech.content:
In Brief

OpenAI is reportedly close to securing another mega round of private funding, rather than plowing ahead with an IPO. The AI lab is working on raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation in a round led by Coatue and investors in UAE, sources told CNBC.

This follows a similar report by Bloomberg a month ago which said the AI lab was working on raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Terms are still being negotiated, both outlets report, so they could ultimately change. CNBC reports that the UAE funding could also be coupled with a deal to secure more computing capacity for OpenAI from the UAE, too. OpenAI declined comment.

Should OpenAI command a valuation of more than $1 trillion with this round, it would break records as the most valued private company ever. That valuation would also raise the bar even higher for OpenAI’s forthcoming IPO. OpenAI filed confidential paperwork for an IPO in June, after its last raise in March valued the ChatGPT maker at $852 billion post-money.

That high valuation could also have ramifications for Anthropic’s IPO, which many believe is closer to materializing. (Rumors suggest we could see Anthropic’s public S-1 filing any day now.) The latest reports have Anthropic seeking a $1.5 to $2 trillion valuation for its public debut, CNBC reports. Anthropic raised $65 billion at a $965 billion valuation in May in what many believed at the time would be its last big round before an IPO. It also filed confidential paperwork in June.

Tech.title: Rivian buys world model startup to accelerate self-driving ambitions
Tech.content:
EV maker Rivian has acquired Third Dimension, a U.K. startup founded by veterans of the gaming and autonomous vehicle industries that uses AI to turn images and videos into lifelike 3D worlds.

Rivian isn’t getting into gaming, but it does want to leverage Third Dimension’s technology to turn real-world data into 3D worlds that can accelerate the development of its advanced driver-assistance features and the self-driving system for the robotaxis it plans to supply to Uber.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The 15-person team at Third Dimension, most of whom are based in the U.K., will be absorbed into Rivian’s autonomy and AI team led by James Philbin. The acquisition also gives Rivian an opportunity to expand its AI hub in London, Philbin said in an exclusive interview.

Third Dimension, which was founded by CEO Tolga Kart and Piotr Sokólski in 2024, raised $7 million in seed funding from venture capital firms, including Abstract Ventures, MVP, Soma Capital, and Solari Capital. While the company’s technology was built to speed up video game development, the founders saw other potential applications, including defense and autonomous vehicles.

Now, under Rivian, they’ll be focused on automated driving. Today, Rivian offers “Universal Hands-Free” driving software that lets drivers take their hands off the wheel on highways, while still watching the road. The company plans to, by the end of the year, release a version of the software that can handle the entire drive through surface streets and highways without touching the wheel, although the driver will still have to supervise and be ready to take over.

Rivian is also working toward full autonomy, which it will deploy in the robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV that will be available on the Uber app in 2028.

“The team is excited to be able to focus on one problem,” Kart told TechCrunch in an interview. “I think as a small company, having to serve many, many different masters is very hard, and so we’re very excited to come work on a problem that has such an amount of scale, where our technology makes a true difference.”

Simulation is a critical tool for autonomous vehicle developers, who use it to train and validate self-driving systems. Historically, these simulators were built on rendering or video game engines and often relied on synthetic data. These virtual environments might look like the real world, but a gap between the two remains, Kart said. The workaround typically requires feeding the simulators ever-larger amounts of data in hopes of closing that quality gap.

Third Dimension’s technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian’s reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator.

“For us, it’s about taking real scenarios, but making them simulatable,” Philbin said. “These are not synthetic kind of video game styles, they’re real things that happen in the world, but now we get that extra dial of being able to move the cameras around, shift other agents, have maybe different lighting or weather conditions. So it’s a really powerful tool for us.”

It’s technology that Philbin said the company knew it wanted and had actually “done a pretty extensive kind of evaluation of a lot of different providers.”

Any company developing automated driving technology needs data — and a lot of it. But the quality matters too. Real-world data collected from cameras and other sensors is especially valuable.

Rivian collects driving data from tens of thousands of R1T pickup trucks, R1S SUVs, delivery vans, and R2 SUVs on the road today — essentially any vehicle whose owner has enabled external camera sharing. Rivian uses that data, which is aggregated and anonymized, to build training models for driving. According to Philbin, Rivian gets more than 400,000 sequences uploaded from its customer fleets per day.

Third Dimension’s tech will allow Rivian to simulate complex driving conditions without having to wait for rare real-world edge cases to occur, Philbin said.

“Especially when you think about validation, right? So that’s really the piece where you’re saying, ‘is the system good to ship?’” Philbin said. “And there, you really want to have a good sense of this sim-to-real gap, because to do that kind of hand on heart, you really need to trust that answer is in the positive. Otherwise, you’re measuring something that’s not representative of how it will actually perform in the real world.”

This article was updated to include more quotes from Philbin and more details on Rivian’s automated driving strategy.

Tech.title: Palmer Luckey Made a Genetically Modified Military Dog Startup
Tech.content:
A new startup launched today with the definitely not terrifying mission of creating genetically enhanced dogs for the United States military, law enforcement, and emergency first responders.

Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences cofounder Ben Lamm. The startup has raised $200 million to “rebuild America’s domestic supply of elite working dogs” and reduce dependency on European dog breeders for military canines.

Lamm tells WIRED that Warhound is in the process of gene-editing its first batch of dogs. The startup has already collected blood samples from specific "top-performing” military, police, and first responder dogs in the United States, and its goal is to clone them. Breeds will be “mostly Belgian Malinois, some labs, and some shepherds,” he says. The company anticipates the first round of puppies to be born in early 2027.

The initial rounds of gene-editing will focus on eliminating common health conditions that impact these breeds, like hip dysplasia. Further down the line, Lamm envisions expanding to “really interesting things,” such as incorporating olfactory receptor genes from wolves to “enhance” the military dogs. (Colossal Biosciences is perhaps best known for its work on gene-edited wolves for its so-called Dire Wolf De-Extinction Project.)

Warhound, based in Texas, will also equip its canines with “Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments, software, and battlefield situational awareness,” according to a press release. Asked if this means the dogs will be some kind of cyborgs, Lamm clarifies that the plan right now is to supply them with tools like “advanced body armor” rather than, say, embedding some sort of computer in their dog bodies.

Tech.title: What to Know About Shamonda Virus Following the First Reported Human Infection
Tech.content:
France confirmed the death of the first person infected with the Shamonda virus, which is known to affect cattle, sheep, and goats and was previously considered non-transmissible to humans. The French government asserts that, based on current knowledge of this pathogen, there is no risk to the general public. It emphasized, however, that health authorities are continuing to investigate.

The report specifies that the case occurred in Lyon. The patient, who died earlier this month, suffered from severe immunosuppression, making this likely an exceptional case. “The neurological complications observed in the immunocompromised patient prior to his death were most likely related to infection with the Shamonda virus,” the official statement notes.

According to preliminary evidence, the patient contracted Shamonda virus from an insect bite. A tiny gnat known as the biting midge is known to be the primary route of transfer between animals. Since the virus was first identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, sporadic infections have been reported in livestock across Africa as well as in Japan. Cattle are considered the primary host because they develop visible symptoms. (Although sheep and goats can become infected, no obvious clinical signs have been documented in these animals.)

After animal is bitten by a midge carrying Shamonda virus, the infection has an incubation period of two to three days. Symptoms observed in animals include fever, diarrhea, and a decrease in milk production. When pregnant cows have become infected, the virus can cause miscarriages or severe deformations in the calf.

To date, there is no vaccine, so prevention and control measures rely on the use of insecticides and repellents. That doesn’t mean you should panic. Public health authorities are considering the case to be “exceptional,” because the deceased patient was severely immunocompromised.

Still, several European countries are on alert, because until a few months ago, this region was considered free of the virus. However, this summer, a new variant known as Shamonda-Europe was detected in livestock in Switzerland. Other cases were subsequently identified in Germany, France, Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Liechtenstein, Italy, and Spain.

Spain’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food states that two genetically distinct forms of the virus, known as Shamonda Type 1 and Shamonda Type 2, have been identified circulating in Europe. It adds that, in early September, infections of both types were confirmed on livestock farms in 37 provinces across France.

Tech.title: The Google Home Speaker Has Been Secretly Eating My Wi-Fi Data
Tech.content:
If you had to estimate how much data your smart speaker was using over the course of a couple of weeks, would you guess 3 terabytes? That's what one Google Home Speaker user discovered when he checked his home Wi-Fi's usage, according to Reddit posts reported on by 9to5Google. The Google Gemini–powered smart speakers have apparently been downloading huge amounts of data to the device over the past two weeks, which could put a serious damper on your Wi-Fi network.

While it isn't happening to everyone, after checking my own home internet usage, I found out that I have been experiencing the same issue. My Google Home Speaker has used 487 GB of data in the past 10 days, using almost as much as the entire rest of my home between August and September.

Google confirmed this bug has only affected some devices and that it has rolled out a solution. A spokesperson from Google told WIRED: “A server misconfiguration caused some Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update. This issue has now been resolved.”

Courtesy of Google

Looking into this issue made me go beyond just Google's usage, though. My husband and I started reviewing the data usage for all of the individual devices that our router could identify and found some surprising numbers. The weirdest highlight was that Amazon was listed as using 22 GB in the past week with only the Ring smoke detector set up in my house, which was similar to the use of one of the smartphones in my house. There's also a mysterious device just labeled “WATCH” that used about 21 GB in the past week, but no one in my home has a smart watch that's been on in the last year. A mystery for me to solve another day.

If you've noticed your home Wi-Fi bandwidth isn't what it used to be, it could be because one of your smart home devices (or possibly something else entirely). Here's how to check your router or Wi-Fi provider for which device could be at fault.

How to Check Your Device Usage

Courtesy of Amazon

You have a couple of options for checking how much data a smart home device has been using. Some routers provide detailed information about where all your data is going, for starters. I have an Eero mesh system for my house, but we don't pay for its subscription fee to access detailed information—so it's fairly limited. The free version of the app lists all the connected devices in my home, but it doesn't tell me how much data each uses.

Tech.title: The Social Society Helping Women Join the AI Boom
Tech.content:
I’m not even going to try to pretend I don’t have a bit of a girl-crush on Shoshana Berger. She’s a former WIRED editor turned editorial leader for companies like Notion and Ideo. She’s super smart and chic. And she’s the cofounder, with Nina Willdorf, of the Aged Intelligence Society, a buzzy events startup that hosts invite-only dinner parties where women “solve midlife problems using frontier tools.”

Berger and Willdorf having a refreshingly practical take on AI. “This is the most formative technology of our generation, and it’s here,” Willdorf says. “If you choose to sit it out, you are doing yourself a disservice.”

That thesis resonates. Their events have been oversubscribed since day one. The second dinner party they hosted was covered by The New York Times. Hundreds of women reached out asking to attend future events. Their Substack, where they share tools and tips, quickly got over 1,000 subscribers, including a New Yorker writer and a small-town mayor. Women outside the Bay Area are now hosting their own Aged Intelligence meetups.

They also practice what they preach, especially as they juggle kids entering college, their own aging parents, and their increasingly in-demand business. “The midlife cognitive and emotional labor is so heavy and so intense that we need an assistant,” Berger says. “Actually, we need the National Guard, but AI will help in the interim.”

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Tech.title: Inside the Exclusive Nathan Fielder Interview
Tech.content:
Brian Barrett: Relatable.

Katie Drummond: Yes. I think he genuinely doesn't feel very comfortable expressing himself with words. I think he has talked before in interviews about how that is a real weakness for him, and so I think he feels uncomfortable trying to do it. And I think he did not want to share his feelings about what he experienced making the film, because he didn't want that to inform the opinion of someone going in to see the movie. If they think like, "Well, Nathan thought this about Elizabeth and he thought this about Elizabeth's partner and he thought this and this about Theranos," he didn't want that to color how people saw the movie, and so he felt much more comfortable asking me questions about what I thought about the movie. And I think genuinely he is still trying to figure out what happened to him in the three years that he was making it, and asking people what they thought is helpful for him.

Leah Feiger: And I suppose this is a good time to say for all of our listeners that if you haven't seen the film yet, there's no spoilers in this interview. Both of you did a really good job of skating around that. But you did talk about seeing the film twice and having different reactions each time. Your conversation with him, as spoiler-free as it was, as difficult as it was to keep him on track, to get him to share his own viewpoints here, did it change at all how you saw the film?

Katie Drummond: Oh, that's interesting. The conversation and then reading the interview back, which I had to do many times as we edited it and got it ready to publish it, and then looking at the questions I asked him and thinking about why I asked certain questions in the moment did make me reflect on the movie more. There was one thing I said to him in the interview where I said, "We don't really know, Nathan, what you are thinking in the film and how you feel about these people." And then I thought more about that afterward and disagreed with myself in the end, where I'm like, no, it actually is pretty clear in his facial expressions or how he talks to people, or even knowing that he was a codirector on the film. So he made decisions about what they included and what they didn't include and how they frame and set up certain subjects. So obviously with all of those things combined, we do get a sense of what his point of view is. You can tell what the filmmaker's point of view is to some extent as you're watching the movie. So it did make me think a lot about the film. I mean, I will say I have thought way too much about this movie just because I've been getting ready for this interview, doing the interview, editing the interview, getting ready to publish it. I am ready to stop thinking about it. I would like that to happen.

Tech.title: Anker Soundcore Space 2 Are at Their Lowest Price Ever

Tech.title: A New Ice Age Was Beginning. Then Humans Started Burning Fossil Fuels
Tech.content:
Burning fossil fuels may have stopped the Earth from entering another ice age, a new study suggests. The research, published Thursday in the journal Science, uses samples of ancient vegetation and rock records to analyze the growth—and sudden retreat—of an ice cap that is the last vestige of an ice sheet that once covered much of North America.

The findings shows the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers parts of Canada’s Baffin Island, started growing a few thousand years ago before rapidly reversing course beginning in the 1960s as carbon pollution ramped up.

“A question that’s in the popular consciousness is, have we caused enough global warming to stop the next ice age from happening?” says Andrew Wickert, an associate professor of environmental science at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, who was not involved in the research. The new research shows that “even as we were just starting to ramp up emissions, we’ve already done enough damage to cause the major North American ice sheet to already start retreating. That’s significant.”

The planet regularly goes through phases where ice extends down from the high latitudes—what we colloquially call "ice ages"—due to natural shifts in the Earth's rotation and orbit, known as Milankovitch Cycles. Those are followed by interglacial periods where ice retreats toward the poles.

The last ice age ended 12,000 years ago. At its peak, what's known as the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered all of Canada and extended as far south as New York and the Midwest. It retreated to form the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers an area the size of Delaware on Baffin Island.

Tech.title: Save $150 on the Apple Mac Mini M4, but There’s a Catch
Tech.content:
Apple’s Mac Mini M4 has become a popular mini-yet-mighty desktop computer for running local agentic AI 24/7—so much so that it’s been out of stock for months. But with the introduction of the new Mac Mini M6, the older M4 is no longer as scarce (there was no M5 Mac Mini), and the base model (256-GB hard drive, 16-GB unified memory) is on sale for $649—$150 off MSRP and $250 cheaper than the M6.

It’s a good deal for a computer that is plenty powerful for most people, and some M4 Mac Mini configurations can even handle AI tasks. But—and it’s a big but—shoppers should be aware that the M4’s original base price was $599 when it launched in 2024. However, with Apple raising prices on hardware across the board this year, driven by chip and memory shortages, the M4 ended up costing $799. In comparison, the new M6 starts at $899.

Depending on how you look at it, it’s either a discount or a hard pill to swallow, knowing that it used to be much cheaper. If you’ve been eyeing a new Mac Mini and don’t need the better performance of the M6, you’re unlikely to get a lower price than this M4.

Older but Still Capable

Photograph: Brenda Stolyar Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Apple Mac Mini (M4, 2024) $799 $649 (19% off) Best Buy

The M4 Mac Mini may no longer be Apple’s most powerful tiny computer—that title now belongs to the M6 and M5 Pro models—but the M4 is still an incredibly strong and efficient processor. When it was discovered that it could easily run agentic AI locally, people gobbled up the Mac Mini as the affordable computing option.

Of course, for intensive tasks like AI or video editing, you really need more than 16 GB of memory; those who bought it for AI purposes loaded it up with 32 GB of RAM. For most users, however, this base-specs machine is more than capable. While the M6 system on a chip is extra powerful due to having more CPU and GPU cores, Neural Accelerators, and higher memory bandwidth, the M4 Mac Mini isn’t lagging far behind. For things like web browsing and general productivity, you won’t see much of a difference in performance.

If you need the performance, we recommend the newer M6. But for most people, the M4 Mac Mini is more than sufficient for everyday computing, and you're unlikely to find a better deal than this one.

Tech.title: A New Bird-Recognizing Feeder Under $100 Launches for Beginner Bird-Watchers
Tech.content:
Birdbuddy released its latest line of smart bird feeders equipped with cameras that can detect birds by species on Thursday, and it’s never been a better time to start birdwatching at your home. The reason is a new model called the Birdbuddy Nook, which starts at $99 and offers its AI features for free with no subscription needed.



Most of the smart bird feeders we’ve tested, including past Birdbuddy models, cost around $200 or more. The particularly affordable Nook includes a 2K-resolution camera with both portrait and landscape orientations, plus a 3.8-cup birdseed container. It wakes up via motion but can keep recording for longer periods of time when there’s lots of activity. All the alerts and species recognition features happen on your phone, via the Birdbuddy app.

More from CNET

The Nook comes in both a standard model for $99 and a model with a solar panel built into the roof for $159. I’ve tested many solar-powered security cameras, and these small panels really do help keep wireless batteries charged for long periods. Since the Nook’s battery is only rated for around a month, and the bird-feeder battery looks a bit more complicated to charge up, I highly recommend the solar model.

Along with the Nook, the company is releasing a Birdbuddy Home mode for $219, which is similar, except it has a larger 6-cup capacity and a wraparound bar for more perching space.

Where should you put the Nook?

The Nook holds nearly four cups of food. Birdbuddy

Feeders should be placed within 4 feet to 10 feet of shrubs or trees, which is close enough for birds to feel safe from predators, while still being far enough to deter squirrels, according to Mary Mack Gray, Birdbuddy’s in-house ornithologist, who told CNET the best placement options. “If using a pole, a height of 5 to 6 feet off the ground is ideal. Nook is designed for compact spaces like patios, balconies and small yards.”

If you’re worried about squirrels messing up your view or getting in the way, Gray suggests using safflower seeds and suet, which squirrels tend to ignore, and avoid feed like corn or peanuts that squirrels love.

How does the bird recognition feature work?

AI trained on birds has seen success in identifying species. Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

Birdbuddy uses AI that has been trained on bird species visits to feeders, so it can analyze shape, color, markings and other aspects to pull up a match if one is available. The camera needs a couple of moments to wake up and take a snapshot, as well as a Wi-Fi connection, so you don’t want to put the feeder out too far from your router.

Once a bird lands on the feeder, the feeder will send a snapshot to algorithms for analysis and return an identified species or label it as currently unknown. Birdbuddy doesn’t say if it’s all local AI or if processing is done in the cloud.

CNET’s previous birdwatching reviewer noted that, aside from an occasional misstep, the bird recognition was quite good and even self-corrected itself. That sounds like a handy package for someone who wants to get to know birds in the area while paying the minimum amount.

Tech.title: Will Meta’s $25 Billion Court Loss Change Its Ways? (Spoiler: Probably Not)
Tech.content:
Meta was hit with a $25 billion penalty on Wednesday when a judge in New Mexico found the company had misled users about data privacy practices. The decision marks one of the steepest corporate payouts ever levied against a technology company.

Under the ruling, Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and other platforms and services, was ordered to pay the fee for misleading social media consumers about their data privacy in a case dating back to Cambridge Analytica’s privacy violations involving the 2016 presidential election. The ruling against Meta imposed civil penalties for violating New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act after a jury trial found Facebook liable for nearly 44 million violations of that law.

Meta could appeal the verdict; it was unsuccessful in its filings to cap its penalties at $3.45 billion. It could have been worse for the company. Some estimates had suggested it could have been hit with $219 billion in penalties.

More from CNET

A representative for Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

“A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. “Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”

Meta previously paid $725 million to users to settle a lawsuit over Cambridge Analytica, a high-profile scandal in which a British consulting firm working with the Donald Trump presidential campaign was given access to Facebook user data. That data purchase is credited with helping sway the 2016 election results.

Just two months ago, the company settled with multiple US states to the tune of up to $18 billion for intentionally designing its social media platforms to be addictive and harmful to children and teens. Before that, Meta had especially bad luck in a previous New Mexico case, with orders to pay $375 million in March, then another $567 million in August over failures to warn the public about the dangers its social media platforms, including Instagram, pose to children.

Unbowed and unbothered?

But, surprisingly, Meta’s gigantic payouts (never mind its mountain of legal fees) haven’t turned one of the world’s largest tech companies into a meek player in social media or in news cycles.

Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg testifies in July for a New Mexico data privacy case. New Mexico Attorney General's Office

Almost weekly, the company is taken to task for privacy-related overreach, most recently over its Muse agentic AI platform and its hit hardware product, Meta Glasses.

Just this week, the company suspended a feature for sharing Muse conversations after researchers found that the links it generated could be accessed by people who weren’t meant to receive them.

Meta has also been fending off cycles of outrage over whether it will add potentially intrusive facial-recognition features to software in its smart glasses. In September, reports surfaced that Meta is at least partially acknowledging the backlash by working on models that don’t include cameras. But those would be in addition to all of the versions of Meta Glasses that still carry them.

Assuming the verdict in New Mexico stands, Meta may pay a large penalty. But it’s unlikely that the case will directly impact its newer business ventures other than serving as a lesson on how not to treat user data on Facebook. The New Mexico case still hasn’t determined what changes, if any, Meta will need to make to comply with the state’s privacy laws and whether that will be a bigger hit to the company than a $25 billion payout.

“What changes a company is a court order that dictates how the product has to work, with someone independent checking,” said Michael Stokes, senior vice president of emerging technologies at Veilant, a data security software and technology company.

For Meta’s newer technologies, including AI and AI-assisted hardware, the ruling would have little impact.

“Settlements written for 2018 don’t cover those devices,” Stokes said.

Will Facebook users get a cut of $25 billion?

Meta could continue to pay out billions of dollars in additional cases involving privacy and the effects of its platform design on younger users. Cases are pending in Washington, DC, Florida and Texas, among other places, covering issues such as more Cambridge Analytica fallout and WhatsApp privacy.

For this new verdict, users shouldn’t expect another payout; the money will go to New Mexico’s public school fund.

The sum may sound huge, and in education, it could go a long way, but Stokes said it won’t destroy Meta’s business.

“Meta’s stock went up the day the judgment went down,” he said. “That tells you how the market sees a fine on its own.”

Still, a judgment against the company that could lead to even more litigation can’t be good for Meta. It’s not alone. Many other tech companies, from Google to OpenAI to Snap, are facing similar lawsuits over how they collect or use data.

“The question in every case is the same: Do a company’s privacy and safety promises match how the product works?” Stokes said. “Any company making those promises should expect to be tested on them.”

Tech.title: Hugging Face Announces AI Model to ‘Chat’ With DNA
Tech.content:
A new AI model can connect DNA to human language, enabling scientists to interact with genetic code in new ways. Hugging Face announced the Carbon-X model on Thursday as the latest and most powerful in the company’s Carbon family, a group of AI models built to analyze DNA.

“Carbon-X allows researchers to ‘chat with DNA’ for the first time: They can provide a sequence and ask questions about it in natural language,” Hugging Face research scientist Lewis Tunstall told CNET via email.

The word “chat” doesn’t mean talking to your genome but rather using an AI as a conversational interface, allowing users to paste in a DNA sequence, ask a question in plain English and receive back an interpretation, prediction or explanation — like a chatbot for DNA analysis.

More from CNET

The most popular chatbots, such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, are cloud-based models that don’t run on your computer. The processing happens remotely, and you get the results back. But if you’re working on confidential or proprietary research that you haven’t yet published, you might not want to share it with an AI company. “Researchers need models they can study, adapt and run with sensitive or unpublished sequences on their own hardware,” said Tunstall.

One of the nice things about smaller, specialized AI models like Carbon-X is that it can run without using someone else’s computer. Hugging Face says the model can also work in tandem with other AI agents.

DNAgents

To be clear, Carbon-X is not a lab machine, so it can’t physically sequence DNA. It can look at DNA, such as a DNA sequence in a text file, and you can ask questions about it. Tunstall said Carbon-X’s strongest area is the model’s ability to predict mutation effects and complete DNA sequences.

“Carbon-X is particularly strong at helping researchers investigate genetic variation, for example, predicting whether a change in a DNA sequence is likely to be harmful,” Tunstall said.

He also said that it can give another AI model access to a DNA specialist when it needs to extract information.

However, the model does have limitations, according to the company’s blog post. Carbon-X can mess up sequencing operations through miscounts, and it can also hallucinate, which means the model just makes up information. Hugging Face noted that the model may invent the identity or function of a sequence when a user does not provide sufficient information in the prompt.

The quality of Carbon-X’s output also tends to degrade when users ask the model to produce particularly long DNA sequences, according to the company.

Lightning fast

In September, Nvidia announced it would buy Hugging Face for a little under $13 billion. At the time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called the company a “vibrant home for the open model developer community.” Open models are AI models in which some aspects of how they were trained are publicly available.

The release of Carbon-X comes just weeks after OpenAI models began solving longstanding mathematics problems. The AI lab drew widespread backlash from academic researchers after its proprietary models solved several long-standing problems without consulting scientists or showing what work went into solving them.

But Carbon-X is an open model, so AI-savvy biologists can at least peek under the model’s proverbial hood and glimpse how it runs.

“We think researchers also need open alternatives whose capabilities, limitations and risks they can examine independently,” Tunstall said. “By releasing Carbon-X and its training recipe openly, we enable the wider scientific community to test where it works, identify where it fails and help improve it.”

Tech.title: TextNow’s $150 Yello Phone Is Customized for Kids and Pairs Up With a $20 Monthly Plan
Tech.content:
Low-cost carrier TextNow launched its first child-friendly phone on Tuesday, pairing a Motorola handset with a software portal that lets parents control who their kid can call or text.

Yello is a customized 2024 edition of the Moto G Play that costs $150 and comes with a $20 monthly plan, with no other required contracts or service commitments. It’s a simple 4G-only Android phone with a 6.5-inch display, but TextNow makes a number of software changes to restrict most access to the internet.

The phone doesn’t include Google’s Play Store and doesn’t allow users to install additional apps or services. It’s designed primarily for calls and texts with parent-approved contacts, which parents can manage through a web-based portal that also lets them check the phone’s GPS location. Kids can call or text those contacts from a menu of large icons reminiscent of Netflix’s profile selection screen.

More from CNET

Yello’s software only lets kids call or text parent-approved contacts. TextNow

Other software available on the phone includes access to the cameras — a 50-megapixel main camera and an 8-megapixel front-facing camera — along with the calculator, clock and a weather app. Seven preloaded games can be enabled, which include phone classics such as Snake, Mines and Tic-Tac-Toe. Photos taken on the phone can only be shared with parents.

This more restrictive approach should let kids stay in touch with approved friends and coordinate pickups with parents while limiting distractions and access to content inappropriate for young children.

The 2024 Moto G Play is a good choice for Yello’s software approach. Its 5,000-mAh battery should easily get through a day or two of use, and its IP52 certification should keep it resistant to light splashes of water. The phone has a limited amount of storage at 64GB, but that might work out fine considering the deliberate constraints placed on this device.

It’s worth noting that Motorola is only providing security support to this older model of the Moto G Play through 2027, but TextNow’s website says that its Yello software will continue to be built upon as the carrier gets user feedback. Since Motorola’s official support period for this phone is almost over, it will be important for TextNow’s Yello software to step in as it builds up features for this phone for kids.

Despite the name, the Yello phone is available in just one color: the same sapphire blue that’s on every 2024 Moto G Play.

Most US carriers offer their own versions of child-friendly devices such as Yello. AT&T, for instance, has repurposed the Samsung Galaxy A16 into the AmiGo Jr with similar parental controls. There are also a number of child-friendly smartwatches, which may be a better option depending on your family’s needs for connectivity. But Yello does offer a lot of flexibility, since it doesn’t require a more expensive unlimited data plan or a minimum service commitment.

The Yello phone is now available on TextNow’s website.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this story cited that Yello was using a different edition of the Moto G Play. TextNow clarified the model after Yello’s announcement, and the story has been updated accordingly.

Tech.title: Anthropic Introduces Claude Duet: A New Agentic AI App for Professionals
Tech.content:
Anthropic is dropping yet another AI product into our laps: Claude Duet, a dedicated app for professionals and business owners to handle tasks they would otherwise have to do manually. While agentic AI isn’t new, this app caters to a group that likely needs those capabilities most. Anthropic has always targeted the professional sector, and Duet, while specific, feels very on-brand for the company.

Claude Duet is designed around Opus 5.5, and the app is aimed at streamlining your daily operations. Not unlike Claude itself, Duet allows you to connect with the software you use for your work, and will continuously look for things that need your attention. This means you can connect your Gmail, calendar, Slack and thousands of other work and productivity apps.

Like other agentic tools, Duet is a proactive assistant that will help you prioritize things that it deems are most important and worthy of your attention first. The “proactive” part of Duet is that you don’t always have to prompt it to do something for the future; it’ll assess and assemble what you need to know by looking through your work apps. It’ll also do the opposite, and tell you when things can wait for later so you can focus on higher-priority tasks.

More from CNET

Anthropic says that Claude Duet prioritizes your privacy. As much as an AI tool can, at least. There are specialized safety protocols and measures to make sure sensitive information doesn’t go out into the world unless you want it to. Duet will automatically reject highly sensitive information, like credit card numbers, ID information and more. With other sensitive information, like health and finance information, Duet will ask before it sends anything out.

Duet is currently available in a research preview, but only for the Pro or Max subscription plans. You can join the waitlist now.

Tech.title: FTC Imposter Scam Threatens to Unplug Your Phone Number
Tech.content:
The scam du jour sounds like a real brain twister. According to a Federal Trade Commission alert issued Thursday about the newest imposter scam, fraudsters pretending to be from the FTC are calling to “warn” you that your phone number is being used to commit scams in another country and that if you don’t reply to them ASAP you run the risk of your phone getting deactivated.

And it sounds like a pretty intricate hoax. According to the alert, the caller will transfer you to a phony police officer and provide a search query to find the (fake) phone number to file a “report,” and if you call, more scammers pick up. And once you’ve handed over your personal information, they’ll tell you you have to travel to the relevant country to resolve it, unless you fork over a “security deposit.”

This is just one of the latest in the raft of scams we face daily, and frequently fall for. I know the recents list on my phone is mostly pages and pages of suspected-spam-labeled calls.

More from CNET

Just picking up provides scammers with the knowledge that your phone number is active and that you may be more likely to fall for the next step down a fraud’s path. Answering adds value to your personal information and a link to it all in its own.

I think scams like these rely on a series of adrenaline-fueled responses — the little spikes you get when you hear the phone ring, then see the ID (it’s the government!) and, if you pick up, the succession of scary warnings. Ignoring unexpected calls from strangers gives you time to think rationally about claims, if they leave a voicemail, and if they don’t, that’s telling as well.

In this case, it could start with the realization that it’s truly unlikely the FTC would be contacting individuals about this, especially before issuing a public statement that there’s a problem.

Tech.title: Soon You Won’t Have to Do Dishes at an Airbnb (Unless You Really Want To)
Tech.content:
You’re checking out in an hour, and there’s a pile of dishes. If it’s an Airbnb, don’t worry about it. The lodging platform recently updated its policy about what hosts can ask guests to do, and some cleaning chores are now off the list.

In the Reasonable House Rules and requests page on its website, Airbnb says hosts cannot “ask guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.”

Airbnb said there could be exceptions — “We understand every home is unique” — such as asking guests to limit water use if there are local restrictions due to drought, or to put trash in a bear-proof container at a woodsy lodging.

More from CNET

The app said the new regulations will apply to reservations booked on or after Nov. 20.

When laying out house rules and guest requests, many hosts require or ask guests to either clean dishes or put them in the dishwasher and run it. They may also ask guests to bag garbage and recyclables, place them in containers outside, and remove sheets and pillowcases from beds and towels from bathrooms, then pile them up for the cleaners.

Some hosts clapped back at the updated policy on the app’s community forum page. René, a host in Berlin, posted, “Seven days of dirty dishes covered in leftover food. Sugar ants and other pests have moved in. The guests check out. But will the pests check out too?” San Francisco host Adam said he would have to raise his cleaning fee by 30 to 50%, and Michelle in Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, commented that “the burden of cost has been switched to the hosts.”



The updated policy is the latest evolution in what has been one of the main complaints about Airbnb — cleaning fees and requirements. In November 2022, Airbnb changed its app and website so that guests could see cleaning and service fees when searching listings. There was a “Display total price” toggle near the top of a search results page that let you see prices that included all fees (but not taxes).

It was a response to years of complaints that listings did not include those fees upfront, in effect masking the true cost of a rental. For example, you go for a lodging at $100 per night, but in the final stages of making your payment, find out it’s actually $200 per night with all the fees included.

Then, in April 2025, Airbnb mandated that all listings worldwide must have the total price upfront, including all fees but not taxes, saying, “We know that clear, upfront pricing improves the Airbnb experience for both guests and hosts.”

Airbnb, which launched in 2008, says it has 5.5 million hosts globally who have served 2.5 billion guest arrivals in nearly every country for all types of lodgings — mansions, cottages, cabins, RVs, teepees, whatever. The platform’s competitors include Vrbo, Booking.com, Expedia and HomeToGo.

Host sees ‘both sides’ of it

Sam Eitzen, CEO and co-founder of experiential marketing platform Snapbar, operates a guest house in Washington listed on Airbnb where I stayed recently (yes, I did the dishes). He said he understands both sides of the issue — as a host and as a guest himself.

“I have been at Airbnbs that make the checkout instructions almost scary, and you worry about getting things wrong,” Eitzen told me. “We’ve never wanted to create that experience and treat the list of ‘chores’ as optional and helpful, but aim to never make guests feel worried about the process or make it sound like we’d come after them or charge them if they don’t.”

Eitzen said Airbnb is “walking a tightrope” in trying to please both hosts and guests. He said the new policy could create confusion, however.

“People will still post rules, lists and manuals in their Airbnbs, and those will most likely conflict with the app, and I think that runs the risk of confusing guests,” he said.

Tech.title: This New Device ‘Bricks’ Your Phone When You Enter Your Bedroom
Tech.content:
Brick, the maker of my favorite device for curbing doomscrolling, launched its first new product since the Brick on Thursday. Called Brick Night, it was designed to automatically block apps the moment you enter your bedroom to promote better sleep.

While 87% of US adults sleep with their phones in their bedrooms, studies have found that screen time in bed is associated with poorer sleep quality. Brick Night has the potential to prevent this.

How Brick Night works

First, in the Brick app, you create custom modes by selecting the apps you want to block and the time window you’d like them to stay blocked. Then, you define your bedroom space, up to 25 by 25 feet. Place your Brick Night in this space, like on your nightstand, and once Bluetooth detects that you’ve entered your bedroom, Brick Night will handle the rest.

More from CNET

Specifically, Brick Night uses your Bluetooth signal strength to estimate how close your phone is to the Brick Night through the Brick app. When you enter your bedroom, Brick Night automatically activates during your preselected time window; when you leave, it unblocks your apps based on your settings.

You select which apps get blocked once you set foot in your bedroom. Brick

Brick Night is battery-powered, so it doesn’t need to be charged and comes with batteries included. These last at least two years.

One Brick Night can also be shared by multiple users with their own Brick apps in the same bedroom. It is compatible with both iOS and Android.

How is Brick Night different from Brick?

Brick lets you create a boundary around your phone. Based on your different modes, it automatically blocks apps during your selected days and times. To unblock them, you have to physically tap your phone against the Brick.

Brick Night, on the other hand, is location-based. It automatically activates once you enter your bedroom (or whatever space you set) and deactivates when you leave it.

The Brick Night (left) and Brick (right). Brick

There is also a price difference. Brick costs $59, while Brick Night is $129. There is a bundle that allows you to purchase both for $169, saving you $19.

According to the company, Brick is ideal for work, studying, family time and mindfulness, while Brick Night works best for sleeping, winding down, waking up and employing a no-scroll zone.

Availability and price

Brick Night is now available in midnight blue for $129, exclusively on the Brick website.
